entry.title: Florida secures arrest warrant for Raúl Castro in 1996 Brothers to the Rescue shootdown
entry.summary: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced Monday that state prosecutors and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement (FDLE) have secured an arrest warrant for former Cuban leader Ral Castro, accusing him of conspiring to murder four men in the 1996 shootdown of two civilian aircraft operated by the anti-Castro group Brothers to the Rescue. According to the Attorney General's Office, Castro has been charged with one count of conspiracy to commit first-degree murder in connection with an incident in which Cuban military fighter jets shot down two unarmed Brothers to the Rescue planes over international waters. Authorities said three unarmed Cessna aircraft departed Opa-locka Airport in Miami-Dade County on Feb. 24, 1996. After crossing the 24th parallel and flying outside Cuba's territorial waters, two of the planes were destroyed by air-to-air missiles fired by Cuban MiG fighter jets. According to the affidavit, the aircraft were traveling away from Cuba at the time and received no warning before being shot down. The warrant, obtained by the Office of Statewide Prosecution and FDLE, alleges Castro played a key role in authorizing the attack that killed four men with ties to Florida: Carlos Costa, Pablo Morales, Mario de la Pea and Armando Alejandre Jr. 'Ral Castro ordered the murder of four Floridians in cold blood, and Florida will never stop pursuing accountability for that communist conspiracy,' Uthmeier said in a statement. According to a probable cause affidavit, Castro, who at the time served as Cuba's minister of the Revolutionary Armed Forces and first vice president, was among the final decision-makers who authorized the operation. Investigators allege Castro issued standing orders to military leaders to shoot down aircraft associated with Brothers to the Rescue if they appeared over the sea. State investigators also allege Cuban intelligence agents operating in South Florida infiltrated Brothers to the Rescue and provided flight information to the Cuban government as part of what was known as 'Operation Scorpion.' Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz called the warrant a 'historic step toward accountability' for the four men killed in the attack, while FDLE Special Agent in Charge Michael Stein said the case demonstrates that 'the passage of time does not diminish the pursuit of justice.' The warrant charges Castro under Florida statutes governing conspiracy and first-degree murder. Prosecutors said the offense is a first-degree felony,

entry.title: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy set for execution Tuesday - WPEC
entry.summary: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy set for execution Tuesday    WPEC
entry.article_text: The man convicted of killing an Indian River County deputy nearly 40 years ago is scheduled to be executed Tuesday. William Reaves, 77, is set to die by lethal injection at 6 p.m. at Florida State Prison near Starke . Ron DeSantis signed the death warrant Sept. According to court records, Cpl. Richard Raczkoski was called to a Zippy Mart near Vero Beach around 3 a.m. 23, 1986, to help Reaves get a cab. During the encounter, a gun fell from Reaves’ shorts and the two struggled over it. Records say Reaves shot the deputy four times in the back. In a taped interview with Indian River County detectives in Albany, Reaves admitted to the shooting. I’ve never met a finer officer in my life, he said, according to a transcript filed by the state. When a detective asked why he would not give up the gun, Reaves said he was a convicted felon and feared prison. I know if I got caught with that gun, and the man take me down there, I’m gonna get a mandatory three years already for the gun, he said. Reaves also told detectives, I was all coked up and I panicked, both of us panicked. Prosecutors have long argued the shooting was premeditated. Court records show the deputy was running away when he was shot, and the .380 handgun required a separate trigger pull for each shot. See also: Florida secures state arrest warrant for Raúl Castro in 1996 shootdown Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death. The Florida Supreme Court rejected his latest appeals last week, and a request for the U.S. Supreme Court to review his case is still pending. His attorneys and supporters, including a group of military veterans, have asked DeSantis to spare his life, pointing to his service in Vietnam. Reaves was first convicted in 1987, but the Florida Supreme Court threw out that conviction in 1991 because one of the prosecutors had previously represented Reaves in another case. A second jury convicted him again in 1992 and voted 10-2 to recommend the death penalty. In a court filing last month, Reaves’ attorneys said he was deployed to Vietnam as a ground combat soldier in 1969, at age 20. They say the Department of Veterans Affairs rates him 100% disabled for post-traumatic stress disorder, and that the jury that sentenced him never heard the details of his combat service. His attorneys also argued that Reaves was shut out of the clemency process. They said the attorney assigned to represent him met with him about five minutes before his clemency interview and never gave him a copy of what was submitted on his behalf. A circuit judge ruled Reaves received a full clemency proceeding. The governor denied clemency the same day he signed the death warrant. In the same filing, the defense accused two former Indian River County deputies of taking bribes from a drug dealer in the 1980s. The defense also said one of them helped shape the testimony of a key witness against Reaves. Circuit Judge Anastasia Norman rejected the claim on Oct. 2, finding the allegations were not backed by any sworn statement and were merely speculative at best. Reaves did not raise that claim in his appeal to the Florida Supreme Court. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers, who pushed for the governor to sign the warrant, describes the moment when he learned the governor signed Reaves' death warrant. "It was not something that I had expected. At this point, our governor is wrapping things up in Tallahassee and finishing out his time. So for him to take time to make sure that this gets handled is just really a blessing," said Flowers. Flowers plans to attend the execution in Raiford on Tuesday. My goal with going tomorrow is ultimately the last thing that he sees is an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office uniform, knowing that justice finally came, Flowers said. Flowers said Raczkoski’s brother will also be there. Raczkoski’s parents have since died. Flowers said the brother told him, Christmas was never the same for our family after Richard was killed. The execution comes nearly a year after the agency lost Sgt. Terri Sweeting-Mashkow, who was killed in the line of duty in November 2025. Flowers said Tuesday will bring the agency some closure. It just really feels like coming full circle, like a moment of healing that we all needed, Flowers said. Supreme Court appeal still pending, Flowers said he will not rest easy until the execution is carried out. I’d hate to see it delayed in any way, he said.

entry.article_text: 27-year-old man is accused of exposing himself in multiple incidents involving women walking alone on the Seaway Bridge in Fort Pierce, and police say two victims identified him as the suspect. Kyle Kennedy was arrested Friday after an investigation by the Fort Pierce Police Department into multiple reports of indecent exposure on the bridge. Investigators reviewed previous reports and spotted patterns linking the incidents, then interviewed victims and conducted photo lineups, police said. See also: Florida divers remove record 36,187 invasive lionfish in statewide challenge Two victims positively identified Kennedy during the lineups, leading to his arrest, according to police. Kennedy faces two counts of indecent exposure and one charge of violation of probation. Police are asking anyone who witnessed suspicious activity or has information about the incidents to call the FPPD at 772-467-6800 . Anonymous tips can also be submitted to Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers.

Kathleen Amber, 62, was arrested Friday near the MidFlorida Event Center , where officers were investigating a disturbance. Police said officers noticed signs of impairment, including slurred speech, lethargy and difficulty maintaining balance. Her breath test result was 0.130, according to the department. James Kirby, 81, was arrested Friday after police received a report of a potentially impaired driver leaving a restaurant. Officers stopped his pickup truck on SW Becker Road after seeing it change lanes without signaling and brake suddenly at a green light, police said. Officers reported that Kirby had slurred speech, watery eyes and difficulty maintaining balance. His breath test result was 0.123, according to police. Tamra Goodman, 57, was arrested Sunday after officers responded to a single-vehicle crash on SE Port St. Lucie Boulevard, west of U.S. Police said her Mustang had struck a curb and was damaged and inoperable. Goodman told officers she had left a restaurant and had three vodka and club soda drinks, police said. Her breath test result was 0.227. entry.title: Man found dead after barricade situation in St. Lucie County, deputies say
entry.summary: A man was found dead from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound Saturday after a barricade situation prompted deputies to evacuate a woman and children from a St. Lucie County home, according to the sheriffs office. The St. Lucie County Sheriffs Office said deputies responded around 10:17 a.m. to a reported domestic violence incident in the 7600 block of Winter Garden Boulevard. WATCH BELOW: Man found dead after St. Lucie County barricade situation Man found dead after barricade situation in St. Lucie County Deputies initially encountered a man in the front yard who went back inside after seeing law enforcement. Authorities later made contact with a man and woman at the front door. During that interaction, a deputy saw what appeared to be a firearm in the man's possession and ordered him to drop it, the sheriffs office said. Instead, the man closed the door and retreated inside, creating a barricaded-subject situation while other people remained in the home. According to investigators, the man came outside several times and said he would surrender after making a phone call, but repeatedly went back inside. During his final retreat into the home, deputies heard what appeared to be a gunshot. Knowing a woman and children were still inside and could be in danger, deputies entered the residence and evacuated them through a side window, the sheriffs office said. Deputies later found the man dead from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound. Authorities said there is no ongoing threat to the community. Detectives, crime scene technicians and investigators from the Medical Examiners Office are expected to remain at the scene for several hours as the investigation continues.

A second jury convicted him again in 1992 and voted 10-2 to recommend the death penalty. In a court filing last month, Reaves’ attorneys said he was deployed to Vietnam as a ground combat soldier in 1969, at age 20. They say the Department of Veterans Affairs rates him 100% disabled for post-traumatic stress disorder, and that the jury that sentenced him never heard the details of his combat service. His attorneys also argued that Reaves was shut out of the clemency process. They said the attorney assigned to represent him met with him about five minutes before his clemency interview and never gave him a copy of what was submitted on his behalf. A circuit judge ruled Reaves received a full clemency proceeding. The governor denied clemency the same day he signed the death warrant. In the same filing, the defense accused two former Indian River County deputies of taking bribes from a drug dealer in the 1980s. The defense also said one of them helped shape the testimony of a key witness against Reaves. Circuit Judge Anastasia Norman rejected the claim on Oct. 2, finding the allegations were not backed by any sworn statement and were merely speculative at best. Reaves did not raise that claim in his appeal to the Florida Supreme Court. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers, who pushed for the governor to sign the warrant, describes the moment when he learned the governor signed Reaves' death warrant. "It was not something that I had expected. At this point, our governor is wrapping things up in Tallahassee and finishing out his time. So for him to take time to make sure that this gets handled is just really a blessing," said Flowers. Flowers plans to attend the execution in Raiford on Tuesday. My goal with going tomorrow is ultimately the last thing that he sees is an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office uniform, knowing that justice finally came, Flowers said. Flowers said Raczkoski’s brother will also be there. Raczkoski’s parents have since died. Flowers said the brother told him, Christmas was never the same for our family after Richard was killed. The execution comes nearly a year after the agency lost Sgt. Terri Sweeting-Mashkow, who was killed in the line of duty in November 2025. Flowers said Tuesday will bring the agency some closure. It just really feels like coming full circle, like a moment of healing that we all needed, Flowers said. Supreme Court appeal still pending, Flowers said he will not rest easy until the execution is carried out. I’d hate to see it delayed in any way, he said.

entry.title: Do seatbelts put students at risk in a school bus rollover? An NTSB expert weighs in
entry.summary: A deadly school bus crash in Polk County is raising new questions about how students are protected when a bus rolls over, including whether wearing a seat belt could create an additional danger. WATCH: AN NTSB EXPERT WEIGHS IN ON SCHOOL BUS SEAT BELTS NTSB on school buses seat belt safety Two weeks after the crash, investigative reporter Katie LaGrone put that question directly to Dr. Kristin Poland, a school bus safety expert with the National Transportation Safety Board . The crash killed 16-year-old Adinaluz Prieto Oyola during the morning commute on Oct. 5. According to investigators, the school bus carrying 37 high school students was on its way to Winter Haven High School when another cut slammed into its rear, causing the bus to collide head-on with another vehicle and flip over. Following the crash, Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd was asked whether any of the dozens of students aboard were wearing seat belts at the time of impact. 'Quite frankly, if you try to make everyone put a seat belt on, then we would have had 37 kids hanging from the roof by a seat belt,' Judd said. His comments raise a key safety question: In a rollover crash, do seat belts protect students or potentially put them at greater risk? While Poland said the NTSB cannot yet discuss specifics of its investigation into the Polk County crash, she pointed to what the agency has learned from other school bus crashes. 'The real risk is when theyre violently thrown during the crash sequence about the inside of the bus, where they hit other occupants, or they could potentially hit hard points inside the school bus,' Poland said. According to Poland, properly worn three-point restraints, which include both a lap and shoulder belt, provide the best protection even when a bus overturns. 'Those seat belts are designed so that students can still release the belts even if they're under tension, like if a student is hanging from the belt,' she said. Poland acknowledged that the image of a child hanging by a seat belt after a rollover may sound frightening. But she said the greater danger comes during the crash itself, when an unrestrained student can be thrown around the bus. The NTSB has not determined whether a three-point seat belt could have changed the outcome of the Polk County crash. The school district confirmed the bus involved was only equipped with lap belts as are all the school buses in its fleet, according to a district spokesperson. A safety issue investigated for years For report

More than a decade ago, she investigated a St. Lucie County school bus crash that killed 9-year-old Aaron Beauchamp, who was wearing a lap belt at the time.The NTSB investigated that crash and produced simulations demonstrating the difference between the protection provided by a lap belt and the protection provided when a shoulder belt is added.A few years later, the agency formally recommended that school districts in the U.S. upgrade school bus restraints to include both lap and shoulder belts. Florida was among the states called on to make three-point seat belts state law.What does Florida require?Currently, Florida only requires school buses to be equipped with lap belts, but students are not required to wear them.Nearly a decade after the NTSB's recommendation, Poland said some Florida school districts are moving toward three-point lap-and-shoulder belts. “We're seeing some progress with some of the school districts in Florida moving to the passenger lap shoulder belts,” she said.But our investigation found that the majority of public school buses in the state still have lap belts only.Cost is one hurdle. entry.article_text: A Vero Beach man accused of restraining a woman in a hotel room and throwing water on her after she tried to leave has been sentenced to nine months in jail. Frank Joseph Lagola pleaded no contest to charges of false imprisonment and battery and was sentenced Thursday, according to court records. Deputies with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office say they were called to Econo Lodge at 950 U.S. Highway 1 in Vero Beach on December 23, 2025, after a witness reported hearing a woman screaming for help. The witness told deputies she saw a man restraining a woman in the hotel doorway, preventing her from leaving. See also: Fort Pierce flasher? String of indecent exposure reports on bridge leads to arrest When deputies arrived, they found Lagola and the victim, who was visibly wet and shaken. Coppeto told deputies she had been staying at the hotel for about a week and wanted to leave the room. She alleged Lagola became increasingly agitated, threw "holy" water on her, and physically restrained her, telling her she wasn't going anywhere. According to the affidavit, Coppeto said Lagola pinned her down and struck her on the top of her head. She also told deputies she screamed for help because she did not have a cellphone and could not physically get away from him. Lagola told deputies he believed Coppeto was possessed by the devil after she began speaking in Latin. He said he was trying to perform an exorcism and admitted holding her down while reading Bible passages, according to the affidavit. Investigators also spoke with a witness who said she heard a woman yelling, Stop, Rape, Help Me, before seeing the man appear to drag the woman back into the room. Lagola was arrested on charges of false imprisonment and battery and was held in St. Lucie County Jail until his sentencing and was given 297 days time served.

entry.title: Miami native and baseball Hall of Famer Andre Dawson receives the Governors Medal of Freedom
entry.summary: Baseball Hall of Famer Andre Dawson received the Governors Medal of Freedom. Gov. Ron DeSantis said the award recognizes Dawson's baseball career, his contributions to Florida AM University, and his lasting impact on the state of Florida. Dawson was born in Miami and went to Southwest Miami Senior High School. He then went to Florida AM and walked on to the Rattlers baseball team. His performance led the Montreal Expos to select him in the 1975 MLB draft. His distinguished career in Major League Baseball, his contributions to the sport, and his lasting impact on our state have earned him this award. 'The Hawk' has represented Florida in the best possible way for decades. His generous support of FAMU and its baseball program has helped generations of student-athletes succeed. The Governors Medal of Freedom is the highest honor I can bestow on any Floridian, and Andre Dawson truly deserves this recognition, DeSantis said. Past recipients of the Governors Medal of Freedom include Florida State University football coach Bobby Bowden, golfer Barbara Nicklaus, musician Jimmy Buffett, Coach Lee Corso, and former Florida Supreme Court Justice Charles Canady.

entry.title: Man dies by suicide after barricaded-subject SWAT situation in Fort Pierce - cw34.com
entry.summary: Man dies by suicide after barricaded-subject SWAT situation in Fort Pierce    cw34.com
entry.article_text: A man was found dead from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound after deputies responded to a reported domestic violence incident Saturday morning in Fort Pierce's Lakewood Park neighborhood. Deputies responded around 10:17 a.m. to a home in the 7600 block of Winter Garden Boulevard, where they encountered a man in the front yard. The man went back inside after seeing law enforcement, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office . Deputies say they later contacted a man and woman at the front door. A deputy saw what appeared to be a firearm in the man's possession and ordered him to drop the weapon, but he shut the door and retreated inside, prompting a barricaded-subject situation with other occupants still in the home. See also: Driver tried to ram deputy before PIT maneuver ended chase, SLCSO says During the incident, the man reportedly came outside several times and indicated he would surrender after making a phone call, but repeatedly went back inside, deputies said. During his final retreat into the home, deputies say they heard what appeared to be a gunshot. Concerned for an adult woman and children who remained inside, deputies entered the home without alerting the occupants and evacuated them through a side window, according to the sheriff's office. Deputies later found the man dead from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound. The sheriff's office said there is no ongoing threat to the community. Detectives with the agency's Criminal Investigations Division, crime scene technicians and investigators from the Medical Examiner's Office remained at the scene to investigate the circumstances surrounding the incident. If you or someone you know is struggling with thoughts of suicide, help is available. Call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline , available 24/7. You can also chat at 988lifeline.org

entry.title: Lake Worth Beach food-sharing ordinance sparks new dispute over weekly Bryant Park gatherings
entry.summary: A weekly community gathering at Bryant Park is drawing renewed scrutiny in Lake Worth Beach as organizers question how the city is enforcing a new ordinance regulating food-sharing events in public parks. Melissa Salerno, a community member involved in the weekly gatherings, says the group continues to meet to share food and spend time together. WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW: This is a picnic: Bryant Park organizers push back on Lake Worth Beach Ordinance But she says members have repeatedly been told by law enforcement that they are violating the city's rules, even as organizers maintain they are keeping attendance below 25 people and gathering for a picnic rather than a food distribution event. The dispute centers on how the city defines a food-sharing event, which rules apply to smaller gatherings, and why Bryant Park is excluded from the locations where these events are permitted. During a recent gathering, attendance appeared significantly lower than at previous events. Legal observers were also present after organizers invited them to monitor the gathering in case tensions escalated, equipped with body cameras and a measuring tape to comply with Florida's Halo law. 'Just to make sure no one's civil rights are being violated, either way we're neutral; we're not here for one side or the other,' White said. Salerno said organizers have attempted to follow the new ordinance by keeping participation below 25 people. She also disputes the city's characterization of the gathering as a food distribution event. 'According to the city, this is a food distribution event, and we are therefore in violation of the ordinance,' Salerno said. 'And what I tried to clarify was that this is not a food distribution event; this is a picnic.' Salerno said the group wants to continue gathering without feeling intimidated or monitored. 'We just share each other's company and time, she said. She also emphasized the importance of transparency and public awareness surrounding the citys decisions. entry.article_text: A weekly community gathering at Bryant Park is drawing renewed scrutiny in Lake Worth Beach as organizers question how the city is enforcing a new ordinance regulating food-sharing events in public parks.Melissa Salerno, a community member involved in the weekly gatherings, says the group continues to meet to share food and spend time together. WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW: But she says members have repeatedly been told by law enforcement that they are violating the city's rules, even as organizers maintain they are keeping attendance below 25 people and gathering for a picnic rather than a food distribution event.The dispute centers on how the city defines a food-sharing event, which rules apply to smaller gatherings, and why Bryant Park is excluded from the locations where these events are permitted.During a recent gathering, attendance appeared significantly lower than at previous events. Legal observers were also present after organizers invited them to monitor the gathering in case tensions escalated, equipped with body cameras and a measuring tape to comply with Florida's Halo law. Rick White, one of the legal observers, said their role was to help ensure participants' rights were respected."Just to make sure no one's civil rights are being violated, either way we're neutral; we're not here for one side or the other," White said.Salerno said organizers have attempted to follow the new ordinance by keeping participation below 25 people. She also disputes the city's characterization of the gathering as a food distribution event."According to the city, this is a food distribution event, and we are therefore in violation of the ordinance," Salerno said. "And what I tried to clarify was that this is not a food distribution event; this is a picnic."Salerno said the group wants to continue gathering without feeling intimidated or monitored."We just share each other's company and time,” she said.She also emphasized the importance of transparency and public awareness surrounding the city’s decisions."I think it's really important that the community at large knows what's going on, how their taxpayer dollars are being spent,” Salerno said.The Lake Worth Beach City Commission approved Ordinance 2026-01 on Feb. 3, 2026, tightening requirements for special events on city property, including organized food-sharing events. The measure followed complaints from downtown businesses and visitors about food-sharing gatherings at Bryant Park, including events serving people experiencing homelessness. Under the ordinance, a special event generally includes a gathering that attracts, is intended to attract, or is likely to attract 25 or more people, including staff, vendors and volunteers. The ordinance defines food-sharing events to include social-service food sharing and public events where food is provided or served at no charge in a public space.Those events are restricted to three designated locations:Memorial Park PavilionHoward Park PavilionNorthwest ParkA special-event permit application must be submitted at least 30 days in advance. The ordinance also limits the number of food-sharing event permits issued to the same person, group or organization at the same public space to 12 within a consecutive 12-month period. Additional requirements may include liability insurance, food-safety credentials for certain food preparation and service, and arrangements for cleanup. The restrictions mean that staying below 25 people does not automatically resolve every question about whether a gathering is allowed. Stuart Sword, interim director of Lake Worth Beach’s Leisure Services Department, said Bryant Park is not one of the approved locations for food-sharing events.Sword said the city selected the three designated parks partly because of their proximity to public transportation, making them accessible to people who rely on those services."Anytime there's a food-sharing event, there are significant implications to the park and also waste management,” Sword said.He said the city is trying to manage the impact of these gatherings while preserving public spaces for other uses."We identified three parks where you can do that, Northwest Ball Field, Memorial Park and Howard Park, and the reason the city picked those is 'cause they're close to public transportation," Sword said.Sword acknowledged a distinction between a picnic and a food-sharing event, adding that it's a clarification that would have to be made by the city attorney. WPTV began reporting on the proposal in June 2025, when organizers said they were serving growing numbers of people facing food insecurity amid rising housing costs and inflation. At the time, Salerno said Bryant Park was important because of its central location and access to bus routes. City leaders argued that organized events involving large numbers of people require planning, cleanup and coordination to protect public spaces and ensure other residents can use them.But advocates have argued that the requirements could create financial and logistical barriers for volunteer-led groups that rely on donations and personal contributions to provide meals.For now, the disagreement between organizers and the city remains focused on the ordinance’s application to the weekly Bryant Park gathering.Organizers say they want to continue meeting and sharing meals while complying with the rules. The city maintains that Bryant Park is not an approved location for food-sharing events and says its goal is to keep public spaces safe, clean and accessible.

entry.title: Delray Beach homeowner says insurance went up $300 a year after replacing her roof through state program
entry.summary: Betty Haygood of Delray Beach says she is happy with her new roof after it was installed in August with help from the My Safe Florida Home program. However, what does not make her happy is her homeowners insurance renewal that's due in December. entry.title: Vero Beach gives Three Corners developers another extension as Dec. 8 deadline looms
entry.summary: WPTV is learning that the Vero Beach City Council approved an extension for developers of the Three Corners project but time is ticking. City council members told the developers, ClearBlue, that they need to negotiate and come to an agreement by Dec. 8 or the city may need to go back to the drawing board. WATCH BELOW: Developers get 4th extension for Three Corners project Developers get fourth extension for negotiations on Three Corners project 'I've been on this thing since 2019,' Vero Beach Mayor John Cotugno said. 'We need to negotiate the best, we'll call it a deal, for our citizens.'  The development project is located at the old Vero Beach Power Plant at the base of the 17th Street Bridge. Plans include hotels, a marina, restaurants, walking paths and more. This is the fourth extension the city council approved for developers to negotiate agreements on financing and lease terms. 'Some progress had been made on the financial aspects of the developer proposal,' Cotugno said. But the mayor said if the council and ClearBlue aren't on the same page, they might have to change course. 'We need to listen and to see if this aligns with our goals and objectives. And if it does, great, we're going to work out a deal that's mutually beneficial,' Cotugno said. 'If not, then you know well we'll have to see what happens.' Cotugno said the city council is also appointing a liaison to aid in negotiations and the developers come to discuss the project in person. Bob Salera, a spokesperson for ClearBlue, said they are meeting with city council Oct. 27. 'It's something that we've actually been asking for for several months,' Salera said. 'We're glad we finally have one on the books now.' Salera said they're committed to the project and have invested over $1 million. 'We wouldn't have put in 21,000 hours of time into this project if we weren't serious,' Salera said. 'We're happy that these negotiations are moving forward, and we're ready to bring it home to a close.' Cotugno said he hopes they do. 'I'm willing to stay at that the table if progress is being made,' Cotugno said.

entry.title: Up to 12-foot waves pound Palm Beach County, Treasure Coast beaches - WPEC
entry.summary: Up to 12-foot waves pound Palm Beach County, Treasure Coast beaches    WPEC
entry.article_text: Waves reaching up to 12 feet are pounding beaches across Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast Monday, drawing experienced surfers into the water while prompting lifeguards in Jupiter to raise double red flags and prohibit swimming. From Boca Raton to Sebastian, beaches are experiencing rough surf and dangerous rip currents, with conditions expected to continue over the next several days. At Jupiter Beach Park Monday, CBS12 News watched surfers battle choppy waves, a kite surfer take advantage of the strong winds and beachgoers enjoy the sunshine from the sand. But lifeguards were taking the conditions seriously. "We're changing our flags from single red to double red, so this entire area is going to be with no swimming," said Ethan Sage, a Jupiter Ocean Rescue lifeguard. Sage said double red flags are typically needed only a few times a year, usually during major storms or unusually rough conditions. He estimated wave faces reaching 12 to 15 feet beyond the sandbars Monday, compared with 4 to 6 feet Sunday. Despite the warnings, some experienced surfers were eager to get into the water. "When it gets this big, I mean, we kind of want to go out there and let the ocean humble us a little bit," said surfer JC Southwell. Southwell said he would rather take on windy, choppy conditions than spend a day watching a flat ocean. Kite surfer Joe Goulet was also excited about the conditions, saying the wind and waves give him an opportunity to challenge himself and improve his skills. "It's a blast," Goulet said. But for other beachgoers, the waves were better enjoyed from a distance. Isis Alize brought her baby to the beach but had no plans to take her swimming. "Definitely a water baby," Alize said of her daughter. "We dipped our toes, and that was a bit scary, actually." What's causing the big waves? CBS12 News meteorologist Lauren Olesky said a nor'easter developing off the East Coast is sending large swells down the coastline. "So, we're dealing with waves breaking up to about 10 to 12 feet," Olesky said. The system developed along the same frontal boundary that brought rain to South Florida late last week and over the weekend. Olesky said high surf advisories extend across the region, with strong onshore winds contributing to the rough conditions. While the waves may be exciting for experienced surfers, Olesky warned that the high risk of rip currents makes swimming especially dangerous. "Even if you are a super strong swimmer, it can get tiring trying to fight the current if you're out there for an extended period of time," she said. Sage warned that even standing close to the water can be dangerous when powerful waves crash onto the shore. See also: 5,543 calls in 13 days: Palm Beach County's trash troubles pile up He said surfers are allowed to enter the water at their own discretion where the Jupiter restrictions are in place, but recommended that only experts consider going out. What beachgoers should know With seasonal visitors beginning to return to South Florida, Olesky encouraged everyone to check the forecast and beach warning flags before heading into the ocean. She recommended swimming only at lifeguarded beaches when conditions allow and paying attention to posted warnings. At the Jupiter beach CBS12 News visited, double red flags mean no swimming. And beachgoers hoping for calmer conditions may have to wait. Olesky said the large waves and high rip current risk are expected to continue over the next several days, giving experienced surfers more opportunities to catch waves while keeping lifeguards on high alert.

entry.title: More than 100 cats rescued from hoarding situation in Port St. Lucie - WPBF
entry.summary: More than 100 cats rescued from hoarding situation in Port St. Lucie    WPBF
entry.article_text: More than 100 cats and kittens rescued from a hoarding situation in Port St. Lucie are now receiving medical care and nourishment at the Humane Society of St. Lucie Animal Control removed the animals over the course of three days last week, with the first group arriving at the shelter on Tuesday. "Some were clearly showing symptoms of upper respiratory. The majority of them had ear mites. They were all covered in fleas. There were a couple that had open sores, from scratching at the flea, scratching at the ear mites and some other issues," said Sarah Wees, executive director of the Humane Society of St. Three pregnant cats gave birth shortly after being rescued, with one too weak to care for her kittens. Those newborns were rushed to an emergency foster home for round-the-clock care, while others remain at the shelter. "We have kittens who are nursing on cats that may or may not be their mom because we really can't tell who belongs with whom because they were all in the same house together," Wees said. The Humane Society is receiving assistance from American Humane, a national organization that supports local communities during large intake cases or natural disasters. "She reached out to me, and by Thursday morning I was on property, and helping just work through those initial days, and also coordinating some volunteers and additional staffing to come in to help with additional personnel," said Taylor Nickelsen, a certified animal responder with American Humane. Nickelsen said their efforts are making a difference, with many of the cats showing significant improvement. "We stay as long as we need to be able to provide the relief that is needed, which ultimately our goal is to help get these animals on their way to foster and on their way to adoption," Nickelsen said. Lucie police are monitoring the case to determine if any criminal charges will be filed. In the meantime, the Humane Society is seeking donations and volunteers to help care for the rescued cats and kittens. entry.summary: Man found dead after barricade situation in St. Lucie County, deputies say    WFLX
entry.article_text: A man was found dead from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound Saturday after a barricade situation prompted deputies to evacuate a woman and children from a St. Lucie County home, according to the sheriff’s office. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said deputies responded around 10:17 a.m. to a reported domestic violence incident in the 7600 block of Winter Garden Boulevard. WATCH BELOW: Man found dead after St. Lucie County barricade situation Deputies initially encountered a man in the front yard who went back inside after seeing law enforcement. Authorities later made contact with a man and woman at the front door. During that interaction, a deputy saw what appeared to be a firearm in the man's possession and ordered him to drop it, the sheriff’s office said. Instead, the man closed the door and retreated inside, creating a barricaded-subject situation while other people remained in the home. According to investigators, the man came outside several times and said he would surrender after making a phone call, but repeatedly went back inside. During his final retreat into the home, deputies heard what appeared to be a gunshot. Knowing a woman and children were still inside and could be in danger, deputies entered the residence and evacuated them through a side window, the sheriff’s office said. Deputies later found the man dead from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound. Authorities said there is no ongoing threat to the community. Detectives, crime scene technicians and investigators from the Medical Examiner’s Office are expected to remain at the scene for several hours as the investigation continues.

entry.title: Martin County woman honored after using CPR to save 3-year-old girl from swimming pool
entry.summary: A 20-year-old Martin County woman is being honored after she used CPR to help save a 3-year-old girl she found motionless at the bottom of a swimming pool. Nearly two months after the August rescue, Martin County Fire Rescue recognized Madison Isler with the department's Heroic Heart Award. WATCH: Martin County woman honored for saving 3-year-old Woman Honored After Using CPR to Save 3-Year-Old Girl | WPTV The rescue happened Aug. 23 as Isler walked past the pool at her apartment complex. She told WPTV something in the water caught her attention. 'It kind of looked like a smudge in your sunglasses,' Isler said. 'And then, so I took my glasses off and I looked, and then I realized that it was a little girl.' That little girl was 3-year-old Luna. 'I jumped in and grabbed her' Isler said Luna was motionless at the bottom of the swimming pool when she spotted her. 'I jumped in and grabbed her and pulled her out, and she was blue,' Isler said. Isler called for her boyfriend to contact 911 and began CPR, using skills she said she learned at a young age from her parents, who both work in fire rescue. 'You just don't really think; you just kind of do, especially in a situation when it's a little baby,' Isler said. 'I pulled a lifeless baby out of a pool.' A family friend who is a pediatric intensive care unit nurse heard the commotion and joined the rescue effort, according to the account shared by Martin County Fire Rescue. 'Together, they continued their life-saving efforts till finally Luna responded,' Martin County Fire Rescue Chief Chad Cianciulli said. Fire rescue officials said Luna was alert and oriented by the time paramedics transported her to the hospital. Luna's mother says Isler was there 'at the right time' Luna's mother, Christine Hernandez, said she is grateful Isler happened to be nearby when her daughter needed help. 'It's God's work that He put her when we needed her, like at the right place at the right time,' Hernandez said. Nearly two months after that frightening day, Isler and Luna reunited at Martin County Fire Rescue headquarters. This time, they were together to celebrate the outcome of the rescue. Martin County Fire Rescue honors Isler Martin County Fire Rescue presented Isler with its Heroic Heart Award in recognition of her actions. 'Today, on behalf of Martin County Fire Rescue and our entire community, we honor Madison for her courage to act with Martin County Fire Rescue's Heroic Heart Award,' Cianciulli said during the recognition

entry.summary: Man dies by suicide after barricaded-subject SWAT situation in Fort Pierce    cw34.com
entry.article_text: A man was found dead from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound after deputies responded to a reported domestic violence incident Saturday morning in Fort Pierce's Lakewood Park neighborhood. Deputies responded around 10:17 a.m. to a home in the 7600 block of Winter Garden Boulevard, where they encountered a man in the front yard. The man went back inside after seeing law enforcement, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office . Deputies say they later contacted a man and woman at the front door. A deputy saw what appeared to be a firearm in the man's possession and ordered him to drop the weapon, but he shut the door and retreated inside, prompting a barricaded-subject situation with other occupants still in the home. See also: Driver tried to ram deputy before PIT maneuver ended chase, SLCSO says During the incident, the man reportedly came outside several times and indicated he would surrender after making a phone call, but repeatedly went back inside, deputies said. During his final retreat into the home, deputies say they heard what appeared to be a gunshot. Concerned for an adult woman and children who remained inside, deputies entered the home without alerting the occupants and evacuated them through a side window, according to the sheriff's office. Deputies later found the man dead from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound. The sheriff's office said there is no ongoing threat to the community. Detectives with the agency's Criminal Investigations Division, crime scene technicians and investigators from the Medical Examiner's Office remained at the scene to investigate the circumstances surrounding the incident. If you or someone you know is struggling with thoughts of suicide, help is available. Call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline , available 24/7. You can also chat at 988lifeline.org

entry.title: 'The unicorn baby': Martin County woman saves 3-year-old from drowning, earns Heroic Heart Award - WPBF
entry.summary: 'The unicorn baby': Martin County woman saves 3-year-old from drowning, earns Heroic Heart Award    WPBF
entry.article_text: A 20-year-old Martin County woman is being honored for rescuing a 3-year-old girl from drowning in an apartment pool, an act that earned her the first-ever Heroic Heart Award. Three-year-old Luna Hernandez, described as shy in front of cameras, clung to her new best friend, Madison Isler, during a recent meeting. Isler, who calls Luna the "unicorn baby," explained the significance of the nickname. "Because this doesn't happen. Drownings don't end like this. When they're babies 3 years old like this, they just go under, slip right under really quick. And she's a unicorn," Isler said. A Moment of Joy: News We Love The incident occurred on Aug. 23 when Isler noticed Luna lying motionless at the bottom of the pool at their apartment complex. "I had to go get my hair clip that I left on, like, the opposite side of the pool. And as I was walking, I saw a shadow, and it kind of looked like a smudge on your sunglasses," Isler said. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Isler immediately jumped into the pool and pulled Luna out of the water. Seeing the child was blue, unresponsive, and not breathing, she began CPR while shouting for someone to call 911. A pediatric intensive care unit nurse heard the commotion and rushed to help. "There were at least 10 adults at the swimming pool when she went down. So, it just happens right in front of you and silently quick, so for me to walk by and see it was a pretty slim chance. I call her the unicorn baby," Isler said. Martin County fire officials presented Isler with the first-ever Heroic Heart Award. Her father, who works for Palm Beach County Fire Rescue, and her mother, who retired from the department, were present to celebrate the moment. "Because of the actions of one young woman who happened to be at the right place at the right time, Luna was given another chance. A chance to go home, a chance to grow up, a chance to make memories with her family. A chance to live a life that she was waiting for, " fire Chief Chad Cianciulli said. "Madison is an incredible young woman." Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. Luna’s mother, Kristine Hernandez, who was out of town when the incident occurred, shared photos of her daughter’s big smile and expressed her gratitude for Isler’s actions. "Stopping on the way to the pool to get a hair clip. There're just minor little details in the story that it's God's work that he put her when we needed her, like at the right place, at the right time," Kristine Hernandez said. She also emphasized that accidents could happen to anyone. "I'm just thankful for the life that Luna gets to live now," she said. Isler will be honored at an upcoming Martin County Commission meeting.

entry.title: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy set for execution Tuesday - WPEC
entry.summary: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy set for execution Tuesday    WPEC
entry.article_text: The man convicted of killing an Indian River County deputy nearly 40 years ago is scheduled to be executed Tuesday. William Reaves, 77, is set to die by lethal injection at 6 p.m. at Florida State Prison near Starke . Ron DeSantis signed the death warrant Sept. According to court records, Cpl. Richard Raczkoski was called to a Zippy Mart near Vero Beach around 3 a.m. 23, 1986, to help Reaves get a cab. During the encounter, a gun fell from Reaves’ shorts and the two struggled over it. Records say Reaves shot the deputy four times in the back. In a taped interview with Indian River County detectives in Albany, Reaves admitted to the shooting. I’ve never met a finer officer in my life, he said, according to a transcript filed by the state. When a detective asked why he would not give up the gun, Reaves said he was a convicted felon and feared prison. I know if I got caught with that gun, and the man take me down there, I’m gonna get a mandatory three years already for the gun, he said. Reaves also told detectives, I was all coked up and I panicked, both of us panicked. Prosecutors have long argued the shooting was premeditated. Court records show the deputy was running away when he was shot, and the .380 handgun required a separate trigger pull for each shot. See also: Florida secures state arrest warrant for Raúl Castro in 1996 shootdown Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death. The Florida Supreme Court rejected his latest appeals last week, and a request for the U.S. Supreme Court to review his case is still pending. His attorneys and supporters, including a group of military veterans, have asked DeSantis to spare his life, pointing to his service in Vietnam. Reaves was first convicted in 1987, but the Florida Supreme Court threw out that conviction in 1991 because one of the prosecutors had previously represented Reaves in another case. A second jury convicted him again in 1992 and voted 10-2 to recommend the death penalty. In a court filing last month, Reaves’ attorneys said he was deployed to Vietnam as a ground combat soldier in 1969, at age 20. They say the Department of Veterans Affairs rates him 100% disabled for post-traumatic stress disorder, and that the jury that sentenced him never heard the details of his combat service. His attorneys also argued that Reaves was shut out of the clemency process. They said the attorney assigned to represent him met with him about five minutes before his clemency interview and never gave him a copy of what was submitted on his behalf. A circuit judge ruled Reaves received a full clemency proceeding. The governor denied clemency the same day he signed the death warrant. In the same filing, the defense accused two former Indian River County deputies of taking bribes from a drug dealer in the 1980s. The defense also said one of them helped shape the testimony of a key witness against Reaves. Circuit Judge Anastasia Norman rejected the claim on Oct. 2, finding the allegations were not backed by any sworn statement and were merely speculative at best. Reaves did not raise that claim in his appeal to the Florida Supreme Court. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers, who pushed for the governor to sign the warrant, describes the moment when he learned the governor signed Reaves' death warrant. "It was not something that I had expected. At this point, our governor is wrapping things up in Tallahassee and finishing out his time. So for him to take time to make sure that this gets handled is just really a blessing," said Flowers. Flowers plans to attend the execution in Raiford on Tuesday. My goal with going tomorrow is ultimately the last thing that he sees is an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office uniform, knowing that justice finally came, Flowers said. Flowers said Raczkoski’s brother will also be there. Raczkoski’s parents have since died. Flowers said the brother told him, Christmas was never the same for our family after Richard was killed. The execution comes nearly a year after the agency lost Sgt. Terri Sweeting-Mashkow, who was killed in the line of duty in November 2025. Flowers said Tuesday will bring the agency some closure. It just really feels like coming full circle, like a moment of healing that we all needed, Flowers said. Supreme Court appeal still pending, Flowers said he will not rest easy until the execution is carried out. I’d hate to see it delayed in any way, he said.

entry.title: What's next for Boca? Mayor outlines plan after city manager resignation
entry.summary: The City of Boca Raton is preparing for a leadership transition after City Manager Mark Sohaney announced he is stepping down after roughly 13 months in the position. City officials say an interim city manager could be selected by mid-November ahead of his expected departure. Sohaney is leaving to join the University of Maryland Global Campus as senior vice president for global military operations, according to Boca Raton Mayor Andy Thomson. The move returns Sohaney to a field closely tied to his background as a retired U.S. Navy captain. The resignation comes as Boca Raton continues work on several major initiatives, including plans for a proposed new police headquarters and other long-term projects expected to shape the city's future. Mayor says city remains on stable footing Mayor Andy Thomson acknowledged it is difficult to see Sohaney leave but said he understands the opportunity. 'For him to have the opportunity to go back and work in a capacity supporting military families and supporting our military makes perfect sense,' Thomson said. Despite the leadership change, Thomson said residents should remain confident in the city's direction. 'Leadership continues to be very strong and the city's in very good hands,' he said. According to Thomson, city staff and elected leaders are prepared to continue advancing major projects while seeking public input and voter approval where required. Leadership changes draw attention Sohaney's departure follows a period of significant turnover within city leadership. In March, WPTV reported on a major shakeup that included the departures of Boca Raton's police chief and two deputy city managers. The latest announcement has prompted some residents to question the city's leadership stability and what comes next for one of Palm Beach County's largest municipalities. When asked how residents can be assured the next city manager will remain in the role long term, Thomson pointed to Boca Raton's history of retaining top leaders for decades. 'The next people who are going to be leading the city will be somebody, I imagine, that is going to have that same level of continuity,' he said. entry.summary: Vero Beach gives Three Corners developers another extension as Dec. 8 deadline looms    WPTV
entry.article_text: WPTV is learning that the Vero Beach City Council approved an extension for developers of the Three Corners project — but time is ticking.City council members told the developers, ClearBlue, that they need to negotiate and come to an agreement by Dec. 8 or the city may need to go back to the drawing board.WATCH BELOW: Developers get 4th extension for Three Corners project"I've been on this thing since 2019," Vero Beach Mayor John Cotugno said. "We need to negotiate the best, we'll call it a deal, for our citizens." The development project is located at the old Vero Beach Power Plant at the base of the 17th Street Bridge. Plans include hotels, a marina, restaurants, walking paths and more.This is the fourth extension the city council approved for developers to negotiate agreements on financing and lease terms."Some progress had been made on the financial aspects of the developer proposal," Cotugno said.But the mayor said if the council and ClearBlue aren't on the same page, they might have to change course."We need to listen and to see if this aligns with our goals and objectives. And if it does, great, we're going to work out a deal that's mutually beneficial," Cotugno said. "If not, then you know well we'll have to see what happens."Cotugno said the city council is also appointing a liaison to aid in negotiations and the developers come to discuss the project in person.Bob Salera, a spokesperson for ClearBlue, said they are meeting with city council Oct. 27."It's something that we've actually been asking for for several months," Salera said. "We're glad we finally have one on the books now."Salera said they're committed to the project and have invested over $1 million."We wouldn't have put in 21,000 hours of time into this project if we weren't serious," Salera said. "We're happy that these negotiations are moving forward, and we're ready to bring it home to a close."Cotugno said he hopes they do."I'm willing to stay at that the table if progress is being made," Cotugno said.

entry.summary: Fort Pierce flasher? String of indecent exposure reports on bridge leads to arrest    cw34.com
entry.article_text: 27-year-old man is accused of exposing himself in multiple incidents involving women walking alone on the Seaway Bridge in Fort Pierce, and police say two victims identified him as the suspect. Kyle Kennedy was arrested Friday after an investigation by the Fort Pierce Police Department into multiple reports of indecent exposure on the bridge. Investigators reviewed previous reports and spotted patterns linking the incidents, then interviewed victims and conducted photo lineups, police said. See also: Florida divers remove record 36,187 invasive lionfish in statewide challenge Two victims positively identified Kennedy during the lineups, leading to his arrest, according to police. "It's just crazy to know that there's something like that going on," Leidi Cruz of Fort Pierce. "I've never had any experience like that. We walk here regularly and we've never had any issues." Kennedy faces two counts of indecent exposure and one charge of violation of probation. Police are asking anyone who witnessed suspicious activity or has information about the incidents to call the FPPD at 772-467-6800 . Anonymous tips can also be submitted to Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers.

entry.article_text: Florida has secured an arrest warrant charging former Cuban leader Raúl Castro with conspiracy to commit first-degree murder in connection with the 1996 shootdown of two unarmed Brothers to the Rescue planes that killed four men, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced Monday.The state case comes months after federal prosecutors indicted Castro and others over the same attack, raising questions about what the new Florida prosecution could mean alongside the existing federal case.WPTV's Michael Hoffman spoke with a former state attorney about the practical impact of the state charges and with a Cuban American woman whose family had a close connection to Brothers to the Rescue."It was not an accident what happened. It was murder," Uthmeier said Monday. "The evidence makes abundantly clear that there was a conspiracy."The Florida Attorney General's Office said its Office of Statewide Prosecution and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement secured the warrant. The state charges Castro with conspiracy to commit first-degree murder.The allegations date back to Feb. 24, 1996, when a Cuban military aircraft shot down two unarmed civilian planes operated by Brothers to the Rescue over international waters.The four men killed were Carlos Costa, Pablo Morales, Mario de la Peña and Armando Alejandre Jr.Brothers to the Rescue was a Miami-based Cuban exile organization whose missions included searching for Cuban migrants at sea."Raúl Castro called for the planes to be shot down," Uthmeier said. "He called for murder."According to the state attorney general's office, Castro is accused of participating in a conspiracy involving Cuban spies operating in South Florida who supplied intelligence to Havana.The arrest warrant affidavitalleges the goal was to kill people aboard the Brothers to the Rescue aircraft "using information provided by spies operating in Miami-Dade and Monroe counties."Florida's case does not stand alone.Federal prosecutors announced an indictment against Castro in May stemming from the same 1996 shootdown. The state prosecution is proceeding alongside that federal case.Former Palm Beach County State Attorney Dave Aronberg told WPTV that federal authorities would ordinarily take the lead on a case such as this."The federal government usually takes the lead on matters like this," Aronberg said.Aronberg questioned how much practical effect a state prosecution would have if Castro were ultimately brought to the United States."If he is brought to the United States to face justice at all, it'll be by the United States to face federal charges in a federal court and then get federal prison time," Aronberg said.Uthmeier, however, argued Monday that the state warrant has consequences. He said it could affect Castro's ability to travel internationally if he enters a country willing and legally able to assist with an arrest or extradition. Such an outcome would depend on the country's laws, applicable extradition arrangements and federal cooperation.The state announcement also brought questions about its timing.Monday marked the first day of early voting in Miami-Dade County, where Uthmeier is seeking election as attorney general.Aronberg told WPTV he believes politics played a role."I think the timing so close to the election is not a coincidence," Aronberg said. "This is a splash that the attorney general wanted to make, and perhaps it's justified under state law. But the timing does indicate that politics came into play here."Uthmeier's opponent also criticized the timing in a statement to WPTV."If we can arrest the murderous Raúl Castro from Tallahassee, I will be the first to do it as Attorney General," the statement said in part.The opponent argued that Uthmeier "somehow chose the first day of early voting in Miami-Dade to make this announcement" and called it "a smokescreen to distract from Hope Florida and Alligator Alcatraz."Beyond the legal and political questions, the case remains deeply personal for members of South Florida's Cuban American community.Hoffman spoke with Mirta Luaces, who said she fled Cuba 65 years ago in search of freedom."I came here in search of freedom, the freedom that I have lost in Cuba," Luaces said.Her son, she said, was a pilot with Brothers to the Rescue and could have been flying with the organization the day of the shootdown."The reason why he wasn't flying that day is because he had moved to Daytona, and he wasn't coming every week," Luaces said. "But otherwise, he could have been one of the victims."Luaces told WPTV she welcomed the new charges and hopes Cuba's political system will someday change."I hope that one day the political system in Cuba will change," Luaces said. "We will have free elections, and democracy will take place in Havana, in Cuba again."Thirty years after the shootdown, Florida's prosecution adds a state case to an already active federal effort to hold Castro accountable. Whether Castro will ever appear in a U.S. courtroom remains an open practical question, but the new warrant adds another legal avenue tied to a case that has remained significant to South Florida's Cuban exile community for decades.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: More than 100 cats rescued from hoarding situation in Port St. Lucie - WPBF
entry.summary: More than 100 cats rescued from hoarding situation in Port St. Lucie    WPBF
entry.article_text: More than 100 cats and kittens rescued from a hoarding situation in Port St. Lucie are now receiving medical care and nourishment at the Humane Society of St. Lucie Animal Control removed the animals over the course of three days last week, with the first group arriving at the shelter on Tuesday. "Some were clearly showing symptoms of upper respiratory. The majority of them had ear mites. They were all covered in fleas. There were a couple that had open sores, from scratching at the flea, scratching at the ear mites and some other issues," said Sarah Wees, executive director of the Humane Society of St. Three pregnant cats gave birth shortly after being rescued, with one too weak to care for her kittens. Those newborns were rushed to an emergency foster home for round-the-clock care, while others remain at the shelter. "We have kittens who are nursing on cats that may or may not be their mom because we really can't tell who belongs with whom because they were all in the same house together," Wees said. The Humane Society is receiving assistance from American Humane, a national organization that supports local communities during large intake cases or natural disasters. "She reached out to me, and by Thursday morning I was on property, and helping just work through those initial days, and also coordinating some volunteers and additional staffing to come in to help with additional personnel," said Taylor Nickelsen, a certified animal responder with American Humane. Nickelsen said their efforts are making a difference, with many of the cats showing significant improvement. "We stay as long as we need to be able to provide the relief that is needed, which ultimately our goal is to help get these animals on their way to foster and on their way to adoption," Nickelsen said. Lucie police are monitoring the case to determine if any criminal charges will be filed. In the meantime, the Humane Society is seeking donations and volunteers to help care for the rescued cats and kittens. entry.summary: Man found dead after barricade situation in St. Lucie County, deputies say    WPTV
entry.article_text: A man was found dead from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound Saturday after a barricade situation prompted deputies to evacuate a woman and children from a St. Lucie County home, according to the sheriff’s office.The St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said deputies responded around 10:17 a.m. to a reported domestic violence incident in the 7600 block of Winter Garden Boulevard.WATCH BELOW: Man found dead after St. Lucie County barricade situationDeputies initially encountered a man in the front yard who went back inside after seeing law enforcement.Authorities later made contact with a man and woman at the front door. During that interaction, a deputy saw what appeared to be a firearm in the man's possession and ordered him to drop it, the sheriff’s office said.Instead, the man closed the door and retreated inside, creating a barricaded-subject situation while other people remained in the home.According to investigators, the man came outside several times and said he would surrender after making a phone call, but repeatedly went back inside.During his final retreat into the home, deputies heard what appeared to be a gunshot.Knowing a woman and children were still inside and could be in danger, deputies entered the residence and evacuated them through a side window, the sheriff’s office said.Deputies later found the man dead from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound.Authorities said there is no ongoing threat to the community.Detectives, crime scene technicians and investigators from the Medical Examiner’s Office are expected to remain at the scene for several hours as the investigation continues.

entry.title: Local court leaders urge residents to respond to jury summonses as turnout drops
entry.summary: Court officials in Floridas 19th Judicial Circuit are warning people who ignore jury duty summonses that they could face fines and other legal consequences. The circuit serves Indian River, Martin, St. Lucie, and Okeechobee counties. Officials say low response rates are making it harder to select juries and can delay court proceedings. At a recent WPTV Lets Hear It meetup in Okeechobee , Jerald D. Bryant, clerk of circuit court and comptroller, spoke with WPTV reporter Brooke Chau about the problem. WATCH: Treasure Coast courts crack down on jury duty no-shows We just ask one thing, and we don't ask you to do it often, but people just ignore them, Bryant said. The numbers illustrate the concern. In April 2026, 300 people were summoned for jury duty, but only 60 reported. That means just one in five people showed up. Bryant said a jury summons is a court order and ignoring it can have legal consequences. It is contempt of court because a jury summons is a court order to appear, Bryant said. Why jury duty participation matters Court officials say low turnout can make it difficult to assemble a jury, potentially delaying trials and affecting defendants waiting for their cases to be heard, as well as victims and their families. Chief Judge Charles A. Schwab told WPTV that higher response rates could also help the court use its resources more efficiently. If we knew that that return rate was going to be 75% to 85%, that money could be diverted to things that we use in the community would rather be spending those on, Schwab said. What happens if you ignore a jury summons? Court leaders say they plan to enforce the consequences for people who fail to appear for jury duty. People who ignore their summonses could receive an order requiring them to explain their absence to a judge. They could face a $100 fine and still be required to serve on a jury. Failing to appear for that court hearing could lead to a bench warrant and potential arrest. Diamond Litty, public defender for the 19th judicial circuit, encouraged anyone with questions or a legitimate issue preventing them from attending to contact the court. I encourage everyone to do the right thing, to not ignore it. If you have an issue, make a phone call. There's a number on the summons, Litty said. 'Please do the right thing.' Chief Judge Schwab said the court intends to enforce the consequences moving forward. Failure to show up there is a consequence, and the courts are going to be enforcing those consequence

entry.summary: Man who claimed woman was possessed by the devil sentenced for Vero Beach hotel attack    cw34.com
entry.article_text: A Vero Beach man accused of restraining a woman in a hotel room and throwing water on her after she tried to leave has been sentenced to nine months in jail. Frank Joseph Lagola pleaded no contest to charges of false imprisonment and battery and was sentenced Thursday, according to court records. Deputies with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office say they were called to Econo Lodge at 950 U.S. Highway 1 in Vero Beach on December 23, 2025, after a witness reported hearing a woman screaming for help. The witness told deputies she saw a man restraining a woman in the hotel doorway, preventing her from leaving. See also: Fort Pierce flasher? String of indecent exposure reports on bridge leads to arrest When deputies arrived, they found Lagola and the victim, who was visibly wet and shaken. Coppeto told deputies she had been staying at the hotel for about a week and wanted to leave the room. She alleged Lagola became increasingly agitated, threw "holy" water on her, and physically restrained her, telling her she wasn't going anywhere. According to the affidavit, Coppeto said Lagola pinned her down and struck her on the top of her head. She also told deputies she screamed for help because she did not have a cellphone and could not physically get away from him. Lagola told deputies he believed Coppeto was possessed by the devil after she began speaking in Latin. He said he was trying to perform an exorcism and admitted holding her down while reading Bible passages, according to the affidavit. Investigators also spoke with a witness who said she heard a woman yelling, Stop, Rape, Help Me, before seeing the man appear to drag the woman back into the room. Lagola was arrested on charges of false imprisonment and battery and was held in St. Lucie County Jail until his sentencing and was given 297 days time served.

Lagola was arrested on charges of false imprisonment and battery and was held in St. Lucie County Jail until his sentencing and was given 297 days time served.

entry.title: Martin County woman honored after using CPR to save 3-year-old girl from swimming pool - WFLX
entry.summary: Martin County woman honored after using CPR to save 3-year-old girl from swimming pool    WFLX
entry.article_text: A 20-year-old Martin County woman is being honored after she used CPR to help save a 3-year-old girl she found motionless at the bottom of a swimming pool. Nearly two months after the August rescue, Martin County Fire Rescue recognized Madison Isler with the department's Heroic Heart Award. WATCH: Martin County woman honored for saving 3-year-old The rescue happened Aug. 23 as Isler walked past the pool at her apartment complex. She told WPTV something in the water caught her attention. "It kind of looked like a smudge in your sunglasses," Isler said. "And then, so I took my glasses off and I looked, and then I realized that it was a little girl." That little girl was 3-year-old Luna. Isler said Luna was motionless at the bottom of the swimming pool when she spotted her. "I jumped in and grabbed her and pulled her out, and she was blue," Isler said. Isler called for her boyfriend to contact 911 and began CPR, using skills she said she learned at a young age from her parents, who both work in fire rescue. "You just don't really think; you just kind of do, especially in a situation when it's a little baby," Isler said. "I pulled a lifeless baby out of a pool." A family friend who is a pediatric intensive care unit nurse heard the commotion and joined the rescue effort, according to the account shared by Martin County Fire Rescue. "Together, they continued their life-saving efforts till finally Luna responded," Martin County Fire Rescue Chief Chad Cianciulli said. Fire rescue officials said Luna was alert and oriented by the time paramedics transported her to the hospital. Luna's mother, Christine Hernandez, said she is grateful Isler happened to be nearby when her daughter needed help. "It's God's work that He put her when we needed her, like at the right place at the right time," Hernandez said. Nearly two months after that frightening day, Isler and Luna reunited at Martin County Fire Rescue headquarters. This time, they were together to celebrate the outcome of the rescue. Martin County Fire Rescue presented Isler with its Heroic Heart Award in recognition of her actions. "Today, on behalf of Martin County Fire Rescue and our entire community, we honor Madison for her courage to act with Martin County Fire Rescue's Heroic Heart Award," Cianciulli said during the recognition. According to the department, Isler is the first person to receive its Heroic Heart Award. For Isler, however, the recognition is secondary to seeing Luna alive and able to grow up. "What means the most to me is that Luna's here with us today and that she gets to grow up and experience life," Isler said. Isler affectionately calls Luna her "unicorn baby." For Hernandez, the outcome comes with overwhelming gratitude. "I'm just very, very thankful, very thankful for Maddie and her family," Hernandez said. For Isler, a skill learned years before an emergency ever happened became critical in the moment Luna needed help, turning CPR training into an action Martin County Fire Rescue says helped save a child's life. entry.summary: Traffic remains slow on Florida's Turnpike in St. Lucie County after a truck fire and a separate crash near the same location Tuesday morning. The truck fire was reported just before 8 a.m. in the southbound lanes near mile marker 161, approximately nine miles south of the Okeechobee Road/State Road 70 exit. Officials initially closed all southbound lanes while crews worked to extinguish the blaze. One lane later reopened before a separate crash in the same area prompted another full closure. As of 11:30 a.m., one southbound lane has reopened, though motorists should continue to expect significant delays near mile marker 161. It's unclear what caused the truck fire or whether anyone was injured in either incident. WPTV has reached out to the Florida Highway Patrol for additional information. This story will be updated as more information becomes available.

entry.title: What's next for Boca Raton? Mayor outlines plan after city manager's resignation
entry.summary: The City of Boca Raton is preparing for a leadership transition after City Manager Mark Sohaney announced he is stepping down after roughly 13 months in the position. City officials say an interim city manager could be selected by mid-November ahead of his expected departure. Sohaney is leaving to join the University of Maryland Global Campus as senior vice president for global military operations, according to Boca Raton Mayor Andy Thomson. The move returns Sohaney to a field closely tied to his background as a retired U.S. Navy captain. The resignation comes as Boca Raton continues work on several major initiatives, including plans for a proposed new police headquarters and other long-term projects expected to shape the city's future. Mayor says city remains on stable footing Mayor Andy Thomson acknowledged it is difficult to see Sohaney leave but said he understands the opportunity. 'For him to have the opportunity to go back and work in a capacity supporting military families and supporting our military makes perfect sense,' Thomson said. In March, WPTV reported on a major shakeup that included the departures of Boca Raton's police chief and two deputy city managers.
