entry.title: William Reaves: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy in 1986 scheduled to be executed Tuesday - WFLX
entry.summary: William Reaves: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy in 1986 scheduled to be executed Tuesday    WFLX
entry.article_text: Florida is set Tuesday to carry out its 18th execution of the year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis’ aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term. William Reaves , 77, was sentenced to death after being convicted of first-degree murder for the 1986 shooting of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski. He would become Florida’s eighth prisoner over the age of 70 to be executed this year, which has highlighted the nation’s aging death-row population and underscored how Florida has outpaced the rest of the country in executions. Reaves was set to receive a three-drug injection starting at 6 p.m. at Florida State Prison near Starke. Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year. Another execution is scheduled for November, which would tie that mark if both are carried out as planned. DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said previously that his goal is to bring justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out. According to court records, Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986. Reaves acknowledged that he had placed the call at a payphone outside the store. While Raczkowski and Reaves spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves’ shorts, officials said. The men struggled over the firearm, and Reaves eventually regained control over it. Investigators said the deputy attempted to run away before Reaves shot him four times. The deputy later died from his wounds. Reaves was initially convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. The Florida Supreme Court reversed the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death a second time in 1992, and subsequent appeals have been unsuccessful. The Florida Supreme Court rejected Reaves’ final appeals last week. One issue raised by his attorneys was Florida’s method of execution. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections. The court has previously upheld this lethal injection protocol against similar challenges. It differs from the single-drug injection used by states like Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike was rushed to the hospital last month after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital. Defense attorneys also argued that the jurors who recommended the death penalty for Reaves were never told that the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs rated Reaves, an Army veteran, as 100% disabled by post-traumatic stress disorder, which was caused by his service in the Vietnam War. More than 100 veterans sent DeSantis a letter on Monday asking him to stop the execution. Final appeals for Reaves were still pending before the U.S. A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half of the 31 total executions in the U.S. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so. Jesse Guardado, 64, is next scheduled to die by injection in Florida on Nov. He was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.

entry.title: Oculina Bank: Rare Florida coral reef faces pivotal federal decision over return of shrimp trawling
entry.summary: A years-long fight over one of the world's rarest ecosystems has reached federal officials, as scientists and conservationists push back against a proposal that could reopen part of the protected Oculina Bank to shrimp trawling for the first time in decades. The Oculina Bank is a deep-water coral reef off Florida's Atlantic coast, with some of its most significant formations off Fort Pierce. Built by the rare Oculina varicosa coral, the reef sits hundreds of feet below the surface and provides habitat for thousands of marine species, including economically important snapper and grouper. Parts of the Oculina Bank were closed to trawling beginning in the 1990s, with protections later expanded and made permanent. Now, conservationists fear some of that progress could be reversed. 'I'd say it's dire. It's a dire situation,' said Mark Perry, executive director of the Florida Oceanographic Society. 'We're desperate to get this protected.' A push to reopen protected waters The latest battle began after a Trump administration executive order directed the nation's regional fishery councils to look for ways to reduce regulatory burdens, expand fishing opportunities and increase economic profitability. The South Atlantic Fishery Management Council subsequently considered proposals that would restore commercial shrimping access to portions of the Oculina Bank that have been protected from trawling for decades. Council documents described the areas as historically important fishing grounds and said the changes were intended to help achieve optimum yield in the rock shrimp fishery. Shrimpers say they need the additional fishing grounds. entry.article_text: A years-long fight over one of the world's rarest ecosystems has reached federal officials, as scientists and conservationists push back against a proposal that could reopen part of the protected Oculina Bank to shrimp trawling for the first time in decades.The Oculina Bank is a deep-water coral reef off Florida's Atlantic coast, with some of its most significant formations off Fort Pierce. Built by the rare Oculina varicosa coral, the reef sits hundreds of feet below the surface and provides habitat for thousands of marine species, including economically important snapper and grouper.WATCH BELOW: Fight over rare coral reef reaches NOAA as public comment opensScientists say decades of shrimp trawling destroyed roughly 90% of the reef before federal protections were put in place. Parts of the Oculina Bank were closed to trawling beginning in the 1990s, with protections later expanded and made permanent.Now, conservationists fear some of that progress could be reversed."I'd say it's dire. It's a dire situation," said Mark Perry, executive director of the Florida Oceanographic Society. "We're desperate to get this protected."The latest battle began after a Trump administration executive order directed the nation's regional fishery councils to look for ways to reduce regulatory burdens, expand fishing opportunities and increase economic profitability.The South Atlantic Fishery Management Council subsequently considered proposals that would restore commercial shrimping access to portions of the Oculina Bank that have been protected from trawling for decades. Council documents described the areas as historically important fishing grounds and said the changes were intended to help achieve optimum yield in the rock shrimp fishery.Shrimpers say they need the additional fishing grounds."The shrimping industry is teetering on the brink of extinction," Bob Zales, executive director of the Southeastern Fisheries Association, previously told WPTV.Council data reviewed by WPTV shows the rock shrimp industry has declined dramatically. The number of annual trips fell from more than 700 in the mid-1990s to fewer than 100 annually since 2010. The number of active rock shrimpers also dropped from 144 in 1996 to fewer than 30 in later years.Zales has blamed the decline on factors including rising costs, imported shrimp and the loss of fishing grounds. Shrimpers have also faced increasing restrictions off Port Canaveral during space launches.Scientists and conservationists argue the potential benefit to the shrimp industry is small compared with the ecological and economic value of protecting the remaining reef.NOAA data previously reviewed by WPTV showed brown rock shrimp landings nationwide totaled about 600,000 pounds in 2023, worth roughly $1 million.Florida fishermen, by comparison, landed nearly 100 million pounds of fish worth just under $300 million that year, including species such as snapper and grouper that use the reef as habitat."We know how valuable this reef system is," Perry said.Scientists also warn that recovery from additional damage could take generations."It would take centuries to grow back even some semblance of the corals," Perry said.Supporters of reopening the area point to mapping that found no live coral, standing dead coral or coral rubble within the proposed trawling zones.But that same research warned sediment kicked up by trawling could drift into nearby living reef and smother coral. Scientists have also raised concerns that snapper and grouper could be caught as bycatch.WPTV Investigates has followed the debate as opposition grew locally and nationally.Earlier public comments to the council overwhelmingly opposed reopening the area. WPTV's review found about 120 of 150 comments opposed both proposals, while 25 supported both and five supported one proposal but not the other.A similar proposal approved by the council in 2022 ultimately failed to win federal approval, garnering thousands of opposing public comments from across the country. The latest proposal nevertheless continued moving forward.WPTV also previously reviewed financial disclosure records for members of the South Atlantic Fishery Management Council and found several disclosed financial interests tied to the fishing or seafood industries. Council officials told WPTV that conflicts of interest are governed by NOAA rules and federal law.Earlier this year, despite opposition from scientists, conservationists and members of the public, the council voted to recommend reopening as much as 24 square nautical miles to shrimp trawling — an area larger than Manhattan.The proposal has now reached the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, which will decide whether to approve it.The Agency has posted the proposals to its Federal Registry, asking the public to weigh in before it votes. The fight is also drawing attention from national conservation organizations.Mike Gravitz, with the Marine Conservation Institute, said the debate comes as coral reefs worldwide already face pressure from warming waters, pollution and overfishing — and as countries around the world work toward protecting more of the planet's oceans."For gosh sakes, it's the last 10% of something that occurs nowhere else on Earth," Gravitz said.He said the United States has close to 25% of its ocean protected in an effective way, while international conservation efforts are moving in the opposite direction."It's really ironic to us that people would be talking about weakening protections for these deep-sea corals at a time when the world needs to do even more, not less," Gravitz said. "This administration is rolling back those protections, especially for the very large marine protected areas, some of which have been protected since Teddy Roosevelt was president." For Perry, the federal review represents the latest — and potentially decisive — stage of a fight that has stretched for years."They understood it, and they protected it," Perry said of previous federal protections, "but now it's being attacked again."Public comment on the proposal is open through Nov. 17 before federal officials make a final decision.Click here to submit a public comment."And we just really need to, you know, stand up and fight for it," Perry said.Multiple organizations have also launched petitions opposing the proposals.

entry.summary: Florida carried out its 18th execution of the year on Tuesday under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis' aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term. William Reaves , 77, was pronounced dead at 6:12 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison near Starke. He was convicted of first-degree murder in the 1986 shooting death of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski. Asked if he had any last statement, he replied, 'No, I do not.' The injection began immediately after that. About 30 seconds later, Reaves took several big breaths and then stopped moving. After a few minutes, the team warden shook Reaves shoulders and yelled his name, but there was no response. entry.article_text: Florida carried out its 18th execution of the year on Tuesday under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis' aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term.William Reaves, 77, was pronounced dead at 6:12 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison near Starke. He was convicted of first-degree murder in the 1986 shooting death of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski.WATCH PREVIOUS COVERAGE BELOW:The death chamber curtain went up promptly at the 6 p.m. execution time, and Reaves was already strapped to a gurney with an IV in his arm. Asked if he had any last statement, he replied, "No, I do not."The injection began immediately after that. About 30 seconds later, Reaves took several big breaths and then stopped moving. After a few minutes, the team warden shook Reaves’ shoulders and yelled his name, but there was no response.A medic was called into the chamber a short time later to check for a heartbeat or any other signs of life, and Reaves was pronounced dead about a minute later.Reaves was the eighth Florida prisoner over age 70 put to death this year, highlighting the nation’s aging death-row population as Florida continues to far outpace the rest of country in total executions.Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year and it would tie that mark if another execution is carried out next month as scheduled.DeSantis, who leaves office in January after two terms, has said his goal is to deliver justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for death sentences to be carried out.Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986, according to court records. Reaves later acknowledged he had placed the call from a payphone outside the store.While Raczkowski and Reaves spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves’ shorts, officials said. The two struggled over the weapon, and Reaves eventually regained control of it. Investigators said the deputy was trying to run away when Reaves shot him four times. The deputy later died from his wounds.Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. But the Florida Supreme Court overturned the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted again and sentenced to death in 1992, and subsequent appeals were unsuccessful.The U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday afternoon rejected Reaves’ final appeal without comment.The Florida Supreme Court last week also rejected Reaves’ appeals to spare his life.One issue raised by his attorneys was Florida’s method of execution. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections.The court has previously upheld this lethal injection protocol against similar challenges. It differs from the single-drug injection used by states such as Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike was rushed to the hospital last month after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital.Defense attorneys also argued that the jurors who recommended the death penalty for Reaves were never told that the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs rated Reaves — an Army veteran — as 100% disabled by post-traumatic stress disorder, which was caused by his service in the Vietnam War. More than 100 veterans sent DeSantis a letter Monday urging him to stop the execution.A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half of the 32 total executions in the U.S. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so.Jesse Guardado, 64, is next scheduled to die by injection in Florida on Nov. He was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.

entry.summary: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy in 1986 executed tonight    WPEC
entry.article_text: Florida carried out the execution of William Reaves at 6 p.m. Tuesday, 40 years after Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkoski was shot and killed outside a convenience store near Vero Beach. Reaves, 77, died by lethal injection at Florida State Prison with an official time of death of 6:12 p.m. Supreme Court denied his final appeal Tuesday, after the Florida Supreme Court rejected his last state appeals on Oct. The Florida Department of Corrections says Reaves had 5 visitors. His brother, sister, nephew, friend, and spiritual advisor all visited Reaves Tuesday. A spokesperson with the department said his final meal was crackers and juice. According to court records, Raczkoski was called to the store around 3 a.m. 23, 1986, to help Reaves get a cab. A gun fell from Reaves’ shorts and the two struggled over it. Records say Reaves shot the deputy in the back four times as he turned away. His son was born after his death. Reaves was arrested two days later in Albany, Georgia. In a taped interview with Indian River County detectives, he admitted to the shooting and said he had been using cocaine. I’ve never met a finer officer in my life, he told them, according to a transcript filed by the state. Reaves was convicted in 1987, but the Florida Supreme Court threw out that verdict in 1991 because one of the prosecutors had previously represented him. A second jury convicted him in 1992 and voted 10-2 to recommend death. DeSantis signed his death warrant Sept. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers, who pushed the governor to sign the warrant, plans to witness the execution. He told CBS12 News on Monday that his goal is that the last thing that he sees is an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office uniform, knowing that justice finally came. Flowers said Raczkoski’s brother is expected to be among the witnesses. Flowers said the brother told him Christmas was never the same for our family after Richard was killed. In court filings, they argued he is a Vietnam veteran rated 100% disabled for post-traumatic stress disorder by the Department of Veterans Affairs, and that the jury that sentenced him never heard the details of his combat service. They also argued he was shut out of the clemency process. The governor denied clemency the same day he signed the death warrant. The Department of Corrections is expected to hold a briefing after the execution. CBS12 News is at Florida State Prison and will update this story.

entry.title: 124 cats, some deceased, surrendered in disturbing Port St. Lucie hoarding case - WPEC
entry.summary: 124 cats, some deceased, surrendered in disturbing Port St. Lucie hoarding case    WPEC
entry.article_text: More than 100 cats were found in unsanitary conditions inside a Port St. Lucie home, including deceased kittens, prompting a criminal investigation. Officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department say 124 cats, both living and deceased, were recovered from a residence in the 2500 block of SW Warwick Street. Animal Control personnel responded to concerns about the number of cats and their living conditions on October 13. They documented accumulated feces and deceased kittens inside the home. See also: Wellington speed camera ticket tossed over missing state approval Two of the three residents have been issued citations for hoarding and failing to provide medical attention to animals, police said. The investigation remains active, and police have not provided details about potential future arrests. All 124 cats have been surrendered and are receiving care through Port St. Lucie Animal Control and the Humane Society of St. Several cats are being treated for ear mites and fleas. Others have needed surgery or additional veterinary care, with some transported to Veterinary Medical Center for treatment. Many of the surviving cats are friendly and could become available for adoption once their medical needs are addressed, police said. The case required a coordinated response involving animal control personnel, police officers, veterinarians and animal welfare organizations. Police said additional information will be released as the investigation continues.

entry.title: More than 100 cats rescued from hoarding situation in Port St. Lucie - WPBF
entry.summary: More than 100 cats rescued from hoarding situation in Port St. Lucie    WPBF
entry.article_text: More than 100 cats and kittens rescued from a hoarding situation in Port St. Lucie are now receiving medical care and nourishment at the Humane Society of St. Lucie Animal Control removed the animals over the course of three days last week, with the first group arriving at the shelter on Tuesday. "Some were clearly showing symptoms of upper respiratory. The majority of them had ear mites. They were all covered in fleas. There were a couple that had open sores, from scratching at the flea, scratching at the ear mites and some other issues," said Sarah Wees, executive director of the Humane Society of St. Three pregnant cats gave birth shortly after being rescued, with one too weak to care for her kittens. Those newborns were rushed to an emergency foster home for round-the-clock care, while others remain at the shelter. "We have kittens who are nursing on cats that may or may not be their mom because we really can't tell who belongs with whom because they were all in the same house together," Wees said. The Humane Society is receiving assistance from American Humane, a national organization that supports local communities during large intake cases or natural disasters. "She reached out to me, and by Thursday morning I was on property, and helping just work through those initial days, and also coordinating some volunteers and additional staffing to come in to help with additional personnel," said Taylor Nickelsen, a certified animal responder with American Humane. Nickelsen said their efforts are making a difference, with many of the cats showing significant improvement. "We stay as long as we need to be able to provide the relief that is needed, which ultimately our goal is to help get these animals on their way to foster and on their way to adoption," Nickelsen said. Lucie police are monitoring the case to determine if any criminal charges will be filed. In the meantime, the Humane Society is seeking donations and volunteers to help care for the rescued cats and kittens. entry.title: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy set for execution Tuesday - WPEC
entry.summary: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy set for execution Tuesday    WPEC
entry.article_text: The man convicted of killing an Indian River County deputy nearly 40 years ago is scheduled to be executed Tuesday. William Reaves, 77, is set to die by lethal injection at 6 p.m. at Florida State Prison near Starke . Ron DeSantis signed the death warrant Sept. According to court records, Cpl. Richard Raczkoski was called to a Zippy Mart near Vero Beach around 3 a.m. 23, 1986, to help Reaves get a cab. During the encounter, a gun fell from Reaves’ shorts and the two struggled over it. Records say Reaves shot the deputy four times in the back. In a taped interview with Indian River County detectives in Albany, Reaves admitted to the shooting. I’ve never met a finer officer in my life, he said, according to a transcript filed by the state. When a detective asked why he would not give up the gun, Reaves said he was a convicted felon and feared prison. I know if I got caught with that gun, and the man take me down there, I’m gonna get a mandatory three years already for the gun, he said. Reaves also told detectives, I was all coked up and I panicked, both of us panicked. Prosecutors have long argued the shooting was premeditated. Court records show the deputy was running away when he was shot, and the .380 handgun required a separate trigger pull for each shot. See also: Florida secures state arrest warrant for Raúl Castro in 1996 shootdown Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death. The Florida Supreme Court rejected his latest appeals last week, and a request for the U.S. Supreme Court to review his case is still pending. His attorneys and supporters, including a group of military veterans, have asked DeSantis to spare his life, pointing to his service in Vietnam. Reaves was first convicted in 1987, but the Florida Supreme Court threw out that conviction in 1991 because one of the prosecutors had previously represented Reaves in another case. A second jury convicted him again in 1992 and voted 10-2 to recommend the death penalty. In a court filing last month, Reaves’ attorneys said he was deployed to Vietnam as a ground combat soldier in 1969, at age 20. They say the Department of Veterans Affairs rates him 100% disabled for post-traumatic stress disorder, and that the jury that sentenced him never heard the details of his combat service. His attorneys also argued that Reaves was shut out of the clemency process. They said the attorney assigned to represent him met with him about five minutes before his clemency interview and never gave him a copy of what was submitted on his behalf. A circuit judge ruled Reaves received a full clemency proceeding. The governor denied clemency the same day he signed the death warrant. In the same filing, the defense accused two former Indian River County deputies of taking bribes from a drug dealer in the 1980s. The defense also said one of them helped shape the testimony of a key witness against Reaves. Circuit Judge Anastasia Norman rejected the claim on Oct. 2, finding the allegations were not backed by any sworn statement and were merely speculative at best. Reaves did not raise that claim in his appeal to the Florida Supreme Court. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers, who pushed for the governor to sign the warrant, describes the moment when he learned the governor signed Reaves' death warrant. "It was not something that I had expected. At this point, our governor is wrapping things up in Tallahassee and finishing out his time. So for him to take time to make sure that this gets handled is just really a blessing," said Flowers. Flowers plans to attend the execution in Raiford on Tuesday. My goal with going tomorrow is ultimately the last thing that he sees is an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office uniform, knowing that justice finally came, Flowers said. Flowers said Raczkoski’s brother will also be there. Raczkoski’s parents have since died. Flowers said the brother told him, Christmas was never the same for our family after Richard was killed. The execution comes nearly a year after the agency lost Sgt. Terri Sweeting-Mashkow, who was killed in the line of duty in November 2025. Flowers said Tuesday will bring the agency some closure. It just really feels like coming full circle, like a moment of healing that we all needed, Flowers said. Supreme Court appeal still pending, Flowers said he will not rest easy until the execution is carried out. I’d hate to see it delayed in any way, he said.

entry.title: Mangonia Park council approves Extraordinary Kids Foundation request, allowing nonprofit to continue services
entry.summary: After months of uncertainty, the Extraordinary Kids Foundation can continue serving families in Mangonia Park following a narrow vote by the town council. The Mangonia Park Town Council voted 3-2 Tuesday night to approve a special exception request tied to code violations first raised in July , allowing the nonprofit to continue operating and providing community services, including services for children with special needs and weekly community outreach. The decision ends a months-long battle that supporters said left the organization's future uncertain and raised concerns about the impact a closure could have on families who depend on its programs and outreach efforts. entry.title: Year-long bridge closure in southern Martin County forces drivers onto detour, adds minutes to commutes
entry.summary: A major road closure is now in effect in southern Martin County, where the bridge at Southeast County Line Road is closed for a year-long reconstruction project. The detour could add several minutes to daily drives, so officials are urging commuters to plan ahead or find an alternate route. George May lives just off Southeast County Line Road, where a road block is now notifying drivers to turn around. 'It'll be inconvenient, for sure. People commuting to work and people that live in little club,' May said. May said the road closure is going to take some getting used to. 'I already drive over an hour to work everyday. It'll probably add about 20 minutes to my commute,' May said. Martin County says the bridge will be closed for a year, with a lot of work ahead. 'There are a lot of utilities ther,' Mark Aveni, Martin County public works deputy director, said. 'There's a lot of coordination that needs to occur. We're removing a pedestrian bridge and we're going to repurpose that somewhere else and unfortunately these things just take time.' Despite the closure, residents say they're glad to see the investment. 'There were large cracks under the bridge. It was deteriorating,' May said. 'It's a little bit of an inconvenience but I'm happy for that to have a new bridge and have better infrastructure in the area,' Daniel Von said. Six of the project's $7 million price tag is covered by state and federal grants. The new bridge will be two feet higher and built to be safer and more resilient. 'We're replacing it with a very resilient type of rebar that's going to be safer. There is a very sharp curve before that bridge, we're going to totally eliminate that and soften the curve. It'll also be much safer for pedestrians,' Aveni said. Residents are now hoping the project will go on without delays. 'I'm fine with it as long as they keep the project on schedule,' May said. Many believed it meant the 206,000 square feet of data center space approved in 2016 would remain the limit at the site.New documents show that was not the end of the story.Documents obtained by Hoffman show PBA Holdings, one of two companies that own property associated with Project Tango, had submitted a separate proposal before the July commission vote.Palm Beach County staff approved that plan Oct. 7 without another vote by county commissioners or a new public hearing before the commission.The approval increases the data center space on that portion of the property from 206,000 square feet to just under 700,000 square feet.The additional data center space uses square footage that had been unassigned under the 2016 approval.Under the newly approved plan, the property would include:Two 288,000-square-foot data center buildingsOne 122,000-square-foot data center building1.2 million square feet of warehouse spaceA utility building and offices occupying the remaining square footageThere is another significant difference between the 2016 plan and the October approval.The latest approval contains conditions governing development of the property. Palm Beach County zoning officials confirmed in July that the original 2016 approval did not include such conditions.Under the newly approved plan, data center buildings cannot be constructed within 850 feet of the property line near Arden.Noise at neighboring homes would be capped between 50 and 60 decibels, depending on the time of day. entry.article_text: More than 100 cats were found in unsanitary conditions inside a Port St. Lucie home, including deceased kittens, prompting a criminal investigation. Officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department say 124 cats, both living and deceased, were recovered from a residence in the 2500 block of SW Warwick Street. Animal Control personnel responded to concerns about the number of cats and their living conditions on October 13. They documented accumulated feces and deceased kittens inside the home. See also: Wellington speed camera ticket tossed over missing state approval Two of the three residents have been issued citations for hoarding and failing to provide medical attention to animals, police said. The investigation remains active, and police have not provided details about potential future arrests. All 124 cats have been surrendered and are receiving care through Port St. Lucie Animal Control and the Humane Society of St. Several cats are being treated for ear mites and fleas. Others have needed surgery or additional veterinary care, with some transported to Veterinary Medical Center for treatment. Many of the surviving cats are friendly and could become available for adoption once their medical needs are addressed, police said. The case required a coordinated response involving animal control personnel, police officers, veterinarians and animal welfare organizations. Police said additional information will be released as the investigation continues.

entry.title: William Reaves: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy in 1986 scheduled to be executed Tuesday - WFLX
entry.summary: William Reaves: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy in 1986 scheduled to be executed Tuesday    WFLX
entry.article_text: Florida is set Tuesday to carry out its 18th execution of the year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis’ aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term. William Reaves , 77, was sentenced to death after being convicted of first-degree murder for the 1986 shooting of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski. He would become Florida’s eighth prisoner over the age of 70 to be executed this year, which has highlighted the nation’s aging death-row population and underscored how Florida has outpaced the rest of the country in executions. Reaves was set to receive a three-drug injection starting at 6 p.m. at Florida State Prison near Starke. Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year. Another execution is scheduled for November, which would tie that mark if both are carried out as planned. DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said previously that his goal is to bring justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out. According to court records, Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986. Reaves acknowledged that he had placed the call at a payphone outside the store. While Raczkowski and Reaves spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves’ shorts, officials said. The men struggled over the firearm, and Reaves eventually regained control over it. Investigators said the deputy attempted to run away before Reaves shot him four times. The deputy later died from his wounds. Reaves was initially convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. The Florida Supreme Court reversed the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death a second time in 1992, and subsequent appeals have been unsuccessful. The Florida Supreme Court rejected Reaves’ final appeals last week. One issue raised by his attorneys was Florida’s method of execution. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections. The court has previously upheld this lethal injection protocol against similar challenges. It differs from the single-drug injection used by states like Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike was rushed to the hospital last month after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital. Defense attorneys also argued that the jurors who recommended the death penalty for Reaves were never told that the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs rated Reaves, an Army veteran, as 100% disabled by post-traumatic stress disorder, which was caused by his service in the Vietnam War. More than 100 veterans sent DeSantis a letter on Monday asking him to stop the execution. Final appeals for Reaves were still pending before the U.S. A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half of the 31 total executions in the U.S. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so. Jesse Guardado, 64, is next scheduled to die by injection in Florida on Nov. He was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.

entry.title: Local court leaders urge residents to respond to jury summonses as turnout drops
entry.summary: Court officials in Floridas 19th Judicial Circuit are warning people who ignore jury duty summonses that they could face fines and other legal consequences. The circuit serves Indian River, Martin, St. Lucie and Okeechobee counties. Officials say low response rates are making it harder to select juries and can delay court proceedings. At a recent WPTV Lets Hear It meetup in Okeechobee , Jerald D. Bryant, clerk of circuit court and comptroller, spoke with WPTV reporter Brooke Chau about the problem. WATCH: Treasure Coast courts crack down on jury duty no-shows We just ask one thing, and we don't ask you to do it often, but people just ignore them, Bryant said. The numbers illustrate the concern. In April 2026, 300 people were summoned for jury duty, but only 60 reported. That means just one in five people showed up. Bryant said a jury summons is a court order and ignoring it can have legal consequences. It is contempt of court because a jury summons is a court order to appear, Bryant said. Why jury duty participation matters Court officials say low turnout can make it difficult to assemble a jury, potentially delaying trials and affecting defendants waiting for their cases to be heard, as well as victims and their families. Chief Judge Charles A. Schwab told WPTV that higher response rates could also help the court use its resources more efficiently. 'If we knew that return rate was going to be 75% to 85%, those other monies could then be diverted to things that we as a community would rather be spending those on,' Schwab said. What happens if you ignore a jury summons? Court leaders say they plan to enforce the consequences for people who fail to appear for jury duty. People who ignore their summonses could receive an order requiring them to explain their absence to a judge. They could face a $100 fine and still be required to serve on a jury. Failing to appear for that court hearing could lead to a bench warrant and potential arrest. Diamond Litty, public defender for the 19th judicial circuit, encouraged anyone with questions or a legitimate issue preventing them from attending to contact the court. It was murder," Uthmeier said Monday. "The evidence makes abundantly clear that there was a conspiracy."The Florida Attorney General's Office said its Office of Statewide Prosecution and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement secured the warrant. The state charges Castro with conspiracy to commit first-degree murder.The allegations date back to Feb. 24, 1996, when a Cuban military aircraft shot down two unarmed civilian planes operated by Brothers to the Rescue over international waters.The four men killed were Carlos Costa, Pablo Morales, Mario de la Peña and Armando Alejandre Jr.Brothers to the Rescue was a Miami-based Cuban exile organization whose missions included searching for Cuban migrants at sea."Raúl Castro called for the planes to be shot down," Uthmeier said. "He called for murder."According to the state attorney general's office, Castro is accused of participating in a conspiracy involving Cuban spies operating in South Florida who supplied intelligence to Havana.The arrest warrant affidavit alleges the goal was to kill people aboard the Brothers to the Rescue aircraft "using information provided by spies operating in Miami-Dade and Monroe counties."Florida's case does not stand alone.Federal prosecutors announced an indictment against Castro in May stemming from the same 1996 shootdown. The state prosecution is proceeding alongside that federal case.Former Palm Beach County State Attorney Dave Aronberg told WPTV that federal authorities would ordinarily take the lead on a case such as this."The federal government usually takes the lead on matters like this," Aronberg said.Aronberg questioned how much practical effect a state prosecution would have if Castro were ultimately brought to the United States."If he is brought to the United States to face justice at all, it'll be by the United States to face federal charges in a federal court and then get federal prison time," Aronberg said.Uthmeier, however, argued Monday that the state warrant has consequences. He said it could affect Castro's ability to travel internationally if he enters a country willing and legally able to assist with an arrest or extradition. Such an outcome would depend on the country's laws, applicable extradition arrangements and federal cooperation.The state announcement also brought questions about its timing.Monday marked the first day of early voting in Miami-Dade County, where Uthmeier is seeking election as attorney general.Aronberg told WPTV he believes politics played a role."I think the timing so close to the election is not a coincidence," Aronberg said. "This is a splash that the attorney general wanted to make, and perhaps it's justified under state law. But the timing does indicate that politics came into play here."Uthmeier's opponent also criticized the timing in a statement to WPTV."If we can arrest the murderous Raúl Castro from Tallahassee, I will be the first to do it as Attorney General," the statement said in part.The opponent argued that Uthmeier "somehow chose the first day of early voting in Miami-Dade to make this announcement" and called it "a smokescreen to distract from Hope Florida and Alligator Alcatraz."Beyond the legal and political questions, the case remains deeply personal for members of South Florida's Cuban American community.Hoffman spoke with Mirta Luaces, who said she fled Cuba 65 years ago in search of freedom."I came here in search of freedom, the freedom that I have lost in Cuba," Luaces said.Her son, she said, was a pilot with Brothers to the Rescue and could have been flying with the organization the day of the shootdown."The reason why he wasn't flying that day is because he had moved to Daytona, and he wasn't coming every week," Luaces said. "But otherwise, he could have been one of the victims."Luaces told WPTV she welcomed the new charges and hopes Cuba's political system will someday change."I hope that one day the political system in Cuba will change," Luaces said. "We will have free elections, and democracy will take place in Havana, in Cuba again."Thirty years after the shootdown, Florida's prosecution adds a state case to an already active federal effort to hold Castro accountable. entry.article_text: A major road closure is now in effect in southern Martin County, where the bridge at Southeast County Line Road is closed for a year-long reconstruction project. The detour could add several minutes to daily drives, so officials are urging commuters to plan ahead or find an alternate route. George May lives just off Southeast County Line Road, where a road block is now notifying drivers to turn around. "It'll be inconvenient, for sure. People commuting to work and people that live in little club," May said. May said the road closure is going to take some getting used to. "I already drive over an hour to work everyday. It'll probably add about 20 minutes to my commute," May said. Martin County says the bridge will be closed for a year, with a lot of work ahead. "There are a lot of utilities ther," Mark Aveni, Martin County public works deputy director, said. "There's a lot of coordination that needs to occur. We're removing a pedestrian bridge and we're going to repurpose that somewhere else and unfortunately these things just take time." Despite the closure, residents say they're glad to see the investment. "There were large cracks under the bridge. It was deteriorating," May said. "It's a little bit of an inconvenience but I'm happy for that — to have a new bridge and have better infrastructure in the area," Daniel Von said. Six of the project's $7 million price tag is covered by state and federal grants. The new bridge will be two feet higher and built to be safer and more resilient. "We're replacing it with a very resilient type of rebar that's going to be safer. There is a very sharp curve before that bridge, we're going to totally eliminate that and soften the curve. It'll also be much safer for pedestrians," Aveni said. Residents are now hoping the project will go on without delays. "I'm fine with it as long as they keep the project on schedule," May said. entry.title: Palm Beach County said no to Project Tango expansion, but data center space still triples

About 600,000 square feet remained unassigned.The site is next to what would later become the Arden community and Saddle View Elementary School.A decade later, a much larger proposal came before the Palm Beach County Commission.On July 15, commissioners spent roughly 12 hours reviewing the application known as Project Tango. That proposal sought to increase the project's data center footprint to more than 1 million square feet.Commissioners voted 5-1 to deny the expansion following significant opposition from nearby residents.The county also passed a moratorium on new data center applications while officials work on new rules.For residents who had fought the expansion, the July decision was a victory. Many believed it meant the 206,000 square feet of data center space approved in 2016 would remain the limit at the site.New documents show that was not the end of the story.Documents obtained by Hoffman show PBA Holdings, one of two companies that own property associated with Project Tango, had submitted a separate proposal before the July commission vote.Palm Beach County staff approved that plan Oct. 7 without another vote by county commissioners or a new public hearing before the commission.The approval increases the data center space on that portion of the property from 206,000 square feet to just under 700,000 square feet.The additional data center space uses square footage that had been unassigned under the 2016 approval.Under the newly approved plan, the property would include:Two 288,000-square-foot data center buildingsOne 122,000-square-foot data center building1.2 million square feet of warehouse spaceA utility building and offices occupying the remaining square footageThere is another significant difference between the 2016 plan and the October approval.The latest approval contains conditions governing development of the property. Palm Beach County zoning officials confirmed in July that the original 2016 approval did not include such conditions.Under the newly approved plan, data center buildings cannot be constructed within 850 feet of the property line near Arden.Noise at neighboring homes would be capped between 50 and 60 decibels, depending on the time of day. Sound monitors would run continuously, with the county receiving access to the monitoring data.The county's water utility would commit to providing no more than 100,000 gallons of water per day for the entire site.Battery storage would also be required to comply with fire safety requirements.Residents have contacted WPTV and Hoffman questioning how the plan could be approved without another commission vote and saying they believed the county's data center moratorium would prevent further movement on the property.Palm Beach County Zoning Director Wendy Hernandez told Hoffman by phone that the proposal was submitted before the moratorium took effect.Because it was already submitted, Hernandez said, county staff were able to continue reviewing it and ultimately approve it.Hernandez declined an on-camera interview.The Oct. 7 approval is not the only application involving the Project Tango property.According to Hernandez, WPB Logistics, the second owner of part of the property, has submitted its own proposal seeking to increase data center space on its roughly 60-acre portion of the site without approval from the County Commission.That proposal could result in approximately 1.2 million square feet of additional data center space.Unlike the PBA Holdings proposal approved Oct. 7, the WPB Logistics application remains under review.Hoffman also reached out to Ernie Cox, the main project manager for Project Tango, seeking a response to concerns from residents who said they felt the latest approval happened without their knowledge or an opportunity for public input.A member of Cox's staff returned Hoffman's call Tuesday and said the team would respond to the question.Hoffman had not received that response at the time of publication.

entry.title: Sheriff witnesses execution of man convicted in 1986 killing of Indian River County deputy - WPBF
entry.summary: Sheriff witnesses execution of man convicted in 1986 killing of Indian River County deputy    WPBF
entry.article_text: Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers witnessed the execution of William Reaves, who was convicted of killing Deputy Richard Raczkowski in 1986, at Florida State Prison on Tuesday night. Flowers said he positioned himself in the front row to ensure Reaves could see his sheriff’s office uniform. "I was in the front row; I was on the side of the room that he could see, so he saw my uniform, and I’m glad that he saw that," Flowers said. Reaves was convicted of killing Raczkowski at a convenience store near Vero Beach in 1986. Following the crime, Reaves was quickly arrested and sentenced to death. The case went through a retrial and several appeals, but the death sentence remained unchanged. "We will never forget Richard; we will never forget his sacrifice," Flowers said. Flowers described the execution process, which lasted about 12 minutes, and noted that Reaves did not make a final statement. "The real kicker on top of it was that he didn’t say anything; he didn’t make a last statement; he didn’t say anything to the family, ask God for forgiveness," Flowers said. Reaves’ last meal consisted of crackers and juice. Flowers said this was the first execution he had ever witnessed. "It’s closure but not justice; that chapter of the book is closed, but that man killed him in cold blood," Flowers said. Flowers also said his office will unveil a monument next month to honor its two fallen deputies.

entry.title: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy in 1986 executed tonight - WPEC
entry.summary: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy in 1986 executed tonight    WPEC
entry.article_text: Florida carried out the execution of William Reaves at 6 p.m. Tuesday, 40 years after Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkoski was shot and killed outside a convenience store near Vero Beach. Reaves, 77, died by lethal injection at Florida State Prison with an official time of death of 6:12 p.m. Supreme Court denied his final appeal Tuesday, after the Florida Supreme Court rejected his last state appeals on Oct. The Florida Department of Corrections says Reaves had 5 visitors. His brother, sister, nephew, friend, and spiritual advisor all visited Reaves Tuesday. A spokesperson with the department said his final meal was crackers and juice. William Reaves Execution Jack Wu's Reporter Notebook Before the execution 5:45 p.m. Notes say 29 people in the room, including 16 spectators: 8 men and 8 women. Sheriff Eric Flowers and Kevin Delisle are listed. The room is white, with no windows. A large viewing window takes up most of one wall. The room is quiet, with muffled talking heard on the other side of the glass. The door to the execution chamber is the same color as the wall, with covered glass and a tan border. Reaves is lying face-up, with his feet toward the witnesses. Three men in suits are in the room; one is on the phone. A spectator in the second row puts his hand on his wife’s shoulder. The man on the phone hangs up. Asked for any final words, Reaves says, No, I do not. Notes describe heavy breathing, his mouth opening and multiple IVs in his left arm. He is bound by brown leather straps. A man in a white shirt says "Reaves, Reaves" while shaking his shoulder. A man in the room is taking notes. (The note doesn’t specify further.) 6:11 p.m. A doctor walks in, puts a hand on Reaves’ face and shines a flashlight in his eyes. The doctor checks Reaves’ heart with a stethoscope. Notes say his face is blocked from view for 10 to 20 seconds. The doctor leaves; the man with the phone makes a call. Reaves is pronounced dead, and the curtain drops. According to court records, Raczkoski was called to the store around 3 a.m. 23, 1986, to help Reaves get a cab. A gun fell from Reaves’ shorts and the two struggled over it. Records say Reaves shot the deputy in the back four times as he turned away. His son was born after his death. Reaves was arrested two days later in Albany, Georgia. In a taped interview with Indian River County detectives, he admitted to the shooting and said he had been using cocaine. I’ve never met a finer officer in my life, he told them, according to a transcript filed by the state. Reaves was convicted in 1987, but the Florida Supreme Court threw out that verdict in 1991 because one of the prosecutors had previously represented him. A second jury convicted him in 1992 and voted 10-2 to recommend death. DeSantis signed his death warrant Sept. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers, who pushed the governor to sign the warrant, plans to witness the execution. He told CBS12 News on Monday that his goal is that the last thing that he sees is an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office uniform, knowing that justice finally came. Flowers said Raczkoski’s brother is expected to be among the witnesses. Flowers said the brother told him Christmas was never the same for our family after Richard was killed. In court filings, they argued he is a Vietnam veteran rated 100% disabled for post-traumatic stress disorder by the Department of Veterans Affairs, and that the jury that sentenced him never heard the details of his combat service. They also argued he was shut out of the clemency process. The governor denied clemency the same day he signed the death warrant. The Department of Corrections is expected to hold a briefing after the execution. CBS12 News is at Florida State Prison and will update this story.

entry.title: Martin County woman honored after using CPR to save 3-year-old girl from swimming pool - WPTV
entry.summary: Martin County woman honored after using CPR to save 3-year-old girl from swimming pool    WPTV
entry.article_text: A 20-year-old Martin County woman is being honored after she used CPR to help save a 3-year-old girl she found motionless at the bottom of a swimming pool. Nearly two months after the August rescue, Martin County Fire Rescue recognized Madison Isler with the department's Heroic Heart Award.WATCH: Martin County woman honored for saving 3-year-oldThe rescue happened Aug. 23 as Isler walked past the pool at her apartment complex. She told WPTV something in the water caught her attention."It kind of looked like a smudge in your sunglasses," Isler said. "And then, so I took my glasses off, and I looked, and then I realized that it was a little girl."That little girl was 3-year-old Luna.Isler said Luna was motionless at the bottom of the swimming pool when she spotted her."I jumped in and grabbed her and pulled her out, and she was blue," Isler said.Isler called for her boyfriend to contact 911 and began CPR, using skills she said she learned at a young age from her parents, who both work in fire rescue."You just don't really think; you just kind of do, especially in a situation when it's a little baby," Isler said. "I pulled a lifeless baby out of a pool."A family friend who is a pediatric intensive care unit nurse heard the commotion and joined the rescue effort, according to the account shared by Martin County Fire Rescue."Together, they continued their life-saving efforts till finally Luna responded," Martin County Fire Rescue Chief Chad Cianciulli said.Fire rescue officials said Luna was alert and oriented by the time paramedics transported her to the hospital.Luna's mother, Christine Hernandez, said she is grateful Isler happened to be nearby when her daughter needed help."It's God's work that He put her when we needed her, like at the right place at the right time," Hernandez said.Nearly two months after that frightening day, Isler and Luna reunited at Martin County Fire Rescue headquarters.This time, they were together to celebrate the outcome of the rescue.Martin County Fire Rescue presented Isler with its Heroic Heart Award to recognize her actions."Today, on behalf of Martin County Fire Rescue and our entire community, we honor Madison for her courage to act with Martin County Fire Rescue's Heroic Heart Award," Cianciulli said during the recognition.According to the department, Isler is the first person to receive its Heroic Heart Award.For Isler, however, the recognition is secondary to seeing Luna alive and able to grow up."What means the most to me is that Luna's here with us today and that she gets to grow up and experience life," Isler said.Isler affectionately calls Luna her "unicorn baby."For Hernandez, the outcome comes with overwhelming gratitude."I'm just very, very thankful, very thankful for Maddie and her family," Hernandez said.For Isler, a skill learned years before an emergency ever happened became critical in the moment Luna needed help, turning CPR training into an action Martin County Fire Rescue says helped save a child's life.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

entry.article_text: All lanes of Florida’s Turnpike have reopened in St. Lucie County after a truck fire and a separate crash caused major delays Tuesday morning. The truck fire was reported just before 8 a.m. in the southbound lanes near mile marker 161, approximately nine miles south of the Okeechobee Road/State Road 70 exit. Officials initially closed all southbound lanes while crews worked to extinguish the blaze. One lane later reopened before a separate crash in the same area led to another closure. As of the latest update, all southbound lanes have reopened and traffic is beginning to move through the area. However, motorists may continue to experience residual delays as congestion clears. It’s unclear what caused the truck fire or whether anyone was injured in either incident. WFLX has reached out to the Florida Highway Patrol for additional information. This story will be updated if more information becomes available.

entry.title: Sheriff witnesses execution of man convicted in 1986 killing of Indian River County deputy - WPBF
entry.summary: Sheriff witnesses execution of man convicted in 1986 killing of Indian River County deputy    WPBF
entry.article_text: Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers witnessed the execution of William Reaves, who was convicted of killing Deputy Richard Raczkowski in 1986, at Florida State Prison on Tuesday night. Flowers said he positioned himself in the front row to ensure Reaves could see his sheriff’s office uniform. "I was in the front row; I was on the side of the room that he could see, so he saw my uniform, and I’m glad that he saw that," Flowers said. Reaves was convicted of killing Raczkowski at a convenience store near Vero Beach in 1986. Following the crime, Reaves was quickly arrested and sentenced to death. The case went through a retrial and several appeals, but the death sentence remained unchanged. "We will never forget Richard; we will never forget his sacrifice," Flowers said. Flowers described the execution process, which lasted about 12 minutes, and noted that Reaves did not make a final statement. "The real kicker on top of it was that he didn’t say anything; he didn’t make a last statement; he didn’t say anything to the family, ask God for forgiveness," Flowers said. Reaves’ last meal consisted of crackers and juice. Flowers said this was the first execution he had ever witnessed. "It’s closure but not justice; that chapter of the book is closed, but that man killed him in cold blood," Flowers said. Flowers also said his office will unveil a monument next month to honor its two fallen deputies. Ron DeSantis' aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term.William Reaves, 77, was pronounced dead at 6:12 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison near Starke. Asked if he had any last statement, he replied, "No, I do not."The injection began immediately after that. About 30 seconds later, Reaves took several big breaths and then stopped moving. After a few minutes, the team warden shook Reaves’ shoulders and yelled his name, but there was no response.A medic was called into the chamber a short time later to check for a heartbeat or any other signs of life, and Reaves was pronounced dead about a minute later.Reaves was the eighth Florida prisoner over age 70 put to death this year, highlighting the nation’s aging death-row population as Florida continues to far outpace the rest of country in total executions.Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year and it would tie that mark if another execution is carried out next month as scheduled.DeSantis, who leaves office in January after two terms, has said his goal is to deliver justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for death sentences to be carried out.Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986, according to court records. Reaves later acknowledged he had placed the call from a payphone outside the store.While Raczkowski and Reaves spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves’ shorts, officials said. The two struggled over the weapon, and Reaves eventually regained control of it. Investigators said the deputy was trying to run away when Reaves shot him four times. The deputy later died from his wounds.Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. But the Florida Supreme Court overturned the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted again and sentenced to death in 1992, and subsequent appeals were unsuccessful.The U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday afternoon rejected Reaves’ final appeal without comment.The Florida Supreme Court last week also rejected Reaves’ appeals to spare his life.One issue raised by his attorneys was Florida’s method of execution. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections.The court has previously upheld this lethal injection protocol against similar challenges. It differs from the single-drug injection used by states such as Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike was rushed to the hospital last month after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital.Defense attorneys also argued that the jurors who recommended the death penalty for Reaves were never told that the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs rated Reaves — an Army veteran — as 100% disabled by post-traumatic stress disorder, which was caused by his service in the Vietnam War. More than 100 veterans sent DeSantis a letter Monday urging him to stop the execution.A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half of the 32 total executions in the U.S. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so.Jesse Guardado, 64, is next scheduled to die by injection in Florida on Nov. entry.summary: Man who claimed woman was possessed by the devil sentenced for Vero Beach hotel attack    WPEC
entry.article_text: A Vero Beach man accused of restraining a woman in a hotel room and throwing water on her after she tried to leave has been sentenced to nine months in jail. Frank Joseph Lagola pleaded no contest to charges of false imprisonment and battery and was sentenced Thursday, according to court records. Deputies with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office say they were called to Econo Lodge at 950 U.S. Highway 1 in Vero Beach on December 23, 2025, after a witness reported hearing a woman screaming for help. The witness told deputies she saw a man restraining a woman in the hotel doorway, preventing her from leaving. See also: Fort Pierce flasher? String of indecent exposure reports on bridge leads to arrest When deputies arrived, they found Lagola and the victim, who was visibly wet and shaken. Coppeto told deputies she had been staying at the hotel for about a week and wanted to leave the room. She alleged Lagola became increasingly agitated, threw "holy" water on her, and physically restrained her, telling her she wasn't going anywhere. According to the affidavit, Coppeto said Lagola pinned her down and struck her on the top of her head. She also told deputies she screamed for help because she did not have a cellphone and could not physically get away from him. Lagola told deputies he believed Coppeto was possessed by the devil after she began speaking in Latin. He said he was trying to perform an exorcism and admitted holding her down while reading Bible passages, according to the affidavit. Investigators also spoke with a witness who said she heard a woman yelling, Stop, Rape, Help Me, before seeing the man appear to drag the woman back into the room. Lagola was arrested on charges of false imprisonment and battery and was held in St. Lucie County Jail until his sentencing and was given 297 days time served.

entry.title: More than 120 cats, kittens found in Port St. Lucie home in alleged hoarding situation
entry.summary: WPTV is learning more about another animal hoarding situation on the Treasure Coast. Port St. Lucie police said more than 124 cats and kittens were found in a home off the 2500 block of Warwick Street. WATCH BELOW: More than 120 cats found in Port St. Lucie home 124 cats recovered from animal hoarding situation in Port St Lucie Investigators said they found the home in unsanitary conditions, including an accumulation of feces and dead kittens. Police said two of the three people living inside the home where the cats were found were issued citations for hoarding and failure to provide medical attention. Sarah Wees, executive director of The Humane Society of St. Lucie County, said they were brought in 106 cats and kittens. 'They likely had to fight for food, which is why some of them are underweight, and some of the kittens that are nursing, they might be nursing on the wrong mother,' Wees said. 'If they got them spayed or neutered, we wouldn't be where we are right now.' Wees said almost all of the cats had fleas and ear mites, and some with open sores needed immediate medical treatment. Now, Wees said staff and volunteers are scrambling to get them well. 'They're feeding them, they're cleaning them, they're doing medical intakes,' Wees said. Taylor Nickelson with the American Humane Society said the cats and kittens are getting better fast. 'We're seeing that in just their liveliness and eagerness to approach us and take food,' Nickelson said.  However, Wees said some of the cats and kittens are still in a dangerous situation and being treated in their sick room. 'They're responding well, but it's still an unknown situation,' Wees said. 'Any of them can fade at any time, so it's very dangerous at this time.' Wees said this situation has doubled their cat population. 'It overwhelms the staff,' Wees said. 'It overwhelms our resources.' Staff are asking for donations, volunteers and fosters during these recovery efforts. 'These little babies can't do it for themselves,' Wee said. 'So, we and the community need to do it for them.' Once medical needs are met, the cats and kittens will be up for adoption.

entry.title: William Reaves executed Tuesday after being convicted of killing Indian River County deputy in 1986
entry.summary: Florida carried out its 18th execution of the year on Tuesday under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis' aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term. William Reaves , 77, was pronounced dead at 6:12 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison near Starke. He was convicted of first-degree murder in the 1986 shooting death of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Man executed after killing Indian River Co. deputy 40 years ago The death chamber curtain went up promptly at the 6 p.m. execution time, and Reaves was already strapped to a gurney with an IV in his arm. Asked if he had any last statement, he replied, 'No, I do not.' The injection began immediately after that. About 30 seconds later, Reaves took several big breaths and then stopped moving. After a few minutes, the team warden shook Reaves shoulders and yelled his name, but there was no response. A medic was called into the chamber a short time later to check for a heartbeat or any other signs of life, and Reaves was pronounced dead about a minute later. Reaves was the eighth Florida prisoner over age 70 put to death this year, highlighting the nations aging death-row population as Florida continues to far outpace the rest of country in total executions. Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year and it would tie that mark if another execution is carried out next month as scheduled. DeSantis, who leaves office in January after two terms, has said his goal is to deliver justice to victims families who have waited decades for death sentences to be carried out. Reaves struggled with a deputy after dropping a gun Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986, according to court records. Reaves later acknowledged he had placed the call from a payphone outside the store. While Raczkowski and Reaves spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves shorts, officials said. The two struggled over the weapon, and Reaves eventually regained control of it. Investigators said the deputy was trying to run away when Reaves shot him four times. The deputy later died from his wounds. Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. entry.article_text: Florida carried out its 18th execution of the year on Tuesday under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis' aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term.William Reaves, 77, was pronounced dead at 6:12 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison near Starke. He was convicted of first-degree murder in the 1986 shooting death of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski.WATCH REPORT BELOW:The death chamber curtain went up promptly at the 6 p.m. execution time, and Reaves was already strapped to a gurney with an IV in his arm. Asked if he had any last statement, he replied, "No, I do not."The injection began immediately after that. About 30 seconds later, Reaves took several big breaths and then stopped moving. After a few minutes, the team warden shook Reaves’ shoulders and yelled his name, but there was no response.A medic was called into the chamber a short time later to check for a heartbeat or any other signs of life, and Reaves was pronounced dead about a minute later.Reaves was the eighth Florida prisoner over age 70 put to death this year, highlighting the nation’s aging death-row population as Florida continues to far outpace the rest of country in total executions.Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year and it would tie that mark if another execution is carried out next month as scheduled.DeSantis, who leaves office in January after two terms, has said his goal is to deliver justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for death sentences to be carried out.Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986, according to court records. Reaves later acknowledged he had placed the call from a payphone outside the store.While Raczkowski and Reaves spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves’ shorts, officials said. The two struggled over the weapon, and Reaves eventually regained control of it. Investigators said the deputy was trying to run away when Reaves shot him four times. The deputy later died from his wounds.Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. But the Florida Supreme Court overturned the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted again and sentenced to death in 1992, and subsequent appeals were unsuccessful.The U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday afternoon rejected Reaves’ final appeal without comment.The Florida Supreme Court last week also rejected Reaves’ appeals to spare his life.One issue raised by his attorneys was Florida’s method of execution. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections.The court has previously upheld this lethal injection protocol against similar challenges. It differs from the single-drug injection used by states such as Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike was rushed to the hospital last month after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital.Defense attorneys also argued that the jurors who recommended the death penalty for Reaves were never told that the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs rated Reaves — an Army veteran — as 100% disabled by post-traumatic stress disorder, which was caused by his service in the Vietnam War. More than 100 veterans sent DeSantis a letter Monday urging him to stop the execution.A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half of the 32 total executions in the U.S. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so.Jesse Guardado, 64, is next scheduled to die by injection in Florida on Nov. He was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.

entry.title: Panthers fans make 100-mile trek from Port St. Lucie to cheer on their team
entry.summary: WPTV anchor and Panthers 360 host Mike Trim joined fans on a 100-mile, one-way trip to Amerant Bank Arena with one goal: cheer on the Panthers to a win. The group of six fans, including Maria Charles and Camilo Medina, meet up before their long rides from Port St. Lucie to Sunrise. WATCH BELOW: Port St. Lucie fans go the distance for Panthers Port St. Lucie Panthers fans drive to game 'We have a strong following here in St. Lucie County,' Medina told Trim. When we talked to these super fans on Thursday, Oct. 15, the Panthers were facing off against the Vancouver Canucks. Leaving Port St. Lucie just before 3:30 p.m., the group hoped to beat rush-hour traffic. 'And the length of the drive doesn't bother you at all?' Trim asked Medina. 'Not at all, no,' Medina replied. The group is not only bonded by the love for the Panthers but also their prior military service. Nearly all in the road-tripping group are veterans. Trim joined Charles for most of the drive. As they departed to make the drive south, Trim asked Charles, 'We're leaving Port St. Lucie now. 100 miles. Do you get in the zone while you're driving? Do you listen to music? What's the drive like?' 'I listen to music, and when it starts getting a little boring, that's when I put on the Latin music,' Charles said. Charles, a Panthers season ticket holder, explained her route. 'I take the Florida Turnpike, drive all the way down until I hit Sawgrass Expressway and take Sawgrass Expressway to Oakland Park, which is the off-ramp for going to the arena,' Charles told Trim. 'Do you keep a running tab of how many miles you've driven to Florida Panthers games?' Trim asked Charles. 'I can honestly say, 20 to 25,000 miles since 2023,' Charles replied. entry.title: 23 kids meet their idol Lionel Messi thanks to Inter Miami and Make-A-Wish
entry.summary: Tuesday was a day to remember for several youngsters who had the chance to meet their sports idols thanks to Make-A-Wish. 'I was so happy I started crying; it's just an amazing experience,' said Yulissa Morales Melendrez, a Make-A-Wish participant. Several kids from around the country had the opportunity to meet the defending MLS Champs, Inter Miami, a moment Make-A-Wish participant Jimmy Hoover could only dream of. 'I was super excited. I was a little in shock. I didn't really know what to do; it was kind of all surreal to me,' Hoover said. Hoover said he's been playing soccer since he was 7 years old. 'I started playing and started watching (Lionel) Messi, and he became my favorite player right away,' said Hoover. On Tuesday afternoon, Hoover sat in the stands at Nu Stadium, watching his idol, Lionel Messi, and Inter Miami train. It was a simple moment, yes, but a moment that nearly didn't happen. 'I was going in (to the hospital) for a couple of months, and they were telling me it was just a stomach ache,' said Hoover. Hoover and his family didn't think much of it until one day at his friend's house. 'My stomach was hurting so bad, I was in agonizing pain,' said Hoover. He rushed to the hospital, where doctors found out he had cancer, so for months he endured chemotherapy, and while he was fighting for his life, he didn't want to let his teammates down, so every day after treatment he'd be with his teammates. 'It was really difficult; I couldn't keep up with everyone; that was the hardest part,' said Hoover. Dedicated to playing soccer and again and again kicking cancer's butt he fought effortlessly, and last July he rang the bell as his cancer went into remission. 'It's been great. I'm still in a little bit of shock from everything,' said Hoover. That shock would soon wear off, and days ago he and his teammates hung out. He got the surprise of a lifetime: he'd be part of the Make-A-Wish Foundation's latest effort to help him and kids from around the world meet Messi and Inter Miami. 'It's super rewarding. It was a bit of a wait to get out here, but after everything, it's been super great,' said Hoover. Kids signed on to join the team for the day, get a jersey, watch the fellas practice, and share joy and hope with the Inter Miami guys.
