entry.title: St. Lucie County fire chief terminated after months of controversy - WPBF
entry.summary: St. Lucie County fire chief terminated after months of controversy    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District Board voted 4-3 to terminate fire Chief Jeff Lee without cause after months of controversy, hazing allegations, and a no-confidence vote. Interim Chief Paul Langel said, "I believe that the fire board moved forward and that was their job. Now my job is going to be to step in and start the healing process." The decision comes two months after five firefighters were displaced for allegedly turning a bug zapper into a makeshift taser and using it to shock coworkers. Videos appear to show the alleged hazing, and three firefighters ultimately lost their jobs. One of the terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson, said, "I think it was a step in the right direction. I don’t think today was about us by any means. I think it was the best thing for the entire department." The disciplined firefighters have called the termination retaliation for previous complaints they filed against district leadership. When asked about the possibility of the terminated firefighters regaining their jobs, Langel said, "I believe that there’s always scenarios that would unfold and happen. I’ve got to get in and get up to speed on all the specifics." The board voted to appoint Langel as interim chief. He is a familiar face in the district, with 30 years of experience. Because Lee was terminated without cause, he is entitled to compensation as his contract ends early.

entry.title: St. Lucie County Fire Board terminates chief after calls for leadership change - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County Fire Board terminates chief after calls for leadership change    WPEC
entry.article_text: After months of controversy, the St. Lucie County Fire District Board voted Wednesday to fire longtime Chief Jeff Lee, following an emotional meeting filled with calls for change and coming less than two weeks after the firefighters' union released the results of a no-confidence vote in the district's top leaders. The meeting was packed with firefighters, union members, retirees and residents, many urged the board to change the district's leadership. Among them was Taylor Baldwin, who pointed to the dozens of supporters wearing yellow shirts throughout the room. Look at everyone wearing yellow," Baldwin told commissioners. "These are not people who want to see the fire district fail. These are people who love this department enough to stand up and beg you to save it." The decision marks the latest development in a controversy that began this summer after a hazing investigation led to the firing of three veteran firefighters and the suspension of two others . The district determined the conduct amounted to hazing, while the firefighters and their union have argued it was consensual horseplay. A Fort Pierce Police Department investigation found no criminal violations. The union is pursuing arbitration to get the three firefighters reinstated . The issue later escalated into a no-confidence vote organized by IAFF Local 1377. According to the union, 423 of its 517 dues-paying members participated. Lee received 314 no-confidence votes and 108 confidence votes, with 74.23% of participants voting they no longer had confidence in his leadership. Several speakers criticized both district leadership and the board's handling of the controversy. "You participated in this cover-up. You protected the lies and you profoundly failed the people you are elected to serve," another resident Katie told the board. Lee, who joined the department in 1997 after serving in the U.S. Navy and became the district's 14th fire chief in May 2023, was not present for Wednesday's meeting. Commissioners spent more than 30 minutes debating whether Lee should be fired with or without cause. Ultimately, the board voted to terminate him without cause, triggering the severance provisions in his contract. "I think we still have to come to the determination of what exactly the final total is of the severance," board member James Clasby said after the vote. "We will only pay what we are legally required to." Those who supported Lee's removal said the district needs a fresh start. "I feel like a weight is lifted," Commissioner Jamie Fowler said. "Firing someone is never an easy decision, regardless of all the factors that come into play. So I feel like we've sort of taken a step in the right direction." Following Lee's termination, the board voted 4-3 to appoint Deputy Chief Paul Langel as interim chief while a search for a permanent replacement begins. The board is also moving forward with hiring outside legal counsel and discussing the process for selecting the district's next chief. See also: Former PBSO dispatcher sentenced after 2023 head-on DUI crash that killed mother This is not the first time the board has faced this choice. In 2017, after a union no-confidence vote, the board accepted then Chief Buddy Emerson’s retirement effective immediately and paid him severance through the end of his contract.

entry.title: St. Lucie County Fire Board terminates fire chief after union vote - cw34.com
entry.summary: St. Lucie County Fire Board terminates fire chief after union vote    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District Board will discuss the future of Fire Chief Jeff Lee on Wednesday afternoon, about two weeks after the district’s firefighters union released the results of a no-confidence vote on its top leaders. The agenda for the board’s 3 p.m. regular meeting includes an item listed under Chair Shannon Martin titled Discussion Regarding Potential Retirement and Leadership Transition. The agenda does not say whose retirement will be discussed, and no supporting documents for the item have been made public. The Professional Fire Fighters and Paramedics of St. Lucie County, IAFF Local 1377, released its vote results Oct. According to the union, 423 of its 517 dues-paying members took part. Lee received 314 votes of no confidence and 108 votes of confidence. Assistant Fire Chief Brian Gonzalez received 390 votes of no confidence, and District Attorney Kim Sabol received 413. Under the rules the union set before the vote, at least 75% of participating members had to vote no confidence before the union would formally present the result to the Fire Board. Gonzalez and Sabol both passed that mark. The union said 74.23% of members voted no confidence in him. Local 1377 calls upon the Board to carefully consider these results and fulfill its responsibility to the employees who serve this county and to the public they have sworn to protect, the union said in its release. Since then, the district has reassigned Gonzalez from assistant chief to a battalion chief training role. The district said Gonzalez and Lee agreed to the move and that it had been discussed before the recent events. Sabol gave the district 90 days’ notice on Sept. 30 and is set to retire Dec. Wednesday’s agenda also includes the selection of a law firm and a new district attorney. See also: Former PBSO dispatcher sentenced after 2023 head-on DUI crash that killed mother The vote followed months of fallout from a hazing investigation. In July, the district f ired three veteran firefighters , Jordon Hutchinson, Christopher Baldwin and Douglas Boudrias, and suspended two others. Videos showed newer firefighters being shocked with a modified bug zapper . An outside investigation hired by the district concluded the conduct was hazing. The firefighters and their union say it was consensual horseplay, and a Fort Pierce Police report found no criminal matter. The union is pursuing arbitration to get the three firefighters reinstated. Board members have said the district has no policy for handling complaints against its top contracted employees, including the fire chief. They can’t investigate themselves. That’s not proper, board member and County Commissioner Jamie Fowler said at an Oct. 6, Lee withdrew a settlement offer that would have brought the three firefighters back with retroactive pay, citing guidance from counsel and the district’s insurance representatives. CBS12 News has also obtained a 2022 recording in which Lee, Gonzalez and Sabol declined to investigate a female firefighter’s complaint of unwanted touching by a coworker. Lee has said the problem is not one he can solve himself. The board has to fix that problem, Lee said at an Aug. County Commissioner James Clasby, who also sits on the fire board, has publicly called on Lee to resign. In August, a motion to suspend Lee and Sabol failed 2 to 4. In a statement after the vote, the district said it recognizes the results and will take appropriate action. It pointed to pay increases, about 100 additional uniformed personnel and three-person engine staffing during Lee’s tenure. Lee joined the district in 1997 after serving in the U.S. He became its 14th fire chief in May 2023. This is not the first time the board has faced this choice. In 2017, after a union no-confidence vote, the board accepted then Chief Buddy Emerson’s retirement effective immediately and paid him severance through the end of his contract. CBS12 News will be at Wednesday’s meeting and will update this story.

The committee is also scheduled to receive an update on the Residential Sound Insulation Program, which aims to reduce aircraft noise inside eligible homes near the airport. entry.title: More than 120 cats, kittens found in Port St. Lucie home in alleged hoarding situation - WPTV
entry.summary: More than 120 cats, kittens found in Port St. Lucie home in alleged hoarding situation    WPTV
entry.article_text: WPTV is learning more about another animal hoarding situation on the Treasure Coast.Port St. Lucie police said more than 124 cats and kittens were found in a home off the 2500 block of Warwick Street.WATCH BELOW: More than 120 cats found in Port St. Lucie homeInvestigators said they found the home in unsanitary conditions, including an accumulation of feces and dead kittens.Police said two of the three people living inside the home where the cats were found were issued citations for hoarding and failure to provide medical attention.Sarah Wees, executive director of The Humane Society of St. Lucie County, said they were brought in 106 cats and kittens."They likely had to fight for food, which is why some of them are underweight, and some of the kittens that are nursing, they might be nursing on the wrong mother," Wees said. "If they got them spayed or neutered, we wouldn't be where we are right now."Wees said almost all of the cats had fleas and ear mites, and some with open sores needed immediate medical treatment.Now, Wees said staff and volunteers are scrambling to get them well."They're feeding them, they're cleaning them, they're doing medical intakes," Wees said.Taylor Nickelson with the American Humane Society said the cats and kittens are getting better fast."We're seeing that in just their liveliness and eagerness to approach us and take food," Nickelson said. However, Wees said some of the cats and kittens are still in a dangerous situation and being treated in their sick room."They're responding well, but it's still an unknown situation," Wees said. "Any of them can fade at any time, so it's very dangerous at this time."Wees said this situation has doubled their cat population."It overwhelms the staff," Wees said. "It overwhelms our resources."Staff are asking for donations, volunteers and fosters during these recovery efforts."These little babies can't do it for themselves," Wee said. "So, we and the community need to do it for them."Once medical needs are met, the cats and kittens will be up for adoption.

entry.title: Trump, tariffs and health care: Takeaways from two Senate debates
entry.summary: Voters in Michigan and Kansas saw their Senate candidates square off in high-stakes debates, with control of the Senate potentially hanging in the balance. In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers traded sharp attacks in one of the countrys most competitive Senate races. El-Sayed sought to tie Rogers closely to President Donald Trump, repeatedly arguing that a vote for Rogers would effectively be a vote for Trump. Rogers, meanwhile, portrayed El-Sayed as too extreme for Michigan. The candidates also clashed over several major policy issues. RELATED STORY | El-Sayed, Rogers debate in closely watched Michigan Senate race El-Sayed said he supports changes to the U.S. Supreme Court and Medicare for All. On Social Security, he has called for raising the cap on income subject to Social Security taxes. Rogers opposes Medicare for All and previously voted against the Affordable Care Act, though he has said he wants to reform the law. On Social Security, Rogers said he wants lawmakers to work together on a solution but did not outline a specific plan during the debate. The debate also featured a heated exchange over foreign policy, campaign funding and national security, with Rogers questioning El-Sayeds positions and El-Sayed criticizing Rogers ties to Trump. Meanwhile, Republican Sen. Roger Marshall and Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton also faced off in Kansas, a state that has become more competitive than many observers expected earlier in the election cycle. RELATED STORY | All eyes on Maine as critical Senate race draws closer Hamilton sought to distance himself from national Democratic leadership, saying he would not support Sen. Chuck Schumer as majority leader if elected. Marshall emphasized his relationship with Trump, arguing that he would be able to work with the president to deliver results for Kansas. The candidates also sparred over tariffs and the economy. Marshall argued that tariffs are helping bring manufacturing jobs back to the United States, while Hamilton said uncertainty surrounding tariffs is making it harder for businesses to operate and increasing costs. With Election Day approaching, both Michigan and Kansas remain closely watched Senate contests.

entry.title: Teachers in Palm Beach County worry voter confusion over a ballot referendum could lead to sizeable pay cut
entry.summary: In less than two weeks, voters in several school districts in Florida will decide whether to renew a local $1 million property tax referendum that is directly tied to teacher pay. For band teachers like Amrutha Murthy, the suspense and concern are building. 'We love our students and we want to be able to provide for them, but we don't want it to come at our cost of living, says Murthy. The Park Vista High School instructor is one of nearly 900 teachers in the Palm Beach County School District who could face an average pay cut of $8,000 a year if voters choose not to renew the referendum that first passed in 2018. WATCH: Teachers in the Palm Beach County School District are relying on voters to keep jobs and pay Teachers in the Palm Beach County School district are relying on voters to keep jobs and pay Some educators say they're worried the property tax renewal supplement will be confused with the highly controversial Amendment Three Property Tax measure. The 'referendum to continue ad valorem levy for school safety, teachers and operational needs' is different. It helps to pay the salaries of music, art and physical education teachers as well as teachers of specialty programs like culinary and aviation. In addition, the Palm Beach County School District says the money is also used to help fund additional security measures and personnel and provide a behavioral health professional at every school. 'It's been a huge boost for teachers in Palm Beach County because it literally creates a more livable situation,' says Gordan Longhofer, president of the Classroom Teachers Association. By next school year, the Palm Beach County School District says some of these teaching positions could be eliminated if the referendum fails. Veteran educators like Marie Chrisphonce could lose the maximum $10,00 annual amount because of their years of experience. She is hoping to keep her job and pay intact. 'It's scary because that's a lot of pay. It's paying the bills. It's very scary,' says Chrisphonce. While Chrisphonce already has a second job, Murthy says with her busy band schedule, there's just no time. Teachers say they can only hope for a forte of support when voters head to the polls next month.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie Election includes Mayors race and trash pick-up - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie Election includes Mayors race and trash pick-up    WPEC
entry.article_text: The CBS12 News I-Team has been closely following Port St. Lucie's election cycle, as there are two headline stories playing out and the future of the city is at stake. Leadership and trash are the hot-button items. On the first day of early voting in St. Lucie County, our crew visited a polling location on Rosser Blvd. We found two tents, side by side. In them, two candidates for mayor-- with such a rift between them-- the race feels like a war. The incumbent, Shannon Martin, is running to stay in office, and she says the city needs to stay on its current course. She points to how she has prioritized infrastructure repairs, like roadwork, as a reason to keep her in City Hall. Her opponent, Steven Giordano, says City Hall is corrupt and has lost touch with everyday people. When pressed on specific things he’d do differently-- he also wanted to talk about roadwork and says the city needs a new traffic study. See also: Martin County airport committee to review overnight flights and noise concerns Mayors serve four-year terms and wield significant influence in the mayor-council form of government. But trash collection is another issue getting people fired up: Should the city switch to twice-a-week pickup? FCC is the company that handles garbage collection in Port St. "I don't want to pay for something I don't need," said resident Rob Buske. Buske is making a point we have seldom heard while covering trash in the city. At many recent city council meetings, members of the public have hurled angry comments at city leaders, saying the trash pickup is sub-par. They’ve demanded an additional collection day. Ironic, then, that on the first day of early voting, everyone we asked for comment said they’d rather keep what they’ve got. The ballot question about trash collection isn't binding; it’s simply a way to poll the residents. The council might or might not go with whatever the majority of voters say. A second pick-up day would cost residents more than a hundred bucks a year, but some are adamant it's necessary. As this story comes to air and online, the election is less than 2 weeks away. Candidates for Mayor do not declare a party, and trash is a non-party matter. Here it's not Republicans vs. Democrats, but it’s somehow more personal, more granular, while also being big-picture. When can my garbage go to the curb? Who will be in charge of the city and what's their vision? The people are about to decide.

entry.title: St. Lucie County Fire Board terminates chief after calls for leadership change - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County Fire Board terminates chief after calls for leadership change    WPEC
entry.article_text: After months of controversy, the St. Lucie County Fire District Board voted Wednesday to fire longtime Chief Jeff Lee, following an emotional meeting filled with calls for change and coming less than two weeks after the firefighters' union released the results of a no-confidence vote in the district's top leaders. The meeting was packed with firefighters, union members, retirees and residents, many urged the board to change the district's leadership. Among them was Taylor Baldwin, who pointed to the dozens of supporters wearing yellow shirts throughout the room. Look at everyone wearing yellow," Baldwin told commissioners. "These are not people who want to see the fire district fail. These are people who love this department enough to stand up and beg you to save it." The decision marks the latest development in a controversy that began this summer after a hazing investigation led to the firing of three veteran firefighters and the suspension of two others . The district determined the conduct amounted to hazing, while the firefighters and their union have argued it was consensual horseplay. A Fort Pierce Police Department investigation found no criminal violations. The union is pursuing arbitration to get the three firefighters reinstated . The issue later escalated into a no-confidence vote organized by IAFF Local 1377. According to the union, 423 of its 517 dues-paying members participated. Lee received 314 no-confidence votes and 108 confidence votes, with 74.23% of participants voting they no longer had confidence in his leadership. Several speakers criticized both district leadership and the board's handling of the controversy. "You participated in this cover-up. You protected the lies and you profoundly failed the people you are elected to serve," another resident Katie told the board. Lee, who joined the department in 1997 after serving in the U.S. Navy and became the district's 14th fire chief in May 2023, was not present for Wednesday's meeting. Commissioners spent more than 30 minutes debating whether Lee should be fired with or without cause. Ultimately, the board voted to terminate him without cause, triggering the severance provisions in his contract. "I think we still have to come to the determination of what exactly the final total is of the severance," board member James Clasby said after the vote. "We will only pay what we are legally required to." Those who supported Lee's removal said the district needs a fresh start. "I feel like a weight is lifted," Commissioner Jamie Fowler said. "Firing someone is never an easy decision, regardless of all the factors that come into play. So I feel like we've sort of taken a step in the right direction." Following Lee's termination, the board voted 4-3 to appoint Deputy Chief Paul Langel as interim chief while a search for a permanent replacement begins. The board is also moving forward with hiring outside legal counsel and discussing the process for selecting the district's next chief. See also: Former PBSO dispatcher sentenced after 2023 head-on DUI crash that killed mother This is not the first time the board has faced this choice. In 2017, after a union no-confidence vote, the board accepted then Chief Buddy Emerson’s retirement effective immediately and paid him severance through the end of his contract.

In Wednesday's Fire Board meeting, those community members packed the Fire Administration building, many of whom held signs or wore shirts in support of the three firefighters. Union Representative Ryan Sapp said he believed Lee's termination is a "positive step forward.""I think moving forward, the ultimate goal here is to just move forward and get things back to a level field and continue providing the services to our community," Sapp told investigative reporter Kate Hussey. "The biggest thing today is we worked together and came together as a local — glad to see my membership stepped up and let their voices be heard." The Fire Board is also searching for a replacement district attorney, who submitted her notice of retirement amid the ongoing controversy.

entry.title: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy in 1986 executed - cw34.com
entry.summary: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy in 1986 executed    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Florida carried out the execution of William Reaves at 6 p.m. Tuesday, 40 years after Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkoski was shot and killed outside a convenience store near Vero Beach. Reaves, 77, died by lethal injection at Florida State Prison with an official time of death of 6:12 p.m. Supreme Court denied his final appeal Tuesday, after the Florida Supreme Court rejected his last state appeals on Oct. The Florida Department of Corrections says Reaves had 5 visitors. His brother, sister, nephew, friend, and spiritual advisor all visited Reaves Tuesday. A spokesperson with the department said his final meal was crackers and juice. William Reaves Execution Jack Wu's Reporter Notebook Before the execution 5:45 p.m. Notes say 29 people in the room, including 16 spectators: 8 men and 8 women. Sheriff Eric Flowers and Kevin Delisle are listed. The room is white, with no windows. A large viewing window takes up most of one wall. The room is quiet, with muffled talking heard on the other side of the glass. The door to the execution chamber is the same color as the wall, with covered glass and a tan border. Reaves is lying face-up, with his feet toward the witnesses. Three men in suits are in the room; one is on the phone. A spectator in the second row puts his hand on his wife’s shoulder. The man on the phone hangs up. Asked for any final words, Reaves says, No, I do not. Notes describe heavy breathing, his mouth opening and multiple IVs in his left arm. He is bound by brown leather straps. A man in a white shirt says "Reaves, Reaves" while shaking his shoulder. A man in the room is taking notes. (The note doesn’t specify further.) 6:11 p.m. A doctor walks in, puts a hand on Reaves’ face and shines a flashlight in his eyes. The doctor checks Reaves’ heart with a stethoscope. Notes say his face is blocked from view for 10 to 20 seconds. The doctor leaves; the man with the phone makes a call. Reaves is pronounced dead, and the curtain drops. According to court records, Raczkoski was called to the store around 3 a.m. 23, 1986, to help Reaves get a cab. A gun fell from Reaves’ shorts and the two struggled over it. Records say Reaves shot the deputy in the back four times as he turned away. His son was born after his death. Reaves was arrested two days later in Albany, Georgia. In a taped interview with Indian River County detectives, he admitted to the shooting and said he had been using cocaine. I’ve never met a finer officer in my life, he told them, according to a transcript filed by the state. Reaves was convicted in 1987, but the Florida Supreme Court threw out that verdict in 1991 because one of the prosecutors had previously represented him. A second jury convicted him in 1992 and voted 10-2 to recommend death. DeSantis signed his death warrant Sept. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers, who pushed the governor to sign the warrant, plans to witness the execution. He told CBS12 News on Monday that his goal is that the last thing that he sees is an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office uniform, knowing that justice finally came. Flowers said Raczkoski’s brother is expected to be among the witnesses. Flowers said the brother told him Christmas was never the same for our family after Richard was killed. See also: 124 cats, some deceased, surrendered in disturbing Port St. Lucie hoarding case Reaves’ attorneys fought the execution to the end. In court filings, they argued he is a Vietnam veteran rated 100% disabled for post-traumatic stress disorder by the Department of Veterans Affairs, and that the jury that sentenced him never heard the details of his combat service. They also argued he was shut out of the clemency process. The governor denied clemency the same day he signed the death warrant. The Department of Corrections is expected to hold a briefing after the execution. CBS12 News is at Florida State Prison and will update this story.

entry.title: 2 vehicles sought in Port St. Lucie hit-and-run investigation, police say
entry.summary: The Port St. Lucie Police Department has released new information in its investigation of a hit-and-run crash that left a 63-year-old man seriously injured earlier this month on Oct. 9. Detectives now believe the victim may have been hit by two separate vehicles near the intersection of Northwest University Boulevard and Northwest California Boulevard. According to police, one vehicle was traveling northbound while the other was traveling southbound at the time of the incident. The crash occurred at approximately 12:56 a.m and the victim, a 63-year-old Port St. Lucie resident, was found unconscious in the roadway suffering from severe head injuries. In a previous update, police said surveillance video from a nearby business captured the incident and showed what investigators believed to be a white four-door sedan striking the man before leaving the scene without stopping. As detectives continued reviewing evidence and surveillance footage, investigators developed information indicating a second vehicle may also have been involved in the crash. Police are now working to identify both vehicles and their drivers. Investigators have released images of the vehicles and are asking for the public's help. Anyone who recognizes either vehicle, was in the area around the time of the crash, witnessed the incident, or has dashcam or surveillance video from the area is asked to contact the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000.

entry.title: WHERE'S WALTER? Having a day of discovery at the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast
entry.summary: This week, I visited a place where learning and fun go hand in hand: the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast. From the moment I walked in, I could tell this wasn't your typical museum. Instead of looking at exhibits from behind a rope or glass case, kids are encouraged to jump in, get involved and learn by doing. As I explored the museum, I discovered exhibits designed to teach important life skills in creative and engaging ways. From learning about money and budgeting to exploring different careers and practicing job skills, every corner of the museum offered a new opportunity to learn something useful. WATCH: WHERE'S WALTER? Discovering the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast One of my favorite stops, of course, involved the weather. As a meteorologist, I was excited to check out the museum's WPTV weather simulator and hurricane simulator. It was fascinating to see how children can experience weather concepts in a hands-on environment and gain a better understanding of the science behind storms and hurricanes. What impressed me most was how interactive everything was. Kids aren't just reading signs or watching demonstrations. They're solving problems, making decisions, using their imaginations and building confidence along the way. The museum creates an environment where learning feels more like an adventure than a lesson. Whether they're exploring future careers, practicing financial skills or learning about science and weather, children are gaining valuable experiences that can help them throughout their lives. My visit was a great reminder that some of the best learning happens when you're having fun. By rolling up their sleeves, asking questions and trying new things, kids can discover skills and interests they never knew they had. If you're looking for a family-friendly destination on the Treasure Coast that combines education, creativity and fun, the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast is definitely worth a visit. That's where I was!

entry.title: Republicans split over condemning controversial Ramaswamy ad targeting Amy Acton
entry.summary: A campaign ad in Ohios governors race is drawing criticism from Democrats and some Republicans and raising questions about how far negative campaigning should go. The ad, paid for by Republican nominee Vivek Ramaswamys campaign, features Democratic nominee Amy Actons birth mother calling her daughter a liar. RELATED STORY | Democrat Amy Actons estranged mother calls her liar in ad, court documents say otherwise The ad has drawn particular attention because Actons mother lost custody of her when Acton was a child amid sexual abuse allegations involving the man her mother was with at the time. Republican Rep. Nancy Mace of South Carolina sharply criticized the ad, calling it the most shameful, disgusting, offensive ad this election season. Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine said the ad needs to come down, but he would not be rescinding his endorsement of Ramaswamy. Acton worked for DeWine as the state's health director during the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance were also asked about the controversy but did not condemn the ad. I know nothing about it, Trump said. But I hear the mother went very rogue on the daughter, doesn't have a lot of respect for the daughter. Trump later added, It's a very unusual situation to have a mother hate a daughter that much. But I don't think that has anything to do with Vivek. RELATED STORY | Barack Obama to campaign with Ohio Democrats as he expands his outreach ahead of Election Day Vance defended Ramaswamys decision to air the commercial. Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is and calls Amy Acton a liar, Vance said. Acton herself condemned the ad, telling CNN that it has 'crossed everyone's boundaries.' The controversy has extended beyond Ohio, prompting a broader debate about negative political advertising. There was no indication that Ramaswamys campaign planned to pull the ad. Republican Sen. John Husted of Ohio also criticized the decision, telling The Associated Press he would not have aired the commercial.

entry.title: Teachers in Palm Beach County worry voter confusion over a ballot referendum could lead to sizeable pay cut
entry.summary: In less than two weeks, voters in several school districts in Florida will decide whether to renew a local $1 million property tax referendum that is directly tied to teacher pay. For band teachers like Amrutha Murthy, the suspense and concern are building. 'We love our students and we want to be able to provide for them, but we don't want it to come at our cost of living, says Murthy. The Park Vista High School instructor is one of nearly 900 teachers in the Palm Beach County School District who could face an average pay cut of $8,000 a year if voters choose not to renew the referendum that first passed in 2018. WATCH: Teachers in the Palm Beach County School District are relying on voters to keep jobs and pay Teachers in the Palm Beach County School district are relying on voters to keep jobs and pay Some educators say they're worried the property tax renewal supplement will be confused with the highly controversial Amendment Three Property Tax measure. The 'referendum to continue ad valorem levy for school safety, teachers and operational needs' is different. It helps to pay the salaries of music, art and physical education teachers as well as teachers of specialty programs like culinary and aviation. In addition, the Palm Beach County School District says the money is also used to help fund additional security measures and personnel and provide a behavioral health professional at every school. 'It's been a huge boost for teachers in Palm Beach County because it literally creates a more livable situation,' says Gordan Longhofer, president of the Classroom Teachers Association. By next school year, the Palm Beach County School District says some of these teaching positions could be eliminated if the referendum fails. Veteran educators like Marie Chrisphonce could lose the maximum $10,00 annual amount because of their years of experience. She is hoping to keep her job and pay intact. 'It's scary because that's a lot of pay. It's paying the bills. It's very scary,' says Chrisphonce. While Chrisphonce already has a second job, Murthy says with her busy band schedule, there's just no time. Teachers say they can only hope for a forte of support when voters head to the polls next month.

entry.article_text: Martin County’s Airport Noise Advisory Committee is scheduled to meet at 9 a.m. Thursday at Witham Field’s Airport Administration Building to review nighttime flight activity and noise concerns. The committee advises the county on airport noise and possible mitigation measures. The airport recorded 7,474 takeoffs and landings in September, including 1,224 jet operations. Of those, 258 took place during the voluntary curfew, which runs from 11 p.m. The airport reported a 96.55% compliance rate. The county also sent 20 letters to aircraft operators about nighttime activity; the report does not specify how many flights, if any, were considered violations. Residents say private jet traffic can increase when flight restrictions are imposed in Palm Beach County during President Donald Trump’s visits to Mar-a-Lago, affecting their quality of life. The committee is also scheduled to receive an update on the Residential Sound Insulation Program, which aims to reduce aircraft noise inside eligible homes near the airport. The agenda does not list a proposal to change the voluntary curfew or a vote on airport rules. If you would like to review the agenda for the meeting, CLICK HERE. This is a developing story.

entry.title: High surf and red flag warnings put St. Lucie County beaches under high hazard advisory this week
entry.summary: A red flag warning was cautioning swimmers about dangerous surf at Fort Pierce Inlet State Park, where waves between four and six feet we're crashing along the shoreline Wednesday. Fort Pierce Inlet State Park was among several beaches in St. Lucie County under a red flag high hazard warning. The conditions are tied to a low pressure system off the eastern U.S. coast in the mid-Atlantic. 'The sea was angry today my friends,' Fort Pierce resident Lee Bertucelli said. St. Lucie County Ocean Rescue says conditions like these make it more important than ever to swim at a lifeguarded beach. There are two in St. Lucie County, at Pepper Park and Waveland Beach. Officials say both will likely be flying red or double red flags for the next few days. 'It was very windy and very choppy and it's really challenging because you have to negotiate all of the chop,' foil surfer Lisa Rose said. 'I went in, not with my surfboard, but like, to my waist and it's just, it's rough and it's just not super safe for like I'm sort of a beginner so not safe for me, but like, some of the other surfers have definitely been out,' surfer Jodi Riley said. 'I went in, you know, not too far. The waves were fun, but again not too far, didn't want to deal with rip tides or anything else,' Bertucelli said. The county says rip currents are possible in these conditions. If you find yourself stuck in one, Ocean Rescue says don't panic and swim parallel with the shoreline. WPTV received several emails from concerned residents that the plug may soon be pulled on this diving dynasty. We're learning the Board of Trustees at Indian River State College are looking to possibly eliminate the men's and women's swimming and diving teams. WATCH BELOW: IRSC swimmers react to possible elimination of program Swimmers rally to save IRSC swim and dive teams This past March, the men's swim and dive team captured its 52nd consecutive national championship title, and the women's team claimed its 48th crown. entry.title: St. Lucie County fire chief terminated after months of controversy - WPBF
entry.summary: St. Lucie County fire chief terminated after months of controversy    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District Board voted 4-3 to terminate fire Chief Jeff Lee without cause after months of controversy, hazing allegations, and a no-confidence vote. Interim Chief Paul Langel said, "I believe that the fire board moved forward and that was their job. Now my job is going to be to step in and start the healing process." The decision comes two months after five firefighters were displaced for allegedly turning a bug zapper into a makeshift taser and using it to shock coworkers. Videos appear to show the alleged hazing, and three firefighters ultimately lost their jobs. One of the terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson, said, "I think it was a step in the right direction. I don’t think today was about us by any means. I think it was the best thing for the entire department." The disciplined firefighters have called the termination retaliation for previous complaints they filed against district leadership. When asked about the possibility of the terminated firefighters regaining their jobs, Langel said, "I believe that there’s always scenarios that would unfold and happen. I’ve got to get in and get up to speed on all the specifics." The board voted to appoint Langel as interim chief. He is a familiar face in the district, with 30 years of experience. Because Lee was terminated without cause, he is entitled to compensation as his contract ends early. entry.title: Treasure Coast group marks 50 years of friendship, service to community
entry.summary: The Treasure Coast (FL) Chapter of The Links, Incorporated is celebrating 50 years of friendship and service in 2026, marking five decades of volunteerism, education, advocacy and philanthropy across the region. Chartered October 30, 1976, by 22 women, the chapter serves Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties. Its approved chapter background reports more than 125,000 volunteer service hours over its history. The chapter works with schools, health providers, civic organizations and nonprofits to address local needs. The chapter organizes its work through five national program facets: Services to Youth, The Arts, National Trends and Services, International Trends and Services, and Health and Human Services. A signature health initiative Launched in 2011, Linking Together Against Syndrome X addresses metabolic syndrome and risk factors associated with diabetes, heart disease and stroke. Activities have included free community health symposiums, Womens Red Dress heart-health education, screenings, nutrition and oral-health education, healthy-lifestyle coaching, and Walk for Healthy Living. The chapters approved background reports more than 1,450 people served through its health symposium over more than 13 years. Florida Community Health Centers, Inc. is a documented partner. According to the chapters 2023-2024 program report, it provided blood glucose and blood pressure screenings, waist-circumference assessments, and COVID-19 testing and education. Other community partners have contributed venues, clinicians, outreach and health education. The 2023-2024 report describes more than 3,000 people educated through the wider Syndrome X initiative over its history and reports broader educational outreach of more than 50,000 people, including public-health campaigns in collaboration with Florida Community Health Centers, Inc. In that report, 90% of surveyed respondents rated educational delivery excellent. Supporting youth and students The chapter supports student learning and career exploration through scientist-led STEAM education and interactive STEAM Day exhibits at the Indian River State College Planetarium. Its scholarship program supports graduating seniors in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties, considering academic achievement, financial need and leadership. entry.title: Trump’s trade fight with Canada hits home along Maine border
entry.summary: Along Maines northern border, ties between the United States and Canada have long extended beyond trade. Families live on both sides, and businesses depend on customers crossing the border. A golf course, the Aroostook Valley Country Club, even straddles the international boundary. But Northern Mainers say President Donald Trumps trade fight with Canada is straining those cross-border relationships and raising economic concerns in communities like Fort Fairfield, located about two miles from the international boundary. The economics certainly is a big deal for us, he said Wednesday. Most towns, he explained, in the U.S. have a 360-degree area that they can haul business from. entry.title: Semi-truck turns into path of SUV, killing Vero Beach driver, FHP says
entry.summary: A man was killed Thursday morning in a crash involving a semi-truck in unincorporated Indian River County, according to the Florida Highway Patrol (FHP). The crash happened around 6:45 a.m. at the intersection of 66th Avenue and 49th Street. According to FHP, a Freightliner semi-truck was attempting to make a left turn from a stop sign at westbound 49th Street onto 66th Avenue. At the same time, a Dodge Durango was traveling north in the inside lane of 66th Avenue, which had no traffic controls at the intersection. Troopers said the Freightliner entered the path of the SUV, causing the front of the Durango to collide with the left side of the semi-trailer. Both vehicles came to rest in the area of the collision. The driver of the SUV, a 60-year-old Vero Beach man, was taken to Health First's Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he was pronounced dead just after 8 a.m., according to FHP. The driver of the Freightliner, a 59-year-old Jacksonville man, was not injured. The crash remains under investigation.

entry.title: Martin County airport committee to review overnight flights and noise concerns - WPEC
entry.summary: Martin County airport committee to review overnight flights and noise concerns    WPEC
entry.article_text: Martin County’s Airport Noise Advisory Committee is scheduled to meet at 9 a.m. Thursday at Witham Field’s Airport Administration Building to review nighttime flight activity and noise concerns. The committee advises the county on airport noise and possible mitigation measures. The airport recorded 7,474 takeoffs and landings in September, including 1,224 jet operations. Of those, 258 took place during the voluntary curfew, which runs from 11 p.m. The airport reported a 96.55% compliance rate. The county also sent 20 letters to aircraft operators about nighttime activity; the report does not specify how many flights, if any, were considered violations. Residents say private jet traffic can increase when flight restrictions are imposed in Palm Beach County during President Donald Trump’s visits to Mar-a-Lago, affecting their quality of life. The committee is also scheduled to receive an update on the Residential Sound Insulation Program, which aims to reduce aircraft noise inside eligible homes near the airport. The agenda does not list a proposal to change the voluntary curfew or a vote on airport rules. If you would like to review the agenda for the meeting, CLICK HERE. This is a developing story.

entry.title: Vero Beach man, 60, dies in crash involving tractor-trailer in Indian River County - WPEC
entry.summary: Vero Beach man, 60, dies in crash involving tractor-trailer in Indian River County    WPEC
entry.article_text: A 60-year-old Vero Beach man died after the SUV he was driving collided with a semi-trailer at an intersection in Indian River County on Thursday. The crash happened as a 2026 Freightliner truck-tractor pulling a flatbed trailer attempted to turn left from a stop sign on westbound 49th Street, according to a crash report from the Florida Highway Patrol . The Freightliner entered the path of a northbound 2006 Dodge Durango traveling on 66th Avenue, and the front of the SUV struck the left side of the trailer. The Durango driver was taken to Health First’s Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he was pronounced dead at 8:02 a.m. His next of kin had not been notified, according to the report. See also: West Palm Beach man faces up to life after conviction in child sex trafficking case The 59-year-old Jacksonville man driving the Freightliner did not report any injuries. The traffic homicide investigation is ongoing.

entry.title: 2 men accused of posing as law enforcement, robberies in Palm Beach County, PBSO seeks more victims
entry.summary: PBSO says two men posed as law enforcement while targeting Hispanic victims in at least three robberies. Deputies are seeking more victims. Two men are under arrest after the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said they posed as law enforcement officers while targeting Hispanic people in at least three strong-arm robberies in Palm Beach County. Investigators said help from victims and witnesses, along with license plate reader cameras, led them to the suspects, and PBSO is now looking for potential additional victims. PBSO identified the men as Sean Armas and Billy Brewer. Investigators said the men used a black truck marked with the word 'STATE TRAPPER' and bearing Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission stickers during at least one of the encounters. First robbery reported near Cresthaven and Military Trail Investigators said the first robbery happened near Cresthaven Boulevard and Military Trail. According to PBSO, the victim was riding an e-bike when the suspects pulled alongside him in the black truck. Investigators said the men demanded a passport or other documents proving the victim was a U.S. citizen. The victim refused because he did not believe the men were legitimate law enforcement officers, according to PBSO. Investigators said the suspects then grabbed the victim's chain and drove away. Woman's necklace taken near Military Trail and Summit Boulevard Investigators said a second robbery happened near South Military Trail and Summit Boulevard. According to PBSO, one of the men got out of the truck, approached a woman and indicated he had a gun. Investigators said the suspect then grabbed the woman's gold necklace before leaving. Third victim was riding an electric scooter PBSO said a third robbery happened in the 400 block of Roberts Way. Investigators said a man was riding an electric scooter when the suspects cut him off with their truck and took his scooter. According to investigators, the suspects told a witness they were law enforcement officers. License plate readers help investigators find suspects PBSO told WPTV that information provided by the victims and witnesses helped investigators use license plate reader cameras to track down the truck. entry.title: Two Palm Beach County nonprofits are expanding youth softball with affordable, accessible programs
entry.summary: On any given Tuesday or Thursday night in the fall, you can expect to see nearly 300 young athletes playing softball at Lake Charleston Park in western Palm Beach County. Two local nonprofits are giving more young athletes the chance to play the sport, with a goal of expanding softball in a way that is affordable and accessible to all. One of those programs is the VSA Lady Lions , a travel softball program whose under-14s team runs a practice packed full of every element softball has to offer from the tee to home plate. 'Our normal practice starts with stretching, throwing,' Coach Ed Kunzweiler said. 'They do a lot of defensive drills. They run a lot of plays. Then we usually do some hitting off coaches, and then we usually try to finish with some live hitting,' Kunzweiler said. Coach Kunzweiler said when he started at the club, they had just two travel teams. 'Now we're at 8 or 9. So it's grown pretty substantially,' Kunzweiler said. He said the VSA Lady Lions are the largest women's travel softball program in South Florida and interest is still growing. 'I'm really proud about what we built here. It's something that has grown every season,' Kunzweiler said. One of the program's star players is Ari Merklein, who plays shortstop, third base and some outfield. She admits her favorite spot on the field is shortstop. 'I got involved in softball because I just didn't know what sport to pick when I was little and I just couldn't get used to 1 sport. But then I joined softball and I made a lot of friends and I got really good at it and just continued doing it,' Merklein said. She never looked back. Merklein said that whether it's at practice or traveling to tournaments on the weekend, her team is having fun. 'It's really fun. We're all like good friends with each other, so we all hang out outside of softball and inside of softball, and we're good at communicating with each other. entry.article_text: Lucie police are asking for the public’s help identifying two vehicles that may have been involved in a hit-and-run crash that left a 63-year-old man with severe injuries. Detectives now believe the man may have been struck by two separate vehicles, one traveling northbound and the other southbound, near Northwest University Boulevard and Northwest California Boulevard, police said. The crash happened at about 12:56 a.m. The man was found unconscious in the roadway with severe head injuries and was later identified as a Port St. Police previously said the man was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in critical condition. See also: More than 4.3 million toothpaste tubes recalled, including children's brands Investigators are working to identify both vehicles and their drivers. Police shared images of the vehicles and asked anyone who recognizes them, witnessed the crash or has dashcam or other video from the area to call the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000.

entry.title: Charges dropped against Indian River County school bus driver accused of child abuse - WPEC
entry.summary: Charges dropped against Indian River County school bus driver accused of child abuse    WPEC
entry.article_text: The child abuse case against an Indian River County school bus driver has ended after prosecutors declined to file formal charges. The State Attorney’s Office filed a no information in the case against Tracy Marie Alpy on Oct. 5, according to a court document. The filing listed the charge as child abuse intentional act, but did not explain why prosecutors decided not to proceed. Alpy, 65, of Sebastian, was arrested Sept. 10 after investigators reviewed surveillance video from a school bus. The allegations were described in an arrest affidavit. The alleged incident happened Aug. 24 as the bus was transporting students to after-school care. The video, recorded from 3:44 to 4:31 p.m., showed the bus waiting at Liberty Magnet School for another bus to exchange children headed to the Gifford Youth Aquatic Center and the Boys & Girls Club, according to the affidavit. Investigators said a student seated near the front of the bus repeatedly got out of the seat. Alpy was seen walking through the aisle and directing the student to sit down. The student also appeared to repeatedly raise a middle finger toward Alpy when her back was turned, the affidavit said. About 15 minutes into the video, Alpy sat on the edge of the student’s seat to keep the child from getting up, investigators said. After more children boarded and the bus began moving, the student again stood up and turned around to interact with other children. The affidavit said Alpy repeatedly told the student to sit down. When the child did not, she pulled the bus over, left the driver’s seat and approached the student. Investigators alleged she grabbed the child, forced the child back into the seat and fastened the seat belt. See also: More than 4.3 million toothpaste tubes recalled, including children's brands The child’s middle finger was extended toward Alpy, according to the affidavit. Investigators said Alpy then grabbed the student’s hand, forced it into the child’s lap and asked, Do you want me to break this finger? The student later told investigators that Alpy grabbed and bent back the child’s middle finger and said she was going to break it off. The child said they were afraid during the encounter, according to the affidavit.

entry.article_text: A 60-year-old Vero Beach man died after the SUV he was driving collided with a semi-trailer at an intersection in Indian River County on Thursday. The crash happened as a 2026 Freightliner truck-tractor pulling a flatbed trailer attempted to turn left from a stop sign on westbound 49th Street, according to a crash report from the Florida Highway Patrol . The Freightliner entered the path of a northbound 2006 Dodge Durango traveling on 66th Avenue, and the front of the SUV struck the left side of the trailer. The Durango driver was taken to Health First’s Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he was pronounced dead at 8:02 a.m. His next of kin had not been notified, according to the report. See also: West Palm Beach man faces up to life after conviction in child sex trafficking case The 59-year-old Jacksonville man driving the Freightliner did not report any injuries. The traffic homicide investigation is ongoing.

entry.summary: Semi-truck turns into path of SUV, killing Vero Beach driver, FHP says    WFLX
entry.article_text: A man was killed Thursday morning in a crash involving a semi-truck in unincorporated Indian River County, according to the Florida Highway Patrol (FHP). The crash happened around 6:45 a.m. at the intersection of 66th Avenue and 49th Street. According to FHP, a Freightliner semi-truck was attempting to make a left turn from a stop sign at westbound 49th Street onto 66th Avenue. At the same time, a Dodge Durango was traveling north in the inside lane of 66th Avenue, which had no traffic controls at the intersection. Troopers said the Freightliner entered the path of the SUV, causing the front of the Durango to collide with the left side of the semi-trailer. Both vehicles came to rest in the area of the collision. The driver of the SUV, a 60-year-old Vero Beach man, was taken to Health First's Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he was pronounced dead just after 8 a.m., according to FHP. The driver of the Freightliner, a 59-year-old Jacksonville man, was not injured. The crash remains under investigation. entry.title: William Reaves: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy in 1986 scheduled to be executed Tuesday - WFLX
entry.summary: William Reaves: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy in 1986 scheduled to be executed Tuesday    WFLX
entry.article_text: Florida is set Tuesday to carry out its 18th execution of the year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis’ aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term. William Reaves , 77, was sentenced to death after being convicted of first-degree murder for the 1986 shooting of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski. He would become Florida’s eighth prisoner over the age of 70 to be executed this year, which has highlighted the nation’s aging death-row population and underscored how Florida has outpaced the rest of the country in executions. Reaves was set to receive a three-drug injection starting at 6 p.m. at Florida State Prison near Starke. Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year. Another execution is scheduled for November, which would tie that mark if both are carried out as planned. DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said previously that his goal is to bring justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out. According to court records, Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986. Reaves acknowledged that he had placed the call at a payphone outside the store. While Raczkowski and Reaves spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves’ shorts, officials said. The men struggled over the firearm, and Reaves eventually regained control over it. Investigators said the deputy attempted to run away before Reaves shot him four times. The deputy later died from his wounds. Reaves was initially convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. The Florida Supreme Court reversed the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death a second time in 1992, and subsequent appeals have been unsuccessful. The Florida Supreme Court rejected Reaves’ final appeals last week. One issue raised by his attorneys was Florida’s method of execution. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections. The court has previously upheld this lethal injection protocol against similar challenges. It differs from the single-drug injection used by states like Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike was rushed to the hospital last month after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital. Defense attorneys also argued that the jurors who recommended the death penalty for Reaves were never told that the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs rated Reaves, an Army veteran, as 100% disabled by post-traumatic stress disorder, which was caused by his service in the Vietnam War. More than 100 veterans sent DeSantis a letter on Monday asking him to stop the execution. Final appeals for Reaves were still pending before the U.S. A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half of the 31 total executions in the U.S. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so. Jesse Guardado, 64, is next scheduled to die by injection in Florida on Nov. He was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.

entry.title: Judge reins in armed ICE agents investigating voter fraud
entry.summary: A federal judge issued a ruling late Wednesday setting limits for ICE agents visiting homes of immigrants to investigate claims of voter fraud and make arrests. With early voting already underway, ICE has taken the unprecedented step of deploying agents into communities to knock on doors and follow up on data the agency has collected that suggests people at those addresses either voted or registered to vote even though they were ineligible to do so as non-U.S. citizens. ICE INC | Major ICE contractors shower Republican candidates with campaign cash The Trump administration continues to share pictures and videos online of ICE armed agents in the field arresting noncitizens as part of its unlawful voting initiative. But U.S. District Judge Araceli Martnez-Olgun said ICE is relying on data that is unreliable, some of it coming from unknown artificial intelligence tools. She pointed to the U.S. governments acknowledgement that the target list could be tainted by similar names, incomplete records or clerical errors. The ruling says ICE cannot target immigrants using a batch of data likely to have errors or question people when there is a reasonable chance they might be eligible to vote. entry.title: St. Lucie County Nuclear Power Plant turns 50
entry.summary: WPTV had the rare opportunity to go inside the St. Lucie County Nuclear Power Plant on Thursday. This year, the facility is celebrating 50 years of operation and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission just granted licenses for 20 more.   On Thursday, WPTV learned about operations inside the plant and spoke with people who keep the power on. Watch report from Tyler Hatfield: WPTV gets an inside look at the St Lucie County Nuclear Power Plant Our Tyler Hatfield listened to Alfred Phillips, a digital INC specialist. 'My job is to calibrate and make sure all the equipment used to work on the equipment that controls the reactor itself meets all the government standards and accuracies.' Phillips said hes been working at the plant for nearly 20 years. 'You have million-dollar homes right down the street. We're here, but yet we're still invisible because what we do, we do it well, .Phillips said.   Alfreds son, Alfred Sinclair Phillips, followed his father's footsteps and works in the operations department. 'There's a pressure with it, but there's also a sense of pride, Phillips said. Knowing that my dad has worked his butt off and he's left an impact with the people here on his work to make this place better. WPTV learned from Carlos Santos, site vice president, how the plant generates power. 'The simplest way to put it is the reactor creates the heat,' Santos said. Santos said that heat comes from nuclear fission from uranium pellets stacked into rods inside the two units on site. The heat from the rods builds up and produces steam, which travels into a secondary closed system into a turbine, which then generates power and produces electricity for the grid. Back in August, the plant had to be manually shut down when three control rods dropped in the reactors core. entry.article_text: Golfers at a Veterans Day fundraiser in Hobe Sound will share the course with local veterans, as Tee It Up for the Troops brings its tournament to The Club at Lost Lake for the first time. The event is scheduled for Wednesday, Nov. The field is capped at 106 golfers, with registration listed at $750 per player. Veterans paired with foursomes will play for free, according to Chris LaRocque, the nonprofit’s president and executive director. It’s very close to my heart, LaRocque said in an ARC Florida interview. I’m an Army Reserve major myself. He said Tee It Up for the Troops has deployed more than $20 million and supported more than 400,000 veterans through programs that include help with the transition to civilian jobs and support for post-traumatic stress disorder and traumatic brain injuries. The tournament will also support local veterans programs, including PGA HOPE in South Florida, LaRocque said. PGA HOPE introduces veterans and active-duty service members to golf to support their physical, mental, social and emotional well-being. The tournament will be held at The Club at Lost Lake, 8300 SE Fazio Drive in Hobe Sound. Registration and event information are available through Tee It Up for the Troops.

entry.title: Homeowner gets better news on insurance after contacting WPTV
entry.summary: A Delray Beach homeowner who got a new roof this year now is finding out her insurance will not go up. Betty Haygood contacted WPTV after finding out her insurance renewal was going up $300 even though she had a new roof installed in August. Her insurer, Universal, based in South Florida, told us they were looking over Haygood's policy and gave her a new quote of $3,087, which is $90 less than what she is paying now. 'Im OK with that,' the 76-year-old home healthcare worker told WPTV. 'You have helped by bringing it to attention because so many people and neighbors and people I didnt know reached out to me about that, because Im not the only one going through something like this,' Haygood said. Haygood says she does plan to shop around some other insurance companies, something insurance experts now recommend. Litigation reforms in Florida have led to more insurers, more competition and lower rates. But lower rates don't always mean lower premiums as inflation has made it more expensive to build and repair homes. Many insurers also focus on the age of a roof in assessing risk, and experts also advise checking with an agent first. Lee Wiglesworth of Wiglesworth-Rindom Insurance Agency in Stuart says one step can solve issues down the road. 'Call an agent who can shop multiple carriers and say what would it save me if I got a new roof,' Wiglesworth says.

entry.title: Supreme Court says New Hampshire can limit use of student IDs for voting
entry.summary: The Supreme Court on Thursday allowed New Hampshire officials to limit when voters may use a student ID to receive a ballot, agreeing that a lower court ruling that blocked enforcement of the policy was too close to Election Day. The unsigned order was a win for New Hampshire Secretary of State David Scanlan, a Republican, and the Republican National Committee, which had supported Scanlan in the fight. The court did not provide a vote count, though it did provide a brief explanation, invoking the Purcell principle that warns against last-minute decisions from courts that change election rules. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, a liberal, wrote a brief dissent questioning the application of the Purcell doctrine. New Hampshire voters will fill an open Senate seat in November to replace the retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. A recent CNN poll found that Democrats enjoy a 31 percentage point advantage over Republicans among younger adults. Lower federal courts allowed the state to enforce the central prohibition of a law enacted by the state legislature this spring. Under that law, student IDs on their own may no longer be used to verify a voters identity. But state law also includes a safety valve that allows voters to attempt to prove their identity through other means and the fight at the Supreme Court was about whether, in those circumstances, student IDs could be used as one factor, along with other evidence, to help officials identify people requesting a ballot. When New Hampshire officials interpreted the new state law as shutting off the ability to use student IDs even in those circumstances, a voting rights group called Coalition for Open Democracy sued. A federal district court blocked enforcement of that interpretation on October 2. New Hampshire filed an emergency appeal at the Supreme Court arguing that the Purcell opinion meant should decide the case in its favor. The RNC had warned that the lower courts order threatens to disrupt identity verification in New Hampshires looming elections. The Supreme Court has been called on to address several high-profile election disputes heading into next months midterms, most notably a decision in mid-September rejecting President Donald Trumps proposal to change how mail ballots are sent to voters across the country. "The District also expanded employee benefits, increased retirement-health contributions, and invested in additional training opportunities, equipment, and facilities to better support personnel in carrying out their responsibilities." “That’s really all I have to say,” Lee told Hussey Thursday. Lee’s termination marks the latest fallout from a controversy that began after videos surfaced showing probationary firefighters being shocked with a modified bug zapper. A third-party investigator concluded the conduct amounted to hazing.Three veteran firefighters were fired following the investigation, prompting significant public backlash from firefighters, their families and community members who argued the punishment went too far.“Not only have they lost their jobs, but they lost their reputation,” one speaker told the board Wednesday.Others said the controversy had damaged confidence in the district.“We need to restore faith in this fire district,” another speaker said.Lee’s departure also follows an overwhelming union vote of no confidence in district leadership.St Lucie County Commissioner and Fire Board Member, Jamie Fowler, said the decision to remove Lee was not based solely on the vote of no confidence. “At the end of the day, it’s gotten very messy,” Fowler said. “It’s not about one single decision that he’s made. It’s about bringing peace and calm and respect.”Lee had already signaled that his time as chief could be nearing an end. 15 letter to the board, Lee wrote that “the position of fire chief requires confidence” and raised the possibility of a mutually agreeable retirement and leadership transition.Deputy Chief Paul Langel has now been appointed interim fire chief as the district searches for Lee’s permanent replacement.Langel inherits a department facing questions about morale, trust and what some speakers Wednesday described as a broader “culture problem.”“Personally, I don’t think there is a culture problem,” Langel said. “But I’m going to do the due diligence and I’m going to evaluate whether that’s visiting fire stations, one-on-one conversations with employees, group settings to get the vibe, what's going on out there, where are we at as an organization, and then once I receive all that, process it, I'll correct the course and move this district forward." The board is now confronting several major issues left unresolved by Lee’s departure.Commissioners plan to hire a headhunter to conduct a search for a permanent chief inside and outside the district. "I'm sure we have a very talented pool right here, but we'll see how it plays out," said Fowler. The district and firefighters union are also expected to continue discussions over the possible reinstatement of the three firefighters fired following the hazing investigation.“I’m excited to see if we can just come back together and collectively work together,” union representative Ryan Sapp said.At the same time, the board is moving forward with an outside law firm to overhaul the district's complaint policies after a heated Sept. 30 meeting identified what board members called "a significant gap" in existing policy. Commissioner James Clasby has also called for reconsidering the terms offered in the next fire chief’s contract, as Lee’s existing contract could leave taxpayers responsible for more than $350,000 in severance following his termination.“That’s the consequences of firing somebody with those terms,” Clasby said. "The next chief — I'm going to be fighting very hard does not get those terms, and I think that could lead to more accountability." For the four board members who supported Lee’s removal, Wednesday’s vote represented an attempt to turn the page after months of controversy.“There was a large desire to have a change in leadership,” Clasby said, “and we delivered that today.”But Lee’s departure does not end the larger fight over the district’s future. Commissioners must now determine who will permanently lead the agency, whether the terminated firefighters will return and whether new leadership can rebuild trust among firefighters and the community.

entry.title: Florida Senate president opposes Amendment 3 months after lawmakers put it on ballot
entry.summary: The president of the Florida State Senate says he is voting 'No' on Amendment 3, just months after the State Senate approved putting the referendum on the November ballot. 'As a native of Florida's Heartland, our rural communities are near and dear to my heart,' Albritton said in a post on the Florida Sheriffs Association's Instagram page. 'Amendment 3 would eliminate up to 30% of resources for Florida's rural counties, gutting essential support for law enforcement, emergency response services and critical infrastructure.' WATCH BELOW: Florida Senate president opposes Amendment 3 Florida Senate president opposes Amendment 3 Albritton also stated the Florida Taxation and Budget Reform Commission presents: 'An ideal opportunity to design property tax reform and create a solution that is meaningful, reasonable and balanced.' Amendment 3 would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. It would also cut property taxes for homesteaded homeowners, excluding school taxes. Cities and counties stand to lose significant revenue and many local leaders say it will lead to budget cuts, reduced services and possibly creating other revenue streams. The referendum needs 60% approval on Election Day to become law in Florida.

entry.title: St. Lucie County fire chief terminated after months of controversy - WPBF
entry.summary: St. Lucie County fire chief terminated after months of controversy    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District Board voted 4-3 to terminate fire Chief Jeff Lee without cause after months of controversy, hazing allegations, and a no-confidence vote. Interim Chief Paul Langel said, "I believe that the fire board moved forward and that was their job. Now my job is going to be to step in and start the healing process." The decision comes two months after five firefighters were displaced for allegedly turning a bug zapper into a makeshift taser and using it to shock coworkers. Videos appear to show the alleged hazing, and three firefighters ultimately lost their jobs. One of the terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson, said, "I think it was a step in the right direction. I don’t think today was about us by any means. I think it was the best thing for the entire department." The disciplined firefighters have called the termination retaliation for previous complaints they filed against district leadership. When asked about the possibility of the terminated firefighters regaining their jobs, Langel said, "I believe that there’s always scenarios that would unfold and happen. I’ve got to get in and get up to speed on all the specifics." The board voted to appoint Langel as interim chief. He is a familiar face in the district, with 30 years of experience. Because Lee was terminated without cause, he is entitled to compensation as his contract ends early. entry.article_text: More than 100 cats were found in unsanitary conditions inside a Port St. Lucie home, including deceased kittens, prompting a criminal investigation. Officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department say 124 cats, both living and deceased, were recovered from a residence in the 2500 block of SW Warwick Street. Animal Control personnel responded to concerns about the number of cats and their living conditions on October 13. They documented accumulated feces and deceased kittens inside the home. See also: Wellington speed camera ticket tossed over missing state approval Two of the three residents have been issued citations for hoarding and failing to provide medical attention to animals, police said. The investigation remains active, and police have not provided details about potential future arrests. All 124 cats have been surrendered and are receiving care through Port St. Lucie Animal Control and the Humane Society of St. Several cats are being treated for ear mites and fleas. Others have needed surgery or additional veterinary care, with some transported to Veterinary Medical Center for treatment. Many of the surviving cats are friendly and could become available for adoption once their medical needs are addressed, police said. The case required a coordinated response involving animal control personnel, police officers, veterinarians and animal welfare organizations. Police said additional information will be released as the investigation continues.
