entry.title: From the fairway to housing: Golf event supports a new shelter model
entry.summary: WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. A celebrity golf tournament in Palm Beach County brought athletes, community leaders, and supporters together for a day on the course, but the larger goal stretched far beyond golf. Par for the Culture, presented by the Higher Learning Foundation, raised support for The Lords Place and its efforts to expand housing and early-intervention services for people experiencing homelessness in Palm Beach County. The need is significant. The Lords Place says the county has more than 500 shelter beds dedicated to people experiencing homelessness, while roughly 1,500 people currently need housing. Those existing beds are generally prioritized for people with the greatest needs, including those who have experienced homelessness for longer periods of time or face significant health and safety concerns. That can leave people who are newly unhoused waiting for help -a gap The Lords Place hopes to address with a new shelter model focused on early intervention. The goal is to provide intensive, short-term support before a temporary housing crisis becomes long-term homelessness. We would really love to shorten their experience in homelessness and get them bridged back and transitioned back into the community as quickly as possible, said Christine Frederick, CEO of The Lords Place. Outreach workers say intervening early can help people maintain jobs, stay in school, address health needs and preserve the support systems that can help them regain stability. Cristina Lucier with The Lords Place said the longer someone remains on the streets, the greater the risk of losing those connections. The longer people spend on the streets, they may lose some of those critical social connections that will help them get back on their feet and retain stability long term, Lucier said. For Devin Perry, that instability was once part of everyday life. The hardest part is knowing where youre gonna sleep at, where youre gonna wake up at, if your stuff is gonna be there when you come back, Perry said. Perry later entered The Lords Place culinary training program, secured housing and began moving toward employment. Having a place of his own has changed what he is able to think about each day. entry.title: Martin County parents win push for school zone outside Citrus Grove Elementary
entry.summary: Martin County parents are celebrating a victory in a long battle to improve safety around their children's school. Citrus Grove Elementary School parents say the 45 mph speed limit outside the school puts their children's safety in jeopardy. They say a recently approved school zone is the first step to making Newfield Parkway a safer place for children who walk to school. On Southwest Newfield Parkway, morning and afternoon traffic is an obstacle for young students. 'It scares me,' parent Kendall George said. 'These cars are driving 45 miles an hour plus.' Kendall is among the many families who live in the Canopy Creek community across the street from Citrus Grove Elementary, so their children walk to school. Kelly Ribaudo, the PTA president and Martin County PTA Advocacy Chair, told WPTV she's spent the last five years asking the county to put in a school zone. 'We've had so many near misses with the kids just from people not paying attention,' Ribaudo said. 'Everyone has a right to a free and public education and they should be safe getting there. Our main priority should be the kids not the traffic.' At the previous Martin County Commission meeting, commissioners unanimously answered their call. entry.title: Conflict of interest? Palm Beach County reconsiders data center consultant
entry.summary: WPTV is staying on top of the future of data centers in Palm Beach County as commissioners rethink who should help develop new regulations for an industry that has already generated significant concern among residents. County commissioners on Wednesday backed away from immediately moving forward with one consultant selected by staff, instead deciding they want to consider other options before making a final selection. At the same time, commissioners agreed to bring back plans for a formal community task force, giving the public a greater role as the county considers what its future data center regulations should look like. The discussion comes less than a month after commissioners approved a one-year moratorium on large-scale data centers on Sept. 24. County staff told commissioners the clock is now running to establish regulations before that moratorium expires. The county staff had proposed hiring VHB (Vanasse Hangen Brustlin, Inc.), an engineering and planning firm, to work alongside staff on a framework designed to protect communities, establish clearer expectations and create standards the county could administer and enforce. It would cost $224,900 for VHB's services. But the proposal quickly drew questions from residents. I have concerns today about the consultant who was chosen, said Rachel Smith, an Acreage resident. Resident Ben Brown questioned how the firm had been selected and whether enough alternatives were considered. I have many questions. When did you reach out to this consultant? Are you interviewing other ones? Brown said. They obviously work with data centers. You are putting the fox in the henhouse. County staff said they issued a request for information and received six proposals that were incomplete. Staff initially told commissioners the proposals ranged from $200,000 for a portion of the needed support to $2 million. Later in the discussion, staff described the range as about $125,000 for an architect who would only be part of the process, requiring additional experts, to about $2.1 million. Those concerns put particular scrutiny on VHB and its existing work involving data centers. Do you have clients that are a part of data centers? Mayor Sara Baxter asked the consultant representative directly. We work for clients that have data centers in Massachusetts and Virginia, answered Curt Ostrodka a VHB representative responded. Staff initially told commissioners the proposals ranged from $200,000 for a portion of the needed support to $2 million.Later in the discussion, staff described the range as about $125,000 for an architect who would only be part of the process, requiring additional experts, to about $2.1 million.Those concerns put particular scrutiny on VHB and its existing work involving data centers.“Do you have clients that are a part of data centers?” Mayor Sara Baxter asked the consultant representative directly.“We work for clients that have data centers in Massachusetts and Virginia,” answered Curt Ostrodka a VHB representative responded. “We don't have any clients in Florida building data centers.”The firm's representative also told commissioners VHB had worked as a consultant for private clients providing civil engineering, utility studies and other technical services supporting data centers.When Commissioner Gregg Weiss asked whether the company had ever developed regulations specifically for data centers, the answer was direct.“Not for data centers," said Ostrodka.VHB maintained it could serve as an objective third party while researching how other communities are handling data centers and studying potential impacts including noise, energy and water.“We don't know the answers right now,” Ostrodka said. “We would do that collaboratively with staff, members of the public.”The company outlined a nine-month process that would also examine applicable state and federal laws and determine thresholds and regulatory mechanisms for potential impacts.Commissioner Maria Sachs was among those who wanted more information before committing to the firm.“This is one company standing here I know nothing about,” Sachs said.But county staff stressed that the push to hire a consultant isn't simply about getting another opinion. Staff told commissioners they need additional capacity and technical expertise to develop the rules.“We are asking for this assistance because we are limited in our capacity to do the work,” staff told commissioners. “We need the technical expertise to help support the staff get this done.”Commissioner Joel Flores asked what it might cost for the county to instead bring in its own people to handle the workload.Staff estimated a dedicated team could require two employees, with an average annual salary of about $125,000 each, or roughly $250,000.Flores said the need for specialized knowledge was part of the reason he supported hiring outside help.“I'm not an expert on data centers and this technology is evolving so quick,” Flores said.Flores said commissioners will ultimately decide what the county's rules look like, but expert information could help them determine what safeguards are necessary.“Having someone on our side who is going to say these are the things you want to watch out for, these are the guardrails you want to put in place, I would feel more comfortable,” Flores said.For some residents, the concern was less about whether the county hires a consultant and more about making sure it hires the right one.“For me, at least, it’s less of a money issue and more of, I want quality information, not just necessarily what people want to hear,” Wellington resident Elizabeth Pandich said. “I want to make sure we pick a consultant that is maybe in an environmental and scientific aspect of it, not someone that’s just good at moving data around.”The timeline also weighed heavily on the discussion.Staff told commissioners the moratorium lasts a year. If it expires before the county has new regulations in place, data center applications would be handled under the regulations in place at that time. County attorneys said extending the moratorium could be possible under certain circumstances, but any extension would be limited.Weiss put the urgency bluntly.“Time is of the essence. The clock is ticking,” Weiss said.What initially appeared to be a decision to move forward with VHB changed dramatically near the end of the discussion.Commissioners first voted to proceed with the consultant, with Baxter and Sachs opposed. But moments later, Commissioner Bobby Powell moved to reconsider the decision.Powell said he wanted commissioners to have choices before committing to a single company.“My motion is not to consider two consultants,” Powell said. “It would be for us to have an option to not only consider this consultant but more options. One consultant, maybe there is another person or another consultant company.”The motion to reconsider passed 3-2.Commissioners then voted 4-1 to give the county the opportunity to look at other available consultants rather than immediately settling on VHB.That doesn't necessarily mean VHB is out of consideration.“I'm sure this gentleman may win out in the end,” Sachs said. “But then at least we would know. Let's find out.”While commissioners debated which experts should advise them, there was considerably more agreement about giving residents a direct role in the process.Several speakers called for commissioners to revive the idea of a community task force, arguing that the two public outreach meetings outlined by staff would not provide enough community involvement.Baxter supported establishing a formal task force and suggested that because the regulations would apply countywide, each commissioner could appoint someone to represent their district.“This new ordinance, it would be countywide,” Commissioner Marci Woodward said earlier in the discussion. “This isn't about a specific parcel.”Baxter said the task force proposal could come back before commissioners at their Nov. 18 meeting.Smith welcomed the idea of combining expert input with residents who could be affected by whatever rules the county ultimately adopts.“I do appreciate that they are looking at expert opinions, although I do think that we have enough experts in this area who are actually affected that could be very beneficial,” Smith said.Pandich said she and others who became involved after Project Tango have already formed the National Data Impact Coalition and hope to participate.“I’m excited about the task force. A couple of friends of mine, after Project Tango, started a national data impact coalition, and we are doing that basically internally. So we are going to put our name in the hat and hopefully get a seat at the table,” Pandich said.For Smith, commissioners' decision to take another look at the consultant while moving toward giving residents a more formal role represented progress.“Yeah, I’d say it’s a victory for the residents,” Smith said. “Thank you to Sachs and Baxter for doing what they did, and Powell, who came in last minute and saved the day.”WPTV reached out to VHB to address concerns raised during the meeting about potential conflicts of interest but has not received a response.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire Chief Jeff Lee is speaking out after the fire board terminated his contract Wednesday, ending his tenure after months of turmoil surrounding a hazing investigation and growing criticism of district leadership.Lee did not attend Wednesday’s heated fire board meeting, where commissioners voted to terminate him without cause.In a statement to WPTV Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey following the vote, Lee pointed to his previous comments highlighting increases in staffing, pay and benefits he fought for during his time leading the district."During the 2023–2026 period, these efforts included approximately 19% average pay-plan growth, an increase of approximately 100 uniformed personnel, and improved minimum engine staffing from two to three firefighters," the Fire District wrote in a statement October 9. "The District also expanded employee benefits, increased retirement-health contributions, and invested in additional training opportunities, equipment, and facilities to better support personnel in carrying out their responsibilities." “That’s really all I have to say,” Lee told Hussey Thursday. Lee’s termination marks the latest fallout from a controversy that began after videos surfaced showing probationary firefighters being shocked with a modified bug zapper. A third-party investigator concluded the conduct amounted to hazing.Three veteran firefighters were fired following the investigation, prompting significant public backlash from firefighters, their families and community members who argued the punishment went too far.“Not only have they lost their jobs, but they lost their reputation,” one speaker told the board Wednesday.Others said the controversy had damaged confidence in the district.“We need to restore faith in this fire district,” another speaker said.Lee’s departure also follows an overwhelming union vote of no confidence in district leadership.St Lucie County Commissioner and Fire Board Member, Jamie Fowler, said the decision to remove Lee was not based solely on the vote of no confidence. “At the end of the day, it’s gotten very messy,” Fowler said. “It’s not about one single decision that he’s made. It’s about bringing peace and calm and respect.”Lee had already signaled that his time as chief could be nearing an end. 15 letter to the board, Lee wrote that “the position of fire chief requires confidence” and raised the possibility of a mutually agreeable retirement and leadership transition.Deputy Chief Paul Langel has now been appointed interim fire chief as the district searches for Lee’s permanent replacement.Langel inherits a department facing questions about morale, trust and what some speakers Wednesday described as a broader “culture problem.”“Personally, I don’t think there is a culture problem,” Langel said. “But I’m going to do the due diligence and I’m going to evaluate whether that’s visiting fire stations, one-on-one conversations with employees, group settings to get the vibe, what's going on out there, where are we at as an organization, and then once I receive all that, process it, I'll correct the course and move this district forward." The board is now confronting several major issues left unresolved by Lee’s departure.Commissioners plan to hire a headhunter to conduct a search for a permanent chief inside and outside the district. "I'm sure we have a very talented pool right here, but we'll see how it plays out," said Fowler. The district and firefighters union are also expected to continue discussions over the possible reinstatement of the three firefighters fired following the hazing investigation.“I’m excited to see if we can just come back together and collectively work together,” union representative Ryan Sapp said.At the same time, the board is moving forward with an outside law firm to overhaul the district's complaint policies after a heated Sept. 30 meeting identified what board members called "a significant gap" in existing policy. Commissioner James Clasby has also called for reconsidering the terms offered in the next fire chief’s contract, as Lee’s existing contract could leave taxpayers responsible for more than $350,000 in severance following his termination.“That’s the consequences of firing somebody with those terms,” Clasby said. "The next chief — I'm going to be fighting very hard does not get those terms, and I think that could lead to more accountability." For the four board members who supported Lee’s removal, Wednesday’s vote represented an attempt to turn the page after months of controversy.“There was a large desire to have a change in leadership,” Clasby said, “and we delivered that today.”But Lee’s departure does not end the larger fight over the district’s future. Commissioners must now determine who will permanently lead the agency, whether the terminated firefighters will return and whether new leadership can rebuild trust among firefighters and the community.

entry.title: WHERE'S WALTER? Having a day of discovery at the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast
entry.summary: This week, I visited a place where learning and fun go hand in hand: the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast. From the moment I walked in, I could tell this wasn't your typical museum. Instead of looking at exhibits from behind a rope or glass case, kids are encouraged to jump in, get involved and learn by doing. As I explored the museum, I discovered exhibits designed to teach important life skills in creative and engaging ways. From learning about money and budgeting to exploring different careers and practicing job skills, every corner of the museum offered a new opportunity to learn something useful. WATCH: WHERE'S WALTER? Discovering the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast One of my favorite stops, of course, involved the weather. As a meteorologist, I was excited to check out the museum's WPTV weather simulator and hurricane simulator. It was fascinating to see how children can experience weather concepts in a hands-on environment and gain a better understanding of the science behind storms and hurricanes. What impressed me most was how interactive everything was. Kids aren't just reading signs or watching demonstrations. They're solving problems, making decisions, using their imaginations and building confidence along the way. The museum creates an environment where learning feels more like an adventure than a lesson. Whether they're exploring future careers, practicing financial skills or learning about science and weather, children are gaining valuable experiences that can help them throughout their lives. My visit was a great reminder that some of the best learning happens when you're having fun. By rolling up their sleeves, asking questions and trying new things, kids can discover skills and interests they never knew they had. If you're looking for a family-friendly destination on the Treasure Coast that combines education, creativity and fun, the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast is definitely worth a visit. That's where I was!

entry.article_text: Golfers at a Veterans Day fundraiser in Hobe Sound will share the course with local veterans, as Tee It Up for the Troops brings its tournament to The Club at Lost Lake for the first time. The event is scheduled for Wednesday, Nov. The field is capped at 106 golfers, with registration listed at $750 per player. Veterans paired with foursomes will play for free, according to Chris LaRocque, the nonprofit’s president and executive director. It’s very close to my heart, LaRocque said in an ARC Florida interview. I’m an Army Reserve major myself. He said Tee It Up for the Troops has deployed more than $20 million and supported more than 400,000 veterans through programs that include help with the transition to civilian jobs and support for post-traumatic stress disorder and traumatic brain injuries. The tournament will also support local veterans programs, including PGA HOPE in South Florida, LaRocque said. PGA HOPE introduces veterans and active-duty service members to golf to support their physical, mental, social and emotional well-being. The tournament will be held at The Club at Lost Lake, 8300 SE Fazio Drive in Hobe Sound. Registration and event information are available through Tee It Up for the Troops.

entry.title: Riviera Beach leaders question city manager absence after crash
entry.summary: Questions about who is leading Riviera Beach and the future of City Manager William E. Wilkins took center stage during a contentious city council discussion Wednesday, as some elected leaders said they were unaware of the extent of his absence following an August car crash. Wilkins has been working remotely since the crash, according to city officials. While assistant city manager staff have handled many day-to-day operations inside city hall, some council members said they only recently learned key details about Wilkins' condition and work arrangements. The debate comes as Riviera Beach continues to navigate leadership challenges following the April 2026 firing of former City Manager Jonathan Evans, with residents and officials alike calling for stability at City Hall. WATCH: Riviera Beach leaders seek answers on city manager's future, status Riviera Beach leaders seek answers on city manager's future, status Council members question communication and leadership During Wednesday's meeting at Marina Village, some council members expressed frustration over what they described as a lack of communication regarding Wilkins' status. Councilwoman Shirley D. Lanier said she had not spoken with Wilkins since August and was unaware he had been injured in a crash. 'I didn't know he was in a car wreck. I didn't know he was on TV and I haven't heard from him since then,' Lanier said. Lanier and Councilwoman Kashamba Miller-Anderson questioned whether the city's leadership structure is sustainable if the city manager remains out of the office for an extended period. 'I understand he has health issues. I understand that. But someone has to run the business of the city,' Lanier said during the discussion. Miller-Anderson argued that city leaders need clarity on Wilkins' plans moving forward. Miller-Anderson also questioned whether Wilkins' remote work arrangement aligns with the terms of his employment agreement. 'Either take leave, resign, or come back. And I think that's only right and that's only fair to ask,' Miller-Anderson said. Other officials say city operations continue Not everyone on the dais agreed with the criticism. Dr. Glen Spiritis, chair pro tem, said he has maintained communication with Wilkins and believes the city manager continues to oversee city operations while working remotely. 'I have had communications with him, and he is clearly in charge right now,' Spiritis said, while also praising the assistant city manager's handling of daily operations.

entry.title: Homebuilding company plans to purchase Boynton Beach Mall
entry.summary: Homebuilidng company Lennar is set to become the buyer of the Boynton Beach Mall, a company spokesperson confirmed to WPTV. The company plans to develop 'a vibrant mixed-use community' on the 91-acre site. a Lennar spokesperson said in a statement. The company said the development could help 'alleviate Palm Beach Countys severe housing shortage.' The purchase is expected to be completed by 'early' 2027, according to a Lennar spokesperson. 'Although planning is in the early stages and we look forward to stakeholder feedback, our vision is to take advantage of this unique opportunity with a mix of single-family attached housing opportunities, complemented by retail, commercial, open space and civic uses that will create a walkable, connected environment,' the statement said. The event is scheduled for Wednesday, Nov. The field is capped at 106 golfers, with registration listed at $750 per player. Veterans paired with foursomes will play for free, according to Chris LaRocque, the nonprofit’s president and executive director. It’s very close to my heart, LaRocque said in an ARC Florida interview. I’m an Army Reserve major myself. He said Tee It Up for the Troops has deployed more than $20 million and supported more than 400,000 veterans through programs that include help with the transition to civilian jobs and support for post-traumatic stress disorder and traumatic brain injuries. The tournament will also support local veterans programs, including PGA HOPE in South Florida, LaRocque said. PGA HOPE introduces veterans and active-duty service members to golf to support their physical, mental, social and emotional well-being. The tournament will be held at The Club at Lost Lake, 8300 SE Fazio Drive in Hobe Sound. Registration and event information are available through Tee It Up for the Troops.

entry.title: St. Lucie County Fire Board terminates fire chief after union vote - cw34.com
entry.summary: St. Lucie County Fire Board terminates fire chief after union vote    cw34.com
entry.article_text: After months of controversy, the St. Lucie County Fire District Board voted Wednesday to fire longtime Chief Jeff Lee, following an emotional meeting filled with calls for change and coming less than two weeks after the firefighters' union released the results of a no-confidence vote in the district's top leaders. The meeting was packed with firefighters, union members, retirees and residents, many urged the board to change the district's leadership. Among them was Taylor Baldwin, who pointed to the dozens of supporters wearing yellow shirts throughout the room. Look at everyone wearing yellow," Baldwin told commissioners. "These are not people who want to see the fire district fail. These are people who love this department enough to stand up and beg you to save it." The decision marks the latest development in a controversy that began this summer after a hazing investigation led to the firing of three veteran firefighters and the suspension of two others . The district determined the conduct amounted to hazing, while the firefighters and their union have argued it was consensual horseplay. A Fort Pierce Police Department investigation found no criminal violations. The union is pursuing arbitration to get the three firefighters reinstated . The issue later escalated into a no-confidence vote organized by IAFF Local 1377. According to the union, 423 of its 517 dues-paying members participated. Lee received 314 no-confidence votes and 108 confidence votes, with 74.23% of participants voting they no longer had confidence in his leadership. Several speakers criticized both district leadership and the board's handling of the controversy. "You participated in this cover-up. You protected the lies and you profoundly failed the people you are elected to serve," another resident Katie told the board. Lee, who joined the department in 1997 after serving in the U.S. Navy and became the district's 14th fire chief in May 2023, was not present for Wednesday's meeting. Commissioners spent more than 30 minutes debating whether Lee should be fired with or without cause. Ultimately, the board voted to terminate him without cause, triggering the severance provisions in his contract. "I think we still have to come to the determination of what exactly the final total is of the severance," board member James Clasby said after the vote. "We will only pay what we are legally required to." Those who supported Lee's removal said the district needs a fresh start. "I feel like a weight is lifted," Commissioner Jamie Fowler said. "Firing someone is never an easy decision, regardless of all the factors that come into play. So I feel like we've sort of taken a step in the right direction." Following Lee's termination, the board voted 4-3 to appoint Deputy Chief Paul Langel as interim chief while a search for a permanent replacement begins. The board is also moving forward with hiring outside legal counsel and discussing the process for selecting the district's next chief. See also: Former PBSO dispatcher sentenced after 2023 head-on DUI crash that killed mother This is not the first time the board has faced this choice. In 2017, after a union no-confidence vote, the board accepted then Chief Buddy Emerson’s retirement effective immediately and paid him severance through the end of his contract.

entry.title: Sheriff witnesses execution of man convicted in 1986 killing of Indian River County deputy - WPBF
entry.summary: Sheriff witnesses execution of man convicted in 1986 killing of Indian River County deputy    WPBF
entry.article_text: Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers witnessed the execution of William Reaves, who was convicted of killing Deputy Richard Raczkowski in 1986, at Florida State Prison on Tuesday night. Flowers said he positioned himself in the front row to ensure Reaves could see his sheriff’s office uniform. "I was in the front row; I was on the side of the room that he could see, so he saw my uniform, and I’m glad that he saw that," Flowers said. Reaves was convicted of killing Raczkowski at a convenience store near Vero Beach in 1986. Following the crime, Reaves was quickly arrested and sentenced to death. The case went through a retrial and several appeals, but the death sentence remained unchanged. "We will never forget Richard; we will never forget his sacrifice," Flowers said. Flowers described the execution process, which lasted about 12 minutes, and noted that Reaves did not make a final statement. "The real kicker on top of it was that he didn’t say anything; he didn’t make a last statement; he didn’t say anything to the family, ask God for forgiveness," Flowers said. Reaves’ last meal consisted of crackers and juice. Flowers said this was the first execution he had ever witnessed. "It’s closure but not justice; that chapter of the book is closed, but that man killed him in cold blood," Flowers said. Flowers also said his office will unveil a monument next month to honor its two fallen deputies. Democrats and many voting rights advocates have long feared the Trump administration will try to block certification of elections the president's party loses much as Trump unsuccessfully tried to do when he lost the 2020 presidential election.Earlier Thursday, Blanche told reporters that was unlikely outside of extreme circumstances. “It is not DOJ’s intention to and it’s never our intention to improperly interfere with elections or the state certification process," the Attorney General told reporters in Virginia.Derek Muller, a law professor at Notre Dame University, said the lawsuit will likely only kick in if Republicans narrowly lose the Alaska Senate race and that it does not seem to have legal merit. “The statute simply doesn't let the Department of Justice enjoin certification,” he said.

entry.title: Democrats tout momentum as early voting rises ahead of midterms
entry.summary: President Donald Trump is continuing to campaign for Republican candidates ahead of the 2026 midterm elections as early voting picks up across the country. Trump stopped in Sioux City, Iowa, on Thursday night to campaign for Republican Senate nominee Ashley Hinson. He is scheduled to travel to Fort Myers, Florida, on Friday to rally for gubernatorial candidate and U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds and other Republicans on the ballot. RELATED STORY | Massive Texas backlog of voter registrations that scrambled workers has been cleared, state says More than 21 million Americans have already cast ballots in the midterm elections, according to the University of Florida. Early voting in a number of states is outpacing levels seen at the same point in the 2022 midterm elections. New ratings from the Cook Political Report also show 19 seats moving toward Democrats, a shift Democratic officials are highlighting in the closing stretch of the campaign. Polling has indicated Democrats are more motivated than Republicans to vote, though a complete partisan breakdown of early voting is not available. Among states that provide party-registration information, registered Democrats account for about 46% of early ballots cast, compared with about 30% for registered Republicans and 23% for independent voters. Party registration does not necessarily indicate which candidates those voters supported. Older Americans are also accounting for a significant share of the early vote. In states where age information is available, voters 65 and older account for about 52% of early ballots cast. RELATED STORY | Midterm voting picks up amid massive shifts in voting districts The totals include ballots cast during in-person early voting and by mail. In some states, in-person early voting has outpaced previous levels. Many requested mail ballots have yet to be returned, meaning the current totals represent only part of the expected vote. Polling has suggested Democrats have an enthusiasm advantage heading into the midterms, but the early-voting figures do not show whether that advantage will translate into stronger overall turnout.

entry.title: Grand jury indicts man accused of killing West Palm Beach minister
entry.summary: Palm Beach County State Attorney Alexcia Cox announced Friday that a grand jury indicted Hugh Earp Milner Jr. on charges of first-degree murder with a firearm, attempted second-degree murder with a firearm, possession of a firearm by a convicted felon and shooting into an occupied vehicle. The charges stem from the Sept. 27 shooting death of 31-year-old Akeem Moore , a local minister and musician. According to investigators, officers responded to reports of a shooting shortly before 3 a.m. on Sept. 27 in the area of 45th Street and Australian Avenue. Moore was found suffering from gunshot wounds inside a vehicle and was pronounced dead at a hospital. Detectives later identified Hugh Earp Milner Jr. as the suspected gunman and obtained an arrest warrant. Investigators said Moore had been sitting in the driver's seat of a vehicle with another person when gunfire erupted. The passenger survived the shooting. Moore, known throughout the community for his ministry and music, was remembered by friends and family as a mentor who worked to inspire young people and strengthen his community. A vigil held in the days following his death drew dozens of mourners. According to the State Attorney's Office, the indictment follows an investigation by the West Palm Beach Police Department. In a statement announcing the charges, Cox described the killing as a senseless act of violence. 'Akeem Moore was a young man who served the community through his ministry and his music,' Cox said. 'This senseless act of violence leaves lasting pain for those who knew and loved him. My office remains committed to holding violent offenders accountable and seeking justice on behalf of victims. This indictment serves as a critical first step.'Milner was previously arrested in connection with the shooting and appeared in Palm Beach County court earlier this month. The case will now be prosecuted by the Homicide Unit of the Palm Beach County State Attorney's Office.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie Election includes Mayors race and trash pick-up - cw34.com
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie Election includes Mayors race and trash pick-up    cw34.com
entry.article_text: The CBS12 News I-Team has been closely following Port St. Lucie's election cycle, as there are two headline stories playing out and the future of the city is at stake. Leadership and trash are the hot-button items. On the first day of early voting in St. Lucie County, our crew visited a polling location on Rosser Blvd. We found two tents, side by side. In them, two candidates for mayor-- with such a rift between them-- the race feels like a war. The incumbent, Shannon Martin, is running to stay in office, and she says the city needs to stay on its current course. She points to how she has prioritized infrastructure repairs, like roadwork, as a reason to keep her in City Hall. Her opponent, Steven Giordano, says City Hall is corrupt and has lost touch with everyday people. When pressed on specific things he’d do differently-- he also wanted to talk about roadwork and says the city needs a new traffic study. See also: Martin County airport committee to review overnight flights and noise concerns Mayors serve four-year terms and wield significant influence in the mayor-council form of government. But trash collection is another issue getting people fired up: Should the city switch to twice-a-week pickup? FCC is the company that handles garbage collection in Port St. "I don't want to pay for something I don't need," said resident Rob Buske. Buske is making a point we have seldom heard while covering trash in the city. At many recent city council meetings, members of the public have hurled angry comments at city leaders, saying the trash pickup is sub-par. They’ve demanded an additional collection day. Ironic, then, that on the first day of early voting, everyone we asked for comment said they’d rather keep what they’ve got. The ballot question about trash collection isn't binding; it’s simply a way to poll the residents. The council might or might not go with whatever the majority of voters say. A second pick-up day would cost residents more than a hundred bucks a year, but some are adamant it's necessary. As this story comes to air and online, the election is less than 2 weeks away. Candidates for Mayor do not declare a party, and trash is a non-party matter. Here it's not Republicans vs. Democrats, but it’s somehow more personal, more granular, while also being big-picture. When can my garbage go to the curb? Who will be in charge of the city and what's their vision? The people are about to decide.

entry.summary: While control of Congress is drawing much of the attention heading into Election Day, voters across the country will also decide the fate of dozens of consequential ballot measures that could influence policy well beyond their states. According to Ballotpedia, 145 state ballot measures are on this Novembers ballot, touching on issues ranging from taxes and abortion to transgender rights and voting requirements. Even for voters who don't see certain questions on their ballots this year, the outcomes could matter. Policies approved in one state can become models for ballot campaigns and legislation elsewhere. In Tennessee, voters will consider a measure that would restrict the state from ever imposing a statewide property tax. Florida voters, meanwhile, will weigh a significant expansion of the state's property tax exemption. The exemption is currently $50,000, but the proposal would increase it to $150,000, with the amount potentially rising in future years. entry.title: 2 vehicles sought in Port St. Lucie hit-and-run investigation, police say
entry.summary: The Port St. Lucie Police Department has released new information in its investigation of a hit-and-run crash that left a 63-year-old man seriously injured earlier this month on Oct. 9. Detectives now believe the victim may have been hit by two separate vehicles near the intersection of Northwest University Boulevard and Northwest California Boulevard. According to police, one vehicle was traveling northbound while the other was traveling southbound at the time of the incident. The crash occurred at approximately 12:56 a.m and the victim, a 63-year-old Port St. Lucie resident, was found unconscious in the roadway suffering from severe head injuries. In a previous update, police said surveillance video from a nearby business captured the incident and showed what investigators believed to be a white four-door sedan striking the man before leaving the scene without stopping. As detectives continued reviewing evidence and surveillance footage, investigators developed information indicating a second vehicle may also have been involved in the crash. Police are now working to identify both vehicles and their drivers. Investigators have released images of the vehicles and are asking for the public's help. Anyone who recognizes either vehicle, was in the area around the time of the crash, witnessed the incident, or has dashcam or surveillance video from the area is asked to contact the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000.

entry.title: St. Lucie County Fire Board votes to terminate Chief Jeff Lee after hazing fallout - WPTV
entry.summary: St. Lucie County Fire Board votes to terminate Chief Jeff Lee after hazing fallout    WPTV
entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire Board voted Wednesday to terminate Chief Jeff Lee's contract without cause."At the end of the day, it's gotten very messy. It's not about one single decision that he's made. It's about bringing peace and calm and respect back to the district and the men and women that serve this community every day, and it just got to a point where he was not effective anymore," said St. Lucie County Commissioner and Board Member Jamie Fowler. WATCH KATE HUSSEY'S REPORT BELOW:This is the latest fallout from a hazing investigation brought to light earlier this year.WPTV reported last week that more than 74% of firefighters who participated in a union vote said they had no confidence in Lee. About 92% said they had no confidence in Assistant Chief Brian Gonzalez, while 97% said the same about District Attorney Kim Sabol.The vote is the latest fallout from an investigation earlier this year into videos involving firefighters at Station 1A.Some show a modified bug zapper being used to shock three apprentice firefighters while on duty in 2024. Other videos show water being dumped on two firefighters and a dead raccoon placed inside a fire vehicle.A third-party investigator concluded the videos depicted hazing. Veteran firefighters Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Chris Baldwin were fired following the investigation, though they disputed the characterization of hazing and said the incidents were "consensual" pranks that were done "all in good fun." “It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," said Hutchinson. “We’re all still friends," added Boudrias. Boudrias, Hutchinson, and Baldwin's firings sparked outcry from firefighters, former firefighters and community members, many of whom felt the punishment was too harsh. In Wednesday's Fire Board meeting, those community members packed the Fire Administration building, many of whom held signs or wore shirts in support of the three firefighters. "Not only have they lost their jobs, but they also lost their reputations," said one public commentator. "We need to restore faith in this fire district," said another. "I think it speaks loud and clear, exactly like the confidence vote that was reported to us. There was a large desire to have a change in leadership, and we delivered that today," said St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire Board member James Clasby. Lee had signaled days earlier that his tenure could be coming to an end. 15 letter to the board, Lee wrote that it may be time to consider a “mutually agreeable retirement and leadership transition," adding "the position of fire chief requires confidence." During the meeting's discussion, fire board member and business owner Travis Leonard said that gave him reason to begin the motion to Fire Lee. "Coming from the private sector, anytime an employee gives their notice, I terminate them; I found they've checked out," said Leonard. After terminating Lee’s contract, the board appointed Deputy Chief Paul Langel as interim fire chief. The district also plans to hire a recruiter to conduct a search for Lee’s permanent replacement."I am excited to move this district forward, to begin the healing process of the issues that we’ve been dealing with, as of recent, and to instill trust,” Langel said.Lee's departure comes with a high cost to the district. His severance package is expected to total about $350,000.The leadership change also comes as the firefighters union continues negotiations with the district in an effort to reinstate three veteran firefighters who were fired. Union Representative Ryan Sapp said he believed Lee's termination is a "positive step forward.""I think moving forward, the ultimate goal here is to just move forward and get things back to a level field and continue providing the services to our community," Sapp told investigative reporter Kate Hussey. "The biggest thing today is we worked together and came together as a local — glad to see my membership stepped up and let their voices be heard." The Fire Board is also searching for a replacement district attorney, who submitted her notice of retirement amid the ongoing controversy.

entry.article_text: President Donald Trump on Friday said he told his administration to file its lawsuit to block certification of the U.S. Senate race in Alaska if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses, kicking off what many fear could become a lengthy battle between the government and states over certifying an election where the president's party is struggling.“I'm the one that said do it,” Trump told reporters as he landed for a campaign rally in Florida.The lawsuit, filed late Thursday, centers on one of the president's longstanding complaints in the Senate race — the presence of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan who Republican fear could siphon away votes from the incumbent in what's likely to be a photo-finish contest with Democrat Mary Peltola, the state's former congresswoman.The second Dan Sullivan, who is Daniel J. Sullivan from the tiny fishing community of Petersburg, has said he decided to run on his own, but Republicans have contended he is a Democratic plant to siphon votes away from their candidate.The lawsuit by the Republican president's Department of Justice in federal court in Alaska demands that the state be blocked from certifying a Peltola win if Daniel J. Sullivan remains on the ballot. “The United States accordingly brings this lawsuit to protect the integrity of the 2026 Senate election in Alaska,” the lawsuit says, contending that federal law requires states to protect the integrity of federal elections.The legal challenge came 11 days before the Nov. 3 election and months after the final ballot was set.The Alaska Supreme Court rejected a previous Republican effort to remove Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot, and the state's Republican officials made the decisions about how to list him on the ballot. He will appear without a party designation next to his name, while the senator will be listed as the Republican incumbent. Alaska's ranked choice voting system also will allow voters to select both of the men if confused.Peltola and Sen. Sullivan were top vote-getters in nonpartisan primaryThe senator received more than 68,000 votes in the August primary, while the challenging Sullivan got 4,107, about 2% of the total vote. Peltola, who had previously served one term in the House, was the top vote-getter in the nonpartisan primary. Both parties expect that whoever wins in November will do so by a tight margin in a state of 738,000 people.The campaign for Sen. Dan Sullivan did not address whether the senator supports the Department of Justice's intervention. “We'll let the DOJ complaint run its course,” campaign spokesman Nate Adams said in a text message. “Alaskans can tell the difference between a Democrat sideshow and Senator Sullivan's strong record of delivering for Alaska.”Daniel J. Sullivan, whose presence on the ballot is at issue in the lawsuit, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.“Donald Trump knows that Dan Sullivan is going to lose the election, so now his Department of Justice is filing a sham lawsuit to overturn the will of Alaska voters and steal an election when he loses,” said Devan Barber, executive director of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee.In a statement on Friday, the Department of Justice noted that Alaska's election officials, who are Republicans, determined the other Sullivan's campaign was an attempt to “mislead:” voters and wanted him removed from the ballot. Both a state court and Alaska's Supreme Court disagreed and kept the second Sullivan on the ballot."The Justice Department, consistent with the National Voter Registration Act enacted by Congress, is taking the necessary steps to ensure that this frivolous candidacy does not undermine the integrity of Alaska’s election or the will of its voters,” the DoJ statement said.The Department of Justice has increasingly been used to bolster the president's political operation, targeting his enemies and suing Democratic-controlled states before the election. Democrats and many voting rights advocates have long feared that the administration will try to block certification of elections that Trump's party loses, much as he unsuccessfully tried to do when he lost the White House race to Democrat Joe Biden.U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said that was unlikely outside of extreme circumstances. “It is not DOJ’s intention to, and it’s never our intention to, improperly interfere with elections or the state certification process," he told reporters Thursday in Virginia before the lawsuit was filed.The lawsuit was signed by Associate U.S. Attorney General Stanley Woodward, who represented Trump allies and Jan. 6 defendants before becoming one of the top appointees at the department.Constitution gives states the power to run electionsDerek Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, said the lawsuit would likely only kick in if Republicans narrowly lost the Alaska Senate race and that it probably would not survive long. “The statute simply doesn't let the Department of Justice enjoin certification,” Muller said. “The lawsuit could well be mooted by a wide Democratic victory or a narrow Republican one, and if not, the court will likely dismiss it next month.”The U.S. Constitution grants states the power to run their own elections. Elections for federal office like the Senate must comply with standards set by Congress. That division of power has frustrated Trump, who repeatedly has tried to seize control of election procedures through executive orders that courts have blocked.The final step for a state election is formally certifying the winner, the act that the administration's lawsuit seeks to prevent, it requests, “pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan."The process in Alaska is complicated by the state's ranked choice voting system, which Trump opposes, and many expect it to take weeks before a winner is known. Also on the state's ballot is an initiative to repeal that system.Trump has stepped up complaints about a ballot with dueling SullivansTrump has complained about Daniel J. Sullivan's presence on the ballot, making reference to it during a rally in Alaska this month and in repeated social media posts, including one this week where he called it “CHEATING.”“We are looking at powerful legal options to remove the fraudulent Daniel J. from the Ballot, and holding the Democrats accountable for their Election Interference, in the pursuit of Justice and Fairness,” the president wrote on Wednesday.Clogging a ballot with third party candidates to siphon off votes from the other major party is a long-standing tactic in the country's two-party system. Republicans have been linked to an effort to persuade Ohio voters to support a socialist in that state's Senate race, which could help Republican Sen. Jon Husted fend off a challenge from former Democratic Sen.

entry.article_text: A 20-year-old Bronx, New York, man was extradited to St. Lucie County after Canadian border authorities arrested him while he was trying to enter Canada , the Sheriff’s Office said. Gibrill Diallo faces charges of money laundering, a scheme to defraud of $50,000 or more and grand theft in connection with an investigation into a check stolen from a Port St. Lucie real estate company, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office . The agency said the check was altered and deposited into a bank account opened using a stolen identity. Detectives traced the funds through multiple bank accounts and Zelle transfers before they were deposited into Diallo’s personal bank account, the Sheriff’s Office said. Authorities arrested Diallo on Oct. He was held at the Niagara County Jail in New York before being extradited to St. 21, according to the agency. entry.title: Port St. Lucie police arrest suspect in hit-and-run that critically injured 63-year-old - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie police arrest suspect in hit-and-run that critically injured 63-year-old    WPEC
entry.article_text: A 60-year-old man was arrested in connection with a hit-and-run crash that critically injured a 63-year-old Port St. Lucie resident, police said. The crash happened shortly before 1 a.m. 9 on NW California Boulevard just south of the intersection with NW University Boulevard. The victim was found unconscious in the road with severe head injuries and remains in critical condition at HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Ft. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said detectives arrested Eric Saint Aude on Oct. 22 and charged him with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury. He said Aude was working as a newspaper delivery driver and was on his way to pick up newspapers when the crash happened. Investigators reviewed video, physical evidence and other leads since the crash two weeks ago. Niemczyk said a geofence warrant which sought cellphone location data from a specific area during a specific time produced a lead showing Aude's phone had pinged off cell phone towers in that area at the time of the crash. That helped detectives identify Aude as the alleged hit and run driver and the vehicles registered to him. Detectives then located and examined the man’s vehicle, which had damage consistent with striking a pedestrian, including damage to the front bumper and hood, Niemczyk said. Investigators also found presumptive positive results for blood on the vehicle. Further testing is needed. Police also recovered pieces of the vehicle’s inner fender-well fasteners at the scene, Niemczyk said. Detectives found that several matching fasteners were missing from the suspect’s vehicle. Investigators are still looking for a second vehicle that was traveling southbound near the crash. Niemczyk said distant video showed a vehicle traveling in each direction, but it was difficult to determine what happened. Police are trying to learn whether the second vehicle also struck the victim or witnessed the crash. We’re very confident that the vehicle that we have and the person that we’ve arrested are responsible for the majority of what occurred, Niemczyk said. The Police Chief said the victim was in the middle of the road when he was struck, but investigators could not determine from the video whether he was walking or jogging. Police learned he often exercised at night and was known to walk on the road and medians. "I've been doing this for 30 years. I'm not surprised by a whole lot anymore. I've seen pedestrians left for dead on the side of the road before. It doesn't make it any easier, but it doesn't surprise me at this point either. You know, it's just difficult to understand how one human being could be so, you know, without compassion for another," Chief Niemczyk said. See also: 2 arrested in killing of transgender woman Jayla McGee in Belle Glade The victim had no identification or cellphone with him, Niemczyk said. Investigators used data from a Garmin exercise watch he was wearing to trace his route back to his house and were able to identify him. Niemczyk said the victim has significant head trauma and is unable to speak. He is expected to survive, but the chief said his quality of life may not be the same as it was before the crash. An arrest cannot undo the harm or uncertainty imposed upon a victim, Niemczyk said, but it’s the first step in accountability. Police have not released a description of the southbound vehicle. Anyone with information is asked to call the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie police arrest suspect in hit-and-run that critically injured 63-year-old - cw34.com
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie police arrest suspect in hit-and-run that critically injured 63-year-old    cw34.com
entry.article_text: A 60-year-old man was arrested in connection with a hit-and-run crash that critically injured a 63-year-old Port St. Lucie resident, police said. The crash happened shortly before 1 a.m. 9 on NW California Boulevard just south of the intersection with NW University Boulevard. The victim was found unconscious in the road with severe head injuries and remains in critical condition at HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Ft. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said detectives arrested Eric Saint Aude on Oct. 22 and charged him with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury. He said Aude was working as a newspaper delivery driver and was on his way to pick up newspapers when the crash happened. Investigators reviewed video, physical evidence and other leads since the crash two weeks ago. Niemczyk said a geofence warrant which sought cellphone location data from a specific area during a specific time produced a lead showing Aude's phone had pinged off cell phone towers in that area at the time of the crash. That helped detectives identify Aude as the alleged hit and run driver and the vehicles registered to him. Detectives then located and examined the man’s vehicle, which had damage consistent with striking a pedestrian, including damage to the front bumper and hood, Niemczyk said. Investigators also found presumptive positive results for blood on the vehicle. Further testing is needed. Police also recovered pieces of the vehicle’s inner fender-well fasteners at the scene, Niemczyk said. Detectives found that several matching fasteners were missing from the suspect’s vehicle. Investigators are still looking for a second vehicle that was traveling southbound near the crash. Niemczyk said distant video showed a vehicle traveling in each direction, but it was difficult to determine what happened. Police are trying to learn whether the second vehicle also struck the victim or witnessed the crash. We’re very confident that the vehicle that we have and the person that we’ve arrested are responsible for the majority of what occurred, Niemczyk said. The Police Chief said the victim was in the middle of the road when he was struck, but investigators could not determine from the video whether he was walking or jogging. Police learned he often exercised at night and was known to walk on the road and medians. "I've been doing this for 30 years. I'm not surprised by a whole lot anymore. I've seen pedestrians left for dead on the side of the road before. It doesn't make it any easier, but it doesn't surprise me at this point either. You know, it's just difficult to understand how one human being could be so, you know, without compassion for another," Chief Niemczyk said. See also: 2 arrested in killing of transgender woman Jayla McGee in Belle Glade The victim had no identification or cellphone with him, Niemczyk said. Investigators used data from a Garmin exercise watch he was wearing to trace his route back to his house and were able to identify him. Niemczyk said the victim has significant head trauma and is unable to speak. He is expected to survive, but the chief said his quality of life may not be the same as it was before the crash. An arrest cannot undo the harm or uncertainty imposed upon a victim, Niemczyk said, but it’s the first step in accountability. Police have not released a description of the southbound vehicle. Anyone with information is asked to call the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000.

entry.title: St. Lucie County Nuclear Power Plant turns 50
entry.summary: WPTV had the rare opportunity to go inside the St. Lucie County Nuclear Power Plant on Thursday. This year, the facility is celebrating 50 years of operation and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission just granted licenses for 20 more.   On Thursday, WPTV learned about operations inside the plant and spoke with people who keep the power on. Watch report from Tyler Hatfield: WPTV gets an inside look at the St Lucie County Nuclear Power Plant Our Tyler Hatfield listened to Alfred Phillips, a digital INC specialist. 'My job is to calibrate and make sure all the equipment used to work on the equipment that controls the reactor itself meets all the government standards and accuracies.' Phillips said hes been working at the plant for nearly 20 years. 'You have million-dollar homes right down the street. We're here, but yet we're still invisible because what we do, we do it well, .Phillips said.   Alfreds son, Alfred Sinclair Phillips, followed his father's footsteps and works in the operations department. 'There's a pressure with it, but there's also a sense of pride, Phillips said. Knowing that my dad has worked his butt off and he's left an impact with the people here on his work to make this place better. WPTV learned from Carlos Santos, site vice president, how the plant generates power. 'The simplest way to put it is the reactor creates the heat,' Santos said. Santos said that heat comes from nuclear fission from uranium pellets stacked into rods inside the two units on site. The heat from the rods builds up and produces steam, which travels into a secondary closed system into a turbine, which then generates power and produces electricity for the grid. Back in August, the plant had to be manually shut down when three control rods dropped in the reactors core. Florida Power Light told WPTV at the time that there was no danger to staff or the public, and no one lost power. But after 50 years, technology has changed how employees work. Nicholas Negron, associate innovation specialist, showed WPTV their robotic dog, Tritium. 'We've named them after nuclear isotopes, Negron said. entry.title: St. Lucie County fire chief terminated after months of controversy - WPBF
entry.summary: St. Lucie County fire chief terminated after months of controversy    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District Board voted 4-3 to terminate fire Chief Jeff Lee without cause after months of controversy, hazing allegations, and a no-confidence vote. Interim Chief Paul Langel said, "I believe that the fire board moved forward and that was their job. Now my job is going to be to step in and start the healing process." The decision comes two months after five firefighters were displaced for allegedly turning a bug zapper into a makeshift taser and using it to shock coworkers. Videos appear to show the alleged hazing, and three firefighters ultimately lost their jobs. One of the terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson, said, "I think it was a step in the right direction. I don’t think today was about us by any means. I think it was the best thing for the entire department." The disciplined firefighters have called the termination retaliation for previous complaints they filed against district leadership. When asked about the possibility of the terminated firefighters regaining their jobs, Langel said, "I believe that there’s always scenarios that would unfold and happen. I’ve got to get in and get up to speed on all the specifics." The board voted to appoint Langel as interim chief. He is a familiar face in the district, with 30 years of experience. Because Lee was terminated without cause, he is entitled to compensation as his contract ends early. entry.title: Turning declining shopping malls into housing developments
entry.summary: Lennar Homes' confirmation of its intent to buy the Boynton Beach Mall reflects a growing trend in which declining retail space is seen as an opportunity for housing developments. In a statement, Lennar Homes says, Lennar expects to complete the purchase of the Boynton Beach Mall site early next year with plans to develop a vibrant mixed-use community that helps alleviate Palm Beach Countys severe housing shortage. Watch report from Matt Sczesny: Turning Declining Shopping Malls Into Housing Developments Although planning is in the early stages and we look forward to stakeholder feedback, our vision is to take advantage of this unique opportunity with a mix of single-family attached housing opportunities, complemented by retail, commercial, open space and civic uses that will create a walkable, connected environment. In South Florida, were developed, theres a need for housing and when we start looking for opportunities to do it, retail centers are an obvious choice to do that,' says Eric Dumbaugh, at FAU's School of Urban and Regional Planning. In Vero Beach the Indian River Mall is being transformed into a mix use development. And in Palm Beach County, the unoccupied Nordstrom building at Wellington Mall is being viewed as a possible site for an apartment complex. As for the Boynton Beach Mall site, Dumbaugh says the location seems ideal. I dont know what affordable means in the South Florida market anymore but it's going to be a lot more affordable than what they expect to pay in a place like Delray or in Boca,' Dumbaugh says.

entry.title: Democrats tout momentum as early voting rises ahead of midterms
entry.summary: President Donald Trump is continuing to campaign for Republican candidates ahead of the 2026 midterm elections as early voting picks up across the country. Trump stopped in Sioux City, Iowa, on Thursday night to campaign for Republican Senate nominee Ashley Hinson. He is scheduled to travel to Fort Myers, Florida, on Friday to rally for gubernatorial candidate and U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds and other Republicans on the ballot. WATCH: Corbin Trent on turning voter frustration into midterm momentum Corbin Trent on turning voter frustration into midterm momentum More than 21 million Americans have already cast ballots in the midterm elections, according to the University of Florida. Early voting in a number of states is outpacing levels seen at the same point in the 2022 midterm elections. New ratings from the Cook Political Report also show 19 seats moving toward Democrats, a shift Democratic officials are highlighting in the closing stretch of the campaign. RELATED STORY | Massive Texas backlog of voter registrations that scrambled workers has been cleared, state says Polling has indicated Democrats are more motivated than Republicans to vote, though a complete partisan breakdown of early voting is not available. Among states that provide party-registration information, registered Democrats account for about 46% of early ballots cast, compared with about 30% for registered Republicans and 23% for independent voters. Party registration does not necessarily indicate which candidates those voters supported. Older Americans are also accounting for a significant share of the early vote. In states where age information is available, voters 65 and older account for about 52% of early ballots cast. RELATED STORY | Midterm voting picks up amid massive shifts in voting districts The totals include ballots cast during in-person early voting and by mail. In some states, in-person early voting has outpaced previous levels. Many requested mail ballots have yet to be returned, meaning the current totals represent only part of the expected vote. Polling has suggested Democrats have an enthusiasm advantage heading into the midterms, but the early-voting figures do not show whether that advantage will translate into stronger overall turnout.

entry.article_text: Golfers at a Veterans Day fundraiser in Hobe Sound will share the course with local veterans, as Tee It Up for the Troops brings its tournament to The Club at Lost Lake for the first time. Veterans paired with foursomes will play for free, according to Chris LaRocque, the nonprofit’s president and executive director. It’s very close to my heart, LaRocque said in an ARC Florida interview. I’m an Army Reserve major myself. entry.title: Treasure Coast water tank wins 2026 Tank of the Year - WPBF
entry.summary: Treasure Coast water tank wins 2026 Tank of the Year    WPBF
entry.article_text: A water storage tank in Fort Pierce was named the winner of the 2026 Tank of the Year. The annual contest held by Tnemec Company, Inc., a leading provider of high-performance coatings, announced the winner and Top 12 finalists on Friday. "Pretty excited," said Christian Stanley of C. Stanley Creative, the artist behind the tank. "I got the call earlier from our sales rep. He was excited to share that we were the first-place winner of Tnemec's Tank of the Year. And yeah, we're just beyond excited, and I'm excited to share that with them and with the community that they have an award-winning piece of public art there in their community." Located in Jaycee Park, the winning ground storage tank showcases a vibrant mural celebrating Florida's coastal environment and native wildlife. The mural features sea turtles, dolphins, manatees, pelicans, and tropical fish, transforming essential water infrastructure into a community landmark. The tank is protected with Tnemec's Series 1026 Enduratone coating. According to Tnemec Company, Inc., a panel of water tank enthusiasts selected the Fort Pierce tank based on its artistic value, significance to the community, and challenges encountered during the project. "For 20 years, this competition has showcased how communities can transform essential infrastructure into something truly special," said Kevin Morris, director of sales for the water tank market at Tnemec. "The creativity and community pride reflected in this year's entries are remarkable. Fort Pierce is a great example of how a water tank can become more than a functional structure. It can become a landmark that residents are proud to call their own." Digital content reporter Camila Pereira visited the tank last week as Stanley and his wife Jessica traveled from Central Florida for a couple of days to apply that UV clear coat. Stanley shared their excitement of it being in the running, and the honor they felt of being selected by Fort Pierce Utilities Authority to leave their mark where he grew up. On Friday, WPBF 25 News reconnected with Stanley and shared how he felt about the win. "We were runners-up in 2024, and that was exciting," he said. "But I was like, man, I really want to try. And I know we can make something that would win the first-place award. So, it's, you know, taken a couple of years for us to get there. But I'm excited that we were able to come some bring something together and that Fort Pierce trusted us to make something that we felt was going to be really impactful and iconic for the community there." Fort Pierce Utilities Authority shared the following statement with WPBF 25 News: "We are thrilled and deeply grateful to receive the Tank of the Year award. Thank you to everyone who voted and supported us, and to the teams who made it happen. It has been an absolute pleasure and honor for our team here at FPUA to collaborate with the artist and the Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency this summer, turning the Jaycee Park Water Tank into a Fort Pierce landmark. Rachel Tennant, FPUA Director of Public Affairs Sustainability Stanley said it's an honor to be recognized nationally, but an even bigger honor to have his work displayed at home for the community to enjoy. "I grew up in Stuart, so it was great to visit kind of my old hometown and just be back in the community and be a part of it again, and to kind of leave a footprint," he said. "This thing will kind of continue to have a life of its own beyond just the just the tank. And it'll have a bigger footprint than even what we could anticipate. So, it's really cool to get some recognition for the for the award. And we're excited to see what comes next from this." The Fort Pierce tank will be featured as January in Tnemec's 2027 water tank calendar, with the remaining finalists and nominees featured throughout the calendar. The 2026 Tank of the Year winner and Top 12 finalists are: Tank of the Year: Fort Pierce, Florida People's Choice: Detroit Lakes, Minnesota Oak Harbor, Washington Percival, Iowa South Haven, Michigan Shreveport, Louisiana Prior Lake, Minnesota Scranton, South Carolina Elloree, South Carolina Cheyenne, Wyoming Pelham, Alabama Walnut Cove, North Carolina

entry.article_text: Lucie have arrested a suspect in connection with a hit-and-run crash two weeks ago on NW California Boulevard that left a 63-year-old man critically injured and in the ICU. Authorities said the victim was exercising when a man, allegedly on his way to work to deliver newspapers, struck him with his car and fled the scene heading north. Surveillance footage appears to show the suspect driving away after the crash. "It’s a sad thing to see; there’s not many people that we see at this time," said a man who works nearby. Police identified the suspect as 60-year-old Eric Saint Aude. Investigators said nearby surveillance footage helped them identify the type of car involved, but the key breakthrough came from the suspect’s phone. Officers obtained a warrant to track phone pings in the area during the time of the crash, which led them to Aude. When officers located the suspect’s vehicle, they found damage on the front and blood evidence, according to police. Investigators questioned Aude about the crash. "He didn't display much emotion," said Chief Leo Niemczyk. "The victim has serious head trauma, which occurred at the point of impact." Police are still searching for a second vehicle they believe was heading south at the time of the crash. It’s rare that anything like that would happen, and the fact that it did, we need to raise awareness that we have to be more careful here," a nearby worker said. The victim remains in critical condition in the ICU, according to the chief. Police are asking anyone with information about the crash to contact them. entry.article_text: A 22-year-old man from New York is facing charges in an organized check fraud and money laundering scheme, the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office said Friday. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office Economic Crimes Unit conducted a multi-jurisdictional investigation, culminating in the arrest of Gibrill Diallo, of the Bronx. A check mailed by a Port St. Lucie real estate company was stolen, fraudulently altered, and deposited into a bank account established using a stolen identity, the sheriff's office said. Detectives traced the stolen funds through multiple bank accounts and Zelle transfers allegedly used to conceal their origin before the money was deposited into Diallo’s personal bank account. Detectives obtained an arrest warrant charging Diallo with money laundering ($300–$20,000), scheme to defraud ($50,000 or more) and grand theft. 14, Diallo was apprehended by Canadian border authorities while attempting to enter Canada from the United States. He was detained at the Niagara County Jail in New York before being extradited to St. Lucie County on Wednesday at 9:39 p.m. Total bond was set at $30,000 for the three charges. “Our detectives followed the money, uncovered a complex financial scheme, and pursued every lead until the suspect was brought back to St. Lucie County to face justice,” Sheriff Richard Del Toro said in a statement. "This case reflects the relentless investigative work and determination of our Economic Crimes Unit. Our residents and businesses work hard for what they earn, and they deserve to know that when someone tries to take advantage of them, our detectives will go the extra mile to hold those responsible accountable.” Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25
