entry.title: St. Lucie County Fire Board terminates chief after calls for leadership change - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County Fire Board terminates chief after calls for leadership change    WPEC
entry.article_text: After months of controversy, the St. Lucie County Fire District Board voted Wednesday to fire longtime Chief Jeff Lee, following an emotional meeting filled with calls for change and coming less than two weeks after the firefighters' union released the results of a no-confidence vote in the district's top leaders. The meeting was packed with firefighters, union members, retirees and residents, many urged the board to change the district's leadership. Among them was Taylor Baldwin, who pointed to the dozens of supporters wearing yellow shirts throughout the room. Look at everyone wearing yellow," Baldwin told commissioners. "These are not people who want to see the fire district fail. These are people who love this department enough to stand up and beg you to save it." The decision marks the latest development in a controversy that began this summer after a hazing investigation led to the firing of three veteran firefighters and the suspension of two others . The district determined the conduct amounted to hazing, while the firefighters and their union have argued it was consensual horseplay. A Fort Pierce Police Department investigation found no criminal violations. The union is pursuing arbitration to get the three firefighters reinstated . The issue later escalated into a no-confidence vote organized by IAFF Local 1377. According to the union, 423 of its 517 dues-paying members participated. Lee received 314 no-confidence votes and 108 confidence votes, with 74.23% of participants voting they no longer had confidence in his leadership. Several speakers criticized both district leadership and the board's handling of the controversy. "You participated in this cover-up. You protected the lies and you profoundly failed the people you are elected to serve," another resident Katie told the board. Lee, who joined the department in 1997 after serving in the U.S. Navy and became the district's 14th fire chief in May 2023, was not present for Wednesday's meeting. Commissioners spent more than 30 minutes debating whether Lee should be fired with or without cause. Ultimately, the board voted to terminate him without cause, triggering the severance provisions in his contract. "I think we still have to come to the determination of what exactly the final total is of the severance," board member James Clasby said after the vote. "We will only pay what we are legally required to." Those who supported Lee's removal said the district needs a fresh start. "I feel like a weight is lifted," Commissioner Jamie Fowler said. "Firing someone is never an easy decision, regardless of all the factors that come into play. So I feel like we've sort of taken a step in the right direction." Following Lee's termination, the board voted 4-3 to appoint Deputy Chief Paul Langel as interim chief while a search for a permanent replacement begins. The board is also moving forward with hiring outside legal counsel and discussing the process for selecting the district's next chief. See also: Former PBSO dispatcher sentenced after 2023 head-on DUI crash that killed mother This is not the first time the board has faced this choice. In 2017, after a union no-confidence vote, the board accepted then Chief Buddy Emerson’s retirement effective immediately and paid him severance through the end of his contract.

entry.article_text: A man was killed Thursday morning in a crash involving a semi-truck in unincorporated Indian River County, according to the Florida Highway Patrol (FHP).The crash happened around 6:45 a.m. at the intersection of 66th Avenue and 49th Street.According to FHP, a Freightliner semi-truck was attempting to make a left turn from a stop sign at westbound 49th Street onto 66th Avenue. At the same time, a Dodge Durango was traveling north in the inside lane of 66th Avenue, which had no traffic controls at the intersection.Troopers said the Freightliner entered the path of the SUV, causing the front of the Durango to collide with the left side of the semi-trailer.Both vehicles came to rest in the area of the collision.The driver of the SUV, a 60-year-old Vero Beach man, was taken to Health First's Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he was pronounced dead just after 8 a.m., according to FHP.The driver of the Freightliner, a 59-year-old Jacksonville man, was not injured.The crash remains under investigation.

entry.title: Could long fingernails, large fingers impact your vote?
entry.summary: Palm Beach County election officials are urging voters to double-check their ballots after some early voters raised concerns about selections they say did not register the way they intended on ExpressVote ballot-marking devices. Boca Raton resident Ceil Friedenthal is one of them. She voted early Tuesday at the South County Civic Center and said she noticed the issue more than once. I went to the machines and I pressed what I wanted and I used the tip of my finger, the pad of my finger, and a couple of times it defaulted to something I wasn't voting for, Friedenthal said. So if I voted for one party, it defaulted to the other, not every single time, but several. Friedenthal said in her case she was attempting to select a Democratic candidate, but the Republican candidate listed above was selected instead. The experience immediately caught her attention. I better get somebody over here to take a look at it because I don't know what to do, she recalled. Friedenthal said she called a poll worker over three separate times because she caught three selections she believed were incorrect. Each time, she said a worker helped correct the issue. For Friedenthal, making sure those selections were right mattered more than simply getting through the voting process quickly. Listen, in my opinion, as an ordinary U.S. citizen, the only thing we can do is vote, she said. There's really nothing else that we can do as an individual, so it's important that your vote be registered correctly. Friedenthal also told WPTV she had spoken with two other women who said they experienced something similar while early voting. WPTV took Friedenthal's concerns directly to Palm Beach County Supervisor of Elections Wendy Sartory Link. Link said her office had received only a couple of reports directly from voters. She stressed that when voters experience a problem, they should notify a poll worker immediately. That not only gives workers a chance to help the voter, but also allows election officials to identify the specific machine and test it. We have the ability to immediately test that machine and see if we can recreate the problem, Link said. Obviously if there is an issue, we're going to replace that machine. Link told WPTV election workers are also proactively checking the equipment. We are throughout the day, if there's not a voter at a machine, we are proactively testing them again, making sure everything's properly calibrated, Link said. To this moment, we have not been able to rec
entry.article_text: “We brought it back to our office, tried to recreate the problem using fingers, and we couldn't, so we don't think it was the machine, but again, in an abundance of caution, we did replace that one because we did know which one it was.”It was unclear which voting center that machine was located in.Elections office points to several possible factorsLink said there is no setting on an ExpressVote machine that defaults a voter to a particular candidate.Instead, Link said a voter's finger or fingernail can sometimes make contact with a different selection than intended.“If your fingernail is a little long, you might be thinking you're hitting one, but you're really hitting the selection above,” Link said. “Or if you happen to have large hands, maybe you're hitting two different types of selections.”Friedenthal disputes that explanation in her case.“No, I use the pad of my finger, not the nail itself, and I pressed twice with the pad, so the nail wasn't involved at all,” she said.While acknowledging that her fingernails are a little long, Friedenthal demonstrated to WPTV how she said she touched the screen.Link also pointed to the age and responsiveness of the ExpressVote equipment as another factor voters should keep in mind.“These machines are a little bit older. We're actually getting new ones,” Link said.She said the newer machines are expected to be used in March.“With the slower, a little bit slower technology, you may find that, like when you're used to hitting an iPhone, something, it shows up right away,” Link said. “And these may have just a slight delay from when you hit it before it acknowledges your selection.”Link said repeatedly touching the screen while waiting for it to respond could potentially result in a voter touching another selection.“So we just say give it a moment, let it make your selection, use the stylus,” Link said.The Supervisor of Elections Office is now emphasizing the use of the stylus available with the ExpressVote machines.“There's a stylus provided with every machine because with that stylus, it is, you know, it is smaller than your finger, and so you're not going to be hitting two areas at the same time,” Link said.Link said her office contacted poll workers after hearing the concerns and asked them to be more proactive about encouraging voters to use the stylus.She said styluses should be available at every machine, with extras available at check-in if one is missing.Friedenthal, however, told WPTV she did not remember seeing one when she voted.“I didn't see anything, and nobody suggested anything,” she said. “They didn't say to me when I checked in, ‘Please use the stylus.’”Voters also don't have to use an ExpressVote device.

entry.title: WHERE'S WALTER? Having a day of discovery at the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast - WPTV
entry.summary: WHERE'S WALTER? Having a day of discovery at the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast    WPTV
entry.article_text: This week, I visited a place where learning and fun go hand in hand: the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast.From the moment I walked in, I could tell this wasn't your typical museum. Instead of looking at exhibits from behind a rope or glass case, kids are encouraged to jump in, get involved and learn by doing.As I explored the museum, I discovered exhibits designed to teach important life skills in creative and engaging ways. From learning about money and budgeting to exploring different careers and practicing job skills, every corner of the museum offered a new opportunity to learn something useful.WATCH: One of my favorite stops, of course, involved the weather.As a meteorologist, I was excited to check out the museum's WPTV weather simulator and hurricane simulator. It was fascinating to see how children can experience weather concepts in a hands-on environment and gain a better understanding of the science behind storms and hurricanes.What impressed me most was how interactive everything was. Kids aren't just reading signs or watching demonstrations. They're solving problems, making decisions, using their imaginations and building confidence along the way.The museum creates an environment where learning feels more like an adventure than a lesson. Whether they're exploring future careers, practicing financial skills or learning about science and weather, children are gaining valuable experiences that can help them throughout their lives.My visit was a great reminder that some of the best learning happens when you're having fun. By rolling up their sleeves, asking questions and trying new things, kids can discover skills and interests they never knew they had.If you're looking for a family-friendly destination on the Treasure Coast that combines education, creativity and fun, the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast is definitely worth a visit.That's where I was!

entry.title: Port St. Lucie Election includes Mayors race and trash pick-up - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie Election includes Mayors race and trash pick-up    WPEC
entry.article_text: The CBS12 News I-Team has been closely following Port St. Lucie's election cycle, as there are two headline stories playing out and the future of the city is at stake. Leadership and trash are the hot-button items. On the first day of early voting in St. Lucie County, our crew visited a polling location on Rosser Blvd. We found two tents, side by side. In them, two candidates for mayor-- with such a rift between them-- the race feels like a war. The incumbent, Shannon Martin, is running to stay in office, and she says the city needs to stay on its current course. She points to how she has prioritized infrastructure repairs, like roadwork, as a reason to keep her in City Hall. Her opponent, Steven Giordano, says City Hall is corrupt and has lost touch with everyday people. When pressed on specific things he’d do differently-- he also wanted to talk about roadwork and says the city needs a new traffic study. See also: Martin County airport committee to review overnight flights and noise concerns Mayors serve four-year terms and wield significant influence in the mayor-council form of government. But trash collection is another issue getting people fired up: Should the city switch to twice-a-week pickup? FCC is the company that handles garbage collection in Port St. "I don't want to pay for something I don't need," said resident Rob Buske. Buske is making a point we have seldom heard while covering trash in the city. At many recent city council meetings, members of the public have hurled angry comments at city leaders, saying the trash pickup is sub-par. They’ve demanded an additional collection day. Ironic, then, that on the first day of early voting, everyone we asked for comment said they’d rather keep what they’ve got. The ballot question about trash collection isn't binding; it’s simply a way to poll the residents. The council might or might not go with whatever the majority of voters say. A second pick-up day would cost residents more than a hundred bucks a year, but some are adamant it's necessary. As this story comes to air and online, the election is less than 2 weeks away. Candidates for Mayor do not declare a party, and trash is a non-party matter. Here it's not Republicans vs. Democrats, but it’s somehow more personal, more granular, while also being big-picture. When can my garbage go to the curb? Who will be in charge of the city and what's their vision? The people are about to decide.

Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. We’ll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They’ll raise up their hands. And then we’re going to send (Secretary of State) Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal.”Both Rubio and Trump have been bullish on action in Cuba, with Trump previously suggesting the country would "be next” in terms of intervention abroad, following the winding down of the Iran war he has long forecast but which has not yet happened.In May, he and Rubio raised the specter of U.S. military intervention in Cuba, a renewed threat that took on greater weight after the administration announced criminal charges against the island’s former leader, Raúl Castro. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that previous U.S. presidents had considered intervening in Cuba for decades but that “it looks like I’ll be the one that does it.”RELATED STORY | Trump rules out attacking Iran before November's midterm electionsRubio told reporters separately that Cuba has been a national security threat for years because of its ties to U.S. adversaries and that Trump is intent on addressing it. While saying the Trump administration wants to resolve differences with Cuba peacefully, Rubio voiced doubts that the U.S. could reach a diplomatic resolution with the island’s current government.Moments after Trump spoke at the rally, Rubio posted on social media that “now is the time” for action on Cuba, addressing his post “to those who seek to create positive change” and urging them “to seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA.”Rubio has not addressed Cuba in depth in public for several weeks, with his last comments coming in a Sept. 29 interview with Fox News host Sean Hannity.“The truth is Cuba has already fallen. It doesn’t have a functional economy and it’s governed by people who continue to preach about some revolution that has been dead for 20 years that’s never worked,” Rubio said, without alluding to any CIA operation.“We are hopeful that Cuba will choose a different path. We are hopeful … that there will be some people in there that open their eyes to the reality of what they’re facing,” he said. “We’re never going to allow Cuba to become a base of operation against American interests or pose a threat to our national security. On that we are abundantly clear.”FOREIGN POLICY NEWS | Trump endorses embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelectionRubio and other top Trump aides have met with Cuban officials in recent months to explore possible improvements in relations. side has come away unimpressed from those talks, leading to even more sanctions imposed on the Cuban government.During his address to the United Nations General Assembly last month, Trump said Rubio — son of Cuban immigrants, who has long taken a hard line against Cuba’s socialist leadership — was “deep into negotiations with Cuba,” saying he would “not allow a haven for foreign adversaries to threaten America on our own doorstep.”Days later, Trump told reporters that he anticipated that the two countries “will make a deal,” adding, “I don’t think we’ll need the military. entry.title: Charges dropped against Indian River County school bus driver accused of child abuse - WPEC
entry.summary: Charges dropped against Indian River County school bus driver accused of child abuse    WPEC
entry.article_text: The child abuse case against an Indian River County school bus driver has ended after prosecutors declined to file formal charges. The State Attorney’s Office filed a no information in the case against Tracy Marie Alpy on Oct. 5, according to a court document. The filing listed the charge as child abuse intentional act, but did not explain why prosecutors decided not to proceed. Alpy, 65, of Sebastian, was arrested Sept. 10 after investigators reviewed surveillance video from a school bus. The allegations were described in an arrest affidavit. The alleged incident happened Aug. 24 as the bus was transporting students to after-school care. The video, recorded from 3:44 to 4:31 p.m., showed the bus waiting at Liberty Magnet School for another bus to exchange children headed to the Gifford Youth Aquatic Center and the Boys & Girls Club, according to the affidavit. Investigators said a student seated near the front of the bus repeatedly got out of the seat. Alpy was seen walking through the aisle and directing the student to sit down. The student also appeared to repeatedly raise a middle finger toward Alpy when her back was turned, the affidavit said. About 15 minutes into the video, Alpy sat on the edge of the student’s seat to keep the child from getting up, investigators said. After more children boarded and the bus began moving, the student again stood up and turned around to interact with other children. The affidavit said Alpy repeatedly told the student to sit down. When the child did not, she pulled the bus over, left the driver’s seat and approached the student. Investigators alleged she grabbed the child, forced the child back into the seat and fastened the seat belt. See also: More than 4.3 million toothpaste tubes recalled, including children's brands The child’s middle finger was extended toward Alpy, according to the affidavit. Investigators said Alpy then grabbed the student’s hand, forced it into the child’s lap and asked, Do you want me to break this finger? entry.title: Port St. Lucie police arrest suspect in hit-and-run that critically injured 63-year-old - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie police arrest suspect in hit-and-run that critically injured 63-year-old    WPEC
entry.article_text: A 60-year-old man was arrested in connection with a hit-and-run crash that critically injured a 63-year-old Port St. Lucie resident, police said. The crash happened shortly before 1 a.m. 9 on NW California Boulevard just south of the intersection with NW University Boulevard. The victim was found unconscious in the road with severe head injuries and remains in critical condition at HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Ft. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said detectives arrested Eric Saint Aude on Oct. 22 and charged him with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury. He said Aude was working as a newspaper delivery driver and was on his way to pick up newspapers when the crash happened. Investigators reviewed video, physical evidence and other leads since the crash two weeks ago. Niemczyk said a geofence warrant which sought cellphone location data from a specific area during a specific time produced a lead showing Aude's phone had pinged off cell phone towers in that area at the time of the crash. That helped detectives identify Aude as the alleged hit and run driver and the vehicles registered to him. Detectives then located and examined the man’s vehicle, which had damage consistent with striking a pedestrian, including damage to the front bumper and hood, Niemczyk said. Investigators also found presumptive positive results for blood on the vehicle. Further testing is needed. Police also recovered pieces of the vehicle’s inner fender-well fasteners at the scene, Niemczyk said. Detectives found that several matching fasteners were missing from the suspect’s vehicle. Investigators are still looking for a second vehicle that was traveling southbound near the crash. Niemczyk said distant video showed a vehicle traveling in each direction, but it was difficult to determine what happened. Police are trying to learn whether the second vehicle also struck the victim or if the driver of the second vehicle witnessed the accident. We’re very confident that the vehicle that we have and the person that we’ve arrested are responsible for the majority of what occurred, Niemczyk said. The Police Chief said the victim was in the middle of the road when he was struck, but investigators could not determine from the video whether he was walking or jogging. Police learned he often exercised at night when the weather was cooler and he was known to walk on the road and medians. "I've been doing this for 30 years. I'm not surprised by a whole lot anymore. I've seen pedestrians left for dead on the side of the road before. It doesn't make it any easier, but it doesn't surprise me at this point either. It's just difficult to understand how one human being could be so, you know, without compassion for another," Chief Niemczyk said. See also: 2 arrested in killing of transgender woman Jayla McGee in Belle Glade The victim had no identification or cellphone with him, Niemczyk said. Investigators used data from a Garmin exercise watch he was wearing to trace his route back to his house and were able to identify him. Niemczyk said the victim has significant head trauma and is unable to speak. He is expected to survive, but the chief said his quality of life may not be the same as it was before the crash. "An arrest cannot undo the harm or uncertainty imposed upon a victim, Niemczyk said, but it’s the first step in accountability. Police have not released a description of the southbound vehicle. Anyone with information is asked to call the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000. Aude is being held on $45,000 bond.

entry.title: Border patrol agents spotted near Florida polling site were there to vote, investigation finds
entry.summary: Witnesses in Florida have reported seeing federal immigration agents outside early voting sites in two separate incidents this week, raising concern because of a federal law that prohibits the presence of armed officers or troops near polling places. One of the incidents now is being described as an isolated instance of Customs and Border Protection agents attempting to vote early before they left for an out-of-state work assignment.   It started on Monday, when two CBP vehicles were spotted parked outside the busiest early voting site in Leon County, according to county election supervisor Mark S. Earley.  The vehicles stayed at the Northeast Branch Library for about 10 minutes and then left, Earley said. The election office said it did not receive calls from voters about the incident, but Earley said he filed a complaint with the FBI because voters may experience intimidation.  On Friday, Earleys office released an update saying the county sheriffs office and FBI investigated and learned the vehicles were assigned to a team of agents normally stationed in south Florida who were recently assigned to another state. As they drove north to their new assignment, they stopped in Leon County at the last polling place before leaving the state, upon realizing they would not be in Florida to vote on Election Day.  Mistakenly, the agents thought they could vote at that location, which is incorrect since they were not Leon County voters, Earley said. Upon realizing this, they immediately left the early voting site. I accept this account of the incident, as it fits the facts as I understand them, and it is in keeping with the guarantees election officials received that federal agents would not be stationed at polling sites. I am satisfied this was an isolated instance of agents attempting to vote before they left Florida. A CPB spokesperson released a statement to Scripps News: This was   not an immigration enforcement action. These CBP officers were traveling in their government vehicle from Florida to Brownsville, Texas, in support of an out-of-state deployment. While en route, the officers, who were out of uniform, briefly stopped at the polling location to ask whether they could vote early before departing the state. Election officials advised them that they were eligible to vote only in their home county. The officers thanked the staff and promptly departed. Their brief stop was solely to inquire about early-voting eligibility

It started on Monday, when two CBP vehicles were spotted parked outside the “busiest early voting site” in Leon County, according to county election supervisor Mark S. The vehicles stayed at the Northeast Branch Library for about 10 minutes and then left, Earley said. The election office said it did not receive calls from voters about the incident, but Earley said he filed a complaint with the FBI because voters may “experience intimidation.” On Friday, Earley’s office released an update saying the county sheriff’s office and FBI investigated and learned the vehicles were assigned to a team of agents normally stationed in south Florida who were recently assigned to another state. As they drove north to their new assignment, they stopped in Leon County at the last polling place before leaving the state, upon realizing they would not be in Florida to vote on Election Day. “Mistakenly, the agents thought they could vote at that location, which is incorrect since they were not Leon County voters,” Earley said. “Upon realizing this, they immediately left the early voting site. I accept this account of the incident, as it fits the facts as I understand them, and it is in keeping with the guarantees election officials received that federal agents would not be stationed at polling sites. I am satisfied this was an isolated instance of agents attempting to vote before they left Florida.”A CPB spokesperson released a statement to Scripps News:“This was not an immigration enforcement action. These CBP officers were traveling in their government vehicle from Florida to Brownsville, Texas, in support of an out-of-state deployment. While en route, the officers, who were out of uniform, briefly stopped at the polling location to ask whether they could vote early before departing the state. Election officials advised them that they were eligible to vote only in their home county. The officers thanked the staff and promptly departed. Their brief stop was solely to inquire about early-voting eligibility before deployment.""Like all eligible Americans, government personnel may exercise their right to vote. We are grateful for the sacrifices DHS personnel and their families make every day to protect the homeland and serve the American people.”RELATED STORY | Judge reins in armed ICE agents investigating voter fraudArrest outside separate polling place in another county causes concernOn Tuesday, a Key Largo community group posted video to social media showing masked and armed federal agents conducting what appeared to be a traffic stop outside the Murray Nelson Government Center. “We do not know why these agents were at this poll,” a representative of the online community group 50501 Key Largo told Scripps News. “They may have stopped there with the intention of bullying and intimidating voters, or they may have carelessly turned into the poll during pursuit of a member of the community. Either way, whether due to ignorance or intention, their presence at a poll is an outrage.” Monroe County election supervisor Sherri Hodies told Keys Weekly she spoke with CBP and was told agents were trying to pull over a suspect who decided to turn toward the government center. She said her office was investigating the incident. A CBP spokesperson gave the following statement to Scripps News:"On October 20, 2026, U.S. Border Patrol agents assigned to the Marathon Station conducted a vehicle stop on U.S. Highway 1 in Key Largo, Florida, as part of a targeted immigration enforcement operation to arrest Arwiin Pillay, a criminal illegal alien from Malaysia. entry.title: Treasure Coast water tank wins 2026 Tank of the Year - WPBF
entry.summary: Treasure Coast water tank wins 2026 Tank of the Year    WPBF
entry.article_text: A water storage tank in Fort Pierce was named the winner of the 2026 Tank of the Year. The annual contest held by Tnemec Company, Inc., a leading provider of high-performance coatings, announced the winner and Top 12 finalists on Friday. "Pretty excited," said Christian Stanley of C. Stanley Creative, the artist behind the tank. "I got the call earlier from our sales rep. He was excited to share that we were the first-place winner of Tnemec's Tank of the Year. And yeah, we're just beyond excited, and I'm excited to share that with them and with the community that they have an award-winning piece of public art there in their community." Located in Jaycee Park, the winning ground storage tank showcases a vibrant mural celebrating Florida's coastal environment and native wildlife. The mural features sea turtles, dolphins, manatees, pelicans, and tropical fish, transforming essential water infrastructure into a community landmark. The tank is protected with Tnemec's Series 1026 Enduratone coating. According to Tnemec Company, Inc., a panel of water tank enthusiasts selected the Fort Pierce tank based on its artistic value, significance to the community, and challenges encountered during the project. "For 20 years, this competition has showcased how communities can transform essential infrastructure into something truly special," said Kevin Morris, director of sales for the water tank market at Tnemec. "The creativity and community pride reflected in this year's entries are remarkable. Fort Pierce is a great example of how a water tank can become more than a functional structure. It can become a landmark that residents are proud to call their own." Digital content reporter Camila Pereira visited the tank last week as Stanley and his wife Jessica traveled from Central Florida for a couple of days to apply that UV clear coat. Stanley shared their excitement of it being in the running, and the honor they felt of being selected by Fort Pierce Utilities Authority to leave their mark where he grew up. On Friday, WPBF 25 News reconnected with Stanley and shared how he felt about the win. "We were runners-up in 2024, and that was exciting," he said. "But I was like, man, I really want to try. And I know we can make something that would win the first-place award. So, it's, you know, taken a couple of years for us to get there. But I'm excited that we were able to come some bring something together and that Fort Pierce trusted us to make something that we felt was going to be really impactful and iconic for the community there." Fort Pierce Utilities Authority shared the following statement with WPBF 25 News: "We are thrilled and deeply grateful to receive the Tank of the Year award. Thank you to everyone who voted and supported us, and to the teams who made it happen. It has been an absolute pleasure and honor for our team here at FPUA to collaborate with the artist and the Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency this summer, turning the Jaycee Park Water Tank into a Fort Pierce landmark. Rachel Tennant, FPUA Director of Public Affairs Sustainability Stanley said it's an honor to be recognized nationally, but an even bigger honor to have his work displayed at home for the community to enjoy. "I grew up in Stuart, so it was great to visit kind of my old hometown and just be back in the community and be a part of it again, and to kind of leave a footprint," he said. "This thing will kind of continue to have a life of its own beyond just the just the tank. And it'll have a bigger footprint than even what we could anticipate. So, it's really cool to get some recognition for the for the award. And we're excited to see what comes next from this." The Fort Pierce tank will be featured as January in Tnemec's 2027 water tank calendar, with the remaining finalists and nominees featured throughout the calendar. The 2026 Tank of the Year winner and Top 12 finalists are: Tank of the Year: Fort Pierce, Florida People's Choice: Detroit Lakes, Minnesota Oak Harbor, Washington Percival, Iowa South Haven, Michigan Shreveport, Louisiana Prior Lake, Minnesota Scranton, South Carolina Elloree, South Carolina Cheyenne, Wyoming Pelham, Alabama Walnut Cove, North Carolina

entry.article_text: A 22-year-old man from New York is facing charges in an organized check fraud and money laundering scheme, the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office said Friday. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office Economic Crimes Unit conducted a multi-jurisdictional investigation, culminating in the arrest of Gibrill Diallo, of the Bronx. A check mailed by a Port St. Lucie real estate company was stolen, fraudulently altered, and deposited into a bank account established using a stolen identity, the sheriff's office said. Detectives traced the stolen funds through multiple bank accounts and Zelle transfers allegedly used to conceal their origin before the money was deposited into Diallo’s personal bank account. Detectives obtained an arrest warrant charging Diallo with money laundering ($300–$20,000), scheme to defraud ($50,000 or more) and grand theft. 14, Diallo was apprehended by Canadian border authorities while attempting to enter Canada from the United States. He was detained at the Niagara County Jail in New York before being extradited to St. Lucie County on Wednesday at 9:39 p.m. Total bond was set at $30,000 for the three charges. “Our detectives followed the money, uncovered a complex financial scheme, and pursued every lead until the suspect was brought back to St. Lucie County to face justice,” Sheriff Richard Del Toro said in a statement. "This case reflects the relentless investigative work and determination of our Economic Crimes Unit. Our residents and businesses work hard for what they earn, and they deserve to know that when someone tries to take advantage of them, our detectives will go the extra mile to hold those responsible accountable.” Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

entry.title: St. Lucie County Fire Board terminates chief after calls for leadership change - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County Fire Board terminates chief after calls for leadership change    WPEC
entry.article_text: After months of controversy, the St. Lucie County Fire District Board voted Wednesday to fire longtime Chief Jeff Lee, following an emotional meeting filled with calls for change and coming less than two weeks after the firefighters' union released the results of a no-confidence vote in the district's top leaders. The meeting was packed with firefighters, union members, retirees and residents, many urged the board to change the district's leadership. Among them was Taylor Baldwin, who pointed to the dozens of supporters wearing yellow shirts throughout the room. Look at everyone wearing yellow," Baldwin told commissioners. "These are not people who want to see the fire district fail. These are people who love this department enough to stand up and beg you to save it." The decision marks the latest development in a controversy that began this summer after a hazing investigation led to the firing of three veteran firefighters and the suspension of two others . The district determined the conduct amounted to hazing, while the firefighters and their union have argued it was consensual horseplay. A Fort Pierce Police Department investigation found no criminal violations. The union is pursuing arbitration to get the three firefighters reinstated . The issue later escalated into a no-confidence vote organized by IAFF Local 1377. According to the union, 423 of its 517 dues-paying members participated. Lee received 314 no-confidence votes and 108 confidence votes, with 74.23% of participants voting they no longer had confidence in his leadership. Several speakers criticized both district leadership and the board's handling of the controversy. "You participated in this cover-up. You protected the lies and you profoundly failed the people you are elected to serve," another resident Katie told the board. Lee, who joined the department in 1997 after serving in the U.S. Navy and became the district's 14th fire chief in May 2023, was not present for Wednesday's meeting. Commissioners spent more than 30 minutes debating whether Lee should be fired with or without cause. Ultimately, the board voted to terminate him without cause, triggering the severance provisions in his contract. "I think we still have to come to the determination of what exactly the final total is of the severance," board member James Clasby said after the vote. "We will only pay what we are legally required to." Those who supported Lee's removal said the district needs a fresh start. "I feel like a weight is lifted," Commissioner Jamie Fowler said. "Firing someone is never an easy decision, regardless of all the factors that come into play. So I feel like we've sort of taken a step in the right direction." Following Lee's termination, the board voted 4-3 to appoint Deputy Chief Paul Langel as interim chief while a search for a permanent replacement begins. The board is also moving forward with hiring outside legal counsel and discussing the process for selecting the district's next chief. See also: Former PBSO dispatcher sentenced after 2023 head-on DUI crash that killed mother This is not the first time the board has faced this choice. In 2017, after a union no-confidence vote, the board accepted then Chief Buddy Emerson’s retirement effective immediately and paid him severance through the end of his contract.

entry.title: Could long fingernails, large fingers impact your vote?
entry.summary: Palm Beach County election officials are urging voters to double-check their ballots after some early voters raised concerns about selections they say did not register the way they intended on ExpressVote ballot-marking devices. Boca Raton resident Ceil Friedenthal is one of them. She voted early Tuesday at the South County Civic Center and said she noticed the issue more than once. I went to the machines and I pressed what I wanted and I used the tip of my finger, the pad of my finger, and a couple of times it defaulted to something I wasn't voting for, Friedenthal said. So if I voted for one party, it defaulted to the other, not every single time, but several. Friedenthal said in her case she was attempting to select a Democratic candidate, but the Republican candidate listed above was selected instead. The experience immediately caught her attention. I better get somebody over here to take a look at it because I don't know what to do, she recalled. Friedenthal said she called a poll worker over three separate times because she caught three selections she believed were incorrect. Each time, she said a worker helped correct the issue. For Friedenthal, making sure those selections were right mattered more than simply getting through the voting process quickly. Listen, in my opinion, as an ordinary U.S. citizen, the only thing we can do is vote, she said. There's really nothing else that we can do as an individual, so it's important that your vote be registered correctly. Friedenthal also told WPTV she had spoken with two other women who said they experienced something similar while early voting. WPTV took Friedenthal's concerns directly to Palm Beach County Supervisor of Elections Wendy Sartory Link. Link said her office had received only a couple of reports directly from voters. She stressed that when voters experience a problem, they should notify a poll worker immediately. That not only gives workers a chance to help the voter, but also allows election officials to identify the specific machine and test it. We have the ability to immediately test that machine and see if we can recreate the problem, Link said. Obviously if there is an issue, we're going to replace that machine. Link told WPTV election workers are also proactively checking the equipment. We are throughout the day, if there's not a voter at a machine, we are proactively testing them again, making sure everything's properly calibrated, Link said. To this moment, we have not been able to rec
entry.article_text: “We brought it back to our office, tried to recreate the problem using fingers, and we couldn't, so we don't think it was the machine, but again, in an abundance of caution, we did replace that one because we did know which one it was.”It was unclear which voting center that machine was located in.Elections office points to several possible factorsLink said there is no setting on an ExpressVote machine that defaults a voter to a particular candidate.Instead, Link said a voter's finger or fingernail can sometimes make contact with a different selection than intended.“If your fingernail is a little long, you might be thinking you're hitting one, but you're really hitting the selection above,” Link said. “Or if you happen to have large hands, maybe you're hitting two different types of selections.”Friedenthal disputes that explanation in her case.“No, I use the pad of my finger, not the nail itself, and I pressed twice with the pad, so the nail wasn't involved at all,” she said.While acknowledging that her fingernails are a little long, Friedenthal demonstrated to WPTV how she said she touched the screen.Link also pointed to the age and responsiveness of the ExpressVote equipment as another factor voters should keep in mind.“These machines are a little bit older. We're actually getting new ones,” Link said.She said the newer machines are expected to be used in March.“With the slower, a little bit slower technology, you may find that, like when you're used to hitting an iPhone, something, it shows up right away,” Link said. “And these may have just a slight delay from when you hit it before it acknowledges your selection.”Link said repeatedly touching the screen while waiting for it to respond could potentially result in a voter touching another selection.“So we just say give it a moment, let it make your selection, use the stylus,” Link said.The Supervisor of Elections Office is now emphasizing the use of the stylus available with the ExpressVote machines.“There's a stylus provided with every machine because with that stylus, it is, you know, it is smaller than your finger, and so you're not going to be hitting two areas at the same time,” Link said.Link said her office contacted poll workers after hearing the concerns and asked them to be more proactive about encouraging voters to use the stylus.She said styluses should be available at every machine, with extras available at check-in if one is missing.Friedenthal, however, told WPTV she did not remember seeing one when she voted.“I didn't see anything, and nobody suggested anything,” she said. “They didn't say to me when I checked in, ‘Please use the stylus.’”Voters also don't have to use an ExpressVote device.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie Election includes Mayors race and trash pick-up - cw34.com
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie Election includes Mayors race and trash pick-up    cw34.com
entry.article_text: The CBS12 News I-Team has been closely following Port St. Lucie's election cycle, as there are two headline stories playing out and the future of the city is at stake. Leadership and trash are the hot-button items. On the first day of early voting in St. Lucie County, our crew visited a polling location on Rosser Blvd. We found two tents, side by side. In them, two candidates for mayor-- with such a rift between them-- the race feels like a war. The incumbent, Shannon Martin, is running to stay in office, and she says the city needs to stay on its current course. She points to how she has prioritized infrastructure repairs, like roadwork, as a reason to keep her in City Hall. Her opponent, Steven Giordano, says City Hall is corrupt and has lost touch with everyday people. When pressed on specific things he’d do differently-- he also wanted to talk about roadwork and says the city needs a new traffic study. See also: Martin County airport committee to review overnight flights and noise concerns Mayors serve four-year terms and wield significant influence in the mayor-council form of government. But trash collection is another issue getting people fired up: Should the city switch to twice-a-week pickup? FCC is the company that handles garbage collection in Port St. "I don't want to pay for something I don't need," said resident Rob Buske. Buske is making a point we have seldom heard while covering trash in the city. At many recent city council meetings, members of the public have hurled angry comments at city leaders, saying the trash pickup is sub-par. They’ve demanded an additional collection day. Ironic, then, that on the first day of early voting, everyone we asked for comment said they’d rather keep what they’ve got. The ballot question about trash collection isn't binding; it’s simply a way to poll the residents. The council might or might not go with whatever the majority of voters say. A second pick-up day would cost residents more than a hundred bucks a year, but some are adamant it's necessary. As this story comes to air and online, the election is less than 2 weeks away. Candidates for Mayor do not declare a party, and trash is a non-party matter. Here it's not Republicans vs. Democrats, but it’s somehow more personal, more granular, while also being big-picture. When can my garbage go to the curb? Who will be in charge of the city and what's their vision? The people are about to decide.

entry.title: Martin County parents win push for school zone outside Citrus Grove Elementary
entry.summary: Martin County parents are celebrating a victory in a long battle to improve safety around their children's school. Citrus Grove Elementary School parents say the 45 mph speed limit outside the school puts their children's safety in jeopardy. They say a recently approved school zone is the first step to making Newfield Parkway a safer place for children who walk to school. On Southwest Newfield Parkway, morning and afternoon traffic is an obstacle for young students. 'It scares me,' parent Kendall George said. 'These cars are driving 45 miles an hour plus.' Kendall is among the many families who live in the Canopy Creek community across the street from Citrus Grove Elementary, so their children walk to school. Kelly Ribaudo, the PTA president and Martin County PTA Advocacy Chair, told WPTV she's spent the last five years asking the county to put in a school zone. 'We've had so many near misses with the kids just from people not paying attention,' Ribaudo said. 'Everyone has a right to a free and public education and they should be safe getting there. Our main priority should be the kids not the traffic.' At the previous Martin County Commission meeting, commissioners unanimously answered their call. 'Whatever the number is there is no price to someone getting hurt,' Martin County Commissioner Edward Ciampi said. 'You will absolutely get a school zone.' School Principal Rose Rynca told WPTV the need is greater than ever, with enrollment growing as new communities pop up in the area. 'The amount of students crossing Newfield Parkway has definitely increased,' Rynca said. 'This speed zone is going to really really improve the safety of students.' 'It's letting drivers know that, hey there's a school here, there's children crossing, and we have to slow down,' George said. WPTV's Cassandra Garcia followed up with the county on Thursday to find out the timeline for adding a school zone on SW Newfield Parkway. In a statement they said: 'Implementation of the school zone is estimated to take 6 to 9 months. The process includes retaining a consultant to complete the design, coordinating utilities, procuring materials, and completing construction. Work includes installing new school zone flashers with concrete footings, installing and relocating signs, and applying pavement markings. entry.title: New York man faces check fraud, money laundering charges in St. Lucie County - WPBF
entry.summary: New York man faces check fraud, money laundering charges in St. Lucie County    WPBF
entry.article_text: A 22-year-old man from New York is facing charges in an organized check fraud and money laundering scheme, the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office said Friday. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office Economic Crimes Unit conducted a multi-jurisdictional investigation, culminating in the arrest of Gibrill Diallo, of the Bronx. A check mailed by a Port St. Lucie real estate company was stolen, fraudulently altered, and deposited into a bank account established using a stolen identity, the sheriff's office said. Detectives traced the stolen funds through multiple bank accounts and Zelle transfers allegedly used to conceal their origin before the money was deposited into Diallo’s personal bank account. Detectives obtained an arrest warrant charging Diallo with money laundering ($300–$20,000), scheme to defraud ($50,000 or more) and grand theft. 14, Diallo was apprehended by Canadian border authorities while attempting to enter Canada from the United States. He was detained at the Niagara County Jail in New York before being extradited to St. Lucie County on Wednesday at 9:39 p.m. Total bond was set at $30,000 for the three charges. “Our detectives followed the money, uncovered a complex financial scheme, and pursued every lead until the suspect was brought back to St. Lucie County to face justice,” Sheriff Richard Del Toro said in a statement. "This case reflects the relentless investigative work and determination of our Economic Crimes Unit. Our residents and businesses work hard for what they earn, and they deserve to know that when someone tries to take advantage of them, our detectives will go the extra mile to hold those responsible accountable.” Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

entry.title: Port St. Lucie police arrest suspect in hit-and-run that left victim in ICU - WPBF
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie police arrest suspect in hit-and-run that left victim in ICU    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie have arrested a suspect in connection with a hit-and-run crash two weeks ago on NW California Boulevard that left a 63-year-old man critically injured and in the ICU. Authorities said the victim was exercising when a man, allegedly on his way to work to deliver newspapers, struck him with his car and fled the scene heading north. Surveillance footage appears to show the suspect driving away after the crash. "It’s a sad thing to see; there’s not many people that we see at this time," said a man who works nearby. Police identified the suspect as 60-year-old Eric Saint Aude. Investigators said nearby surveillance footage helped them identify the type of car involved, but the key breakthrough came from the suspect’s phone. Officers obtained a warrant to track phone pings in the area during the time of the crash, which led them to Aude. When officers located the suspect’s vehicle, they found damage on the front and blood evidence, according to police. Investigators questioned Aude about the crash. "He didn't display much emotion," said Chief Leo Niemczyk. "The victim has serious head trauma, which occurred at the point of impact." Police are still searching for a second vehicle they believe was heading south at the time of the crash. It’s rare that anything like that would happen, and the fact that it did, we need to raise awareness that we have to be more careful here," a nearby worker said. The victim remains in critical condition in the ICU, according to the chief. Police are asking anyone with information about the crash to contact them. The St. Lucie County Fire District first announced the firefighters death Saturday, saying the department was deeply saddened by the loss. Our thoughts are with the firefighters family, loved ones, and our fellow firefighters as we navigate this difficult loss, the district said. The Indian River County Sheriffs Office later said the firefighter unexpectedly passed away this morning. The Port St. Lucie Police Department also offered condolences to the firefighters family, friends and colleagues. Behind every uniform is a person who has answered a calling greater than themselves, the department said. A life devoted to service, a commitment to protecting others, and a family who makes sacrifices alongside them. Port St. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk and the department said they stand with the St. Lucie County Fire District as it mourns. When one of us grieves, we all grieve, the department said. The firefighters identity and additional details surrounding his death have not been released. The St. Lucie County Fire District said further information will be released when appropriate. WPTV has reached out to the fire district for additional details. This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

entry.title: Martin County woman honored after using CPR to save 3-year-old girl from swimming pool - WPTV
entry.summary: Martin County woman honored after using CPR to save 3-year-old girl from swimming pool    WPTV
entry.article_text: A 20-year-old Martin County woman is being honored after she used CPR to help save a 3-year-old girl she found motionless at the bottom of a swimming pool. Nearly two months after the August rescue, Martin County Fire Rescue recognized Madison Isler with the department's Heroic Heart Award.WATCH: Martin County woman honored for saving 3-year-oldThe rescue happened Aug. 23 as Isler walked past the pool at her apartment complex. She told WPTV something in the water caught her attention."It kind of looked like a smudge in your sunglasses," Isler said. "And then, so I took my glasses off, and I looked, and then I realized that it was a little girl."That little girl was 3-year-old Luna.Isler said Luna was motionless at the bottom of the swimming pool when she spotted her."I jumped in and grabbed her and pulled her out, and she was blue," Isler said.Isler called for her boyfriend to contact 911 and began CPR, using skills she said she learned at a young age from her parents, who both work in fire rescue."You just don't really think; you just kind of do, especially in a situation when it's a little baby," Isler said. "I pulled a lifeless baby out of a pool."A family friend who is a pediatric intensive care unit nurse heard the commotion and joined the rescue effort, according to the account shared by Martin County Fire Rescue."Together, they continued their life-saving efforts till finally Luna responded," Martin County Fire Rescue Chief Chad Cianciulli said.Fire rescue officials said Luna was alert and oriented by the time paramedics transported her to the hospital.Luna's mother, Christine Hernandez, said she is grateful Isler happened to be nearby when her daughter needed help."It's God's work that He put her when we needed her, like at the right place at the right time," Hernandez said.Nearly two months after that frightening day, Isler and Luna reunited at Martin County Fire Rescue headquarters.This time, they were together to celebrate the outcome of the rescue.Martin County Fire Rescue presented Isler with its Heroic Heart Award to recognize her actions."Today, on behalf of Martin County Fire Rescue and our entire community, we honor Madison for her courage to act with Martin County Fire Rescue's Heroic Heart Award," Cianciulli said during the recognition.According to the department, Isler is the first person to receive its Heroic Heart Award.For Isler, however, the recognition is secondary to seeing Luna alive and able to grow up."What means the most to me is that Luna's here with us today and that she gets to grow up and experience life," Isler said.Isler affectionately calls Luna her "unicorn baby."For Hernandez, the outcome comes with overwhelming gratitude."I'm just very, very thankful, very thankful for Maddie and her family," Hernandez said.For Isler, a skill learned years before an emergency ever happened became critical in the moment Luna needed help, turning CPR training into an action Martin County Fire Rescue says helped save a child's life.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

entry.article_text: A man was killed Thursday morning in a crash involving a semi-truck in unincorporated Indian River County, according to the Florida Highway Patrol (FHP). The crash happened around 6:45 a.m. at the intersection of 66th Avenue and 49th Street. According to FHP, a Freightliner semi-truck was attempting to make a left turn from a stop sign at westbound 49th Street onto 66th Avenue. At the same time, a Dodge Durango was traveling north in the inside lane of 66th Avenue, which had no traffic controls at the intersection. Troopers said the Freightliner entered the path of the SUV, causing the front of the Durango to collide with the left side of the semi-trailer. Both vehicles came to rest in the area of the collision. The driver of the SUV, a 60-year-old Vero Beach man, was taken to Health First's Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he was pronounced dead just after 8 a.m., according to FHP. The driver of the Freightliner, a 59-year-old Jacksonville man, was not injured. The crash remains under investigation. entry.summary: Port St. Lucie police arrest suspect in hit-and-run that left victim in ICU    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie have arrested a suspect in connection with a hit-and-run crash two weeks ago on NW California Boulevard that left a 63-year-old man critically injured and in the ICU. Authorities said the victim was exercising when a man, allegedly on his way to work to deliver newspapers, struck him with his car and fled the scene heading north. Surveillance footage appears to show the suspect driving away after the crash. "It’s a sad thing to see; there’s not many people that we see at this time," said a man who works nearby. Police identified the suspect as 60-year-old Eric Saint Aude. Investigators said nearby surveillance footage helped them identify the type of car involved, but the key breakthrough came from the suspect’s phone. Officers obtained a warrant to track phone pings in the area during the time of the crash, which led them to Aude. When officers located the suspect’s vehicle, they found damage on the front and blood evidence, according to police. Investigators questioned Aude about the crash. "He didn't display much emotion," said Chief Leo Niemczyk. "The victim has serious head trauma, which occurred at the point of impact." Police are still searching for a second vehicle they believe was heading south at the time of the crash. It’s rare that anything like that would happen, and the fact that it did, we need to raise awareness that we have to be more careful here," a nearby worker said. The victim remains in critical condition in the ICU, according to the chief. Police are asking anyone with information about the crash to contact them. entry.article_text: Lucie County firefighter-paramedic died while on duty Saturday, more than a year after his younger brother, who also served as a firefighter-paramedic, died at age 26. Lucie County Fire District announced the line-of-duty death of Austin Hodge on Saturday, Oct. 24, calling his death a profound loss to the department and the fire service community. Hodge joined the district on July 17, 2017, and served the community for more than nine years. He was assigned to Station 9. Neighboring Indian River County Fire Rescue also shared condolences following the firefighter’s unexpected death Saturday morning. Lucie County Fire District asked the public to respect Hodge’s family as they grieve. Information about memorial arrangements will be shared as details are finalized. Read more: Missing 5-year-old girl found dead in Fort Pierce body of water Brothers shared a career in firefighting Austin Hodge’s death comes more than a year after his younger brother, Jarius Hodge, also a St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic, died on July 22, 2025. The brothers shared a close bond and a passion for serving their community. This was my best friend, my twin, Austin Hodge previously told CBS12 News. We had the same hairstyle. He described Jarius as someone who loved his family and his work as a first responder. He loved going to work, loved working beside me. I loved working beside him, Austin said. He always pushed me to keep going. He was someone who loved his family, his community and his country. Family sought accountability after Jarius’ death In an interview with CBS12 News , Austin said Jarius became ill after catching the flu from a patient at work in July 2025. Austin said his younger brother went to Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital in Port St. Lucie on July 22, struggling to breathe, but died hours later. He alleged that medical staff made critical errors in treating his brother, including taking three attempts to intubate him. He said Jarius had been healthy before becoming ill. Austin also spoke publicly about Florida’s medical malpractice laws, arguing that restrictions on who can pursue certain wrongful-death claims prevented his family from seeking legal accountability for Jarius’ death. This is unjust, and it's been going on for too long, Austin said in the earlier interview. He emphasized that his family was seeking accountability rather than financial compensation. For me personally, for my family, this has nothing to do with any type of dollar, he said. We just want those physicians to be held accountable. The circumstances surrounding Austin Hodge’s death have not been released. Lucie County Fire District said additional information about ways to honor his service will be shared in coordination with his family.

entry.title: St. Lucie Fire District identifies firefighter who died on duty
entry.summary: A St. Lucie County Fire District firefighter who died unexpectedly Saturday morning has been identified as Austin Hodge, a firefighter paramedic and nine-year veteran of the department. The fire district announced Saturday evening that Hodge, who was assigned to Firehouse 9, died while on duty earlier in the day. 'Today, our St. Lucie County Fire District family mourns the loss of one of our own,' the district said in a statement. In the hours following his death, firefighters, the department's Honor Guard and fellow first responders gathered to honor Hodge and support one another. The district said the response reflected the strong bond shared throughout the fire service. The district thanked the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Fort Pierce Police Department, Port St. Lucie Police Department and peer support teams from Martin and Indian River counties for providing assistance and standing alongside firefighters during the difficult day. 'Together, they offered strength, compassion, and support while ensuring Austin was honored with the dignity and respect he deserves,' the district said. The district said its thoughts are with Hodge's family, loved ones and everyone who served alongside him. 'We are deeply grateful to our fellow first responders and community for the outpouring of support during this tremendous loss,' the district said. 'Today and always, we stand together.' WPTV has reached out to the fire district for additional information. This remains a developing story.

entry.article_text: A firefighter/paramedic died Saturday morning while on duty, one year after his brother, also with the St. Lucie County Fire District, passed away, the agency said. Austin Hodge, 34, joined the St. Lucie County Fire District on July 17, 2017. He was assigned to Station 9 in Fort Pierce. A procession of firefighters and personnel from other agencies went from HCA Lawnwood Hospital to the morgue in Fort Pierce on Saturday morning. His brother, Jarius Hodge, died on July 22, 2025, after falling ill at work at Station 3. His family said he had the flu, felt weak and was later rushed to the hospital, where he died hours later. People gathered on May 30 to celebrate what would have been his 27th birthday with a cookout and balloon release. Austin Hodge told WPBF at the time: "He was a quiet leader, and we take a lot from him. He was my younger brother, but I looked up to him in many ways to keep me poised, keep me patient. And I think that's what he's teaching everybody today." In June, another firefighter, Connor Whitehead, 21, died on May 31 but the cause of death wasn't released. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 There are 20 fire stations and 523 firefighters in the county, according to the agency's website. The brotherhood of the fire service extends far beyond the walls of a fire station. It is a bond built on trust, shared experiences, and an unwavering commitment to one another. "Today, that bond was especially evident through the incredible support of the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Fort Pierce Police Department, Port St. Lucie Police Department, and peer support teams from Martin and Indian River counties. entry.title: Martin County parents win push for a school zone outside Citrus Grove Elementary - WPTV
entry.summary: Martin County parents win push for a school zone outside Citrus Grove Elementary    WPTV
entry.article_text: Martin County parents are celebrating a victory in a long battle to improve safety around their children's school.Citrus Grove Elementary School parents say the 45 mph speed limit outside the school puts their children's safety in jeopardy. They say a recently approved school zone is the first step to making Newfield Parkway a safer place for children who walk to school.On Southwest Newfield Parkway, morning and afternoon traffic is an obstacle for young students."It scares me," parent Kendall George said. "These cars are driving 45 miles an hour plus."Kendall is among the many families who live in the Canopy Creek community across the street from Citrus Grove Elementary, so their children walk to school. Kelly Ribaudo, the PTA president and Martin County PTA Advocacy Chair, told WPTV she's spent the last five years asking the county to put in a school zone."We've had so many near misses with the kids just from people not paying attention," Ribaudo said. "Everyone has a right to a free and public education and they should be safe getting there. Our main priority should be the kids not the traffic."At the previous Martin County Commission meeting, commissioners unanimously answered their call."Whatever the number is there is no price to someone getting hurt," Martin County Commissioner Edward Ciampi said. "You will absolutely get a school zone."School Principal Rose Rynca told WPTV the need is greater than ever, with enrollment growing as new communities pop up in the area."The amount of students crossing Newfield Parkway has definitely increased," Rynca said. "This speed zone is going to really really improve the safety of students.""It's letting drivers know that, hey there's a school here, there's children crossing, and we have to slow down," George said.WPTV's Cassandra Garcia followed up with the county on Thursday to find out the timeline for adding a school zone on SW Newfield Parkway. In a statement they said:In the meantime, these parents are asking drivers to be cautious."Slow down if you see a school — even if there's not a school zone sign, slow down," Ribaudo said.With a school zone on the horizon, these parents said the next step is getting better street lighting.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie police: Suspect's car had blood, damage after hit-and-run - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie police: Suspect's car had blood, damage after hit-and-run    WPEC
entry.article_text: A 60-year-old man was arrested in connection with a hit-and-run crash that critically injured a 63-year-old Port St. Lucie resident, police said. The crash happened shortly before 1 a.m. 9 on NW California Boulevard just south of the intersection with NW University Boulevard. The victim was found unconscious in the road with severe head injuries and remains in critical condition at HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Ft. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said detectives arrested Eric Saint Aude on Oct. 22 and charged him with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury. He said Aude was working as a newspaper delivery driver and was on his way to pick up newspapers when the crash happened. Investigators reviewed video, physical evidence and other leads since the crash two weeks ago. Niemczyk said a geofence warrant which sought cellphone location data from a specific area during a specific time produced a lead showing Aude's phone had pinged off cell phone towers in that area at the time of the crash. That helped detectives identify Aude as the alleged hit and run driver and the vehicles registered to him. Detectives then located and examined the man’s vehicle, which had damage consistent with striking a pedestrian, including damage to the front bumper and hood, Niemczyk said. Investigators also found presumptive positive results for blood on the vehicle. Further testing is needed. Police also recovered pieces of the vehicle’s inner fender-well fasteners at the scene, Niemczyk said. Detectives found that several matching fasteners were missing from the suspect’s vehicle. Investigators are still looking for a second vehicle that was traveling southbound near the crash. Niemczyk said distant video showed a vehicle traveling in each direction, but it was difficult to determine what happened. Police are trying to learn whether the second vehicle also struck the victim or if the driver of the second vehicle witnessed the accident. We’re very confident that the vehicle that we have and the person that we’ve arrested are responsible for the majority of what occurred, Niemczyk said. The Police Chief said the victim was in the middle of the road when he was struck, but investigators could not determine from the video whether he was walking or jogging. Police learned he often exercised at night when the weather was cooler and he was known to walk on the road and medians. "I've been doing this for 30 years. I'm not surprised by a whole lot anymore. I've seen pedestrians left for dead on the side of the road before. It doesn't make it any easier, but it doesn't surprise me at this point either. It's just difficult to understand how one human being could be so, you know, without compassion for another," Chief Niemczyk said. See also: 2 arrested in killing of transgender woman Jayla McGee in Belle Glade The victim had no identification or cellphone with him, Niemczyk said. Investigators used data from a Garmin exercise watch he was wearing to trace his route back to his house and were able to identify him. Niemczyk said the victim has significant head trauma and is unable to speak. He is expected to survive, but the chief said his quality of life may not be the same as it was before the crash. "An arrest cannot undo the harm or uncertainty imposed upon a victim, Niemczyk said, but it’s the first step in accountability. Police have not released a description of the southbound vehicle. Anyone with information is asked to call the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000. Aude is being held on $45,000 bond.

entry.article_text: Lucie police have arrested a suspect in connection with a hit-and-run crash that critically injured a 63-year-old resident earlier this month, the department said Friday. The crash happened about 12:56 a.m. 9 near NW University Boulevard and NW California Boulevard. The victim was found unconscious in the roadway with severe head injuries and taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where the victim remained in critical condition, police said. Detectives reviewed surveillance video and gathered additional evidence as they worked to identify the vehicle or vehicles involved and those who left the scene, according to the department. On Thursday, deputies believed they were looking for two vehicles. See also: Grand jury indicts man in fatal shooting of West Palm Beach minister Akeem Moore Police planned to provide more information at a news conference scheduled for 1 p.m. Friday at department headquarters. The release did not identify the suspect or list any charges.
