entry.article_text: The Justice Department on Friday ordered California election officials to identify suspected noncitizens on voter rolls and set aside their mail-in ballots — warning that officials who knowingly count ballots cast by noncitizens could face criminal liability.The action marks an escalation in the Trump administration’s efforts to scrutinize voter rolls ahead of the midterm elections as it continues to double down on claims of voter fraud, fueled by President Donald Trump’s baseless allegations of widespread election cheating.Letters sent to California county election officials asked them to work with the Justice Department and Department of Homeland Security to “identify who on the accompanying list is a citizen and who is not.”“If persons knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime,” First Assistant US Attorney Bill Essayli said to San Bernardino County officials in a letter, which was seen by CNN.Santa Cruz County received a letter with 81 names, which it said is still under review. So far, officials have found most of the records belong to voters who are no longer actively registered in the county, County Clerk Tricia Webber told CNN on Saturday.“They are either canceled or inactive records,” Webber said. At least one name has never been registered in the county, Webber added.RELATED STORY | DOJ threatens California with legal action over claim of noncitizens on voter rollsRural Modoc County also received a list with one voter who appears to have never been registered in the county, according to an election official.Marin County, north of San Francisco, received a list of 48 “likely aliens,” according to a letter seen by CNN. Nearby Solano County said its list had 170 names.Nevada County has reviewed a list of 10 names and is “confident that state and federal laws are being followed,” according to a statement shared with CNN.Santa Clara, Napa, Butte and Amador counties confirmed they have also received a letter but Riverside County told CNN as of Saturday afternoon, it had not.“All of this is simply meant to raise huge doubts about the integrity of this election,” John Tuteur, registrar of voters for Napa County, told The Associated Press.Tuteur said two uniformed Department of Homeland Security officers delivered a letter with 42 names to his office late on Friday afternoon, according to the AP.“We’re not changing anything we’re doing. We’re proceeding with the election,” Tuteur added.The letters follow a demand earlier this month from acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter, who gave Los Angeles County and California Secretary of State Shirley Weber 48 hours to review a federal list of suspected noncitizens who had been sent mail-in ballots. McCotter threatened to seek “emergency relief” if officials did not comply.The earlier letter, sent October 13, included a password-protected thumb drive containing names of people the administration “believes are likely non-citizens” who had been sent ballots for the November election. It asked officials to temporarily set aside ballots from people whose citizenship could not be confirmed, rather than cancel their registrations.“Maintaining accurate voter registration records is a fundamental responsibility of our office,” Los Angeles County Clerk Dean C. Logan said in a statement, after receiving the October 13 letter.“Federal and state laws are clear on how voter eligibility is established – and any action to remove a voter from eligibility must be based on verifiable information, not assertions of unconfirmed data matching.”RELATED STORY | Records show ICE reviewed tens of millions of voter records looking for noncitizen votersLogan sent an email to the California Association of Clerks and Election Officials on Friday, saying the latest DOJ letter includes a “posture of intimidation and threats leveled against local election officials just twelve days before the election.”Logan said that the DOJ “misrepresents” the county’s response to the earlier letter as “resistance to a civil lawsuit that was not yet filed” and is now giving an “unenforceable 48-hour deadline” to provide information that it has previously “obtained through subpoenas.”The Justice Department last week sued California and Los Angeles County, seeking to prevent officials from counting more than 20,000 mail-in ballots associated with people the government believes are likely noncitizens. A federal judge scheduled a hearing on the case for next week, but the Justice Department on Friday asked the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals to intervene before then.“Every minute of processing that occurs without segregating the ballots of suspected ineligible voters causes untraceable disenfranchisement and dilution of the votes of United States citizens,” the motion noted.Logan, in Friday’s email, said the DOJ provided in its letter a list of the 20,000 noncitizens it believes are on the county’s voter rolls. But a review of those names, he said, showed that many “were associated with addresses throughout California, not solely within Los Angeles County.”A similar legal battle is unfolding in Alaska, where the Trump administration is seeking to block certification of the state’s Senate race under certain circumstances if Republican Sen. The race is being closely watched as Democrats seek to regain control of the Senate.The administration has repeatedly alleged that hundreds of thousands of noncitizens are on voter rolls. Only US citizens are allowed to vote in federal and state elections. But some states, including California, have passed laws allowing noncitizens to cast ballots in local or school board elections.In August, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said his department had identified 250,000 people it believed were noncitizens and registered to vote in four states — California, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Nevada — by comparing voter-registration records with federal immigration data.But the administration’s claims have faced scrutiny, and some initial findings have not held up under further review. In Nevada, for example, DHS told state officials that its initial finding of 15,900 potentially noncitizen registrants was preliminary and unvetted, and that it had confirmed only 185 through manual review.Last month, Nevada officials told DHS their subsequent review found that all 185 were US citizens, a conclusion the federal agency disputes.In response to Friday’s letters, California Sen. Alex Padilla, a ranking member of the Senate Rules and Administration Committee with oversight over federal elections, called the administration “afraid and desperate.”“Trump’s DOJ has not provided any evidence for their claims of massive voter fraud. They’ve admitted that the data they point to is inaccurate and unreliable. No matter how many lawsuits they file or how many election officials they threaten, they do not have the authority to interfere,” Padilla said.“The Trump administration is afraid and desperate. Their attempts to take over our elections will fail. Election officials: We have your back. California: Your vote is your voice. Use it and let’s hold this administration accountable.”The-CNN-Wire™ & © 2026 Cable News Network, Inc., a Warner Bros.

entry.title: Missing 5-year-old found dead in Fort Pierce, police say
entry.summary: A 5-year-old girl who was reported missing in Fort Pierce was found dead in a nearby body of water Saturday afternoon, according to the Fort Pierce Police Department. Police identified the child as Mayra Glory Odelus. Mayra was reported missing at approximately 11:39 a.m. Saturday, police said. In an update issued at 4:13 p.m., the department said officers were on scene after Mayra was located deceased in a nearby body of water. Our deepest condolences are with Mayras family and loved ones during this tragic time, police said. Authorities have not released additional details about the circumstances surrounding her death or where she was found.

entry.summary: St. Lucie County Fire District confirms firefighter's death; Treasure Coast agencies mourn the loss    WFLX
entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District firefighter who died unexpectedly Saturday morning has been identified as Austin Hodge, a firefighter paramedic and nine-year veteran of the department. The fire district announced Saturday evening that Hodge, who was assigned to Firehouse 9, died while on duty earlier in the day. Lucie County Fire District family mourns the loss of one of our own," the district said in a statement. In the hours following his death, firefighters, the department's Honor Guard and fellow first responders gathered to honor Hodge and support one another. The district said the response reflected the strong bond shared throughout the fire service. The district thanked the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Fort Pierce Police Department, Port St. Lucie Police Department and peer support teams from Martin and Indian River counties for providing assistance and standing alongside firefighters during the difficult day. "Together, they offered strength, compassion, and support while ensuring Austin was honored with the dignity and respect he deserves," the district said. The district said its thoughts are with Hodge's family, loved ones and everyone who served alongside him. "We are deeply grateful to our fellow first responders and community for the outpouring of support during this tremendous loss," the district said. "Today and always, we stand together." WPTV has reached out to the fire district for additional information. This remains a developing story.

entry.summary: Bronx man accused in St. Lucie County check fraud scheme arrested at Canadian border    cw34.com
entry.article_text: A 20-year-old Bronx, New York, man was extradited to St. Lucie County after Canadian border authorities arrested him while he was trying to enter Canada , the Sheriff’s Office said. Gibrill Diallo faces charges of money laundering, a scheme to defraud of $50,000 or more and grand theft in connection with an investigation into a check stolen from a Port St. Lucie real estate company, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office . The agency said the check was altered and deposited into a bank account opened using a stolen identity. Detectives traced the funds through multiple bank accounts and Zelle transfers before they were deposited into Diallo’s personal bank account, the Sheriff’s Office said. Authorities arrested Diallo on Oct. He was held at the Niagara County Jail in New York before being extradited to St. 21, according to the agency. See also: Boynton woman held on $20M bond, accused of selling high-THC products, money laundering Sheriff Richard Del Toro said detectives followed the money and pursued leads across jurisdictions.

entry.title: St. Lucie County Fire District confirms firefighter’s death - WPBF
entry.summary: St. Lucie County Fire District confirms firefighter’s death    WPBF
entry.article_text: A firefighter/paramedic died Saturday morning while on duty, one year after his brother, also with the St. Lucie County Fire District, passed away, the agency said. Austin Hodge, 34, joined the St. Lucie County Fire District on July 17, 2017. He was assigned to Station 9 in Fort Pierce. A procession of firefighters and personnel from other agencies went from HCA Lawnwood Hospital to the morgue in Fort Pierce on Saturday morning. His brother, Jarius Hodge, died on July 22, 2025, after falling ill at work at Station 3. His family said he had the flu, felt weak and was later rushed to the hospital, where he died hours later. People gathered on May 30 to celebrate what would have been his 27th birthday with a cookout and balloon release. Austin Hodge told WPBF at the time: "He was a quiet leader, and we take a lot from him. He was my younger brother, but I looked up to him in many ways to keep me poised, keep me patient. And I think that's what he's teaching everybody today." In June, another firefighter, Connor Whitehead, 21, died on May 31 but the cause of death wasn't released. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 There are 20 fire stations and 523 firefighters in the county, according to the agency's website. Information regarding memorial arrangements and opportunities to honor Hodge's service iwll be shared in coordination with his family as details are finalized. "His death is a profound loss to the St. Lucie County Fire District and the fire service community," the agency said. "The District extends its heartfelt condolences to Hodge’s family, friends, and fellow firefighters during this difficult time." Several agencies offered their condolences, including Port St. Lucie Fire Rescue, Fort Pierce Police Officers Association, Port St. Lucie Police Department, Indian River County Sheriff's Office, Indian River County Emergency Services Department, Indian River County Fire Rescue, Palm Beach County Fire Rescue, Riviera Beach Fire Rescue. https://www.facebook.com/stluciesheriff/posts/pfbid0cPopWYk7mLx2z6QfJqkd99ZUoP9dWGSRx3Y7yjuN21oLAqBUmr6n8RYoUYP9RGaZl The St. Lucie agency thanked other agencieson Facebook. https://www.facebook.com/slcfd/posts/pfbid02FGoAgmLryFmnkCkLqRQfwhzpBpGAX3Bh285A6jFqKysGajonPUPDHeKjxdFm2KQvl "In the hours following this heartbreaking loss, our firefighters, Honor Guard, and public safety partners came together to honor our fallen brother and stand alongside one another during an incredibly difficult time. The brotherhood of the fire service extends far beyond the walls of a fire station. It is a bond built on trust, shared experiences, and an unwavering commitment to one another. "Today, that bond was especially evident through the incredible support of the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Fort Pierce Police Department, Port St. Lucie Police Department, and peer support teams from Martin and Indian River counties. "Together, they offered strength, compassion, and support while ensuring Austin was honored with the dignity and respect he deserves. Our hearts are with Austin’s family, loved ones, and everyone who had the privilege of serving alongside him. We are deeply grateful to our fellow first responders and community for the outpouring of support during this tremendous loss." Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

entry.title: 11-year-old, other minors among 11 shot near Florida A&M University stadium
entry.summary: A shooting near a college stadium in Tallahassee, Florida, left 11 people with gunshot wounds Saturday night, officials said. Among the victims near Florida AM University were six juveniles, including an 11-year-old, Tallahassee Police Chief Lawrence Revell told reporters at a news conference late Saturday. No deaths had been reported, police said. The shooting took place just hours after a homecoming football game at the stadium, where the ArkansasPine Bluff Golden Lions beat the Florida AM Rattlers 31-28. Its unclear whether the shooting was connected to the game. In addition to those shot, a victims grandmother was injured while fleeing the scene near Florida AMs Bragg Memorial Stadium. As of Sunday morning, five victims had been released from the hospital, while six remained hospitalized, Tallahassee police said. Of those still being treated, one was in critical condition, police said. There have been at least 383 mass shootings in the US so far this year, according to the Gun Violence Archive, which, like CNN, defines a mass shooting as one in which four or more people are shot, not including the shooter. The police chief told reporters the shooting likely stemmed from an altercation between two to three individuals and that the departments Violent Crimes Unit would lead the ongoing investigation. Tallahassee police detectives have reviewed digital evidence and canvassed the area, police said in a statement Sunday. We need our communitys help. No detail is too small, and no piece of information should go unreported, the statement said. If you know something, please share it with our detectives. Your information could be the key to holding those responsible accountable. Investigators established a tip hotline and a link for people to submit evidence. As our detectives work to determine exactly what happened and identify those responsible, we remain committed to getting answers for these families. Tallahassee Mayor John Dailey called the incident a truly horrific and heartbreaking tragedy. Tonight and in the days ahead, the FAMU family is not alone. Our entire community stands with you, Dailey wrote on X. Florida AM said in a statement late Saturday it was aware of an incident that occurred near campus on Perry Street on the evening of October 24. Our hearts go out to the victims and all those affected by this tragic incident. entry.article_text: Lucie County firefighter-paramedic died while on duty Saturday, more than a year after his younger brother, who also served as a firefighter-paramedic, died at age 26. Lucie County Fire District announced the line-of-duty death of Austin Hodge on Saturday, Oct. 24, calling his death a profound loss to the department and the fire service community. Hodge joined the district on July 17, 2017, and served the community for more than nine years. He was assigned to Station 9. Neighboring Indian River County Fire Rescue also shared condolences following the firefighter’s unexpected death Saturday morning. Lucie County Fire District asked the public to respect Hodge’s family as they grieve. Information about memorial arrangements will be shared as details are finalized. Read more: Missing 5-year-old girl found dead in Fort Pierce body of water Brothers shared a career in firefighting Austin Hodge’s death comes more than a year after his younger brother, Jarius Hodge, also a St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic, died on July 22, 2025. The brothers shared a close bond and a passion for serving their community. This was my best friend, my twin, Austin Hodge previously told CBS12 News. We had the same hairstyle. He described Jarius as someone who loved his family and his work as a first responder. He loved going to work, loved working beside me. I loved working beside him, Austin said. He always pushed me to keep going. He was someone who loved his family, his community and his country. Family sought accountability after Jarius’ death In an interview with CBS12 News , Austin said Jarius became ill after catching the flu from a patient at work in July 2025. Austin said his younger brother went to Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital in Port St. Lucie on July 22, struggling to breathe, but died hours later. He alleged that medical staff made critical errors in treating his brother, including taking three attempts to intubate him. He said Jarius had been healthy before becoming ill. Austin also spoke publicly about Florida’s medical malpractice laws, arguing that restrictions on who can pursue certain wrongful-death claims prevented his family from seeking legal accountability for Jarius’ death. This is unjust, and it's been going on for too long, Austin said in the earlier interview. He emphasized that his family was seeking accountability rather than financial compensation. For me personally, for my family, this has nothing to do with any type of dollar, he said. We just want those physicians to be held accountable. The circumstances surrounding Austin Hodge’s death have not been released. Lucie County Fire District said additional information about ways to honor his service will be shared in coordination with his family.

entry.article_text: A 22-year-old man from New York is facing charges in an organized check fraud and money laundering scheme, the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office said Friday. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office Economic Crimes Unit conducted a multi-jurisdictional investigation, culminating in the arrest of Gibrill Diallo, of the Bronx. A check mailed by a Port St. Lucie real estate company was stolen, fraudulently altered, and deposited into a bank account established using a stolen identity, the sheriff's office said. Detectives traced the stolen funds through multiple bank accounts and Zelle transfers allegedly used to conceal their origin before the money was deposited into Diallo’s personal bank account. Detectives obtained an arrest warrant charging Diallo with money laundering ($300–$20,000), scheme to defraud ($50,000 or more) and grand theft. 14, Diallo was apprehended by Canadian border authorities while attempting to enter Canada from the United States. He was detained at the Niagara County Jail in New York before being extradited to St. Lucie County on Wednesday at 9:39 p.m. Total bond was set at $30,000 for the three charges. “Our detectives followed the money, uncovered a complex financial scheme, and pursued every lead until the suspect was brought back to St. Lucie County to face justice,” Sheriff Richard Del Toro said in a statement. "This case reflects the relentless investigative work and determination of our Economic Crimes Unit. Our residents and businesses work hard for what they earn, and they deserve to know that when someone tries to take advantage of them, our detectives will go the extra mile to hold those responsible accountable.” Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

entry.title: Detainees allege abusive, unconstitutional conditions inside 'Deportation Depot' immigration facility
entry.summary: Civil rights advocates are investigating what they call abusive conditions inside a state-run immigration detention facility, telling me they've received a surge of complaints after the Everglades detention camp known as 'Alligator Alcatraz' closed over the summer. When Alligator Alcatraz shut down over the summer, it didn't end Florida's involvement in immigration detention. There's a second state-run facility that's been open for a year in a former prison about 50 minutes west of Jacksonville. Because its location is less controversial than the Everglades, it's flown largely under the radar. But now, detainees are speaking up about the alleged horrors inside what state officials have dubbed 'Deportation Depot.' 'It's insane. There's no other word [to describe the situation] than insanity. Just how bad these conditions were,' said a man who asked that we hide his face and refer to him by his middle name, Ryan. He fears being publicly identified could jeopardize his still-pending immigration case. 'I'm happy to be here, and I'm grateful, and obviously I'm gonna do everything I can to complete my immigration journey, and hopefully I can put this behind me,' Ryan said. I learned from the American Civil Liberties Union and confirmed through federal court records and local news reports that Ryan was detained by immigration authorities in late February and sent to the Baker Correctional Institution in Sanderson, where he spent four months. According to the most recent ICE detention data from July, roughly a thousand migrant men are housed at Baker. The ACLU put the number even higher, at about 1,200, during Ryan's stay. 'They were businessmen, entrepreneurs, paramedics, people that had been in the military. It was just, it was just everyone,' Ryan said. Ryan told me about 100 people in his dorm, with four working toilets and four working showers. He described the bathrooms as filthy, toiletries as scarce, and extreme heat as a persistent problem. 'We had one small AC unit in the corner of the room, which didn't work because the windows were smashed open anyway and kind of had been left broken,' Ryan said. 'We had black mold, brown mold. Like I said, those infestations of creatures. We had spiders, fire ants, cockroaches, bugs of all description.' On Oct. 8, the ACLU, Southern Poverty Law Center and Americans for Immigrant Justice sent a demand letter decrying the alleged conditions inside Baker to the state of Florida, the federal government, and the private co
entry.article_text: The advocacy groups wrote that they have conducted dozens of interviews with people currently or recently detained at the facility, their loved ones, and attorneys representing people detained there, and that those interviews confirm the widespread abuses occurring there.The letter identifies seven categories of abuse: life-threatening medical neglect; lack of adequate food and clean drinking water; excessive, life-threatening heat; squalid, unsanitary, and unsafe living conditions; deprivation of necessities for physical, mental, and emotional wellbeing, such as sleep, family visitation, and outdoor recreation; verbal and physical abuse and retaliation; and lack of access to the courts and to confidential communications with attorneys.On food and water, the letter alleges that the facility fails to provide people detained there with enough nutritious food, with detained people reporting receiving only "extremely small, infant-sized food portions that are not filling" and lacking adequate protein or nutrients. It states that people are losing dangerous amounts of weight, citing examples including one person who lost 29 pounds in less than two months and another who lost 44 pounds over seven months. On water, it alleges that the facility is failing to provide adequate access to clean drinking water, that most of the time the only drinking water available is from the dorms' visibly rusty water fountains, and that newly detained people are quickly warned not to drink from those fountains because many have gotten sick from drinking that water.Ryan said he and other detainees often spent part of their brief mealtimes drinking as much water as they could from the cafeteria, which he said provided clean drinking water."You had no alternative sometimes than just to kind of take your chances with the water (in the dorm)," Ryan said. "It had a very strong metallic taste, and as soon as it settled in your stomach, it felt like something was kicking and punching your stomach.""It's very much a cruel facility that's designed to deny people every aspect of humanity and decency and dignity, and is designed to make people physically weak, mentally weak, and just pressured to agree to the point— where they agree to self deportation," said ACLU attorney Amy Godshall, who wrote the letter.The letter alleges that this pressure is deliberate, stating there is evidence of a deliberate effort to make immigration detention unbearable so that people abandon their rights and accept departure or removal, and that whether intentional or not, these abusive living conditions are punitive and unconstitutional. Ryan told me he was pulled aside on three or four occasions by guards and asked to sign forms consenting to his deportation."The question that a lot of us had is, well, if we were deportable, then why would we have to sign this document to make us deportable?" Ryan said.I sent detailed questions about the allegations to the Florida Division of Emergency Management, ICE and the Department of Homeland Security, and all three private contractors named in the letter.

entry.title: From Jensen Beach to Louisiana Tech: Andrew Burnette gets one more shot at college football
entry.summary: A young man from the Midwest with South Florida roots describes how Andrew Burnette moved from Michigan around the age of 12 and found home on the football field in Martin County. 'I played football my whole life, and I can say football is a little harder in Florida than it is in Michigan,' said Burnette. WATCH BELOW: Local football standout gets one more shot at college football From Jensen Beach to Louisiana Tech: Andrew Burnette gets one more shot at college football While football was his first sport, during his high school days at Jensen Beach High School, he fell in love with takedowns and pins. 'I wasn't zoned for that school, but I went there for wrestling originally; that was my first passion,' said Burnette. While he was doing well in wrestling, football kept calling to him. 'Moving through high school, I knew football was what I wanted to do,' said Burnette. He established himself as a force at Jensen Beach High School, but he didn't receive much interest from college football programs, similar to many Treasure Coast football recruits. 'One of my main struggles was recruitment out of high school, because I felt like our area was a little under-recruited,' said Burnette. Betting on himself, he decided to play at Highland Community College in Kansas. Burnette played in nine games and rushed for 340 yards and two touchdowns, but he still wasn't on any other college football program's radar. 'I transferred to Independence Junior College, and I was cut from the team,' said Burnette. entry.title: St. Lucie County Fire District confirms firefighter's death; Treasure Coast agencies mourn the loss - WFLX
entry.summary: St. Lucie County Fire District confirms firefighter's death; Treasure Coast agencies mourn the loss    WFLX
entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District firefighter who died unexpectedly Saturday morning has been identified as Austin Hodge, a firefighter paramedic and nine-year veteran of the department. The fire district announced Saturday evening that Hodge, who was assigned to Firehouse 9, died while on duty earlier in the day. Lucie County firefighter dies on duty "Today, our St. Lucie County Fire District family mourns the loss of one of our own," the district said in a statement. In the hours following his death, firefighters, the department's Honor Guard and fellow first responders gathered to honor Hodge and support one another. The district said the response reflected the strong bond shared throughout the fire service. The district thanked the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Fort Pierce Police Department, Port St. Lucie Police Department and peer support teams from Martin and Indian River counties for providing assistance and standing alongside firefighters during the difficult day. "Together, they offered strength, compassion, and support while ensuring Austin was honored with the dignity and respect he deserves," the district said. The district said its thoughts are with Hodge's family, loved ones and everyone who served alongside him. "We are deeply grateful to our fellow first responders and community for the outpouring of support during this tremendous loss," the district said. "Today and always, we stand together." The tragedy comes more than a year after the community mourned the sudden loss of his brother, Jarius Hodge , 26, who was also a St. Lucie County firefighter and died from septic shock in July 2025. WPTV has reached out to the fire district for additional information. This remains a developing story.

entry.title: Indiantown council sets November 5 meeting to consider data center moratorium - WPEC
entry.summary: Indiantown council sets November 5 meeting to consider data center moratorium    WPEC
entry.article_text: The Village of Indiantown is moving forward with plans to consider a temporary moratorium on large-scale data center development, but three sites already in the works would be excluded from the proposed restrictions. During Thursday night's Village Council meeting, members voted to schedule a special meeting for November 5, when they will take up the first reading of an ordinance that would temporarily halt new data center development applications, reviews, approvals and the start of construction on projects subject to the restrictions. The council also identified three sites that would be excluded from the proposed moratorium: Project Silver Fox Associated with Silver Fox 606 LLC. Project Growler Associated with Warfield 18 LLC. Tesoro Groves A large, planned development associated with Florida Power & Light property. The exemptions would allow those sites to remain outside the proposed restrictions while the village considers how to regulate future large-scale data center development. Council seeks negotiations and an end to litigation Council members also called for lawsuits surrounding the developments to be dropped as the village seeks to negotiate with developers. The request comes amid ongoing legal disputes involving data center development in Indiantown. Silver Fox 606 LLC filed a lawsuit against the village challenging its handling of an appeal involving the project's development approvals. A Martin County circuit judge issued an injunction earlier this month blocking a planned zoning appeals hearing while the legal dispute proceeds. It remains unclear whether the developers will agree to dismiss pending litigation or what conditions could be attached to any negotiations. Councilwoman pushes for community benefits See also: Palm Beach County district says 12 K-8 schools made Florida’s top 100 in new rankings During Thursday's meeting, Councilwoman Vernestine Williams-Palmer expressed frustration over the lengthy discussions surrounding data centers and emphasized the need to secure financial benefits for Indiantown residents. Palmer said the village needs additional tax revenue and investments in community infrastructure, particularly improvements to its water system. We need all the things, all the things that's been promised. We need the community impacts. We need all of that," Palmer said, according to a transcript of the meeting. She also encouraged residents to identify improvements they would like developers to help fund, mentioning a proposed $3 million gymnasium as one example discussed. Palmer said she has visited a data center in Texas and spoken with facility managers as part of her efforts to better understand the industry. While acknowledging that residents remain divided over data center development, Palmer said council members are working to protect the community's interests. The November 5 special meeting will focus on the first reading of the proposed moratorium ordinance. If ultimately adopted, the measure would temporarily restrict new large-scale data center applications and development activity covered by the ordinance while excluding the three identified sites. The length of the proposed moratorium and the precise conditions governing the exemptions still need to be established. The council's October 22 vote scheduled the special meeting and addressed the proposed exclusions. It did not enact the moratorium. Village leaders are expected to continue discussions over development restrictions, infrastructure needs and potential community benefits as the ordinance moves forward.

entry.title: Dolphins cornerback Julius 'Juju' Brents on injuries, mental toughness and chasing a healthy season in Miami
entry.summary: The Miami Dolphins cornerback known to friends and teammates as 'Juju' is in his fourth season in the NFL. Julius 'Juju' Brents came to Miami in 2025, but his football journey began long before that. WPTVs Eleanor Sheahan sat down with Brents this week in Miami Gardens to talk about his path to the pros, the mental demands of playing cornerback and how he's approaching the challenge of staying healthy. WATCH: Dolphins' Juju Brents talks injuries and mental warfare of playing cornerback with WPTV's Eleanor Sheahan Dolphins' Juju Brents talks injuries and mental warfare of playing cornerback Off the top, Brents mentioned how the nickname Juju stuck. 'Funny thing about that, my mom gave me that nickname as a kid. So when I tell people my first name is Julius, they'd be like, are you for real? Like, because everybody calls me Juju. It's been like that since I was a child,' Brents said. Brents said he has been playing football for a long time and he even remembers one of his first football drills. 'I got a vivid memory from when I was a kid. I remember they teach you how to tackle, right? They got like a, kind of like those little orange tall things, but it was red... Run up to that, they make you tackle and whatnot. I remember just running up to it and just kind of spear it. I'm supposed to be doing this, and it's like, I vividly remember that as a kid. So I still had that feeling when I come out here playing,' Brents said. Now, roughly 20 years later, he's playing in the pros and thinking back to his 6-year-old self who is discovering the game for the first time. 'As a child, like I always told my mom, I think I want to be a football player and then it was like, no, I'm going to be a football player. Kind of build it to that,' Brents said. entry.article_text: The Miami Dolphins cornerback — known to friends and teammates as "Juju" — is in his fourth season in the NFL. Julius "Juju" Brents came to Miami in 2025, but his football journey began long before that.WPTV’s Eleanor Sheahan sat down with Brents this week in Miami Gardens to talk about his path to the pros, the mental demands of playing cornerback and how he's approaching the challenge of staying healthy. WATCH: Dolphins' Juju Brents talks injuries and ‘mental warfare’ of playing cornerback with WPTV's Eleanor Sheahan Off the top, Brents mentioned how the nickname “Juju” stuck."Funny thing about that, my mom gave me that nickname as a kid. So when I tell people my first name is Julius, they'd be like, are you for real? Like, because everybody calls me Juju. It's been like that since I was a child," Brents said.Brents said he has been playing football for a long time and he even remembers one of his first football drills."I got a vivid memory from when I was a kid. I remember they teach you how to tackle, right? They got like a, kind of like those little orange tall things, but it was red... Run up to that, they make you tackle and whatnot. I remember just running up to it and just kind of spear it. I'm supposed to be doing this, and it's like, I vividly remember that as a kid. So I still had that feeling when I come out here playing," Brents said.Now, roughly 20 years later, he's playing in the pros and thinking back to his 6-year-old self who is discovering the game for the first time."As a child, like I always told my mom, I think I want to be a football player and then it was like, no, I'm going to be a football player. Kind of build it to that," Brents said.On the field, Brents is a cornerback. When asked about the position and what being a defender entails, Brents said it's a constant mental battle."It's like mental warfare for sure. You know, being a corner is not an easy task at hand. Sometimes you lose a rep, but you don't have time to really sorrow in that loss. Your losses are on the grand scheme, like, you give up a big explosive play like that's noticeable, right? Compared to other positions. So I don't care who's in front of me. Being a competitor, I try to win every single snap," Brents said.Tackles are the forefront for defensive backs, but what is the secret to interceptions? Brents said it's all about preparation and watching film goes a long way."A lot of film study goes into it. Just intentionality for sure. You have to be big on the details and you got to be a little sad, you got to have some sadness to, you know, when those opportunities do come because it's not going to get a whole lot. But when they do come, you have to capitalize," Brents said.He said his in-game instincts are rooted in his work off the field. Brents credits his routine."Sure, you say naturally, and it can't be seen as natural, but at the end of the day, I like to say you just fall down to the level of your preparation," Brents said.Injuries have shaped much of his career, including his recent years in the NFL."I know early on in my career was tough. Going through college, I didn't have a whole lot of injuries. Then I get to the league and it was just like, injury after injury, trying to balance it, figure it out. So I faced a lot of adversity, but honestly, I think it was just a blessing in disguise. Now I feel like I got a better understanding of my body," Brents said.Throughout the conversation, Brents returned often to the mental side of the game — something he said he's had to grow into."I've had to grow in that space for sure. I'm not used to be one of the guys around thinking I'm so big and focusing on what everybody's saying and worried about it. Now I just let it be noise in the air, just having a clear focus, focusing on my path, my goals that I set out for myself, team goals, and just being focused on that," Brents said.For Brents, a fully healthy season would mean everything."I can't really control everything, so I'm trying to do my best to control my controllables. But I know the work that I have put in, and now that I do have the opportunity, like, I'm doing everything in my power to make sure I stay out here. It will mean everything to me just to finish this year strong, hopefully get some wins, which I know are coming here soon. Just being healthy," Brents said.Adding wins to the column and staying healthy are top of mind for Brents this season.

entry.title: Detainees allege abusive, unconstitutional conditions inside 'Deportation Depot' immigration facility
entry.summary: Civil rights advocates are investigating what they call abusive conditions inside a state-run immigration detention facility, telling me they've received a surge of complaints after the Everglades detention camp known as 'Alligator Alcatraz' closed over the summer. When Alligator Alcatraz shut down over the summer, it didn't end Florida's involvement in immigration detention. There's a second state-run facility that's been open for a year in a former prison about 50 minutes west of Jacksonville. Because its location is less controversial than the Everglades, it's flown largely under the radar. But now, detainees are speaking up about the alleged horrors inside what state officials have dubbed 'Deportation Depot.' 'It's insane. There's no other word [to describe the situation] than insanity. Just how bad these conditions were,' said a man who asked that we hide his face and refer to him by his middle name, Ryan. He fears being publicly identified could jeopardize his still-pending immigration case. 'I'm happy to be here, and I'm grateful, and obviously I'm gonna do everything I can to complete my immigration journey, and hopefully I can put this behind me,' Ryan said. I learned from the American Civil Liberties Union and confirmed through federal court records and local news reports that Ryan was detained by immigration authorities in late February and sent to the Baker Correctional Institution in Sanderson, where he spent four months. According to the most recent ICE detention data from July, roughly a thousand migrant men are housed at Baker. The ACLU put the number even higher, at about 1,200, during Ryan's stay. 'They were businessmen, entrepreneurs, paramedics, people that had been in the military. It was just, it was just everyone,' Ryan said. Ryan told me about 100 people in his dorm, with four working toilets and four working showers. He described the bathrooms as filthy, toiletries as scarce, and extreme heat as a persistent problem. 'We had one small AC unit in the corner of the room, which didn't work because the windows were smashed open anyway and kind of had been left broken,' Ryan said. 'We had black mold, brown mold. Like I said, those infestations of creatures. We had spiders, fire ants, cockroaches, bugs of all description.' On Oct. 8, the ACLU, Southern Poverty Law Center and Americans for Immigrant Justice sent a demand letter decrying the alleged conditions inside Baker to the state of Florida, the federal government, and the private co
entry.article_text: The advocacy groups wrote that they have conducted dozens of interviews with people currently or recently detained at the facility, their loved ones, and attorneys representing people detained there, and that those interviews confirm the widespread abuses occurring there.The letter identifies seven categories of abuse: life-threatening medical neglect; lack of adequate food and clean drinking water; excessive, life-threatening heat; squalid, unsanitary, and unsafe living conditions; deprivation of necessities for physical, mental, and emotional wellbeing, such as sleep, family visitation, and outdoor recreation; verbal and physical abuse and retaliation; and lack of access to the courts and to confidential communications with attorneys.On food and water, the letter alleges that the facility fails to provide people detained there with enough nutritious food, with detained people reporting receiving only "extremely small, infant-sized food portions that are not filling" and lacking adequate protein or nutrients. It states that people are losing dangerous amounts of weight, citing examples including one person who lost 29 pounds in less than two months and another who lost 44 pounds over seven months. On water, it alleges that the facility is failing to provide adequate access to clean drinking water, that most of the time the only drinking water available is from the dorms' visibly rusty water fountains, and that newly detained people are quickly warned not to drink from those fountains because many have gotten sick from drinking that water.Ryan said he and other detainees often spent part of their brief mealtimes drinking as much water as they could from the cafeteria, which he said provided clean drinking water."You had no alternative sometimes than just to kind of take your chances with the water (in the dorm)," Ryan said. "It had a very strong metallic taste, and as soon as it settled in your stomach, it felt like something was kicking and punching your stomach.""It's very much a cruel facility that's designed to deny people every aspect of humanity and decency and dignity, and is designed to make people physically weak, mentally weak, and just pressured to agree to the point— where they agree to self deportation," said ACLU attorney Amy Godshall, who wrote the letter.The letter alleges that this pressure is deliberate, stating there is evidence of a deliberate effort to make immigration detention unbearable so that people abandon their rights and accept departure or removal, and that whether intentional or not, these abusive living conditions are punitive and unconstitutional. Ryan told me he was pulled aside on three or four occasions by guards and asked to sign forms consenting to his deportation."The question that a lot of us had is, well, if we were deportable, then why would we have to sign this document to make us deportable?" Ryan said.I sent detailed questions about the allegations to the Florida Division of Emergency Management, ICE and the Department of Homeland Security, and all three private contractors named in the letter.

entry.title: Indiantown council sets November 5 meeting to consider data center moratorium - cw34.com
entry.summary: Indiantown council sets November 5 meeting to consider data center moratorium    cw34.com
entry.article_text: The Village of Indiantown is moving forward with plans to consider a temporary moratorium on large-scale data center development, but three sites already in the works would be excluded from the proposed restrictions. During Thursday night's Village Council meeting, members voted to schedule a special meeting for November 5, when they will take up the first reading of an ordinance that would temporarily halt new data center development applications, reviews, approvals and the start of construction on projects subject to the restrictions. The council also identified three sites that would be excluded from the proposed moratorium: Project Silver Fox Associated with Silver Fox 606 LLC. Project Growler Associated with Warfield 18 LLC. Tesoro Groves A large, planned development associated with Florida Power & Light property. The exemptions would allow those sites to remain outside the proposed restrictions while the village considers how to regulate future large-scale data center development. Council seeks negotiations and an end to litigation Council members also called for lawsuits surrounding the developments to be dropped as the village seeks to negotiate with developers. The request comes amid ongoing legal disputes involving data center development in Indiantown. Silver Fox 606 LLC filed a lawsuit against the village challenging its handling of an appeal involving the project's development approvals. A Martin County circuit judge issued an injunction earlier this month blocking a planned zoning appeals hearing while the legal dispute proceeds. It remains unclear whether the developers will agree to dismiss pending litigation or what conditions could be attached to any negotiations. Councilwoman pushes for community benefits See also: Palm Beach County district says 12 K-8 schools made Florida’s top 100 in new rankings During Thursday's meeting, Councilwoman Vernestine Williams-Palmer expressed frustration over the lengthy discussions surrounding data centers and emphasized the need to secure financial benefits for Indiantown residents. Palmer said the village needs additional tax revenue and investments in community infrastructure, particularly improvements to its water system. We need all the things, all the things that's been promised. We need the community impacts. We need all of that," Palmer said, according to a transcript of the meeting. She also encouraged residents to identify improvements they would like developers to help fund, mentioning a proposed $3 million gymnasium as one example discussed. Palmer said she has visited a data center in Texas and spoken with facility managers as part of her efforts to better understand the industry. While acknowledging that residents remain divided over data center development, Palmer said council members are working to protect the community's interests. The November 5 special meeting will focus on the first reading of the proposed moratorium ordinance. If ultimately adopted, the measure would temporarily restrict new large-scale data center applications and development activity covered by the ordinance while excluding the three identified sites. The length of the proposed moratorium and the precise conditions governing the exemptions still need to be established. The council's October 22 vote scheduled the special meeting and addressed the proposed exclusions. It did not enact the moratorium. Village leaders are expected to continue discussions over development restrictions, infrastructure needs and potential community benefits as the ordinance moves forward.

entry.title: St. Lucie County firefighter paramedic Austin Hodge dies unexpectedly while on duty
entry.summary: A St. Lucie County Fire District firefighter who died unexpectedly Saturday morning has been identified as Austin Hodge, a firefighter paramedic and nine-year veteran of the department. The fire district announced Saturday evening that Hodge, who was assigned to Firehouse 9, died while on duty earlier in the day. WATCH REPORT BELOW: St. Lucie County firefighter dies on duty St. Lucie County community mourns firefighter who died on duty 'Today, our St. Lucie County Fire District family mourns the loss of one of our own,' the district said in a statement. In the hours following his death, firefighters, the department's Honor Guard and fellow first responders gathered to honor Hodge and support one another. The district said the response reflected the strong bond shared throughout the fire service. The district thanked the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Fort Pierce Police Department, Port St. Lucie Police Department and peer support teams from Martin and Indian River counties for providing assistance and standing alongside firefighters during the difficult day. 'Together, they offered strength, compassion, and support while ensuring Austin was honored with the dignity and respect he deserves,' the district said. The district said its thoughts are with Hodge's family, loved ones and everyone who served alongside him. 'We are deeply grateful to our fellow first responders and community for the outpouring of support during this tremendous loss,' the district said. 'Today and always, we stand together.' The tragedy comes more than a year after the community mourned the sudden loss of his brother, Jarius Hodge , 26, who was also a St. Lucie County firefighter and died from septic shock in July 2025. WPTV has reached out to the fire district for additional information. This remains a developing story.

entry.article_text: A firefighter/paramedic died Saturday morning while on duty, one year after his brother, also with the St. Lucie County Fire District, passed away, the agency said. Austin Hodge, 34, joined the St. Lucie County Fire District on July 17, 2017. He was assigned to Station 9 in Fort Pierce. A procession of firefighters and personnel from other agencies went from HCA Lawnwood Hospital to the morgue in Fort Pierce on Saturday morning. His brother, Jarius Hodge, died on July 22, 2025, after falling ill at work at Station 3. His family said he had the flu, felt weak and was later rushed to the hospital, where he died hours later. People gathered on May 30 to celebrate what would have been his 27th birthday with a cookout and balloon release. Austin Hodge told WPBF at the time: "He was a quiet leader, and we take a lot from him. He was my younger brother, but I looked up to him in many ways to keep me poised, keep me patient. And I think that's what he's teaching everybody today." In June, another firefighter, Connor Whitehead, 21, died on May 31 but the cause of death wasn't released. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 There are 20 fire stations and 523 firefighters in the county, according to the agency's website. Information regarding memorial arrangements and opportunities to honor Hodge's service iwll be shared in coordination with his family as details are finalized. "His death is a profound loss to the St. Lucie County Fire District and the fire service community," the agency said. "The District extends its heartfelt condolences to Hodge’s family, friends, and fellow firefighters during this difficult time." Several agencies offered their condolences, including Port St. Lucie Fire Rescue, Fort Pierce Police Officers Association, Port St. Lucie Police Department, Indian River County Sheriff's Office, Indian River County Emergency Services Department, Indian River County Fire Rescue, Palm Beach County Fire Rescue, Riviera Beach Fire Rescue. https://www.facebook.com/stluciesheriff/posts/pfbid0cPopWYk7mLx2z6QfJqkd99ZUoP9dWGSRx3Y7yjuN21oLAqBUmr6n8RYoUYP9RGaZl The St. Lucie agency thanked other agencieson Facebook. https://www.facebook.com/slcfd/posts/pfbid02FGoAgmLryFmnkCkLqRQfwhzpBpGAX3Bh285A6jFqKysGajonPUPDHeKjxdFm2KQvl "In the hours following this heartbreaking loss, our firefighters, Honor Guard, and public safety partners came together to honor our fallen brother and stand alongside one another during an incredibly difficult time. The brotherhood of the fire service extends far beyond the walls of a fire station. It is a bond built on trust, shared experiences, and an unwavering commitment to one another. "Today, that bond was especially evident through the incredible support of the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Fort Pierce Police Department, Port St. Lucie Police Department, and peer support teams from Martin and Indian River counties. The truck fire was reported just before 8 a.m. in the southbound lanes near mile marker 161, approximately nine miles south of the Okeechobee Road/State Road 70 exit. Officials initially closed all southbound lanes while crews worked to extinguish the blaze. One lane later reopened before a separate crash in the same area led to another closure. Note: Alert expiration times may differ across the region because Palm Beach County is covered by the Miami forecast office, while Indian River, St. Lucie, Martin and Okeechobee counties are covered by the Melbourne office. Coastal Flood Warning A Coastal Flood Warning is in effect until 8 p.m. Wednesday, October 28th for coastal Palm Beach County. One is in effect until 2 a.m. Thursday, October 29th for coastal Indian River, St. Lucie, and Martin counties. Coastal roads may be closed. Low lying property including homes, businesses and some critical infrastructure will be inundated. Significant shoreline erosion will occur. entry.title: Is it cheaper to fly or drive this Thanksgiving?
entry.summary: If you're traveling for Thanksgiving, one question could have a big impact on your holiday budget: Is it cheaper to fly or drive? The answer can depend on where you're going, how many people are traveling, and when you plan to leave and return. Travelers we spoke with were divided. WATCH: Is it cheaper to fly or drive this Thanksgiving? Is it cheaper to fly or drive this Thanksgiving? It depends where you're going, Leticia Rivera said. But I would say fly right now. Others would rather stay on the road. For the preference, regardless of pricing, drive, Erik Eliassen said. Oh, definitely drive, Calvin Landau added. Carol Baxter, meanwhile, has already made her decision: I'm flying. Airfare can add up quickly for families According to Hopper data provided for this story, the average domestic round-trip flight for Thanksgiving is currently about $402 per person, compared with $307 last year. For a family of four, four tickets at the $402 average would total about $1,608 in airfare alone, before adding other potential travel expenses. Driving can look much different because expenses such as fuel are shared by everyone in the vehicle. Using the example in our comparison, the driving cost is about $160. That means families should consider the total cost of the trip rather than simply comparing the price of one plane ticket with one tank of gas. Your return date could make a big difference For people planning to fly, choosing a different return date could also affect the cost. Hopper data provided for this story shows a round trip with a return on the Sunday after Thanksgiving averaging about $604. Returning on Monday or Tuesday, however, could bring that average down to around $350. That's a difference of roughly $254 per ticket. For a family of four, that difference could potentially add up to more than $1,000. The bottom line There isn't one answer that works for every Thanksgiving traveler. Flying may save time on a long-distance trip, while driving can make the cost easier to spread across several people traveling together. Before booking, compare the total cost for everyone traveling, including airfare or fuel and any additional expenses associated with the trip. Also consider whether changing your travel dates could bring down the price. For families in particular, doing the math on the entire trip could make a significant difference in the Thanksgiving travel budget.

entry.title: Appeals court appears skeptical of Trump administration's California ballot lawsuit
entry.summary: A panel of federal appellate judges on Sunday questioned the timing, constitutionality and authority of the Justice Department's demand that California election officials set aside thousands of mail ballots from people the federal government suspects may not be citizens. During rare weekend arguments, two of the three judges on the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals appeared skeptical of a lawsuit brought by President Donald Trump's administration in mid-October. The lawsuit accuses California officials of failing to meet a 48-hour deadline to review 20,000 names the administration flagged as likely noncitizens on the state's voter rolls. The administration asked a federal judge to require the state to withhold counting those ballots until the voters immigration status could be verified. The district judge scheduled a hearing for Oct. 27, days after the case was assigned, but the federal government appealed to the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, seeking an expedited decision. Justice Department attorney Matthew Donnelly told the panel that California is causing irreparable harm by allowing noncitizens to vote in violation of their own state laws. The damage is irreversible and irrevocable. Circuit Judge Mark Bennett, a Trump appointee, questioned whether the appellate court even has jurisdiction to hear the case even before a ruling by the lower court. Donnelly argued that the schedule set by the lower court judge was too slow and effectively a denial of the government's request, as state elections officials process thousands of mail ballots every day. The lawsuit accuses California officials of failing to meet a 48-hour deadline to review 20,000 names the administration flagged as likely noncitizens on the state's voter rolls.The administration asked a federal judge to require the state to withhold counting those ballots until the voters’ immigration status could be verified. The district judge scheduled a hearing for Oct. 27, days after the case was assigned, but the federal government appealed to the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, seeking an expedited decision.Justice Department attorney Matthew Donnelly told the panel that California is causing irreparable harm “by allowing noncitizens to vote in violation of their own state laws. The damage is irreversible and irrevocable.”RELATED STORY | DOJ threatens California with legal action over claim of noncitizens on voter rollsThe Trump administration has made efforts to identify noncitizen voters a priority this year, even though noncitizen voting is exceptionally rare.Circuit Judge Mark Bennett, a Trump appointee, questioned whether the appellate court even has jurisdiction to hear the case even before a ruling by the lower court.Donnelly argued that the schedule set by the lower court judge was too slow and effectively a denial of the government's request, as state elections officials process thousands of mail ballots every day.Judge Gabriel Sanchez, appointed by former President Joe Biden, questioned whether the federal government was violating the Tenth Amendment, essentially commandeering the state to enforce a federal law that makes it a misdemeanor for a noncitizen to vote.The federal government is simply asking California to enforce their own law, which also bans noncitizens from voting, Donnelly said. He argued the state's refusal to comply with the federal request to set aside the ballots for review was “frustrating the purpose” of the federal law against noncitizen voting.The Elections Clause of the U.S. Constitution gives state legislatures the power to set the time, place and manner of congressional elections, Bennett said. The executive branch may be “unhappy with what they’re doing, and doesn’t like the manner,” Bennett said, but under the Election Clause the state has the right to determine those issues — including how it sorts out any noncitizen voters.Attorney Seth Waxman, representing Los Angeles County Clerk Dean Logan, said the federal government's list was unreliable and that segregating the ballots for a review process would effectively disenfranchise thousands of eligible voters.Even if election staffers spent just three minutes checking each of the expected 2.75 million mail ballots against the government's list, the process would take 140,000 man-hours, Waxman said — or about 16 years of working time.Waxman cited a review of 200 records from the Trump administration's list conducted by Los Angeles County staffers. Assistant Registrar-Recorder Monica Flores said in a court filing that the sample included canceled or inactive registrations, individuals with no voting history and voters who appeared to have been born in the United States, which the filing notes “is strong evidence of citizenship.”If the administration disagrees with how California runs its elections, it can ask Congress to change that process, said attorney Sam Siegel, representing California Secretary of State Shirley Weber.The federal government has provided no credible evidence to support its suspicions, said Siegal.“It has no basis in law or in fact,” he told the panel. “We just dispute the premise that noncitizens are voting."But Judge Patrick Bumatay, who was appointed by Trump, said everyone has an interest in ensuring that only eligible citizens vote. He suggested that granting the administration's request for an emergency order could provide clarity.“Without an injunction, you will never know” if that is happening, Bumatay told Seigel.Bennett said the panel would try to issue a ruling as quickly as possible.

entry.title: 23-year-old man killed after car enters I-95 crash scene, hits FHP cruiser in Lantana
entry.summary: A 23-year-old West Palm Beach man was killed early Sunday after a driver entered a lane closure at an Interstate 95 crash investigation scene and struck him before hitting a Florida Highway Patrol cruiser, according to FHP. The crash happened around 2:07 a.m. on northbound I-95 near Lantana Road in Palm Beach County. According to FHP, a 2019 Mercedes sedan driven by an 18-year-old Lake Worth woman was traveling north in the inside center lane. At the time, a marked FHP Dodge Charger was stationary across the inside and inside center lanes with its emergency lights activated as part of a lane closure for an ongoing crash investigation. Investigators said the Mercedes entered the closed lane and struck the 23-year-old man. The car then rotated and collided with the FHP cruiser. The man was pronounced dead at the scene. His identity has not been released. The 18-year-old driver suffered non-incapacitating injuries and was taken to JFK South for treatment. The outside northbound lane of I-95 reopened at 8:34 a.m., according to FHP.

entry.title: LagoonFest brings free family fun to West Palm Beach waterfront
entry.summary: LagoonFest returns to the downtown West Palm Beach waterfront Saturday with free boat tours, wildlife encounters, children's activities and opportunities to learn about the Lake Worth Lagoon. The free festival runs from 8:30 a.m. to 1:30 p.m. near the West Palm Beach GreenMarket. Benji Studt of Palm Beach County Environmental Resources Management said the event is designed to help residents and visitors connect with the lagoon. 'It's all about connecting people with the lagoon,' Studt said. Shell hunts, wildlife and more at LagoonFest Boat tours offer a closer look at the lagoon Visitors can explore the Lake Worth Lagoon aboard the Hakuna Matata or through Aqua Adventure tours, according to Studt. The boat tours provide a chance to experience the lagoon from the water while learning more about the natural area and the work being done around it. Wildlife encounters and hands-on activities Studt said participating organizations include the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, Busch Wildlife Sanctuary and Manatee Lagoon. The festival will feature touch tanks, wildlife experiences and a live python capture demonstration from FWC. Throughout the morning, families can also meet Laguna, the spotted eagle ray mascot representing Lake Worth Lagoon. Shell hunts and fishing lessons for children Studt said this year's children's zone includes a shell hunt, giveaways and calendars featuring work from local artists. Volunteers from the West Palm Beach Fishing Foundation will teach children how to cast and fish. Participating children will also get to take home a rod and reel, according to Studt. 'The kids can come, and they can do a little shell hunt, look for their shell treasures,' Studt said. Why LagoonFest matters now LagoonFest gives South Florida families a free way to spend time together while learning about a waterway that is part of Palm Beach County's environmental identity. Its location also allows visitors to pair the festival with a stop at the nearby West Palm Beach GreenMarket. Studt said the variety of activities makes the event accessible to visitors with different interests. 'There's something for everybody at LagoonFest,' Studt said. 'It's going to be an awesome time.' LagoonFest takes place Saturday from 8:30 a.m. to 1:30 p.m. along the downtown West Palm Beach waterfront. entry.title: Trump heads to Mississippi as more red states enter the midterm conversation with 8 days to go
entry.summary: The final full week of campaigning has begun after a weekend of bitter attacks on all sides. This week, more red states are entering the conversation for being potentially competitive and so are legal challenges from the Trump administration. President Donald Trump is heading to Mississippi Monday, another traditionally conservative state that few talked about as being competitive earlier this year. But after a number of high-profile visits by Democrats to campaign for Democrat Scott Colom, including former Vice President Kamala Harris, it has entered the conversation. RELATED STORY | Democrats tout momentum as early voting rises ahead of midterms While current Mississippi Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith is still favored, she has faced criticism for months after being asked about beef prices and suggesting there are other proteins to eat. Trump told reporters he thinks his frequent rallies are helping. 'I have heard we have turned the whole thing around and for whatever reason presidents don't win the midterms and I think we really turned it around and I think the rallies have turned it,' Trump said. Trump and Obama duel on the campaign trail Trump is also dueling with former President Barack Obama on the campaign trail this week, with Obama campaigning in Ohio and Michigan and mocking the former president in the process. 'Guy's building a ballroom bigger than White House, paved over the Rose Garden, put a helipad on the south lawn,' Obama said at one rally. 'And there is gold everywhere. What's up with the gold? He has got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.' MORE ELECTION NEWS | Young voter turnout could be pivotal in this year's midterms Polls show Democrats maintaining an edge in both House races and many Senate races with 8 days to go. But Republicans remain very skeptical of polling. A closely watched race in Alaska One of the biggest races is in Alaska, where Democratic nominee Mary Peltola was involved in a car accident over the weekend, sustaining minor injuries. This comes after the Department of Justice has sued to block Alaska certification, citing concerns that incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan is facing another Dan Sullivan on the ballot. 'That is very unfair, that's just outright cheating,' Trump said.

entry.summary: Watches, warnings, and advisories in place across the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches    WPEC
entry.article_text: A long list of watches, warnings and advisories is in place across the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches, with coastal flooding, strong winds and dangerous beach and boating conditions among the main concerns. Note: Alert expiration times may differ across the region because Palm Beach County is covered by the Miami forecast office, while Indian River, St. Lucie, Martin and Okeechobee counties are covered by the Melbourne office. Coastal Flood Warning A Coastal Flood Warning is in effect until 8 p.m. Wednesday, October 28th for coastal Palm Beach County. One is in effect until 2 a.m. Thursday, October 29th for coastal Indian River, St. Lucie, and Martin counties. Coastal roads may be closed. Low lying property including homes, businesses and some critical infrastructure will be inundated. Significant shoreline erosion will occur. Wind Advisory A Wind Advisory is in effect from 11 a.m. Monday, October 26th, until 8 p.m. Tuesday, October 27th, for metro and coastal Palm Beach County. One is in effect until 8 p.m. Monday, October 26th, for coastal Indian River, St. Lucie and Martin counties. Northeast winds of 20 to 25 mph are expected, with gusts up to 40 mph in Palm Beach County and up to 35 mph along the Treasure Coast. Gusts could blow around unsecured objects, break tree limbs and cause isolated power outages. High Surf Advisory A High Surf Advisory is in effect until 8 p.m. Wednesday, October 28th, for coastal Palm Beach County. One is in effect until 2 a.m. Thursday, October 29th, for coastal Indian River, St. Lucie and Martin counties. Breaking waves of 8 to 13 feet are possible along the Palm Beaches, with 7 to 11 feet forecast for the Treasure Coast. Dangerous swimming and surfing conditions are expected, along with localized beach erosion. High Rip Current Risk A High Rip Current Risk is in effect through Wednesday evening, October 28th, for coastal Palm Beach County. One is in effect through late Wednesday night for coastal Indian River, St. Lucie and Martin counties. Dangerous rip currents can pull even experienced swimmers away from shore. Entering the water is strongly discouraged. Gale Warning A Gale Warning is in effect until 2 a.m. Wednesday, October 28th, for nearshore waters from Sebastian Inlet to Jupiter Inlet and nearby offshore waters. One is in effect until 8 a.m. Wednesday, October 28th, for nearshore and offshore waters from Jupiter Inlet to Deerfield Beach. Northeast winds of 25 to 30 knots, with gusts up to 35 knots, and hazardous seas are expected. Small vessels could capsize or be damaged. Mariners should avoid these conditions and remain in port or seek safe harbor. Small Craft Advisory A Small Craft Advisory is scheduled from 8 a.m. Wednesday, October 28th, for nearshore and offshore waters from Jupiter Inlet to Deerfield Beach. Another is in effect until 8 p.m. Wednesday, October 28th, for Lake Okeechobee. Hazardous boating conditions are expected. Small craft operators should avoid heading out in these conditions.

entry.title: Police arrest 15-year-old after 11 shot near Florida A&M University stadium

The investigation suggests a physical altercation took place among individuals known to one another before shots were fired near the Florida AM football stadium, Revell said. At this stage of the investigation, none of the victims appear to have been the intended targets, the police chief said. The investigation remains active and additional arrests are possible, Revell said. Six juveniles, including an 11-year-old, are among the injured, Revell said late Saturday. No deaths have been reported. entry.title: From Jensen Beach to Louisiana Tech: Andrew Burnette gets one more shot at college football - WFLX
entry.summary: From Jensen Beach to Louisiana Tech: Andrew Burnette gets one more shot at college football    WFLX
entry.article_text: A young man from the Midwest with South Florida roots describes how Andrew Burnette moved from Michigan around the age of 12 and found home on the football field in Martin County. "I played football my whole life, and I can say football is a little harder in Florida than it is in Michigan," said Burnette. WATCH BELOW: Local football standout gets one more shot at college football While football was his first sport, during his high school days at Jensen Beach High School, he fell in love with takedowns and pins. "I wasn't zoned for that school, but I went there for wrestling originally; that was my first passion," said Burnette. While he was doing well in wrestling, football kept calling to him. "Moving through high school, I knew football was what I wanted to do," said Burnette. He established himself as a force at Jensen Beach High School, but he didn't receive much interest from college football programs, similar to many Treasure Coast football recruits. "One of my main struggles was recruitment out of high school, because I felt like our area was a little under-recruited," said Burnette. Betting on himself, he decided to play at Highland Community College in Kansas. Burnette played in nine games and rushed for 340 yards and two touchdowns, but he still wasn't on any other college football program's radar. "I transferred to Independence Junior College, and I was cut from the team," said Burnette. Independence was featured on the hit Netflix show Last Chance U, but once his chance there was short-lived, he reached out to Keiser University in West Palm Beach. "I spoke with the coach there and told him, 'You guys offered me in high school,' and he said, 'I don't really remember. Send me your film.' He saw my film and said, 'Hey, bring it,'" said Burnette. And he did "bring it." In the two years he played at Keiser, he rushed for over 2,300 yards and 30 touchdowns. With stats like that, Division I programs finally came calling, starting with Louisiana Tech. "Last year I played there; it was my first year at the Division I level, and then my eligibility ran out," said Burnette. At the time, the NCAA granted student-athletes only four years of eligibility unless they were injured, so Burnette rolled up his sleeves and got to work. "I called my dad and told him, 'Hey, I need to do something. I can't just sit here,' so I went and worked with my dad in Michigan," said Burnette. He worked with his dad at a steel mill in Detroit for a few months, but this summer the NCAA announced the 5-in-5 rule, meaning student-athletes can compete for up to five seasons across a continuous five-year period. So he hired a lawyer and went to court with the NCAA to get his final year of eligibility, and they granted him one last year, and now he's making the most of it. "It was amazing; I would rather play football than do anything, and for me to have this opportunity again, it's a blessing," said Burnette.
