entry.article_text: The race to be Florida's next governor is a competitive one — a statistical tie, according to a poll released last week by the University of North Florida.I caught up with Republican Byron Donalds and Democrat David Jolly as they each campaigned across the state, pitching different visions of Florida's future to voters.WATCH BELOW: Donalds, Jolly pitch competing visions in tight governor's raceDonalds, a Republican congressman, told me in a video call from his campaign bus on the road that he wants to build on the policies he likes from Gov. Ron DeSantis' outgoing administration."We live in a great state, and what has separated us from the other states is we continue to choose common sense conservative policy," Donalds said.That includes immigration enforcement."We're going to continue that mission here in the great state of Florida because we are going to continue to follow the law. I think that's the appropriate use of state authority and state powers," Donalds said.It also includes Florida's Department of Government Efficiency, which DeSantis formed through an executive order in 2025 and has since conducted audits of multiple counties across Florida."We are going to DOGE all governments, both local and state agencies in the state of Florida, because it's not our tax money. It belongs to the people of Florida. We need to make sure that government lives within its means, the way families have to live within their means," Donalds said.Donalds told me that effort will be important if Amendment 3 passes, raising homestead tax exemptions and reducing local revenue. I asked him whether, as governor, he would be prepared if some of the municipalities that need help come to Tallahassee asking for it."Yes, we will, and we've already made a public commitment to the fiscally constrained counties in the state of Florida," Donalds said. "Those that we know that their budgets are going to change in a major way, that we're prepared to provide a funding formula for those fiscally constrained counties so that they can be able to make ends meet."Jolly, a Democrat who served as a Republican in Congress during the 2010s, visited WPTV as his campaign traveled through Palm Beach County. He has said he personally opposes Amendment 3, but will support the will of the voters if it passes."I think we all want the math behind Amendment 3 to work, but it just doesn't," Jolly said.Florida hasn't elected a Democrat as governor since the 1990s. I asked Jolly why he thinks that is and why he believes his campaign could overcome that."Look, we're a state that trended Republican, particularly in the last eight years, and we know by voter registration it's still a predominantly Republican state," Jolly said. "I think we're in a moment most akin to a 1974 post-Watergate moment, where voters are saying, 'Burn the ships. Let's go in a new direction.'"Jolly said that direction should be simple."Housing, healthcare, education, and no data centers. "The answers are not in ideology. The answers are in solutions."He also said he wants to reach across the aisle to achieve those goals."If we expand health care access, we reduce costs. So you can be a conservative that wants to save money or a progressive that wants more health care. When we invest in public education, we create a resilient economy that should be attractive to Republicans. The economic argument behind that, I think, on housing, when more people have stable housing, the economy is better. I think we can work with Republicans," Jolly said.One issue where the two candidates agree is on school choice. Both told me they support keeping universal vouchers in place.Jolly also emphasized his desire to increase transparency requirements in Florida's charter schools and increase teacher pay in public schools."Let's engage in a little bit of consumer protection here on behalf of kids and families, and say that if you're going to take a voucher as a school, you should have to provide the same services, standards and offerings and be measured by the same measuring stick that our public schools are," Jolly said.Asked whether financial records of charter schools should be public records, as they are for public schools, Donalds replied, "I think if you're talking about what parents are looking for, what they want to basically see, are the children being educated? What are the mathematical attainment scores of that school? What are the reading attainment scores of that school? And if you're talking about high school, what's the ACT scores and what's the SAT scores? I think that's the accountability and the transparency that parents are looking for in the state of Florida, because at the end of the day, they're looking to make sure that the output is where it needs to be."Donalds' wife, Erika Donalds, founded a charter school company and currently runs a nonprofit promoting school choice. "My wife is actually not in the charter school business anymore. She's actually been out of that business for a couple of years," Donalds told me. "But I just want to be clear: she will not be contracting with the state of Florida in any way, shape, or form."On data center policy, the candidates differ. Jolly said he supports a moratorium on data center construction, while Donalds believes those decisions should be left up to local governments."If a local government says no data centers, then no data centers. If they do, then where the state steps in is we make sure that utility bills, utility costs are not passed on to consumers, and we also make sure that we are going to protect water resources in our state," Donalds said.For the first time in decades, Florida voters did not get to see a gubernatorial debate for this election.Asked what he would say to Jolly had the two candidates faced one another on the debate stage, Donalds said, "I would like him to explain why and how the people of Florida are going to be able to pay for his insurance plan, because by independent analysis, his insurance plan will drive up premiums on the people of our state, and everybody will be hit with a $1,000 hurricane tax when the next time the big storm comes through," referring to the funding the sovereign wealth fund Jolly says he would like to create to cover windstorm damage for Florida homeowners. (Jolly has denied that the fund would impose a new tax.)"I'm not sure debates improve our politics at this point. I think they just platform the division and the vitriol and the ugliness," Jolly told me. "My wife says in a world of Donald Trump, I'm trying to be Ted Lasso. We have two young kids, and I want them to look back and know that Dad acted in a way that he spoke of, which was not to further devolve our politics into vitriol and ugliness and division. Debates are about who can score the greatest insult, and I just I don't think that helps."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.summary: St. Lucie County Fire District mourns unexpected loss of firefighter    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Lucie County firefighter-paramedic died while on duty Saturday, more than a year after his younger brother, who also served as a firefighter-paramedic, died at age 26. Lucie County Fire District announced the line-of-duty death of Austin Hodge on Saturday, Oct. 24, calling his death a profound loss to the department and the fire service community. Hodge joined the district on July 17, 2017, and served the community for more than nine years. He was assigned to Station 9. Neighboring Indian River County Fire Rescue also shared condolences following the firefighter’s unexpected death Saturday morning. Lucie County Fire District asked the public to respect Hodge’s family as they grieve. Information about memorial arrangements will be shared as details are finalized. Read more: Missing 5-year-old girl found dead in Fort Pierce body of water Brothers shared a career in firefighting Austin Hodge’s death comes more than a year after his younger brother, Jarius Hodge, also a St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic, died on July 22, 2025. The brothers shared a close bond and a passion for serving their community. This was my best friend, my twin, Austin Hodge previously told CBS12 News. We had the same hairstyle. He described Jarius as someone who loved his family and his work as a first responder. He loved going to work, loved working beside me. I loved working beside him, Austin said. He always pushed me to keep going. He was someone who loved his family, his community and his country. Family sought accountability after Jarius’ death In an interview with CBS12 News , Austin said Jarius became ill after catching the flu from a patient at work in July 2025. Austin said his younger brother went to Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital in Port St. Lucie on July 22, struggling to breathe, but died hours later. He alleged that medical staff made critical errors in treating his brother, including taking three attempts to intubate him. He said Jarius had been healthy before becoming ill. Austin also spoke publicly about Florida’s medical malpractice laws, arguing that restrictions on who can pursue certain wrongful-death claims prevented his family from seeking legal accountability for Jarius’ death. This is unjust, and it's been going on for too long, Austin said in the earlier interview. He emphasized that his family was seeking accountability rather than financial compensation. For me personally, for my family, this has nothing to do with any type of dollar, he said. We just want those physicians to be held accountable. The circumstances surrounding Austin Hodge’s death have not been released. Lucie County Fire District said additional information about ways to honor his service will be shared in coordination with his family.

entry.summary: St. Lucie County Fire District confirms firefighter's death; Treasure Coast agencies mourn the loss    WFLX
entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District firefighter who died unexpectedly Saturday morning has been identified as Austin Hodge, a firefighter paramedic and nine-year veteran of the department. The fire district announced Hodge was found unresponsive in his bunk during a shift change. He was taken to the hospital and passed away. Lucie County firefighter dies on duty "Today, our St. Lucie County Fire District family mourns the loss of one of our own," the district said in a statement. In the hours following his death, firefighters, the department's Honor Guard and fellow first responders gathered to honor Hodge and support one another. The district said the response reflected the strong bond shared throughout the fire service. entry.title: From Jensen Beach to Louisiana Tech: Andrew Burnette gets one more shot at college football - WFLX
entry.summary: From Jensen Beach to Louisiana Tech: Andrew Burnette gets one more shot at college football    WFLX
entry.article_text: A young man from the Midwest with South Florida roots describes how Andrew Burnette moved from Michigan around the age of 12 and found home on the football field in Martin County. "I played football my whole life, and I can say football is a little harder in Florida than it is in Michigan," said Burnette. WATCH BELOW: Local football standout gets one more shot at college football While football was his first sport, during his high school days at Jensen Beach High School, he fell in love with takedowns and pins. "I wasn't zoned for that school, but I went there for wrestling originally; that was my first passion," said Burnette. While he was doing well in wrestling, football kept calling to him. "Moving through high school, I knew football was what I wanted to do," said Burnette. He established himself as a force at Jensen Beach High School, but he didn't receive much interest from college football programs, similar to many Treasure Coast football recruits. "One of my main struggles was recruitment out of high school, because I felt like our area was a little under-recruited," said Burnette. Betting on himself, he decided to play at Highland Community College in Kansas. Burnette played in nine games and rushed for 340 yards and two touchdowns, but he still wasn't on any other college football program's radar. "I transferred to Independence Junior College, and I was cut from the team," said Burnette. Independence was featured on the hit Netflix show Last Chance U, but once his chance there was short-lived, he reached out to Keiser University in West Palm Beach. "I spoke with the coach there and told him, 'You guys offered me in high school,' and he said, 'I don't really remember. Send me your film.' He saw my film and said, 'Hey, bring it,'" said Burnette. And he did "bring it." In the two years he played at Keiser, he rushed for over 2,300 yards and 30 touchdowns. With stats like that, Division I programs finally came calling, starting with Louisiana Tech. "Last year I played there; it was my first year at the Division I level, and then my eligibility ran out," said Burnette. At the time, the NCAA granted student-athletes only four years of eligibility unless they were injured, so Burnette rolled up his sleeves and got to work. "I called my dad and told him, 'Hey, I need to do something. I can't just sit here,' so I went and worked with my dad in Michigan," said Burnette. He worked with his dad at a steel mill in Detroit for a few months, but this summer the NCAA announced the 5-in-5 rule, meaning student-athletes can compete for up to five seasons across a continuous five-year period. So he hired a lawyer and went to court with the NCAA to get his final year of eligibility, and they granted him one last year, and now he's making the most of it. "It was amazing; I would rather play football than do anything, and for me to have this opportunity again, it's a blessing," said Burnette.

entry.summary: Strong winds, king tides flood parts of Martin County as officials warn of more high water    WFLX
entry.article_text: WPTV has been following flooding on the Treasure Coast caused by strong winds and king tides on Monday. In Martin County, off Dyer Point Road in Palm City, parts of the area were completely underwater. WATCH BELOW: Flooding swamps parts of Palm City amid king tides, strong winds Terresa Baldwin, who lives off the roadway, said it was flooded for a few hours, but water has since retreated. "You could smell the sewage; it was really stinky, it was bad," Baldwin said. "There were dead copperheads, so the snakes are coming out. They're getting flushed out with the water." Baldwin said she was also dealing with flooding in her backyard along one of the finger canals. She showed WPTV the water over her dock and in her new patio. "The wind was blowing so hard, so it was like waves crashing in your backyard, and you're like, no, nobody wants to see that," Baldwin said. Despite the water going down, she is still worried about what could happen in the next few days. "The biggest concern for us is getting water from both sides. What do you do, especially when you're trying to sleep, and you don't know if the water's going to come up more or what's going to get damaged at night when you really can't see," Baldwin said. With high tide later Monday night, the sheriff’s office told WPTV the situation could get worse. Dave Rosko said they have three high-water vehicles ready for rescue efforts and urged neighbors to think twice before driving through the water. "Understand the limitations of your vehicle and do not drive through the high waters," Rosko said. "If your vehicle gets disabled there, it may turn into a rescue event where we need to come out and ensure your safety." Rosko said neighbors living in coastal communities should be aware of future tides before traveling.

The proposal comes amid residents' concerns about the future of data center development.

entry.title: Frankel, Adeimy outline affordability priorities in race for Florida's redrawn 23rd congressional district
entry.summary: With just a week left until the General Election, the candidates vying for the newly redrawn 23rd congressional district in Florida sat down with WPTV morning anchor Hollani Davis to talk about their priorities for voters here at home if they're elected. U.S. Rep. Louis Frankel, D-Fla., is fighting to continue representing South Florida. She says affordability is at the top of her list to tackle. WATCH REPORT BELOW: District 23 candidates focus on affordability Candidates vying to represent Florida's 23rd District lay out priorities to tackle affordability 'When I'm at the supermarket, and people can't afford their food, that's a pretty big message,' says Frankel. Frankel, who is seeking an eighth term in Congress, says Democrats must seek to end the war with Iran and rein in the Trump administration's tariffs to help bring costs under control. She also says there is another glaring issue that can't be ignored. '(There's) probably nothing more important for the people of Palm Beach County, where we have a big senior population, is (the need) to protect Social Security and Medicare,' Frankel said. Challenging Frankel in the race is Deborah Adeimy. The Republican, is a native of Palm Beach County who's worked as a financial adviser to companies like Morgan Stanley, JP Morgan Chase. She says she'd use her financial acumen to help solve South Florida's affordable housing problem by rewriting the playbook. 'Currently in Palm Beach County, there are real estate developers who are taking advantage of antiquated tax incentives, tax breaks that are driving up costs here in Palm Beach County (including) rent,' says Adeimy. Florida's 23rd congressional district previously straddled the Palm Beach-Broward County line with a heavy focus on Broward County. After the districts were redrawn this year, it now covers a portion of West Palm Beach and extends south to include Boynton Beach.

entry.title: Boca Raton Fire Rescue expands lifesaving whole blood program through new health network partnership
entry.summary: A new partnership between Boca Raton Fire Rescue and Palm Beach Health Network is strengthening a whole blood program that has already saved lives in the field this summer. Boca Raton's fire rescue crews have had access to whole blood since a new program kicked off this summer; paramedics say the capability is transforming how they treat patients before they reach the hospital. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Boca Raton expands whole blood program According to Red Cross Blood Services, whole blood is blood as it flows in our bodies, with none of its components separated or removed. 'Whole blood has been shown to save lives, and now that we have the capability in our arsenal, it's a world of difference in treating patients and getting the right care,' Kacper Palej, Boca Raton firefighter paramedic, said. Jo Thomas was critically injured in a motorcycle crash this summer. Crews administered whole blood for the first time under the new program. 'I've been told I got flown from the bike into a crosswalk pole about 20 to 30 feet and then hit a crosswalk pole with my body,' Thomas said. 'When somebody's bleeding out on the street, the one thing that will really help out is being able to feed blood back into them to keep them alive, just until they can make it to the hospital to be fully treated.' Months later, Thomas is surrounded by fire rescue again, but for a different reason. Crew members who responded to his crash call received a firefighter challenge coin as a token of appreciation. 'Seeing him walking into the station today and we're gonna go and have something to eat, break bread with him... It's a great day,' Steven Wright, driver engineer, said. A recent partnership with Palm Beach Health Network now means that when blood in fire rescue units is close to expiring, crews return it to Palm Beach Health Network for patient care. In exchange, crews receive fresh blood for future emergency calls.

entry.title: 'A smile that lights up the room': Loved ones remember St. Lucie County firefighter - WPEC
entry.summary: 'A smile that lights up the room': Loved ones remember St. Lucie County firefighter    WPEC
entry.article_text: Family and friends are mourning St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge, a man those closest to him describe as endlessly positive and devoted to serving his community. A funeral procession for Hodge left the Medical Examiner’s Office in Fort Pierce at 2 p.m. Monday and traveled to Stone Brothers Funeral Home. Lucie County Sheriff's Office went to the station at 7:25 a.m. 24, regarding a "full cardiac arrest," and Hoge was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. His death comes about 15 months after his younger brother, Jarius Hodge, also a St. Lucie County Fire District firefighter and paramedic, died in July 2025 after falling ill during a shift. The district honored Jarius with line-of-duty honors. After his brother’s death, Austin spent months searching for answers. He told CBS12 News in January that Jarius caught the flu from a patient and died hours after arriving at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital in Port St. Lucie, struggling to breathe. Austin said medical records showed doctors made critical mistakes, including needing three attempts to intubate his brother. CBS12 reached out to the hospital at the time and did not receive a response before that story was published. Because Jarius was over 25 and had no spouse or children, Florida’s so-called free kill law barred his family from suing for medical malpractice. Austin pushed state lawmakers to repeal it and started a petition in his brother’s honor. He said the fight was about accountability, not money. Bernard Taylor has known Austin since their school days in Sebastian. Taylor was a senior and Austin a freshman when they met at the Boys and Girls Club, where Taylor worked as a counselor and Austin was one of the kids he mentored. Taylor said Austin always wanted to keep up with the older kids, and the two formed a bond that lasted for years. Later, when Taylor decided to change careers, Austin was one of the first people he called. Taylor said Austin supported him through becoming a firefighter, from answering questions to helping him with his conditioning. Just a ball of positive energy. A smile that lights up the room. No matter what you’re going through, he had the right words to kind of get you through it, Taylor said. Taylor said he spoke with Austin about a week before his death to make sure he was doing well. He said he is most heartbroken for Austin’s mother, who has now lost both of her sons. That’s one of the strongest people I’ve ever met in my life. I don’t know if I can hold it together if I was her, Taylor said. Bonnie Hill, a family friend who helped raise Austin’s mother, said she has been by her side and that the family is leaning on its faith and a strong circle of support. I say on my watch, I’m not going to let you die. You’re going to live, and we’re going to get through this, Hill said of what she has told Austin’s mother. Hill said that faith is what is carrying the family now. See also: King tides cause coastal flooding, beach closures in Palm Beach County and Treasure Coast We believe God even in this. entry.title: King tides cause coastal flooding, beach closures in Palm Beach County and Treasure Coast - WPEC
entry.summary: King tides cause coastal flooding, beach closures in Palm Beach County and Treasure Coast    WPEC
entry.article_text: King tides flooded streets and reached homes across Palm Beach County on Monday, while beach and road closures were reported as more high tides were expected through Wednesday. In Palm City, flooding made SW Dyer Point Road impassable. Martin County Sheriff’s Office deputies brought in three high-water vehicles to help reach anyone stranded in a vehicle or home. Flooding also was reported on SW 34th Street and Cornell Avenue. One driver told CBS12 the water was about waist-deep in part of the area. Resident Terresa Baldwin said water came up around both the front and back of her home, and that Monday’s flooding was the worst she had seen in eight years. Baldwin also raised concerns about the water’s source and smell. This is not only runoff water, it’s sewage and it’s bad and you can smell it, she said. Deputies urged people to avoid flooded areas and not to drive through standing water. These vehicles can travel through several feet of water safely, Martin County Sheriff’s Office Lt. Flooding also reached Flagler Drive in downtown West Palm Beach and Sunset Avenue on Palm Beach Island, where water covered parts of the roadway and disrupted pedestrians and cyclists. In Boynton Beach, flooding led to road closures, including at Ocean Avenue and Federal Highway. The Ocean Inlet Marina also closed because of high tides. In Boca Raton, water reached a Cub Scout pack’s campsite at Spanish River Park, prompting campers to move supplies to higher ground. Elsewhere, Midtown Beach was temporarily closed because of large surf and high tides. The northbound lane of South Ocean Boulevard between Chilean and Australian avenues was scheduled to close from 10 a.m. to noon while crews moved a lifeguard tower. Delray Beach officials raised red flags because of high surf and flooding, and the Juno Beach Pier remained closed because of damage from a recent offshore surge and high surf. See also: 15-year-old FAMU shooting suspect ordered to be held as prosecutors seek adult charges A coastal flood warning covers low-lying areas near the water in Palm Beach, Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties. The National Weather Service said the warning runs through 8 p.m. Wednesday in coastal Palm Beach County and 2 a.m. Thursday in coastal Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties. The forecast high tides were: Monday: 9:06 p.m. The sheriff’s office advised residents not to drive through floodwater and to call 911 if they need emergency assistance.

entry.title: Strong winds, king tides flood parts of Martin County as officials warn of more high water
entry.summary: WPTV has been following flooding on the Treasure Coast caused by strong winds and king tides on Monday. In Martin County, off Dyer Point Road in Palm City, parts of the area were completely underwater. WATCH BELOW: Flooding swamps parts of Palm City amid king tides, strong winds King tides, strong winds flood areas of Martin County Terresa Baldwin, who lives off the roadway, said it was flooded for a few hours, but water has since retreated. 'You could smell the sewage; it was really stinky, it was bad,' Baldwin said. 'There were dead copperheads, so the snakes are coming out. They're getting flushed out with the water.' Baldwin said she was also dealing with flooding in her backyard along one of the finger canals. She showed WPTV the water over her dock and in her new patio. 'The wind was blowing so hard, so it was like waves crashing in your backyard, and you're like, no, nobody wants to see that,' Baldwin said. Despite the water going down, she is still worried about what could happen in the next few days. 'The biggest concern for us is getting water from both sides. What do you do, especially when you're trying to sleep, and you don't know if the water's going to come up more or what's going to get damaged at night when you really can't see,' Baldwin said.  With high tide later Monday night, the sheriffs office told WPTV the situation could get worse. Lt. Dave Rosko said they have three high-water vehicles ready for rescue efforts and urged neighbors to think twice before driving through the water. 'Understand the limitations of your vehicle and do not drive through the high waters,' Rosko said. 'If your vehicle gets disabled there, it may turn into a rescue event where we need to come out and ensure your safety.' Rosko said neighbors living in coastal communities should be aware of future tides before traveling.

entry.title: Buc-ee's plan for St. Lucie County moves forward, with opening still listed for 2027
entry.summary: Plans to bring a Buc-ee's travel center to the Treasure Coast are continuing to move forward. During questioning from a St. Lucie County commissioner last week, county Planning Director Ben Balser said Buc-ee's has received site plan approval and its building permits are currently under review. Balser said the county is ready to move forward once Buc-ee's addresses the remaining comments from county staff. Plans for the travel center were first announced in 2023. The project calls for a 120-pump location off Indrio Road off Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County. Buc-ee's website continues to list the location as opening in 2027. The Texas-based travel center chain is known for its large stores and expansive fueling areas. The St. Lucie County location would bring the popular chain to the Treasure Coast.

entry.title: From Jensen Beach to Louisiana Tech: Andrew Burnette gets one more shot at college football - WFLX
entry.summary: From Jensen Beach to Louisiana Tech: Andrew Burnette gets one more shot at college football    WFLX
entry.article_text: A young man from the Midwest with South Florida roots describes how Andrew Burnette moved from Michigan around the age of 12 and found home on the football field in Martin County. "I played football my whole life, and I can say football is a little harder in Florida than it is in Michigan," said Burnette. WATCH BELOW: Local football standout gets one more shot at college football While football was his first sport, during his high school days at Jensen Beach High School, he fell in love with takedowns and pins. "I wasn't zoned for that school, but I went there for wrestling originally; that was my first passion," said Burnette. While he was doing well in wrestling, football kept calling to him. "Moving through high school, I knew football was what I wanted to do," said Burnette. He established himself as a force at Jensen Beach High School, but he didn't receive much interest from college football programs, similar to many Treasure Coast football recruits. "One of my main struggles was recruitment out of high school, because I felt like our area was a little under-recruited," said Burnette. Betting on himself, he decided to play at Highland Community College in Kansas. Burnette played in nine games and rushed for 340 yards and two touchdowns, but he still wasn't on any other college football program's radar. "I transferred to Independence Junior College, and I was cut from the team," said Burnette. Independence was featured on the hit Netflix show Last Chance U, but once his chance there was short-lived, he reached out to Keiser University in West Palm Beach. "I spoke with the coach there and told him, 'You guys offered me in high school,' and he said, 'I don't really remember. Send me your film.' He saw my film and said, 'Hey, bring it,'" said Burnette. And he did "bring it." In the two years he played at Keiser, he rushed for over 2,300 yards and 30 touchdowns. With stats like that, Division I programs finally came calling, starting with Louisiana Tech. "Last year I played there; it was my first year at the Division I level, and then my eligibility ran out," said Burnette. At the time, the NCAA granted student-athletes only four years of eligibility unless they were injured, so Burnette rolled up his sleeves and got to work. "I called my dad and told him, 'Hey, I need to do something. I can't just sit here,' so I went and worked with my dad in Michigan," said Burnette. He worked with his dad at a steel mill in Detroit for a few months, but this summer the NCAA announced the 5-in-5 rule, meaning student-athletes can compete for up to five seasons across a continuous five-year period. So he hired a lawyer and went to court with the NCAA to get his final year of eligibility, and they granted him one last year, and now he's making the most of it. "It was amazing; I would rather play football than do anything, and for me to have this opportunity again, it's a blessing," said Burnette.

entry.title: LagoonFest brings free family fun to West Palm Beach waterfront
entry.summary: LagoonFest returns to the downtown West Palm Beach waterfront Saturday with free boat tours, wildlife encounters, children's activities and opportunities to learn about the Lake Worth Lagoon. The free festival runs from 8:30 a.m. to 1:30 p.m. near the West Palm Beach GreenMarket. Benji Studt of Palm Beach County Environmental Resources Management said the event is designed to help residents and visitors connect with the lagoon. 'It's all about connecting people with the lagoon,' Studt said. Shell hunts, wildlife and more at LagoonFest Boat tours offer a closer look at the lagoon Visitors can explore the Lake Worth Lagoon aboard the Hakuna Matata or through Aqua Adventure tours, according to Studt. The boat tours provide a chance to experience the lagoon from the water while learning more about the natural area and the work being done around it. Wildlife encounters and hands-on activities Studt said participating organizations include the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, Busch Wildlife Sanctuary and Manatee Lagoon. The festival will feature touch tanks, wildlife experiences and a live python capture demonstration from FWC. Throughout the morning, families can also meet Laguna, the spotted eagle ray mascot representing Lake Worth Lagoon. Shell hunts and fishing lessons for children Studt said this year's children's zone includes a shell hunt, giveaways and calendars featuring work from local artists. Volunteers from the West Palm Beach Fishing Foundation will teach children how to cast and fish. Participating children will also get to take home a rod and reel, according to Studt. 'The kids can come, and they can do a little shell hunt, look for their shell treasures,' Studt said. Why LagoonFest matters now LagoonFest gives South Florida families a free way to spend time together while learning about a waterway that is part of Palm Beach County's environmental identity. Its location also allows visitors to pair the festival with a stop at the nearby West Palm Beach GreenMarket. Studt said the variety of activities makes the event accessible to visitors with different interests. 'There's something for everybody at LagoonFest,' Studt said. 'It's going to be an awesome time.' LagoonFest takes place Saturday from 8:30 a.m. to 1:30 p.m. along the downtown West Palm Beach waterfront. Participating children will also get to take home a rod and reel, according to Studt."The kids can come, and they can do a little shell hunt, look for their shell treasures," Studt said.LagoonFest gives South Florida families a free way to spend time together while learning about a waterway that is part of Palm Beach County's environmental identity.Its location also allows visitors to pair the festival with a stop at the nearby West Palm Beach GreenMarket. Studt said the variety of activities makes the event accessible to visitors with different interests."There's something for everybody at LagoonFest," Studt said. "It's going to be an awesome time."LagoonFest takes place Saturday from 8:30 a.m. along the downtown West Palm Beach waterfront.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.summary: St. Lucie County firefighter paramedic Austin Hodge dies after being found unresponsive on duty    WPTV
entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District firefighter who died unexpectedly Saturday morning has been identified as Austin Hodge, a firefighter paramedic and nine-year veteran of the department.The fire district announced Hodge was found unresponsive in his bunk during a shift change. He was taken to the hospital and passed away.WATCH REPORT BELOW: St. Lucie County firefighter dies on duty"Today, our St. Lucie County Fire District family mourns the loss of one of our own," the district said in a statement. In the hours following his death, firefighters, the department's Honor Guard and fellow first responders gathered to honor Hodge and support one another. The district said the response reflected the strong bond shared throughout the fire service. The district thanked the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Fort Pierce Police Department, Port St. Lucie Police Department and peer support teams from Martin and Indian River counties for providing assistance and standing alongside firefighters during the difficult day."Together, they offered strength, compassion, and support while ensuring Austin was honored with the dignity and respect he deserves," the district said. The district said its thoughts are with Hodge's family, loved ones and everyone who served alongside him. They respectfully ask that Hodge's family be given privacy during this time."We are deeply grateful to our fellow first responders and community for the outpouring of support during this tremendous loss," the district said. "Today and always, we stand together." The tragedy comes more than a year after the community mourned the sudden loss of his brother, Jarius Hodge, 26, who was also a St. Lucie County firefighter and died from septic shock in July 2025.The district said it will share information on funeral and memorial services in coordination with the family when it becomes available.

Advocates say more than 150,000 Haitian TPS beneficiaries live in Florida, contributing $2.6 billion to the state's economy, and that they became unable to legally work when Homeland Security revoked their status. entry.title: New $17 million Boys & Girls Club opens in West Palm Beach, offering opportunities for hundreds of kids
entry.summary: A new Boys Girls Club officially opened its doors Tuesday in West Palm Beach, bringing a new place for hundreds of children and teens to learn, explore their interests and prepare for their futures. The Julie Mike Connors Boys Girls Club, located at 1150 Southern Blvd., celebrated its grand opening after years of planning. WATCH REPORT BELOW: New Boys Girls Club opens in West Palm Beach 'To have this come to fruition is more beautiful than I ever thought it could be,' Julie Connors said during the celebration. The $17 million, 31,000-square-foot facility is the 21st location for the Boys Girls Clubs of Palm Beach County and is expected to serve approximately 800 children and teens each year, with about 220 attending daily. The club will serve kids ages 6 to 18. For the Connors, however, the bigger story is the need they say exists in the surrounding community. 'People don't realize how big a need there is in West Palm Beach,' Mike Connors said. 'There are a lot of single families that need a lot of help, especially to get kids off the streets.' Inside the new facility are spaces designed for academics, recreation, the arts and career exploration. The club includes a gym and stage, academic center, cultural arts center, computer labs, dance studio, cafeteria, commercial kitchen, sound and recording studio, maker space and outdoor playground. Students will also have access to daily homework help and tutoring programs with certified teachers, along with STEM education, sports, health and fitness programs, cultural arts and leadership programs. For teens, the opportunities extend into career exploration and workforce readiness. They can get hands-on experience in areas such as robotics, health care, content creation, design and culinary arts while being introduced to potential college and career pathways. 'I can be a journalist, a content creator; I can do anything that's possible because we provide essential tools, systems and environment to help them grow,' said Pablo Tejada, Chief Impact Officer for the Boys Girls Club. WPTV reporter Christy Waite spoke with one family who came to the grand opening to tour the new facility. College student Christian Smith said he believes the opportunities being offered could help break cycles of poverty and create new opportunities for young people in the community. entry.title: Powerful waves damage Juno Beach Pier, forcing indefinite closure as officials await full assessment
entry.summary: Powerful waves and strong winds have left their mark on the Juno Beach Pier, forcing officials to close the popular fishing spot indefinitely while crews wait for conditions to improve enough to assess the damage. For people who came to Juno Beach on Tuesday to see the conditions firsthand, the strength of the ocean was impossible to miss. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Rough surf damages Juno Beach Pier, forcing indefinite closure 'It's just amazing the way they roll in and pound and the power,' said Melissa Stolz, who lives in Jupiter but came to Juno Beach to see the rough conditions. 'Between the full moon and the gale-force winds, everything, it's just a perfect storm.' Kristine Galganski lives in North Palm Beach and said Tuesdays are typically her days to visit Juno Beach. After hearing about the damage, she came out to see the pier for herself. 'That's Mother Nature at her best,' Galganski said, 'and she's saying I'm here and I'm ready.' Aerial footage from local photographer Paul Dabill showed floor panels lifted throughout the pier, with some panels missing. Bud Gilfillan, who lives in Jupiter but was visiting Juno Beach, said the conditions stood out to him. 'I'm seeing the heaviest northeast winds and currents that I've seen in a long time,' Gilfillan said. Gilfillan was struck by the amount of force it would take to move the decking. 'I mean, can you imagine the force of those waves pushing that decking up in the air and washing it down,' Gilfillan said. WPTV worked to find answers to understand the extent of the damage the pier had received and contacted Palm Beach County Parks and Recreation Director Jennifer Cirillo. 'The wooden panels are designed to pop out in high surf conditions and in order to save greater structural damage on the pier,' Cirillo said in a statement. The missing panels may be part of the pier's design, but officials believe there could be other damage that would impact when the pier will reopen. 'It does appear during this event, however, that some of the railing may also be damaged, which would require repair,' Cirillo said. For Stolz, seeing the pier closed was difficult. 'I'm just sad it's such a landmark for locals to come down and walk on the fishing pier,' she said. entry.article_text: Powerful waves and strong winds have left their mark on the Juno Beach Pier, forcing officials to close the popular fishing spot indefinitely while crews wait for conditions to improve enough to assess the damage.For people who came to Juno Beach on Tuesday to see the conditions firsthand, the strength of the ocean was impossible to miss.WATCH REPORT BELOW: "It's just amazing the way they roll in and pound and the power," said Melissa Stolz, who lives in Jupiter but came to Juno Beach to see the rough conditions. "Between the full moon and the gale-force winds, everything, it's just a perfect storm."Kristine Galganski lives in North Palm Beach and said Tuesdays are typically her days to visit Juno Beach. After hearing about the damage, she came out to see the pier for herself."That's Mother Nature at her best," Galganski said, "and she's saying I'm here and I'm ready."Aerial footage from local photographer Paul Dabill showed floor panels lifted throughout the pier, with some panels missing.Bud Gilfillan, who lives in Jupiter but was visiting Juno Beach, said the conditions stood out to him."I'm seeing the heaviest northeast winds and currents that I've seen in a long time," Gilfillan said.Gilfillan was struck by the amount of force it would take to move the decking."I mean, can you imagine the force of those waves pushing that decking up in the air and washing it down," Gilfillan said.WPTV worked to find answers to understand the extent of the damage the pier had received and contacted Palm Beach County Parks and Recreation Director Jennifer Cirillo."The wooden panels are designed to pop out in high surf conditions and in order to save greater structural damage on the pier," Cirillo said in a statement.The missing panels may be part of the pier's design, but officials believe there could be other damage that would impact when the pier will reopen."It does appear during this event, however, that some of the railing may also be damaged, which would require repair," Cirillo said.For Stolz, seeing the pier closed was difficult."I'm just sad it's such a landmark for locals to come down and walk on the fishing pier," she said.County staff must now wait for the high surf to subside before they can safely assess the entire pier and determine what will need to be repaired."It's very damaging," Gilfillan said. "It's going to last a couple more days."Cirillo said it typically takes county crews a few days after high-surf events to retrieve loose panels and put them back into the pier. However, the county won't know whether there will be additional costs to reopen the pier until crews can safely determine the full impact."Once high surf conditions subside, our staff will be able to do a full assessment of this public park infrastructure," Cirillo said. "It typically takes our team a few days following high surf events to retrieve any loose panels and place them back into the pier structure. We will not know what costs above staff time are required for reopening until after we can safely assess the entire event's impacts."For now, there is no clear reopening timeline."It's gonna take time. We can't put a time limit on what she does," Stolz said.The pier isn't the only place where the rough conditions are having an impact. Some stairs at beach access points have also been damaged, and the Town of Jupiter has closed some access points because of erosion.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.summary: The Indian River State College Board of Trustees has delayed taking action on a recommendation to eliminate the college's swimming and diving team. This past March, the men's swim and dive team captured its 52nd consecutive national championship title, and the women's team claimed its 48th crown. entry.title: 15-year-old seriously injured after wrong-way crash following police pursuit in Stuart
entry.summary: A 15-year-old driver and another motorist were seriously injured early Tuesday after a police pursuit ended in a wrong-way crash on U.S. Highway 1, according to the Stuart Police Department. Police said officers were conducting traffic enforcement near Southwest Federal Highway and Southwest St. Lucie Crescent at about 3:45 a.m. when they spotted a vehicle traveling north at what officers described as an extremely high rate of speed. An officer attempted to make a traffic stop, but police said the driver refused to stop and fled. The pursuit eventually continued onto U.S. 1, where police said the driver began traveling north in the southbound lanes from Wright Boulevard. Officers continued trying to stop the vehicle because of the danger posed to other motorists, according to the department. Police said officers also attempted to alert drivers traveling on Northwest Federal Highway. The fleeing vehicle eventually collided with a vehicle traveling south at the Mall South Entrance intersection, police said. After the crash, officers learned the driver of the fleeing vehicle was 15 years old. Both drivers were taken to Lawnwood Medical Center in Fort Pierce with serious injuries. The Stuart Police Department is investigating the incident, while the Florida Highway Patrol is conducting a separate investigation into the crash. Police said no additional information would be released at this time because the investigation remains ongoing.

entry.title: 'A smile that lights up the room': Loved ones remember St. Lucie County firefighter - WPEC
entry.summary: 'A smile that lights up the room': Loved ones remember St. Lucie County firefighter    WPEC
entry.article_text: Family and friends are mourning St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge, a man those closest to him describe as endlessly positive and devoted to serving his community. A funeral procession for Hodge left the Medical Examiner’s Office in Fort Pierce at 2 p.m. Monday and traveled to Stone Brothers Funeral Home. Lucie County Sheriff's Office went to the station at 7:25 a.m. 24, regarding a "full cardiac arrest," and Hoge was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. His death comes about 15 months after his younger brother, Jarius Hodge, also a St. Lucie County Fire District firefighter and paramedic, died in July 2025 after falling ill during a shift. The district honored Jarius with line-of-duty honors. After his brother’s death, Austin spent months searching for answers. He told CBS12 News in January that Jarius caught the flu from a patient and died hours after arriving at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital in Port St. Lucie, struggling to breathe. Austin said medical records showed doctors made critical mistakes, including needing three attempts to intubate his brother. CBS12 reached out to the hospital at the time and did not receive a response before that story was published. Because Jarius was over 25 and had no spouse or children, Florida’s so-called free kill law barred his family from suing for medical malpractice. Austin pushed state lawmakers to repeal it and started a petition in his brother’s honor. He said the fight was about accountability, not money. Bernard Taylor has known Austin since their school days in Sebastian. Taylor was a senior and Austin a freshman when they met at the Boys and Girls Club, where Taylor worked as a counselor and Austin was one of the kids he mentored. Taylor said Austin always wanted to keep up with the older kids, and the two formed a bond that lasted for years. Later, when Taylor decided to change careers, Austin was one of the first people he called. Taylor said Austin supported him through becoming a firefighter, from answering questions to helping him with his conditioning. Just a ball of positive energy. A smile that lights up the room. No matter what you’re going through, he had the right words to kind of get you through it, Taylor said. Taylor said he spoke with Austin about a week before his death to make sure he was doing well. He said he is most heartbroken for Austin’s mother, who has now lost both of her sons. That’s one of the strongest people I’ve ever met in my life. I don’t know if I can hold it together if I was her, Taylor said. Bonnie Hill, a family friend who helped raise Austin’s mother, said she has been by her side and that the family is leaning on its faith and a strong circle of support. I say on my watch, I’m not going to let you die. You’re going to live, and we’re going to get through this, Hill said of what she has told Austin’s mother. Hill said that faith is what is carrying the family now. See also: King tides cause coastal flooding, beach closures in Palm Beach County and Treasure Coast We believe God even in this. We believe God, and we stand on the promises because they won’t fail, Hill said. Taylor said he hopes people remember Austin for his love of serving others. He was a person who loved what he did. He was a person who loved serving his community, Taylor said. Lucie County Fire District has not released details about Austin Hodge’s death.

entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District firefighter who died unexpectedly Saturday morning has been identified as Austin Hodge, a firefighter paramedic and nine-year veteran of the department. The fire district announced Hodge was found unresponsive in his bunk during a shift change. He was taken to the hospital and passed away. Lucie County Fire District family mourns the loss of one of our own,” the district said in a statement. In the hours following his death, firefighters, the department’s Honor Guard and fellow first responders gathered to honor Hodge and support one another. The district said the response reflected the strong bond shared throughout the fire service. The district thanked the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office, Fort Pierce Police Department, Port St. Lucie Police Department and peer support teams from Martin and Indian River counties for providing assistance and standing alongside firefighters during the difficult day. “Together, they offered strength, compassion, and support while ensuring Austin was honored with the dignity and respect he deserves,” the district said. The district said its thoughts are with Hodge’s family, loved ones and everyone who served alongside him. They respectfully ask that Hodge’s family be given privacy during this time. “We are deeply grateful to our fellow first responders and community for the outpouring of support during this tremendous loss,” the district said. “Today and always, we stand together.” The tragedy comes more than a year after the community mourned the sudden loss of his brother, Jarius Hodge , 26, who was also a St. Lucie County firefighter and died from septic shock in July 2025. The district said it will share information on funeral and memorial services in coordination with the family when it becomes available.

entry.title: St. Lucie County honors firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge after line-of-duty death
entry.summary: St. Lucie County firefighters and community members gathered to honor firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge, escorting him through the community he served after the fire district said he died Saturday and is being honored with a line-of-duty death designation. WATCH: St. Lucie County Honors Firefighter-Paramedic Austin Hodge St. Lucie County Honors Firefighter-Paramedic Austin Hodge | WPTV Hodge served the St. Lucie County Fire District for more than nine years. According to the district, he was found unresponsive in his bunk at the firehouse during shift change. Firefighters escorted Hodge from the medical examiner's office to the funeral home as colleagues and community members paid their respects along his final journey through Fort Pierce. 'A bright light' Dr. Aleta Paschal, who worked alongside Hodge outside the fire district, described him as someone whose personality made an impression on those around him. 'Austin is just a bright light,' Paschal said. 'He always made me smile. He had the biggest bear hugs. Everybody loved him.' Paschal said Hodge had a way of making the people around him feel welcomed. 'Anybody he interacted with, he made you feel like family for sure,' she said. His service extended beyond the firehouse Hodge's work caring for people extended beyond his role as a firefighter-paramedic. Paschal said Hodge also worked as a respiratory therapist, where the two cared for critically ill patients together. 'Everybody loved him,' Paschal said. 'He was a critical part of our team. He's going to be very missed at the hospital.' Within the St. Lucie County Fire District, Hodge also served on the Honor Guard and the district's Firefighter Challenge Team. Those roles added to a legacy of service that spanned more than nine years with the district. Community says goodbye As Hodge's colleagues escorted him through Fort Pierce, Paschal said she hopes people remember the qualities that made him special to those who knew him. 'Remember his smile. Remember his presence,' Paschal said. 'Just remember his strength and who he was.' The procession offered firefighters, colleagues and members of the community a chance to pay tribute to someone who spent years helping others, both at the fire district and in health care. entry.title: Seminole Ridge flag football eyes third straight state title
entry.summary: Greatness doesn't happen overnight; it takes countless hours and endless repetition. Over the past two years, the girls' flag football team at Seminole Ridge High School has won 37 games and lost only four, while winning two straight championships. WATCH BELOW: Seminole Ridge flag football eyes 3rd straight state title Seminole Ridge flag football eyes 3rd straight state title 'It's an amazing feeling that the girls are so hungry and into flag football. They love what they do and work so hard. It's really a joy to be the coach,' head coach Scott O'Hara said. His joy as a coach comes from having the best team in Florida. The girls are sure-handed, disciplined, and have fun while doing it. 'If we're too serious with the team, then it's going to be a lot of tension with the team, but adding the jokes and the calmness helps keep the balance between everything,' said Samantha Musgrave, the team captain. She knows the girls have a chance to win three straight titles, but takes it day by day. 'This upcoming season I expect for us to win some games. It's all about who puts in the most work, and I think our team puts in even more work than we need to, for sure,' said Musgrave. One reason the girls can let their hair down and be free is thanks to Chachi Saunders, but on the field she's a playmaker. From game-winning catches in the championship to leading the team in almost every statistical category, 17 interceptions last season, and even earning First Team All-Defensive honors. To cap it all off, she's the first flag footballer in Palm Beach County to commit to a Division I school for flag football. 'I didn't know this would ever happen, but I'm so proud and so happy to have all of my coaches to help me and my team being on my back,' said Saunders.

It's all about who puts in the most work, and I think our team puts in even more work than we need to, for sure," said Musgrave.One reason the girls can let their hair down and be free is thanks to Chachi Saunders, but on the field she's a playmaker.From game-winning catches in the championship to leading the team in almost every statistical category, 17 interceptions last season, and even earning First Team All-Defensive honors.To cap it all off, she's the first flag footballer in Palm Beach County to commit to a Division I school for flag football."I didn't know this would ever happen, but I'm so proud and so happy to have all of my coaches to help me and my team being on my back," said Saunders.

entry.article_text: WPTV has been following flooding on the Treasure Coast caused by strong winds and king tides on Monday.In Martin County, off Dyer Point Road in Palm City, parts of the area were completely underwater.WATCH BELOW: Flooding swamps parts of Palm City amid king tides, strong windsTerresa Baldwin, who lives off the roadway, said it was flooded for a few hours, but water has since retreated."You could smell the sewage; it was really stinky, it was bad," Baldwin said. "There were dead copperheads, so the snakes are coming out. They're getting flushed out with the water."Baldwin said she was also dealing with flooding in her backyard along one of the finger canals.She showed WPTV the water over her dock and in her new patio."The wind was blowing so hard, so it was like waves crashing in your backyard, and you're like, no, nobody wants to see that," Baldwin said.Despite the water going down, she is still worried about what could happen in the next few days."The biggest concern for us is getting water from both sides. What do you do, especially when you're trying to sleep, and you don't know if the water's going to come up more or what's going to get damaged at night when you really can't see," Baldwin said. With high tide later Monday night, the sheriff’s office told WPTV the situation could get worse.Lt. Dave Rosko said they have three high-water vehicles ready for rescue efforts and urged neighbors to think twice before driving through the water."Understand the limitations of your vehicle and do not drive through the high waters," Rosko said. "If your vehicle gets disabled there, it may turn into a rescue event where we need to come out and ensure your safety."Rosko said neighbors living in coastal communities should be aware of future tides before traveling.

entry.title: From Jensen Beach to Louisiana Tech: Andrew Burnette gets one more shot at college football - WPTV
entry.summary: From Jensen Beach to Louisiana Tech: Andrew Burnette gets one more shot at college football    WPTV
entry.article_text: A young man from the Midwest with South Florida roots describes how Andrew Burnette moved from Michigan around the age of 12 and found home on the football field in Martin County."I played football my whole life, and I can say football is a little harder in Florida than it is in Michigan," said Burnette.WATCH BELOW: Local football standout gets one more shot at college footballWhile football was his first sport, during his high school days at Jensen Beach High School, he fell in love with takedowns and pins."I wasn't zoned for that school, but I went there for wrestling originally; that was my first passion," said Burnette.While he was doing well in wrestling, football kept calling to him."Moving through high school, I knew football was what I wanted to do," said Burnette.He established himself as a force at Jensen Beach High School, but he didn't receive much interest from college football programs, similar to many Treasure Coast football recruits."One of my main struggles was recruitment out of high school, because I felt like our area was a little under-recruited," said Burnette.Betting on himself, he decided to play at Highland Community College in Kansas.Burnette played in nine games and rushed for 340 yards and two touchdowns, but he still wasn't on any other college football program's radar."I transferred to Independence Junior College, and I was cut from the team," said Burnette.Independence was featured on the hit Netflix show Last Chance U, but once his chance there was short-lived, he reached out to Keiser University in West Palm Beach."I spoke with the coach there and told him, 'You guys offered me in high school,' and he said, 'I don't really remember. Send me your film.' He saw my film and said, 'Hey, bring it,'" said Burnette.And he did "bring it." In the two years he played at Keiser, he rushed for over 2,300 yards and 30 touchdowns.With stats like that, Division I programs finally came calling, starting with Louisiana Tech."Last year I played there; it was my first year at the Division I level, and then my eligibility ran out," said Burnette.At the time, the NCAA granted student-athletes only four years of eligibility unless they were injured, so Burnette rolled up his sleeves and got to work."I called my dad and told him, 'Hey, I need to do something. I can't just sit here,' so I went and worked with my dad in Michigan," said Burnette.He worked with his dad at a steel mill in Detroit for a few months, but this summer the NCAA announced the 5-in-5 rule, meaning student-athletes can compete for up to five seasons across a continuous five-year period.So he hired a lawyer and went to court with the NCAA to get his final year of eligibility, and they granted him one last year, and now he's making the most of it."It was amazing; I would rather play football than do anything, and for me to have this opportunity again, it's a blessing," said Burnette.

entry.summary: Floodwaters have inundated parking spaces, roads and walkways at a Boynton Beach condominium complex, leaving residents struggling to get in and out as king tides, strong onshore winds and heavy rain push water onto the property. Cotanch was waiting for his daughter, Heather, who was visiting from New York. Her Uber driver had to take a detour, and she ultimately had to roll up her pants, put on sandals and wade through the water to reach the complex.Chrissy Ryan, the property's manager, said Coastal Towers installed a new seawall about two years ago, but flooding remains a concern.Ryan said water is entering the property from both sides, including areas near neighboring properties with lower seawalls."We've got both properties that have lower seawalls, and now with this king tide they come in from both sides," Ryan said.Ryan is asking the City of Boynton Beach and the Florida Department of Transportation to investigate the flooding and evaluate the surrounding infrastructure, including neighboring seawalls, drainage outfalls and backflow prevention systems.She also raised concerns about valve checks she said were discussed about a year and a half ago but still need to be addressed."I want them to see this so something gets done about it," Ryan said.In an email, Ryan described the flooding as a serious concern for resident safety and potential property damage. entry.title: Indian River State College trustees table recommendation to eliminate swimming and diving team
entry.summary: The Indian River State College Board of Trustees has delayed taking action on a recommendation to eliminate the college's swimming and diving team. During a meeting held in Okeechobee, the board voted Tuesday to table the president's recommendation to eliminate the program. WATCH REPORT BELOW: IRSC trustees table recommendation to eliminate swimming, diving team Indian River State College trustees table recommendation to eliminate swimming and diving team Instead, trustees asked the college administration to prepare a comprehensive report on the swimming and diving program. The board requested that the report include input from the community. President Timothy Moore said at Tuesday's meeting that the proposal to cut the programs comes down to money. 'It's a tremendous opportunity to leave this college with that kind of skill, resource and talent here, but it comes at a price,' Moore said. The school president said the program currently costs around $1.4 to $2 million, money that isn't coming in through donations. 'What's required to maintain it as it sits today? We will require $15 to $20 million of an endowment to throw off enough revenue per year to sustain the program as it sits today,' Moore said. There's also a proposal to transition the remaining sports to Division II, resulting in potential savings of around $500,000. But if the swimming and diving program stays, Moore said the school may be forced to cut 50 percent for sports across the board. 'It's elimination of one or impose a penalty across all, and I would imagine that our championships will suffer because of that decision,' Moore said. The administration is expected to present the report at the Board of Trustees Nov. 17 meeting, when recommendations on how to move forward will be considered. This past March, the men's swim and dive team captured its 52nd consecutive national championship title, and the women's team claimed its 48th crown. Former swimmer Ella Smith started a petition last week to save the program, which has more than 12,500 signatures.

Throughout her campaign, Nixon has focused on affordability and economic issues, arguing working families are struggling with rising costs while politicians benefit from the current system. She has highlighted her background as a federal prosecutor, judge and attorney general, frequently emphasizing law enforcement and public safety issues.During a recent campaign stop in Martin County with Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz, Moody pointed to President Donald Trump's "One Big Beautiful Bill" and touted tax cuts enacted during his administration.Moody has framed the race starkly, telling voters the election is a choice between "safety or chaos" and "freedom or socialism."Democratic challenger Angie Nixon is a state representative and labor organizer from Jacksonville.Nixon emerged from a competitive Democratic primary, defeating a more centrist opponent who significantly outraised her campaign.A member of the Democratic Socialists of America, Nixon has campaigned alongside U.S. Bernie Sanders and supports policies including a $25 minimum wage and Medicare for All.Throughout her campaign, Nixon has focused on affordability and economic issues, arguing working families are struggling with rising costs while politicians benefit from the current system.Florida has not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 2012, presenting a difficult path for Nixon.Recent polling shows Moody holding a narrow lead of about four percentage points heading into the final week of the campaign.Gillespie is also running for the seat without party affiliation.With early voting underway and Election Day approaching, the race remains one of the most closely watched contests in Florida. The outcome will determine who represents the state in the Senate for the next two years before voters return to the polls for the seat again in 2028.

entry.title: Frankel, Adeimy outline affordability priorities in race for Florida's redrawn 23rd congressional district
entry.summary: With just a week left until the General Election, the candidates vying for the newly redrawn 23rd congressional district in Florida sat down with WPTV morning anchor Hollani Davis to talk about their priorities for voters here at home if they're elected. U.S. Rep. Louis Frankel, D-Fla., is fighting to continue representing South Florida. She says affordability is at the top of her list to tackle. WATCH REPORT BELOW: District 23 candidates focus on affordability Candidates vying to represent Florida's 23rd District lay out priorities to tackle affordability 'When I'm at the supermarket, and people can't afford their food, that's a pretty big message,' says Frankel. Frankel, who is seeking an eighth term in Congress, says Democrats must seek to end the war with Iran and rein in the Trump administration's tariffs to help bring costs under control. She also says there is another glaring issue that can't be ignored. '(There's) probably nothing more important for the people of Palm Beach County, where we have a big senior population, is (the need) to protect Social Security and Medicare,' Frankel said. Challenging Frankel in the race is Deborah Adeimy. The Republican, is a native of Palm Beach County who's worked as a financial adviser to companies like Morgan Stanley, JP Morgan Chase. She says she'd use her financial acumen to help solve South Florida's affordable housing problem by rewriting the playbook. 'Currently in Palm Beach County, there are real estate developers who are taking advantage of antiquated tax incentives, tax breaks that are driving up costs here in Palm Beach County (including) rent,' says Adeimy. Florida's 23rd congressional district previously straddled the Palm Beach-Broward County line with a heavy focus on Broward County. After the districts were redrawn this year, it now covers a portion of West Palm Beach and extends south to include Boynton Beach.

entry.title: 'A smile that lights up the room': Loved ones remember St. Lucie County firefighter - cw34.com
entry.summary: 'A smile that lights up the room': Loved ones remember St. Lucie County firefighter    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Family and friends are mourning St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge, a man those closest to him describe as endlessly positive and devoted to serving his community. A funeral procession for Hodge left the Medical Examiner’s Office in Fort Pierce at 2 p.m. Monday and traveled to Stone Brothers Funeral Home. Lucie County Sheriff's Office went to the station at 7:25 a.m. 24, regarding a "full cardiac arrest," and Hoge was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. His death comes about 15 months after his younger brother, Jarius Hodge, also a St. Lucie County Fire District firefighter and paramedic, died in July 2025 after falling ill during a shift. The district honored Jarius with line-of-duty honors. After his brother’s death, Austin spent months searching for answers. He told CBS12 News in January that Jarius caught the flu from a patient and died hours after arriving at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital in Port St. Lucie, struggling to breathe. Austin said medical records showed doctors made critical mistakes, including needing three attempts to intubate his brother. CBS12 reached out to the hospital at the time and did not receive a response before that story was published. Because Jarius was over 25 and had no spouse or children, Florida’s so-called free kill law barred his family from suing for medical malpractice. Austin pushed state lawmakers to repeal it and started a petition in his brother’s honor. He said the fight was about accountability, not money. Bernard Taylor has known Austin since their school days in Sebastian. Taylor was a senior and Austin a freshman when they met at the Boys and Girls Club, where Taylor worked as a counselor and Austin was one of the kids he mentored. Taylor said Austin always wanted to keep up with the older kids, and the two formed a bond that lasted for years. Later, when Taylor decided to change careers, Austin was one of the first people he called. Taylor said Austin supported him through becoming a firefighter, from answering questions to helping him with his conditioning. Just a ball of positive energy. A smile that lights up the room. No matter what you’re going through, he had the right words to kind of get you through it, Taylor said. Taylor said he spoke with Austin about a week before his death to make sure he was doing well. He said he is most heartbroken for Austin’s mother, who has now lost both of her sons. That’s one of the strongest people I’ve ever met in my life. I don’t know if I can hold it together if I was her, Taylor said. Bonnie Hill, a family friend who helped raise Austin’s mother, said she has been by her side and that the family is leaning on its faith and a strong circle of support. I say on my watch, I’m not going to let you die. You’re going to live, and we’re going to get through this, Hill said of what she has told Austin’s mother. Hill said that faith is what is carrying the family now. See also: King tides cause coastal flooding, beach closures in Palm Beach County and Treasure Coast We believe God even in this. We believe God, and we stand on the promises because they won’t fail, Hill said. Taylor said he hopes people remember Austin for his love of serving others. He was a person who loved what he did. He was a person who loved serving his community, Taylor said. Lucie County Fire District has not released details about Austin Hodge’s death.

entry.summary: St. Lucie County deputy accused of DUI in Vero Beach crash that injured woman and child    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie County sheriff's deputy has been charged with DUI following a March 1 crash in Vero Beach that left a woman seriously injured and her son hospitalized. The crash happened at the intersection of Beachland Boulevard and A1A in Vero Beach. Investigators said Tyler Horstman, an off-duty St. Lucie County sheriff's detective, was driving an unmarked agency pickup truck when it collided with an SUV carrying a woman and her son. According to investigators, the SUV's driver ran a red light, while Horstman had a green light. All three individuals involved in the crash were hospitalized. The child was later released, but the woman suffered a traumatic brain injury, according to the affidavit. Police said the crash could have been fatal. "Given the nature of the vehicles at a decent rate of speed, I mean, I don't want to say it worked out in its best. I mean, obviously injuries were still sustained, possibly long-lasting injuries, but at the end of the day, it's very feasible that a fatality could have occurred," Lt. Investigators determined that Horstman's blood alcohol level was above the legal limit. According to the affidavit, Horstman stated during his assessment that he had "a few beers" earlier in the evening. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates Police also said the truck was traveling about 64 mph in a 35-mph zone just before the crash. Horstman turned himself in on Monday. Police explained that the investigation took several months to complete. "It was a matter of investigators going through search warrants, subpoenas, and obtaining all different records," Kerensky said. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro, Horstman subsequently turned himself in to the Indian River County Jail and was placed on unpaid administrative leave in accordance with agency policy. Sheriff Del Toro released this statement: "Our responsibility to uphold the law comes with an expectation that we follow it ourselves. When an employee is accused of violating that responsibility, we must address it fairly and hold them accountable through the appropriate process," said Sheriff Richard R. "The men and women of this agency work every day to earn the trust of our community, and we will continue to hold ourselves to the standards that trust requires." Horstman faces several charges, including DUI, and his arraignment is scheduled for Dec. "Our job is to investigate no matter who's involved, and we're going to do the due diligence to make sure what we do is right. At the end of the day, it happens to be a warrant was issued for Tyler Horstman," Kerensky said.
