entry.title: St. Lucie County sheriff's deputy faces DUI charge after Vero Beach crash - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County sheriff's deputy faces DUI charge after Vero Beach crash    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County sheriff’s deputy turned himself in Monday afternoon after a felony warrant was issued in connection with an off-duty crash in Vero Beach, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office. Read also: Road Ranger killed, hit at crash scene on I-95 near Lantana Road Deputy Tyler Horstman was driving an agency vehicle when he was involved in the crash on March 1, the sheriff’s office said. On September 9, the Sheriff’s Office received Horstman’s blood-test results. They showed a blood alcohol concentration of 0.246, more than three times Florida’s legal limit. According to the arrest report, March 1 at about 11:25pm at the intersection of Beachland Boulevard and A1A in Vero Beach, Horstman was off-duty driving an unmarked St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office pickup truck when he hit a Chevy Equinox with a woman and an infant inside. The arrest report says: "Horstman stated he had a few beers earlier in the evening." It says Horstman had a "faint odor or alcohol on his breath" and it says Horstman was "lethargic and dazed" and that he was "drowsy and periodically dozing off." The woman in the vehicle he hit suffered "a traumatic brain injury" and the infant was alert and responsive. The arrest report says Horstman had a blood-alcohol level of .246, which is three times the legal limit at which a person is considered too impaired to drive in Florida. Horstman was placed on administrative leave on September 15, according to the St. A felony arrest warrant was issued Monday. It lists charges of DUI impairment involving a blood or breath alcohol level of 0.15 or higher and serious personal injury. The crash happened in March, but Horstman was not arrested until late October. "It's very typical in cases like this take months and months, and it's very frustrating for victims and their families, and also for the public, who are waiting for justice," said Dave Aronberg, former Palm Beach County State Attorney. He is now an attorney in private practice in West Palm Beach. Aronberg says it's not unusual at all that it would take seven months for someone, in this case a Sheriff's detective, to be arrested for DUI with serious bodily injury. "Proving felony DUI with serious bodily injury requires two hard sciences. You have to have crash physics to prove causation. That's crucial to any case like this, and you also have to have toxicology to prove impairment, and neither of those things happens overnight," Aronberg said. Horstman was booked into the Indian River County Jail at 4:59 p.m. and later posted $15,000 bond at 6:24 p.m. His arraignment is scheduled for December 9. Vero Beach police are leading the criminal investigation, according to the Sheriff’s Office. The agency’s internal investigation is on hold pending the outcome of the criminal case.

entry.title: From Jensen Beach to Louisiana Tech: Andrew Burnette gets one more shot at college football - WFLX
entry.summary: From Jensen Beach to Louisiana Tech: Andrew Burnette gets one more shot at college football    WFLX
entry.article_text: A young man from the Midwest with South Florida roots describes how Andrew Burnette moved from Michigan around the age of 12 and found home on the football field in Martin County. “I played football my whole life, and I can say football is a little harder in Florida than it is in Michigan,” said Burnette. While football was his first sport, during his high school days at Jensen Beach High School, he fell in love with takedowns and pins. “I wasn’t zoned for that school, but I went there for wrestling originally; that was my first passion,” said Burnette. While he was doing well in wrestling, football kept calling to him. “Moving through high school, I knew football was what I wanted to do,” said Burnette. He established himself as a force at Jensen Beach High School, but he didn’t receive much interest from college football programs, similar to many Treasure Coast football recruits. “One of my main struggles was recruitment out of high school, because I felt like our area was a little under-recruited,” said Burnette. Betting on himself, he decided to play at Highland Community College in Kansas. Burnette played in nine games and rushed for 340 yards and two touchdowns, but he still wasn’t on any other college football program’s radar. “I transferred to Independence Junior College, and I was cut from the team,” said Burnette. Independence was featured on the hit Netflix show Last Chance U, but once his chance there was short-lived, he reached out to Keiser University in West Palm Beach. “I spoke with the coach there and told him, ‘You guys offered me in high school,’ and he said, ‘I don’t really remember. Send me your film.’ He saw my film and said, ‘Hey, bring it,’” said Burnette. And he did “bring it.” In the two years he played at Keiser, he rushed for over 2,300 yards and 30 touchdowns. With stats like that, Division I programs finally came calling, starting with Louisiana Tech. “Last year I played there; it was my first year at the Division I level, and then my eligibility ran out,” said Burnette. At the time, the NCAA granted student-athletes only four years of eligibility unless they were injured, so Burnette rolled up his sleeves and got to work. “I called my dad and told him, ‘Hey, I need to do something. I can’t just sit here,’ so I went and worked with my dad in Michigan,” said Burnette. He worked with his dad at a steel mill in Detroit for a few months, but this summer the NCAA announced the 5-in-5 rule, meaning student-athletes can compete for up to five seasons across a continuous five-year period. So he hired a lawyer and went to court with the NCAA to get his final year of eligibility, and they granted him one last year, and now he’s making the most of it. “It was amazing; I would rather play football than do anything, and for me to have this opportunity again, it’s a blessing,” said Burnette.

entry.title: 14,000 turtle nests: Decades of protection pay off in Indian River County - WPEC
entry.summary: 14,000 turtle nests: Decades of protection pay off in Indian River County    WPEC
entry.article_text: Indian River County’s sea turtles broke a record. The county documented 14,083 nests as of Thursday, its highest total ever recorded. Coastal Specialist Dakota Whalen credits decades of conservation efforts for the milestone. This is actually a really big deal because what we’re seeing is decades of conservation paying off, Whalen said. But the record season is facing a rough finish. Powerful waves and high tides are eroding beaches, threatening some remaining nests. Loggerheads lead the record season The county’s latest dashboard lists 10,045 loggerhead nests, 3,970 green turtle nests and 68 leatherback nests. The total surpassed the previous record, set in 2023, by approximately 2,000 nests, according to Whalen. Loggerheads drove much of that increase. They’re dominating with 10,000 nests across our entire coastline, which is an insane number, Whalen said. The orange markers beachgoers see represent only a fraction of the nesting activity. The county marks approximately one in 10 nests along its 22.4-mile coastline. If we mark 14,000 nests you wouldn’t have anywhere to sit on the beach, Whalen said. And like seriously it would be a sea of orange. Researchers evaluate those marked nests to help measure reproductive success. Whalen said the long-term gains reflect years of work protecting turtles and their nesting beaches. Those efforts include monitoring, partnerships with conservation groups and encouraging turtle-friendly beach practices. Rough surf threatens remaining nests A nor’easter and king tides have brought challenging conditions as nesting season winds down. Waves strip away sand, potentially exposing eggs buried beneath the beach. Unsafe conditions have delayed surveys needed to determine the full extent of the damage. Whalen estimated that 75% to 90% of the county’s nests had already hatched before the recent rough weather. A lot of them have already hatched out, a lot of them have made it to the water safely, Whalen said. Indian River County’s nesting season officially ends on Halloween. Some nests may continue incubating beyond that date. Nesting numbers across the Treasure Coast Other counties also provided nesting figures. The totals cover different reporting dates and monitoring areas. Indian River County : As of Oct. 22, the county recorded 14,083 nests: 10,045 loggerhead, 3,970 green turtle and 68 leatherback nests. Lucie County : As of Sept. 30, the county recorded 10,239 nests: 9,111 loggerhead, 956 green turtle and 172 leatherback nests. Martin County: As of Sept. 28, its Hutchinson Island monitoring area recorded 4,874 nests: 4,532 loggerhead, 161 green turtle and 181 leatherback nests. Martin County’s figures cover approximately 7.5 miles of Hutchinson Island shoreline. That area stretches from the north side of St. Lucie Inlet to the Martin St. CBS12 News has requested Palm Beach County’s latest countywide figures from FWC and is awaiting those numbers. Boca Raton sees high nest counts, lower hatch success In Boca Raton, a strong nesting season did not translate into equally strong hatching results. David Anderson, sea turtle conservation coordinator at Gumbo Limbo Nature Center, reported the city’s third-highest nesting season. That included record counts of 1,118 loggerhead nests and 43 leatherback nests. But an average of only about 50% of the eggs in inventoried nests hatched. Anderson said a typical hatch rate would be 70% to 80% or more. He attributed some losses to prolonged hot, dry conditions during peak incubation. High sand temperatures can prevent embryos from continuing to develop. Storms and high tides also washed out approximately 185 nests, Anderson said. Predators affected another 13 nests. Artificial lighting created additional problems after hatching. Anderson said hatchlings from at least 85 nests became disoriented and headed into the dunes. Staff plan to evaluate beachfront lighting and work with nearby properties before next season. So sure, it’s sad to see so many hatchlings and eggs not fully developed, but once again, we had a great nesting season, Anderson said. So as long as the nesting numbers continue to climb, it gives us hope. What to do if you find eggs or hatchlings The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission says sea turtles spread their nests across the season. That strategy helps some nests survive even when storms damage others. After rough weather, beachgoers may find exposed eggs or young turtles washed ashore. FWC says to leave exposed eggs in place. Eggs swept from their nests rarely survive, and people should not collect or rebury them. Storm currents can also carry young turtles back ashore, sometimes tangled in seaweed. These washback turtles may need specialized care. Do not pick them up or return them to the ocean. Instead, immediately call FWC’s 24-hour Wildlife Alert Hotline at 888-404-3922 for instructions. Hatchlings actively crawling toward the ocean do not need assistance, according to FWC. Beachgoers can help by keeping beaches clean, flat and dark. Remove beach gear, fill holes, flatten sandcastles and keep lights off the beach at night.

entry.title: St. Lucie County sheriff's deputy faces DUI charge after Vero Beach crash - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County sheriff's deputy faces DUI charge after Vero Beach crash    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County sheriff’s deputy turned himself in Monday afternoon after a felony warrant was issued in connection with an off-duty crash in Vero Beach, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office. Read also: Road Ranger killed, hit at crash scene on I-95 near Lantana Road Deputy Tyler Horstman was driving an agency vehicle when he was involved in the crash on March 1, the sheriff’s office said. On September 9, the Sheriff’s Office received Horstman’s blood-test results. They showed a blood alcohol concentration of 0.246, more than three times Florida’s legal limit. According to the arrest report, March 1 at about 11:25pm at the intersection of Beachland Boulevard and A1A in Vero Beach, Horstman was off-duty driving an unmarked St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office pickup truck when he hit a Chevy Equinox with a woman and an infant inside. Vero Beach police say Horstman was driving at 63 mph in a posted 35 mph zone and entered the intersection on a green light. The other driver entered the intersection against a red light. Both drivers were injured and taken to the hospital, and the infant was not injured. The arrest report says: "Horstman stated he had a few beers earlier in the evening." It says Horstman had a "faint odor of alcohol on his breath" and it says Horstman was "lethargic and dazed" and that he was "drowsy and periodically dozing off." The woman in the vehicle he hit suffered "a traumatic brain injury" and the infant was alert and responsive. The arrest report says Horstman had a blood-alcohol level of .246, which is three times the legal limit at which a person is considered too impaired to drive in Florida. Horstman was placed on administrative leave on September 15, according to the St. A felony arrest warrant was issued Monday. It lists charges of DUI impairment involving a blood or breath alcohol level of 0.15 or higher and serious personal injury. The crash happened in March, but Horstman was not arrested until late October. "It's very typical in cases like this take months and months, and it's very frustrating for victims and their families, and also for the public, who are waiting for justice," said Dave Aronberg, former Palm Beach County State Attorney. He is now an attorney in private practice in West Palm Beach. Aronberg says it's not unusual at all that it would take seven months for someone, in this case a Sheriff's detective, to be arrested for DUI with serious bodily injury. "Proving felony DUI with serious bodily injury requires two hard sciences. You have to have crash physics to prove causation. That's crucial to any case like this, and you also have to have toxicology to prove impairment, and neither of those things happens overnight," Aronberg said. Horstman was booked into the Indian River County Jail at 4:59 p.m. and later posted $15,000 bond at 6:24 p.m. His arraignment is scheduled for December 9. Vero Beach police are leading the criminal investigation, according to the Sheriff’s Office. The agency’s internal investigation is on hold pending the outcome of the criminal case.

entry.title: 15-year-old seriously injured after wrong-way crash following police pursuit in Stuart
entry.summary: A 15-year-old driver and another motorist were seriously injured early Tuesday after a police pursuit ended in a wrong-way crash on U.S. Highway 1, according to the Stuart Police Department. Police said officers were conducting traffic enforcement near Southwest Federal Highway and Southwest St. Lucie Crescent at about 3:45 a.m. when they spotted a vehicle traveling north at what officers described as an extremely high rate of speed. An officer attempted to make a traffic stop, but police said the driver refused to stop and fled. The pursuit eventually continued onto U.S. 1, where police said the driver began traveling north in the southbound lanes from Wright Boulevard. Officers continued trying to stop the vehicle because of the danger posed to other motorists, according to the department. Police said officers also attempted to alert drivers traveling on Northwest Federal Highway. The fleeing vehicle eventually collided with a vehicle traveling south at the Mall South Entrance intersection, police said. After the crash, officers learned the driver of the fleeing vehicle was 15 years old. Both drivers were taken to Lawnwood Medical Center in Fort Pierce with serious injuries. The Stuart Police Department is investigating the incident, while the Florida Highway Patrol is conducting a separate investigation into the crash. Police said no additional information would be released at this time because the investigation remains ongoing.

entry.title: Martin County commissioners approve one-year pause on large-scale data center applications - WPBF
entry.summary: Martin County commissioners approve one-year pause on large-scale data center applications    WPBF
entry.article_text: Martin County commissioners unanimously voted during a second public hearing to implement a one-year moratorium on large-scale data center applications, giving staff time to study potential environmental impacts and establish rules for future projects. During the hearing, every resident who spoke during public comment opposed the possibility of data centers in the county. "We simply do not have enough information on what we may be introducing to this ecologically sensitive region and the world's most extensive restoration effort. We need more study and the evaluation of potential impacts, especially in the 16-county greater Everglades region," said Casey Darling, policy director for Friends of the Everglades. "I don’t want to spend another year or longer where somebody that I know is trying to do me great bodily harm. Folks, it’s in your hands. These things are not to be near people that are trying to conduct their ordinary lives," said resident Richard Miller. Commissioner Blake Capps confirmed there is an applicant for a data center. "One of them is the Florida Gateway Project, where this one project has been ... a data center application has come on Kanner Highway," Capps said. A resident who lives near the proposed site raised concerns about the scale of the project. "I happen to live one mile from this new proposed mega center, 100 MW, and 100 MW is like unbelievable to power 100,000 homes, and that's going to be a mile from me. Who knows how much water it's going to use," the resident said. Commissioner Vargas expressed frustration with the application process. "I was not too happy about hearing this application. I even requested the receipt, which I have here in my hand, and the date ... We should give them back and say they don't want you here. It's okay, you go elsewhere," Vargas said. The application for the Florida Gateway Project was submitted on Oct. 12, with the first public hearing held the following day. "We got the information late on the Monday before the 13th ... so, I didn't have the information in advance of the 13th. At the meeting on the 13th, I disclosed to everybody that I had just found out about it. I'm sorry, Commissioner, we did alert the commission as soon as we could," said County Attorney Elysse A. "I understand, but somebody took the money on this date is what I'm trying to say. Doesn't anybody talk to anybody here?" Vargas said. The application will go through the development review process, which staff said is expected to take a year. Aside from this application, there are currently no other large-scale data center applications pending. entry.summary: 'A smile that lights up the room': Loved ones remember St. Lucie County firefighter    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Family and friends are mourning St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge, a man those closest to him describe as endlessly positive and devoted to serving his community. A funeral procession for Hodge left the Medical Examiner’s Office in Fort Pierce at 2 p.m. Monday and traveled to Stone Brothers Funeral Home. Lucie County Sheriff's Office went to the station at 7:25 a.m. 24, regarding a "full cardiac arrest," and Hoge was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. His death comes about 15 months after his younger brother, Jarius Hodge, also a St. Lucie County Fire District firefighter and paramedic, died in July 2025 after falling ill during a shift. The district honored Jarius with line-of-duty honors. After his brother’s death, Austin spent months searching for answers. He told CBS12 News in January that Jarius caught the flu from a patient and died hours after arriving at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital in Port St. Lucie, struggling to breathe. Austin said medical records showed doctors made critical mistakes, including needing three attempts to intubate his brother. CBS12 reached out to the hospital at the time and did not receive a response before that story was published. Because Jarius was over 25 and had no spouse or children, Florida’s so-called free kill law barred his family from suing for medical malpractice. Austin pushed state lawmakers to repeal it and started a petition in his brother’s honor. He said the fight was about accountability, not money. Bernard Taylor has known Austin since their school days in Sebastian. Taylor was a senior and Austin a freshman when they met at the Boys and Girls Club, where Taylor worked as a counselor and Austin was one of the kids he mentored. Taylor said Austin always wanted to keep up with the older kids, and the two formed a bond that lasted for years. Later, when Taylor decided to change careers, Austin was one of the first people he called. Taylor said Austin supported him through becoming a firefighter, from answering questions to helping him with his conditioning. Just a ball of positive energy. A smile that lights up the room. No matter what you’re going through, he had the right words to kind of get you through it, Taylor said. Taylor said he spoke with Austin about a week before his death to make sure he was doing well. He said he is most heartbroken for Austin’s mother, who has now lost both of her sons. That’s one of the strongest people I’ve ever met in my life. I don’t know if I can hold it together if I was her, Taylor said. Bonnie Hill, a family friend who helped raise Austin’s mother, said she has been by her side and that the family is leaning on its faith and a strong circle of support. I say on my watch, I’m not going to let you die. You’re going to live, and we’re going to get through this, Hill said of what she has told Austin’s mother. Hill said that faith is what is carrying the family now. See also: King tides cause coastal flooding, beach closures in Palm Beach County and Treasure Coast We believe God even in this. We believe God, and we stand on the promises because they won’t fail, Hill said. Taylor said he hopes people remember Austin for his love of serving others. He was a person who loved what he did. He was a person who loved serving his community, Taylor said. Lucie County Fire District has not released details about Austin Hodge’s death.

entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District is honoring the life and service of firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge, who died Saturday while on duty. On Monday afternoon, firefighters escorted Hodge’s body from the medical examiner’s office to a funeral home in Fort Pierce. Tears, respect and a sense of loss were visible on the faces of those gathered to pay tribute. FIREFIGHTER MOURNED: Family honors late St. Lucie County firefighter’s birthday with cookout and balloon release His fellow firefighters, friends and members of the community came together to honor Hodge’s more than nine years of service. Diana Harrison, who has known Hodge’s mother since the early 1990s, shared her memories of him. “So, we actually homeschooled our kids together. Austin was just a little bitty guy back then,” Harrison said. Friends and coworkers expressed the heartbreak of losing Hodge, especially as his brother, Jarius Hodge, also a firefighter-paramedic with the St. Lucie County Fire District, died last year after falling ill while on duty. “I have no words, there’s no words, and the brokenness, the sadness — you can’t imagine losing not one son but two sons,” Harrison said. The fire district reported that Austin Hodge was found unresponsive in his bunk at the firehouse during a shift change Saturday. Crews immediately began life-saving measures, but Hodge later died at the hospital. Lucie County Fire District holds procession for firefighter Austin Hodge Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates Hodge joined the district’s firefighter challenge team in 2018 and helped the team win a world championship in 2021. "He was always a giver, even from a little bitty kid, you know. And if I remember right, even when he was a little kid, he wanted to be a firefighter, and then that's what he became," Harrison said. Howard Dunn Jr., founder of the Howard Dunn Jr. Foundation, which supports first responders, shared his personal connection to Hodge. “A couple of years ago I had a close call, and when the rescue came to me, I met Austin. I had an emergency; they transported me to the hospital. He made me feel better — I forgot what I was going for,” Dunn said. Retired lieutenant and former fire district chaplain Thomas Neiman reflected on the Hodge family’s impact on the community. “Knowing that we saw those kids as grade school kids in the library for our homeschool co-op meetings,” Neiman said. “And of course, we can’t begin to imagine what the family and mom and dad are going through, but we’re holding on to them as best we can, and they know we love them." entry.title: 14,000 turtle nests: Decades of protection pay off in Indian River County - WPEC
entry.summary: 14,000 turtle nests: Decades of protection pay off in Indian River County    WPEC
entry.article_text: Indian River County’s sea turtles broke a record. The county documented 14,083 nests as of Thursday, its highest total ever recorded. Coastal Specialist Dakota Whalen credits decades of conservation efforts for the milestone. This is actually a really big deal because what we’re seeing is decades of conservation paying off, Whalen said. But the record season is facing a rough finish. Powerful waves and high tides are eroding beaches, threatening some remaining nests. Loggerheads lead the record season The county’s latest dashboard lists 10,045 loggerhead nests, 3,970 green turtle nests and 68 leatherback nests. The total surpassed the previous record, set in 2023, by approximately 2,000 nests, according to Whalen. Loggerheads drove much of that increase. They’re dominating with 10,000 nests across our entire coastline, which is an insane number, Whalen said. The orange markers beachgoers see represent only a fraction of the nesting activity. The county marks approximately one in 10 nests along its 22.4-mile coastline. If we mark 14,000 nests you wouldn’t have anywhere to sit on the beach, Whalen said. And like seriously it would be a sea of orange. Researchers evaluate those marked nests to help measure reproductive success. Whalen said the long-term gains reflect years of work protecting turtles and their nesting beaches. Those efforts include monitoring, partnerships with conservation groups and encouraging turtle-friendly beach practices. Rough surf threatens remaining nests A nor’easter and king tides have brought challenging conditions as nesting season winds down. Waves strip away sand, potentially exposing eggs buried beneath the beach. Unsafe conditions have delayed surveys needed to determine the full extent of the damage. Whalen estimated that 75% to 90% of the county’s nests had already hatched before the recent rough weather. A lot of them have already hatched out, a lot of them have made it to the water safely, Whalen said. Indian River County’s nesting season officially ends on Halloween. Some nests may continue incubating beyond that date. Nesting numbers across the Treasure Coast Other counties also provided nesting figures. The totals cover different reporting dates and monitoring areas. Indian River County : As of Oct. 22, the county recorded 14,083 nests: 10,045 loggerhead, 3,970 green turtle and 68 leatherback nests. Lucie County : As of Sept. 30, the county recorded 10,239 nests: 9,111 loggerhead, 956 green turtle and 172 leatherback nests. Martin County: As of Sept. 28, its Hutchinson Island monitoring area recorded 4,874 nests: 4,532 loggerhead, 161 green turtle and 181 leatherback nests. Martin County’s figures cover approximately 7.5 miles of Hutchinson Island shoreline. That area stretches from the north side of St. Lucie Inlet to the Martin St. CBS12 News has requested Palm Beach County’s latest countywide figures from FWC and is awaiting those numbers. Boca Raton sees high nest counts, lower hatch success In Boca Raton, a strong nesting season did not translate into equally strong hatching results. David Anderson, sea turtle conservation coordinator at Gumbo Limbo Nature Center, reported the city’s third-highest nesting season. That included record counts of 1,118 loggerhead nests and 43 leatherback nests. But an average of only about 50% of the eggs in inventoried nests hatched. Anderson said a typical hatch rate would be 70% to 80% or more. He attributed some losses to prolonged hot, dry conditions during peak incubation. High sand temperatures can prevent embryos from continuing to develop. Storms and high tides also washed out approximately 185 nests, Anderson said. Predators affected another 13 nests. Artificial lighting created additional problems after hatching. Anderson said hatchlings from at least 85 nests became disoriented and headed into the dunes. Staff plan to evaluate beachfront lighting and work with nearby properties before next season. So sure, it’s sad to see so many hatchlings and eggs not fully developed, but once again, we had a great nesting season, Anderson said. So as long as the nesting numbers continue to climb, it gives us hope. What to do if you find eggs or hatchlings The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission says sea turtles spread their nests across the season. That strategy helps some nests survive even when storms damage others. After rough weather, beachgoers may find exposed eggs or young turtles washed ashore. FWC says to leave exposed eggs in place. Eggs swept from their nests rarely survive, and people should not collect or rebury them. Storm currents can also carry young turtles back ashore, sometimes tangled in seaweed. These washback turtles may need specialized care. Do not pick them up or return them to the ocean. Instead, immediately call FWC’s 24-hour Wildlife Alert Hotline at 888-404-3922 for instructions. Hatchlings actively crawling toward the ocean do not need assistance, according to FWC. Beachgoers can help by keeping beaches clean, flat and dark. Remove beach gear, fill holes, flatten sandcastles and keep lights off the beach at night.

Trump International Airport and Mar-a-Lago. The North American Aerospace Defense Command has said the deployment was made at the request of the U.S. Secret Service. What are the air defense systems? 'What you see here are three trailer-mounted anti-aircraft, anti-drone, actually even anti-vehicle defense systems,' Ingram told Hoffman. Ingram said the weapons are surface-to-air missile systems, commonly known as SAMs, and described them as a final layer of protection. 'This is the last line of defense that will eliminate the threat to the president of the United States,' Ingram said. entry.article_text: Lucie County sheriff's deputy has been charged with DUI following a March 1 crash in Vero Beach that left a woman seriously injured and her son hospitalized. The crash happened at the intersection of Beachland Boulevard and A1A in Vero Beach. Investigators said Tyler Horstman, an off-duty St. Lucie County sheriff's detective, was driving an unmarked agency pickup truck when it collided with an SUV carrying a woman and her son. According to investigators, the SUV's driver ran a red light, while Horstman had a green light. All three individuals involved in the crash were hospitalized. The child was later released, but the woman suffered a traumatic brain injury, according to the affidavit. Police said the crash could have been fatal. "Given the nature of the vehicles at a decent rate of speed, I mean, I don't want to say it worked out in its best. I mean, obviously injuries were still sustained, possibly long-lasting injuries, but at the end of the day, it's very feasible that a fatality could have occurred," Lt. Investigators determined that Horstman's blood alcohol level was above the legal limit. According to the affidavit, Horstman stated during his assessment that he had "a few beers" earlier in the evening. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates Police also said the truck was traveling about 64 mph in a 35-mph zone just before the crash. Horstman turned himself in on Monday. Police explained that the investigation took several months to complete. "It was a matter of investigators going through search warrants, subpoenas, and obtaining all different records," Kerensky said. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro, Horstman subsequently turned himself in to the Indian River County Jail and was placed on unpaid administrative leave in accordance with agency policy. Sheriff Del Toro released this statement: "Our responsibility to uphold the law comes with an expectation that we follow it ourselves. When an employee is accused of violating that responsibility, we must address it fairly and hold them accountable through the appropriate process," said Sheriff Richard R. "The men and women of this agency work every day to earn the trust of our community, and we will continue to hold ourselves to the standards that trust requires." Horstman faces several charges, including DUI, and his arraignment is scheduled for Dec. "Our job is to investigate no matter who's involved, and we're going to do the due diligence to make sure what we do is right. At the end of the day, it happens to be a warrant was issued for Tyler Horstman," Kerensky said. Deputies responded and found Oswald, who appeared to be under the influence of an unknown substance, the sheriff's office said. See also: Woman with 28 prior felony convictions arrested in Okeechobee drug investigation Oswald has an extensive criminal history, with as many as 14 prior arrests in Martin County on charges ranging from grand theft and burglary to loitering and prowling, according to the sheriff's office. He now faces charges of loitering, prowling, and trespassing. The sheriff's office praised residents for quickly reporting the activity, saying community members play an important role in keeping their neighborhoods safe when they report suspicious behavior.

entry.title: St. Lucie County sheriff's deputy faces DUI charge after Vero Beach crash - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County sheriff's deputy faces DUI charge after Vero Beach crash    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County sheriff’s deputy turned himself in Monday afternoon after a felony warrant was issued in connection with an off-duty crash in Vero Beach, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office. Read also: Road Ranger killed, hit at crash scene on I-95 near Lantana Road Deputy Tyler Horstman was driving an agency vehicle when he was involved in the crash on March 1, the sheriff’s office said. On September 9, the Sheriff’s Office received Horstman’s blood-test results. They showed a blood alcohol concentration of 0.246, more than three times Florida’s legal limit. According to the arrest report, March 1 at about 11:25pm at the intersection of Beachland Boulevard and A1A in Vero Beach, Horstman was off-duty driving an unmarked St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office pickup truck when he hit a Chevy Equinox with a woman and an infant inside. Vero Beach police say Horstman was driving at 63 mph in a posted 35 mph zone and entered the intersection on a green light. The other driver entered the intersection against a red light. Both drivers were injured and taken to the hospital, and the infant was not injured. The arrest report says: "Horstman stated he had a few beers earlier in the evening." It says Horstman had a "faint odor of alcohol on his breath" and it says Horstman was "lethargic and dazed" and that he was "drowsy and periodically dozing off." The woman in the vehicle he hit suffered "a traumatic brain injury" and the infant was alert and responsive. The arrest report says Horstman had a blood-alcohol level of .246, which is three times the legal limit at which a person is considered too impaired to drive in Florida. Horstman was placed on administrative leave on September 15, according to the St. A felony arrest warrant was issued Monday. It lists charges of DUI impairment involving a blood or breath alcohol level of 0.15 or higher and serious personal injury. The crash happened in March, but Horstman was not arrested until late October. "It's very typical in cases like this take months and months, and it's very frustrating for victims and their families, and also for the public, who are waiting for justice," said Dave Aronberg, former Palm Beach County State Attorney. He is now an attorney in private practice in West Palm Beach. Aronberg says it's not unusual at all that it would take seven months for someone, in this case a Sheriff's detective, to be arrested for DUI with serious bodily injury. "Proving felony DUI with serious bodily injury requires two hard sciences. You have to have crash physics to prove causation. That's crucial to any case like this, and you also have to have toxicology to prove impairment, and neither of those things happens overnight," Aronberg said. Horstman was booked into the Indian River County Jail at 4:59 p.m. and later posted $15,000 bond at 6:24 p.m. His arraignment is scheduled for December 9. Vero Beach police are leading the criminal investigation, according to the Sheriff’s Office. The agency’s internal investigation is on hold pending the outcome of the criminal case.

entry.title: King tides cause coastal flooding, beach closures in Palm Beach County and Treasure Coast - WPEC
entry.summary: King tides cause coastal flooding, beach closures in Palm Beach County and Treasure Coast    WPEC
entry.article_text: King tides flooded streets and reached homes across Palm Beach County on Monday, while beach and road closures were reported as more high tides were expected through Wednesday. In Palm City, flooding made SW Dyer Point Road impassable. Martin County Sheriff’s Office deputies brought in three high-water vehicles to help reach anyone stranded in a vehicle or home. Flooding also was reported on SW 34th Street and Cornell Avenue. One driver told CBS12 the water was about waist-deep in part of the area. Resident Terresa Baldwin said water came up around both the front and back of her home, and that Monday’s flooding was the worst she had seen in eight years. Baldwin also raised concerns about the water’s source and smell. This is not only runoff water, it’s sewage and it’s bad and you can smell it, she said. Deputies urged people to avoid flooded areas and not to drive through standing water. These vehicles can travel through several feet of water safely, Martin County Sheriff’s Office Lt. Flooding also reached Flagler Drive in downtown West Palm Beach and Sunset Avenue on Palm Beach Island, where water covered parts of the roadway and disrupted pedestrians and cyclists. In Boynton Beach, flooding led to road closures, including at Ocean Avenue and Federal Highway. The Ocean Inlet Marina also closed because of high tides. In Boca Raton, water reached a Cub Scout pack’s campsite at Spanish River Park, prompting campers to move supplies to higher ground. Elsewhere, Midtown Beach was temporarily closed because of large surf and high tides. The northbound lane of South Ocean Boulevard between Chilean and Australian avenues was scheduled to close from 10 a.m. to noon while crews moved a lifeguard tower. Delray Beach officials raised red flags because of high surf and flooding, and the Juno Beach Pier remained closed because of damage from a recent offshore surge and high surf. See also: 15-year-old FAMU shooting suspect ordered to be held as prosecutors seek adult charges A coastal flood warning covers low-lying areas near the water in Palm Beach, Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties. The National Weather Service said the warning runs through 8 p.m. Wednesday in coastal Palm Beach County and 2 a.m. Thursday in coastal Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties. The forecast high tides were: Monday: 9:06 p.m. The sheriff’s office advised residents not to drive through floodwater and to call 911 if they need emergency assistance.

entry.title: Martin County commissioners approve one-year pause on large-scale data center applications - WPBF
entry.summary: Martin County commissioners approve one-year pause on large-scale data center applications    WPBF
entry.article_text: Martin County commissioners unanimously voted during a second public hearing to implement a one-year moratorium on large-scale data center applications, giving staff time to study potential environmental impacts and establish rules for future projects. During the hearing, every resident who spoke during public comment opposed the possibility of data centers in the county. "We simply do not have enough information on what we may be introducing to this ecologically sensitive region and the world's most extensive restoration effort. We need more study and the evaluation of potential impacts, especially in the 16-county greater Everglades region," said Casey Darling, policy director for Friends of the Everglades. "I don’t want to spend another year or longer where somebody that I know is trying to do me great bodily harm. Folks, it’s in your hands. These things are not to be near people that are trying to conduct their ordinary lives," said resident Richard Miller. Commissioner Blake Capps confirmed there is an applicant for a data center. "One of them is the Florida Gateway Project, where this one project has been ... a data center application has come on Kanner Highway," Capps said. A resident who lives near the proposed site raised concerns about the scale of the project. "I happen to live one mile from this new proposed mega center, 100 MW, and 100 MW is like unbelievable to power 100,000 homes, and that's going to be a mile from me. Who knows how much water it's going to use," the resident said. Commissioner Vargas expressed frustration with the application process. "I was not too happy about hearing this application. I even requested the receipt, which I have here in my hand, and the date ... We should give them back and say they don't want you here. It's okay, you go elsewhere," Vargas said. The application for the Florida Gateway Project was submitted on Oct. 12, with the first public hearing held the following day. "We got the information late on the Monday before the 13th ... so, I didn't have the information in advance of the 13th. At the meeting on the 13th, I disclosed to everybody that I had just found out about it. I'm sorry, Commissioner, we did alert the commission as soon as we could," said County Attorney Elysse A. "I understand, but somebody took the money on this date is what I'm trying to say. Doesn't anybody talk to anybody here?" Vargas said. The application will go through the development review process, which staff said is expected to take a year. Aside from this application, there are currently no other large-scale data center applications pending. entry.summary: The family of St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge is searching for answers after the 34-year-old died in the line of duty , just over a year after his younger brother, Jairus Jay Hodge, who also served with the fire district. Austin Hodge was found unresponsive in his bunk at the firehouse early Saturday and was taken to a hospital, according to information provided to his family. He later died. His family told WPTV they do not yet know what happened. The feeling is unbearable, his sister, Alexis Hodge, told WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache during an exclusive interview. Alexis and her brother, Javan Hodge, gathered at Austins home as they remembered a brother they described as strong, fun, caring and dedicated to serving others. Hes strong. Hes fun. Hes caring. Hes smart. Its so much, Alexis said. Family says Austin appeared normal hours before his death Alexis said the family has been told Austin appeared to be himself in the hours before he was found unresponsive. They were told he had been cooking, talking on the phone and making jokes before going to bed. Everybody that saw him said he was normal, she said. She said the sudden loss has left the family with questions they cannot yet answer. Its a shock to literally all of us, Alexis said. Nobody knows what happened. Along with his work as a firefighter-paramedic, Austin also worked as a respiratory therapist, according to his family. Family loses second firefighter brother in just over a year Austins death comes just over a year after the death of his 26-year-old brother , Jairus Jay Hodge, who also served with the fire district. The family told WPTV that Jairus became sick while on shift in July 2025 and later died. We lost two brothers in one year, Alexis Hodge said. I cant describe to you the pain. The family said Jairus death raised concerns about the medical care he received, and Austin sought answers and advocated for his brother. He would not rest until he could get to the bottom of it, Javan said. He would not rest until he could spread Jays legacy globally. Family seeks answers about Austins death Now, Austins family says they are determined to understand what happened in his final hours. I want to know A to Z what happened, Javan said. They were told he had been cooking, talking on the phone and making jokes before going to bed.“Everybody that saw him said he was normal,” she said.She said the sudden loss has left the family with questions they cannot yet answer.“It’s a shock to literally all of us,” Alexis said. “Nobody knows what happened.”Along with his work as a firefighter-paramedic, Austin also worked as a respiratory therapist, according to his family.Family loses second firefighter brother in just over a yearAustin’s death comes just over a year after the death of his 26-year-old brother, Jairus “Jay” Hodge, who also served with the fire district.The family told WPTV that Jairus became sick while on shift in July 2025 and later died.“We lost two brothers in one year,” Alexis Hodge said. “I can’t describe to you the pain.”The family said Jairus’ death raised concerns about the medical care he received, and Austin sought answers and advocated for his brother.“He would not rest until he could get to the bottom of it,” Javan said. “He would not rest until he could spread Jay’s legacy globally.”Family seeks answers about Austin’s deathNow, Austin’s family says they are determined to understand what happened in his final hours.“I want to know A to Z what happened,” Javan said.Alexis said the family wants to know who was around Austin and who saw him before he was found unresponsive.“We are trying to find out what happened to him, who was around him, who saw him. All those questions that we have,” Alexis said.As the family waits for answers, Alexis said she is relying on her faith.“I just have to lean on God for now and have him direct my path. And direct the path of this investigation most importantly because things that are done in dark will always come to light,” Alexis said.For Alexis, getting those answers is an important part of being able to move forward with her grief.“After I get my answers, then I can rest and heal from my grief,” she said.Siblings promise to carry on their brothers’ legacyAs the Hodge family grieves, Alexis and Javan say they are determined to make both Austin and Jairus proud.For Javan, Austin’s influence is already shaping his future. He said Austin inspired him to pursue a career in healthcare. Javan is studying to become a nurse and is preparing to graduate in December.Javan said he knows Austin will still be with him when he walks across the stage.“I do know I want to make him proud. I do know I want to make both of my brothers proud,” Javan said. “The love I have for them is unimaginable. It has no bounds.”Alexis is also holding on to the plans she shared with Austin.“I’m gonna do everything we talked about. And I’m gonna make him proud,” she said. “I love him and I wish I could just pick up the phone and call him.”This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.summary: Social Security faces a funding deadline in 2032. The senators elected this year could help decide what happens next. See why your midterm vote matters in our interactive story.
entry.article_text: Verdict: false Former Social Security Commissioner Martin O Malley was explicit: every current beneficiary could face a 20% reduction in benefits if Congress doesn t act. The cut applies across the board — retirees, disabled recipients, and survivors. Verdict: true O Malley cited polling showing that eliminating or altering the Social Security tax cap is supported by over 80% of people — making it one of the rare proposals with genuine cross-partisan backing. Verdict: false The 1980s presented a similar moment, and Congress ultimately reached a deal — though not until the deadline was just months away. That precedent cuts both ways: a fix is possible, but it may not come early. A report from the Trump administration found that lower fertility rates, higher deportations, and tax changes have contributed to fewer dollars flowing into Social Security. The finding is notable because it ties specific policy decisions — not just demographic trends — to the program s funding pressures.

entry.title: The new renter is getting older
entry.summary: Renting a place to live isn't just for the young anymore. According to a 2026 analysis by Realtor.com , the typical family renter household is headed by a 42-year-old. The data also shows today's long-term renter is 55 years old, with a median household income of $48,500. Experts say for some households, staying in the same rental property is more about affordability and not just preference. However, the dream of homeownership hasn't disappeared. The same research shows around 65% of renters would like to own a home if they had the financial means. WATCH: The new renter is getting older The new renter is getting older Home warranty specialists 'Cinch Home Services' released a list this month of the states where it takes the longest to save for a home down payment. Florida ranks number 5 behind Hawaii, California, Montana and New York. In Florida, the study found it takes about 3.5 years to save up for a 15% down payment of $56,320 for a home valued around the median price of $375,470. Based on these figures, a potential homeowner in Florida would need to save about $1,341 a month. The analysis accounted for household earnings, factoring in the state's median income and the earnings that remain after paying rent, groceries, health care costs and transportation. Across the country, the estimated time to save for a home down payment is around two years and nine months, based on monthly savings of approximately $1,692. Cinch Services asked for a credit. There is nothing that ties directly to this study, but here is their website that was provided in the press release.

entry.title: Heart Walk aims to spread an important message on heart health
entry.summary: WTPV is the proud media sponsor of the American Heart Association 2026 Palm Beach Heart Walk, and we'd like to invite everyone to join the important community gathering! WPTV morning anchor Ashley Glass is glad to emcee the Heart Walk for a second year. entry.title: Murray Middle School breaks ground on $33 million rebuild after Hurricane Milton damage
entry.summary: Murray Middle School has broken ground on a $33 million phase of its campus rebuild after Hurricane Milton spawned a tornado that damaged three main buildings , forcing students and school programs into portable classrooms, according to Martin County school officials. District leaders said improvements to Murray Middle School were already planned, but the hurricane damage added urgency to the project. The new construction will include learning and performing arts spaces, while the school's gym will also be renovated. WATCH: Murray Middle is rebuilding after Hurricane Milton. entry.title: Surface-to-air missile systems deployed near Trump airport, Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach
entry.summary: New surface-to-air missile systems have been deployed in Palm Beach as part of expanded security around President Donald Trump, with air defense assets visible near Donald J. Trump International Airport and Mar-a-Lago. The North American Aerospace Defense Command has said the deployment was made at the request of the U.S. Secret Service. WATCH: Surface-to-air missiles deployed in Palm Beach Surface-to-air missile systems deployed near Trump airport, Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach The new equipment is attracting attention from people traveling around the airport and near the president's private club. What are the air defense systems? 'What you see here are three trailer-mounted anti-aircraft, anti-drone, actually even anti-vehicle defense systems,' Ingram told Hoffman. Ingram said the weapons are surface-to-air missile systems, commonly known as SAMs, and described them as a final layer of protection. 'This is the last line of defense that will eliminate the threat to the president of the United States,' Ingram said. Hoffman also sat down with Buckley, a decorated former U.S. Navy fighter pilot and graduate of the Navy's elite TOPGUN flight school. 'I'm surprised those SAMs haven't been there longer,' Buckley said. Buckley said the systems are capable of defending against more than conventional aircraft. 'It's anti-aircraft, anti-drone, anti-anything that's a potential threat,' he said. Buckley identified some of the equipment visible near the airport as Avenger systems carrying Stinger missiles. entry.title: Martin County approves 1-year pause on new data center development
entry.summary: By a 4-0 vote, commissioners in Martin County on Tuesday unanimously passed a one-year moratorium on data centers as county leaders consider how to handle future development of the facilities. This was the second reading after commissioners moved forward with the moratorium during a meeting held Oct. 13. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Martin County approves 1-year pause on new data center development Tuesday's vote comes after Martin County recently received an application to build its first data center proposed in unincorporated Martin County. That application is for the construction of a hyperscale data center off Kanner Highway west of Interstate 95. However, because the application was submitted before the moratorium, it will not be affected by Tuesday's vote. The proposal comes amid residents' concerns about the future of data center development.

entry.title: Palm Beach Co. voters to decide whether to renew school tax funding teacher pay, safety and student programs
entry.summary: Palm Beach County voters will decide Nov. 3 whether to renew an existing 1-mill property tax for public schools for four more years, continuing funding for teacher pay, school safety, mental health services and student programs through June 30, 2031. The referendum is a renewal, not a new tax. According to the School District of Palm Beach County, the 1-mill levy has supported local schools since 2019. Voters approved the levy in 2018 and renewed it in 2022. If approved again, the measure would take effect July 1, 2027, after the current authorization expires, and automatically end June 30, 2031. What would the Palm Beach County school referendum fund? The ballot language says money from the tax would be dedicated to school safety, school police, mental health services, arts, music, physical education, career and choice program teachers, and improved teacher pay. An independent committee of citizens and experts would oversee the funds. According to the district, half of the funding currently supports teacher salary supplements, while 25% supports more than 900 career and choice, arts, music and other specialized teaching positions. The remaining 25% supports mental health services, school police and security staff. Students speak out in support Some students who are too young to cast ballots are speaking in support of the referendum and highlighting the impact they believe the measure has on their schools. 'Teacher issues are everybody's issues,' referendum supporter Sawyer Tinsley told WPTV. Tinsley said the issue extends beyond what students experience inside the classroom. 'It goes much further than just high school and high school education. It really impacts our future and the future of our country,' Tinsley said. What happens if the referendum fails? The School District of Palm Beach County says the local funding currently provides teachers salary supplements averaging about $8,000 annually. The money also funds more than 900 teaching positions in areas including art, music and physical education. According to the district, those teaching positions and programs would face cuts without the funding. The League of Women Voters of Palm Beach County's referendum synopsis also states that if voters reject the measure, teachers would face an average $8,000 annual reduction in pay and more than 900 teaching positions in the arts, physical education and choice programs would be eliminated. entry.title: St. Lucie County detective faces felony DUI charge, accused of driving 3 times the legal limit, sheriff says
entry.summary: The St. Lucie County Sheriffs Office said a felony arrest warrant was issued for a detective accused of driving 3 times the legal drinking limit. On March 2, detective Tyler Horstman was involved in an off-duty crash in an agency vehicle in Vero Beach. SLCSO said on Sept. 9, the sheriffs office was notified Horstmans blood alcohol concentration was .246. Sheriff Richard Del Toro Jr. said Horstman was placed on administrative leave on Sept. 15. On Oct. 26, a felony arrest warrant was issued for Horstman for driving under the influence- impairment- blood or breath of .15 or more. SLCSO said Horstman turned himself in at the Indian River Jail. SLCSO said he has been placed on administrative leave and the internal investigation is on hold pending the criminal proceedings. 'The men and women of this agency work every day to earn the trust of our community, and we will continue to hold ourselves to the standards that trust requires,' Sheriff Del Toro said.

entry.title: USAA auto insurance rates dropping for nearly 500,000 Florida policies
entry.summary: Nearly half a million USAA auto insurance policies in Florida are set to see lower rates after state regulators approved a series of reductions, according to the Florida Office of Insurance Regulation. Florida Insurance Commissioner Mike Yaworsky approved several auto insurance program rate decreases for USAA Group that average 7%. The changes affect more than 498,000 policies across the state. Individual policyholders could see different savings depending on their program. According to the state, average rate changes range from a decrease of 0.4% to as much as 11.2%. USAA has its highest concentration of Florida business in Brevard, Escambia and Okaloosa counties. Average decreases in those counties are 5.8% in Brevard, 8% in Escambia and 8.4% in Okaloosa. 'The Office of Insurance Regulation is constantly reaching out to insurers to inquire about rate relief, and USAA is always stepping up to the plate and looking out for their consumers,' Yaworsky said in the release. He encouraged other insurers to consider additional rate reductions. Florida Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia pointed to the reductions as another sign of improvement in the state's insurance market and credited Florida's tort reforms. 'These auto insurance rate decreases will help Florida families keep more of their hard-earned money in their pockets, especially our military families,' Ingoglia said. The latest reductions follow other savings announced by USAA over the past year. According to the release, the company provided nearly $1 billion in rate reductions and direct member returns to Florida members between December 2025 and July 2026. That included a $500 million dividend distributed to approximately 830,000 members. State regulators also said Florida's five largest auto insurance groups are showing a combined indicated rate change of negative 12.6% for 2026. Those companies represent 81% of Florida's auto insurance market, according to the release. The state also reported that Florida had the nation's lowest personal auto liability loss ratio in 2025 at 52.5%, its lowest level in 15 years.

entry.title: Is it cheaper to fly or drive this Thanksgiving?
entry.summary: If you're traveling for Thanksgiving, one question could significantly affect your holiday budget: Is it cheaper to fly or drive? The answer can depend on where you're going, how many people are traveling, and when you plan to leave and return. Travelers we spoke with were divided. WATCH: Is it cheaper to fly or drive this Thanksgiving? Is it cheaper to fly or drive this Thanksgiving? 'It depends where you're going,' Leticia Rivera said. 'But I would say fly right now.' Others would rather stay on the road. 'For the preference, regardless of pricing, drive,' Erik Eliassen said. 'Oh, definitely drive,' Calvin Landau added. Carol Baxter, meanwhile, has already made her decision: 'I'm flying.' Airfare can add up quickly for families According to Hopper data provided for this story, the average domestic round-trip flight for Thanksgiving is currently about $402 per person, compared with $307 last year. For a family of four, four tickets at the $402 average would total about $1,608 in airfare alone, before adding other potential travel expenses. Driving can look very different because everyone in the vehicle shares expenses such as fuel. Using the example in our comparison, the driving cost is about $160. That means families should consider the total cost of the trip rather than simply comparing the price of one plane ticket with one tank of gas. Your return date could make a big difference For people planning to fly, choosing a different return date could also affect the cost. Hopper data provided for this story shows a round trip with a return on the Sunday after Thanksgiving averaging about $604. Returning on Monday or Tuesday, however, could bring that average down to around $350. That's a difference of roughly $254 per ticket. For a family of four, that difference could potentially add up to more than $1,000. The bottom line There isn't one answer that works for every Thanksgiving traveler. Flying may save time on a long-distance trip, while driving can make the cost easier to spread across several people traveling together. Before booking, compare the total cost for everyone traveling, including airfare or fuel and any additional expenses associated with the trip. Also consider whether changing your travel dates could bring down the price. For families in particular, doing the math on the entire trip could make a significant difference in the Thanksgiving travel budget.

entry.article_text: President Donald Trump on Friday told a rally for candidates in South Florida that U.S. warships returning from the Middle East could stop over in Cuba on their way back from the Iran war, his latest suggestion of taking an interventionist approach to the nearby country.Trump first floated this idea earlier this year, but has not mentioned it in recent months. But he revived it in response to a shouted question from the crowd about the island nation. He was campaigning just days ahead of midterm elections in which voters have expressed concern about the impact the U.S. war on Iran has had on prices of goods from gas to groceries.“We’ll do a little stopover,” Trump said. “Actually, what we’re going to do with Cuba is, we’re going to come back from Iran. Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. We’ll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They’ll raise up their hands. And then we’re going to send (Secretary of State) Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal.”Both Rubio and Trump have been bullish on action in Cuba, with Trump previously suggesting the country would "be next” in terms of intervention abroad, following the winding down of the Iran war he has long forecast but which has not yet happened.In May, he and Rubio raised the specter of U.S. military intervention in Cuba, a renewed threat that took on greater weight after the administration announced criminal charges against the island’s former leader, Raúl Castro. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that previous U.S. presidents had considered intervening in Cuba for decades but that “it looks like I’ll be the one that does it.”RELATED STORY | Trump rules out attacking Iran before November's midterm electionsRubio told reporters separately that Cuba has been a national security threat for years because of its ties to U.S. adversaries and that Trump is intent on addressing it. While saying the Trump administration wants to resolve differences with Cuba peacefully, Rubio voiced doubts that the U.S. could reach a diplomatic resolution with the island’s current government.Moments after Trump spoke at the rally, Rubio posted on social media that “now is the time” for action on Cuba, addressing his post “to those who seek to create positive change” and urging them “to seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA.”Rubio has not addressed Cuba in depth in public for several weeks, with his last comments coming in a Sept. 29 interview with Fox News host Sean Hannity.“The truth is Cuba has already fallen. It doesn’t have a functional economy and it’s governed by people who continue to preach about some revolution that has been dead for 20 years that’s never worked,” Rubio said, without alluding to any CIA operation.“We are hopeful that Cuba will choose a different path. We are hopeful … that there will be some people in there that open their eyes to the reality of what they’re facing,” he said. “We’re never going to allow Cuba to become a base of operation against American interests or pose a threat to our national security. On that we are abundantly clear.”FOREIGN POLICY NEWS | Trump endorses embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelectionRubio and other top Trump aides have met with Cuban officials in recent months to explore possible improvements in relations. side has come away unimpressed from those talks, leading to even more sanctions imposed on the Cuban government.During his address to the United Nations General Assembly last month, Trump said Rubio — son of Cuban immigrants, who has long taken a hard line against Cuba’s socialist leadership — was “deep into negotiations with Cuba,” saying he would “not allow a haven for foreign adversaries to threaten America on our own doorstep.”Days later, Trump told reporters that he anticipated that the two countries “will make a deal,” adding, “I don’t think we’ll need the military. Cuba is failing very badly.”Earlier this week, the two countries clashed at the United Nations as the Trump administration sought once again to build opposition for an upcoming annual vote condemning Washington’s decades-long economic embargo against Havana.Cuba has struggled since 2020 with an economic and energy crisis. Its gross domestic product has shrunk, and its 10 million residents have endured blackouts, food shortages and inflation. There have been waves of protests, and hundreds of thousands of Cubans have migrated, many to the United States.

entry.title: A pumpkin wonderland in the Florida sunshine: Inside the fall fun at Bedner's Farm
entry.summary: Just outside Boynton Beach, Bedner's Farm offers a little bit of country, a whole lot of fall fun and a reminder that autumn magic doesn't require chilly weather. Fall fun in the Florida sunshine: Inside Bedner's Farm near Boynton Beach At the family-owned South Florida staple tucked away in west Boynton Beach, even the goats get in on the hospitality. According to Judi Brooker, who has been sharing the farm's charm with visitors for more than a decade, they're a crowd favorite. 'They're so soft, and everybody loves the goats,' Brooker said. I mentioned that the little kids probably love them. 'And by little kids, everybody under the age of 100,' Brooker joked. Bedner's is one of South Florida's last family-owned markets, with a farming legacy that stretches back generations. 'A lot of people don't realize there is life in west Boynton off 441,' Brooker said. 'I know I live here!' More than 50 years ago, Arthur and Henrietta Bedner brought their Pennsylvania farming roots to South Florida, trading harsh winters for a warmer climate and new opportunities. 'They came from farming families in Pennsylvania, but they'd had enough of the winter,' Brooker said. The family began farming in the area in the mid-20th century before purchasing the property that would become home to the farm visitors know today. Their mission remains simple: grow fresh, flavorful produce that's affordable, too. And there's plenty growing here. The farm grows about 60 crops, including tomatoes, corn, strawberries, broccoli, kale, lettuce, cauliflower, peppers and zucchini. The farm also grows sunflowers, adding a splash of color to the agricultural landscape. October is one of the best months to visit. Fall at Bedner's means family outings, festive photo opportunities and plenty of seasonal fun. 'It's a day full of fun. Bring the family, cousins, aunties, grandmas it's great,' Brooker said. One of the biggest attractions is finding the perfect pumpkin. 'We have this beautiful greenery and all the pumpkins on top,' Brooker said. 'It's just a pumpkin wonderland.' Pumpkins aren't the only seasonal stars. Visitors can also spot an assortment of colorful gourds, adding even more variety to the fall display from the popping orange of the pumpkins to the golden glow of the sunflower fields. Those cheerful blooms also play an important role in the farm's ecosystem. Bedner's keeps beehives on the property, recognizing the essential role pollinators play in agriculture. entry.article_text: Fall at Bedner's means family outings, festive photo opportunities and plenty of seasonal fun."It's a day full of fun. Bring the family, cousins, aunties, grandmas — it's great," Brooker said.One of the biggest attractions is finding the perfect pumpkin."We have this beautiful greenery and all the pumpkins on top," Brooker said. "It's just a pumpkin wonderland."Pumpkins aren't the only seasonal stars. Visitors can also spot an assortment of colorful gourds, adding even more variety to the fall display — from the popping orange of the pumpkins to the golden glow of the sunflower fields.Those cheerful blooms also play an important role in the farm's ecosystem. Bedner's keeps beehives on the property, recognizing the essential role pollinators play in agriculture."We do have hives on the farm because the honeybee is the farmer's best friend," Brooker said.It's a reminder that behind the colorful fields and family-friendly attractions, there's a working farm where growing food and caring for the land go hand in hand.For a closer look at the operation, visitors can climb aboard one of the farm's tractor rides, which take you around all 80 acres of Bedner's. The ride offers more than a scenic tour. It's a glimpse into the technology and planning that keep the farm productive in South Florida's challenging climate.Tall crops help protect other plants from the wind, while drip irrigation delivers water directly where it's needed — helping keep the fields hydrated through changing weather conditions.The farm has a long agricultural history to match its modern techniques."Palm Beach County was once known as the winter produce capital of the United States," Brooker said.That legacy is still visible in the fields, where agriculture remains at the heart of the experience.Of course, no fall adventure would be complete without a corn maze — and at Bedner's, finding the exit is easier said than done. Each year brings a new maze to explore, with twists, turns and a few surprises along the way.The maze comes with its own cast of characters, including the occasional zombie and a few strategically placed scarecrows."Sometimes we have some zombie friends along the way," Brooker said.There may be a few spooky sights, but the experience is designed to be more playful than frightening. Still, the maze comes with its share of wrong turns and dead ends, but after plenty of backtracking, the exit finally comes into view.After all that walking, exploring and navigating the maze, there's only one thing left to do: cool off with a sweet treat.At Bedner's, the fall experience is about more than pumpkins and photo ops. It's about spending time outdoors, learning a little about where food comes from, and making memories with family and friends.And the best part? You can soak up all those autumn vibes without bundling up for cold weather. Because at Bedner's Farm, fall magic comes with sunshine, fresh air and just a little bit of Florida flair.Watch "Finding Florida" each Sunday at 10 a.m.

entry.title: Martin County parents win push for school zone outside Citrus Grove Elementary
entry.summary: Martin County parents are celebrating a victory in a long battle to improve safety around their children's school. Citrus Grove Elementary School parents say the 45 mph speed limit outside the school puts their children's safety in jeopardy. They say a recently approved school zone is the first step to making Newfield Parkway a safer place for children who walk to school. On Southwest Newfield Parkway, morning and afternoon traffic is an obstacle for young students. 'It scares me,' parent Kendall George said. 'These cars are driving 45 miles an hour plus.' Kendall is among the many families who live in the Canopy Creek community across the street from Citrus Grove Elementary, so their children walk to school. Kelly Ribaudo, the PTA president and Martin County PTA Advocacy Chair, told WPTV she's spent the last five years asking the county to put in a school zone. 'We've had so many near misses with the kids just from people not paying attention,' Ribaudo said. 'Everyone has a right to a free and public education and they should be safe getting there. Our main priority should be the kids not the traffic.' At the previous Martin County Commission meeting, commissioners unanimously answered their call. 'Whatever the number is there is no price to someone getting hurt,' Martin County Commissioner Edward Ciampi said. 'You will absolutely get a school zone.' School Principal Rose Rynca told WPTV the need is greater than ever, with enrollment growing as new communities pop up in the area. 'The amount of students crossing Newfield Parkway has definitely increased,' Rynca said. 'This speed zone is going to really really improve the safety of students.' 'It's letting drivers know that, hey there's a school here, there's children crossing, and we have to slow down,' George said. WPTV's Cassandra Garcia followed up with the county on Thursday to find out the timeline for adding a school zone on SW Newfield Parkway. In a statement they said: 'Implementation of the school zone is estimated to take 6 to 9 months. The process includes retaining a consultant to complete the design, coordinating utilities, procuring materials, and completing construction. Work includes installing new school zone flashers with concrete footings, installing and relocating signs, and applying pavement markings. entry.title: WHERE'S WALTER? Having a day of discovery at the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast
entry.summary: This week, I visited a place where learning and fun go hand in hand: the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast. From the moment I walked in, I could tell this wasn't your typical museum. Instead of looking at exhibits from behind a rope or glass case, kids are encouraged to jump in, get involved and learn by doing. As I explored the museum, I discovered exhibits designed to teach important life skills in creative and engaging ways. From learning about money and budgeting to exploring different careers and practicing job skills, every corner of the museum offered a new opportunity to learn something useful. WATCH: WHERE'S WALTER? Discovering the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast One of my favorite stops, of course, involved the weather. As a meteorologist, I was excited to check out the museum's WPTV weather simulator and hurricane simulator. It was fascinating to see how children can experience weather concepts in a hands-on environment and gain a better understanding of the science behind storms and hurricanes. What impressed me most was how interactive everything was. Kids aren't just reading signs or watching demonstrations. They're solving problems, making decisions, using their imaginations and building confidence along the way. The museum creates an environment where learning feels more like an adventure than a lesson. Whether they're exploring future careers, practicing financial skills or learning about science and weather, children are gaining valuable experiences that can help them throughout their lives. My visit was a great reminder that some of the best learning happens when you're having fun. By rolling up their sleeves, asking questions and trying new things, kids can discover skills and interests they never knew they had. If you're looking for a family-friendly destination on the Treasure Coast that combines education, creativity and fun, the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast is definitely worth a visit. That's where I was!

entry.title: Year-long bridge closure in southern Martin County forces drivers onto detour, adds minutes to commutes
entry.summary: A major road closure is now in effect in southern Martin County, where the bridge at Southeast County Line Road is closed for a year-long reconstruction project. The detour could add several minutes to daily drives, so officials are urging commuters to plan ahead or find an alternate route. George May lives just off Southeast County Line Road, where a road block is now notifying drivers to turn around. 'It'll be inconvenient, for sure. People commuting to work and people that live in little club,' May said. May said the road closure is going to take some getting used to. 'I already drive over an hour to work everyday. It'll probably add about 20 minutes to my commute,' May said. Martin County says the bridge will be closed for a year, with a lot of work ahead. 'There are a lot of utilities ther,' Mark Aveni, Martin County public works deputy director, said. 'There's a lot of coordination that needs to occur. We're removing a pedestrian bridge and we're going to repurpose that somewhere else and unfortunately these things just take time.' Despite the closure, residents say they're glad to see the investment. 'There were large cracks under the bridge. It was deteriorating,' May said. 'It's a little bit of an inconvenience but I'm happy for that to have a new bridge and have better infrastructure in the area,' Daniel Von said. Six of the project's $7 million price tag is covered by state and federal grants. The new bridge will be two feet higher and built to be safer and more resilient. 'We're replacing it with a very resilient type of rebar that's going to be safer. There is a very sharp curve before that bridge, we're going to totally eliminate that and soften the curve. It'll also be much safer for pedestrians,' Aveni said. Residents are now hoping the project will go on without delays. 'I'm fine with it as long as they keep the project on schedule,' May said.
