entry.summary: A 20-year-old Martin County woman is being honored after she used CPR to help save a 3-year-old girl she found motionless at the bottom of a swimming pool. Nearly two months after the August rescue, Martin County Fire Rescue recognized Madison Isler with the department's Heroic Heart Award. WATCH: Martin County woman honored for saving 3-year-old Woman Honored After Using CPR to Save 3-Year-Old Girl | WPTV The rescue happened Aug. 23 as Isler walked past the pool at her apartment complex. She told WPTV something in the water caught her attention. 'It kind of looked like a smudge in your sunglasses,' Isler said. 'And then, so I took my glasses off, and I looked, and then I realized that it was a little girl.' That little girl was 3-year-old Luna. 'I jumped in and grabbed her' Isler said Luna was motionless at the bottom of the swimming pool when she spotted her. 'I jumped in and grabbed her and pulled her out, and she was blue,' Isler said. 'You just don't really think; you just kind of do, especially in a situation when it's a little baby,' Isler said. 'I pulled a lifeless baby out of a pool.' 'Together, they continued their life-saving efforts till finally Luna responded,' Martin County Fire Rescue Chief Chad Cianciulli said. entry.title: Man exercising at night critically injured in hit-and-run crash in Port St. Lucie, man arrested, police say
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie police (PSLPD) said it has arrested a person in connection with an Oct. 9 hit-and-run crash that injured a 63-year-old man. The crash happened at around 12:56 a.m. near NW University Boulevard and NW California Boulevard. 'Our officers that work night we're used to seeing him out exercising in the evening and he was known to jog, walk in the street medians,' Chief Leo Niemczyk said. The victim was identified through information on his Garmin watch and traced back to his home. PSLPD said the man was found unconscious in the roadway with severe head injuries, was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, and remains in critical condition.' Watch report: Man exercising at night critically injured in hit-and-run crash in Port St. Lucie, man arrested: Officials Detectives reviewed surveillance video and additional evidence, identified Eric Saint Aude, 60, as a suspect, and arrested him, PSLPD said. He was arrested for leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury.

entry.title: St. Lucie County Nuclear Power Plant turns 50
entry.summary: WPTV had the rare opportunity to go inside the St. Lucie County Nuclear Power Plant on Thursday. This year, the facility is celebrating 50 years of operation and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission just granted licenses for 20 more.   On Thursday, WPTV learned about operations inside the plant and spoke with people who keep the power on. Watch report from Tyler Hatfield: WPTV gets an inside look at the St Lucie County Nuclear Power Plant Our Tyler Hatfield listened to Alfred Phillips, a digital INC specialist. 'My job is to calibrate and make sure all the equipment used to work on the equipment that controls the reactor itself meets all the government standards and accuracies.' Phillips said hes been working at the plant for nearly 20 years. 'You have million-dollar homes right down the street. We're here, but yet we're still invisible because what we do, we do it well, .Phillips said.   Alfreds son, Alfred Sinclair Phillips, followed his father's footsteps and works in the operations department. 'There's a pressure with it, but there's also a sense of pride, Phillips said. Knowing that my dad has worked his butt off and he's left an impact with the people here on his work to make this place better. WPTV learned from Carlos Santos, site vice president, how the plant generates power. 'The simplest way to put it is the reactor creates the heat,' Santos said. Santos said that heat comes from nuclear fission from uranium pellets stacked into rods inside the two units on site. The heat from the rods builds up and produces steam, which travels into a secondary closed system into a turbine, which then generates power and produces electricity for the grid. Back in August, the plant had to be manually shut down when three control rods dropped in the reactors core. entry.title: 2 vehicles sought in Port St. Lucie hit-and-run investigation, police say
entry.summary: The Port St. Lucie Police Department has released new information in its investigation of a hit-and-run crash that left a 63-year-old man seriously injured earlier this month on Oct. 9. Detectives now believe the victim may have been hit by two separate vehicles near the intersection of Northwest University Boulevard and Northwest California Boulevard. According to police, one vehicle was traveling northbound while the other was traveling southbound at the time of the incident. The crash occurred at approximately 12:56 a.m and the victim, a 63-year-old Port St. Lucie resident, was found unconscious in the roadway suffering from severe head injuries. In a previous update, police said surveillance video from a nearby business captured the incident and showed what investigators believed to be a white four-door sedan striking the man before leaving the scene without stopping. As detectives continued reviewing evidence and surveillance footage, investigators developed information indicating a second vehicle may also have been involved in the crash. Police are now working to identify both vehicles and their drivers. Investigators have released images of the vehicles and are asking for the public's help. Anyone who recognizes either vehicle, was in the area around the time of the crash, witnessed the incident, or has dashcam or surveillance video from the area is asked to contact the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000.

entry.title: High surf and red flag warnings put St. Lucie County beaches under high hazard advisory this week
entry.summary: A red flag warning was cautioning swimmers about dangerous surf at Fort Pierce Inlet State Park, where waves between four and six feet we're crashing along the shoreline Wednesday. Fort Pierce Inlet State Park was among several beaches in St. Lucie County under a red flag high hazard warning. The conditions are tied to a low pressure system off the eastern U.S. coast in the mid-Atlantic. 'The sea was angry today my friends,' Fort Pierce resident Lee Bertucelli said. St. Lucie County Ocean Rescue says conditions like these make it more important than ever to swim at a lifeguarded beach. There are two in St. Lucie County, at Pepper Park and Waveland Beach. Officials say both will likely be flying red or double red flags for the next few days. 'It was very windy and very choppy and it's really challenging because you have to negotiate all of the chop,' foil surfer Lisa Rose said. 'I went in, not with my surfboard, but like, to my waist and it's just, it's rough and it's just not super safe for like I'm sort of a beginner so not safe for me, but like, some of the other surfers have definitely been out,' surfer Jodi Riley said. 'I went in, you know, not too far. The waves were fun, but again not too far, didn't want to deal with rip tides or anything else,' Bertucelli said. The county says rip currents are possible in these conditions. If you find yourself stuck in one, Ocean Rescue says don't panic and swim parallel with the shoreline. entry.summary: It is as dominant a college sports program as there is anywhere in the country, and it's located on the Treasure Coast. WPTV received several emails from concerned residents that the plug may soon be pulled on this diving dynasty. We're learning the Board of Trustees at Indian River State College are looking to possibly eliminate the men's and women's swimming and diving teams. entry.title: St. Lucie County Fire Board votes to terminate Chief Jeff Lee after hazing fallout
entry.summary: In a 4-3 vote, the St. Lucie County Fire Board voted Wednesday to terminate Chief Jeff Lee's contract without cause. 'At the end of the day, it's gotten very messy. It's not about one single decision that he's made. It's about bringing peace and calm and respect back to the district and the men and women that serve this community every day, and it just got to a point where he was not effective anymore,' said St. Lucie County Commissioner and Board Member Jamie Fowler. WATCH KATE HUSSEY'S REPORT BELOW: St. Lucie Fire District chief fired in 4-3 vote This is the latest fallout from a hazing investigation brought to light earlier this year. WPTV reported last week that more than 74% of firefighters who participated in a union vote said they had no confidence in Lee. About 92% said they had no confidence in Assistant Chief Brian Gonzalez, while 97% said the same about District Attorney Kim Sabol. Vote follows hazing investigation The vote is the latest fallout from an investigation earlier this year into videos involving firefighters at Station 1A. Some show a modified bug zapper being used to shock three apprentice firefighters while on duty in 2024. Other videos show water being dumped on two firefighters and a dead raccoon placed inside a fire vehicle. A third-party investigator concluded the videos depicted hazing. Veteran firefighters Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Chris Baldwin were fired following the investigation , though they disputed the characterization of hazing and said the incidents were 'consensual' pranks that were done 'all in good fun.' It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun,' said Hutchinson. Were all still friends,' added Boudrias. Boudrias, Hutchinson, and Baldwin's firings sparked outcry from firefighters, former firefighters and community members, many of whom felt the punishment was too harsh. In Wednesday's Fire Board meeting, those community members packed the Fire Administration building, many of whom held signs or wore shirts in support of the three firefighters. About 92% said they had no confidence in Assistant Chief Brian Gonzalez, while 97% said the same about District Attorney Kim Sabol.The vote is the latest fallout from an investigation earlier this year into videos involving firefighters at Station 1A.Some show a modified bug zapper being used to shock three apprentice firefighters while on duty in 2024. Other videos show water being dumped on two firefighters and a dead raccoon placed inside a fire vehicle.A third-party investigator concluded the videos depicted hazing. Veteran firefighters Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Chris Baldwin were fired following the investigation, though they disputed the characterization of hazing and said the incidents were "consensual" pranks that were done "all in good fun." “It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," said Hutchinson. “We’re all still friends," added Boudrias. Boudrias, Hutchinson, and Baldwin's firings sparked outcry from firefighters, former firefighters and community members, many of whom felt the punishment was too harsh. In Wednesday's Fire Board meeting, those community members packed the Fire Administration building, many of whom held signs or wore shirts in support of the three firefighters. "Not only have they lost their jobs, but they also lost their reputations," said one public commentator. "We need to restore faith in this fire district," said another. "I think it speaks loud and clear, exactly like the confidence vote that was reported to us. There was a large desire to have a change in leadership, and we delivered that today," said St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire Board member James Clasby. Lee had signaled days earlier that his tenure could be coming to an end. 15 letter to the board, Lee wrote that it may be time to consider a “mutually agreeable retirement and leadership transition," adding "the position of fire chief requires confidence." During the meeting's discussion, fire board member and business owner Travis Leonard said that gave him reason to begin the motion to Fire Lee. "Coming from the private sector, anytime an employee gives their notice, I terminate them; I found they've checked out," said Leonard. After terminating Lee’s contract, the board appointed Deputy Chief Paul Langel as interim fire chief. The district also plans to hire a recruiter to conduct a search for Lee’s permanent replacement."I am excited to move this district forward, to begin the healing process of the issues that we’ve been dealing with, as of recent, and to instill trust,” Langel said.Lee's departure comes with a high cost to the district. His severance package is expected to total about $350,000.The leadership change also comes as the firefighters union continues negotiations with the district in an effort to reinstate three veteran firefighters who were fired. Union Representative Ryan Sapp said he believed Lee's termination is a "positive step forward.""I think moving forward, the ultimate goal here is to just move forward and get things back to a level field and continue providing the services to our community," Sapp told investigative reporter Kate Hussey. "The biggest thing today is we worked together and came together as a local — glad to see my membership stepped up and let their voices be heard." The Fire Board is also searching for a replacement district attorney, who submitted her notice of retirement amid the ongoing controversy.

entry.title: Indian River State College trustees to consider eliminating men's, women's swimming and diving programs
entry.summary: Indian River State College trustees are expected to consider a major restructuring of the college's athletic programs next week that would eliminate men's and women's swimming and diving and move several remaining sports to Division II competition. The recommendations are included on the agenda for the college's Governance Legislative Affairs Committee meeting on Tuesday, Oct. 27, at the Dixon Hendry Campus in Okeechobee. The committee meetings begin at 9:30 a.m., followed by the full District Board of Trustees meeting at 1 p.m. WATCH TYLER HATFIELD'S REPORT BELOW: Swimmers rally to save IRSC swim and dive teams Under the proposed athletic restructuring plan, both the men's and women's swimming and diving programs would be eliminated beginning with the fall 2027-28 academic year. The proposal would also transition baseball, softball and men's basketball to Division II competition beginning that same academic year. Volleyball already competes at the Division 2 level, according to the agenda. College administrators would also be directed to evaluate whether the women's basketball program could be reinstated for the 2028-29 season. The agenda says that possibility would depend on the availability of resources. The recommendations come from the college president and cabinet and are scheduled to be presented to the Governance Legislative Affairs Committee for approval. The agenda itself does not provide a reason for the proposed elimination of swimming and diving or detail the financial impact of the restructuring. All of this comes after Indian River State College's men's swim and dive team in March captured its 52nd consecutive national championship title, with the women's team also claiming its 48th national title. The meeting will take place at the Williamson Conference Center Auditorium on Indian River State College's Dixon Hendry Campus at 2229 NW 9th Avenue in Okeechobee.

entry.summary: Florida carried out its 18th execution of the year on Tuesday under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis' aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term. William Reaves , 77, was pronounced dead at 6:12 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison near Starke. He was convicted of first-degree murder in the 1986 shooting death of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski. After a few minutes, the team warden shook Reaves shoulders and yelled his name, but there was no response. Ron DeSantis' aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term.William Reaves, 77, was pronounced dead at 6:12 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison near Starke. He was convicted of first-degree murder in the 1986 shooting death of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski.WATCH REPORT BELOW:The death chamber curtain went up promptly at the 6 p.m. execution time, and Reaves was already strapped to a gurney with an IV in his arm. Asked if he had any last statement, he replied, "No, I do not."The injection began immediately after that. About 30 seconds later, Reaves took several big breaths and then stopped moving. After a few minutes, the team warden shook Reaves’ shoulders and yelled his name, but there was no response.A medic was called into the chamber a short time later to check for a heartbeat or any other signs of life, and Reaves was pronounced dead about a minute later.Reaves was the eighth Florida prisoner over age 70 put to death this year, highlighting the nation’s aging death-row population as Florida continues to far outpace the rest of country in total executions.Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year and it would tie that mark if another execution is carried out next month as scheduled.DeSantis, who leaves office in January after two terms, has said his goal is to deliver justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for death sentences to be carried out.Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986, according to court records. Reaves later acknowledged he had placed the call from a payphone outside the store.While Raczkowski and Reaves spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves’ shorts, officials said. The two struggled over the weapon, and Reaves eventually regained control of it. Investigators said the deputy was trying to run away when Reaves shot him four times. The deputy later died from his wounds.Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. But the Florida Supreme Court overturned the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted again and sentenced to death in 1992, and subsequent appeals were unsuccessful.The U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday afternoon rejected Reaves’ final appeal without comment.The Florida Supreme Court last week also rejected Reaves’ appeals to spare his life.One issue raised by his attorneys was Florida’s method of execution. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections.The court has previously upheld this lethal injection protocol against similar challenges. It differs from the single-drug injection used by states such as Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike was rushed to the hospital last month after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital.Defense attorneys also argued that the jurors who recommended the death penalty for Reaves were never told that the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs rated Reaves — an Army veteran — as 100% disabled by post-traumatic stress disorder, which was caused by his service in the Vietnam War. More than 100 veterans sent DeSantis a letter Monday urging him to stop the execution.A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half of the 32 total executions in the U.S. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so.Jesse Guardado, 64, is next scheduled to die by injection in Florida on Nov. He was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.

entry.title: Vero Beach gives Three Corners developers another extension as Dec. 8 deadline looms
entry.summary: WPTV is learning that the Vero Beach City Council approved an extension for developers of the Three Corners project but time is ticking. City council members told the developers, ClearBlue, that they need to negotiate and come to an agreement by Dec. 8 or the city may need to go back to the drawing board. WATCH BELOW: Developers get 4th extension for Three Corners project Developers get fourth extension for negotiations on Three Corners project 'I've been on this thing since 2019,' Vero Beach Mayor John Cotugno said. 'We need to negotiate the best, we'll call it a deal, for our citizens.'  The development project is located at the old Vero Beach Power Plant at the base of the 17th Street Bridge. Plans include hotels, a marina, restaurants, walking paths and more. This is the fourth extension the city council approved for developers to negotiate agreements on financing and lease terms. 'Some progress had been made on the financial aspects of the developer proposal,' Cotugno said. But the mayor said if the council and ClearBlue aren't on the same page, they might have to change course. 'We need to listen and to see if this aligns with our goals and objectives. And if it does, great, we're going to work out a deal that's mutually beneficial,' Cotugno said. 'If not, then you know well we'll have to see what happens.' Cotugno said the city council is also appointing a liaison to aid in negotiations and the developers come to discuss the project in person. Bob Salera, a spokesperson for ClearBlue, said they are meeting with city council Oct. 27. 'It's something that we've actually been asking for for several months,' Salera said. 'We're glad we finally have one on the books now.' Salera said they're committed to the project and have invested over $1 million. 'We wouldn't have put in 21,000 hours of time into this project if we weren't serious,' Salera said. 'We're happy that these negotiations are moving forward, and we're ready to bring it home to a close.' Cotugno said he hopes they do. 'I'm willing to stay at that the table if progress is being made,' Cotugno said.

entry.title: Palm Beach County families face a youth mental health gap. A new FAU program aims to fill it.
entry.summary: For years, Palm Beach County has faced a shortage of mental health resources for children, leaving families vulnerable. Now, members of the community are stepping up to fill the need. Florida Atlantic University is launching a new program to provide that support for free. The program, called 'OWLS-FLY' (short for Opportunity, Wellness, Leadership Strength with Families Leading Youth), is being spearheaded by researchers Kelly Emelianchik-Key and Alex Fields inside the education building at FAU. It was made possible by a $1.2 million grant from the Children's Services Council of Palm Beach County. The program will provide free mental health counseling for kids ages 6 through 17 and their families. 'We provide group counseling, individual counseling, family counseling, and we'll have some different parental supports that are going to take place,' Emelianchik-Key said. The space is still coming together with different rooms for family and individual therapy. There's also a room set up to provide care via telehealth. Emelianchik-Key said she anticipates the first clients to be served in January. Fields said the stakes for young people are high. 'If you don't have solid mental health support, you can't build the foundation for a really healthy and high quality of life down the road,' Fields said. The program serves two needs: it helps families who need services, and it provides work experience for the people who are learning to provide them. 'We've worked with clinicians in the community, specifically for youth with intellectual and developmental disabilities, and I've heard how long their wait lists are, and that they're not able to provide services for months and on out,' Fields said. Master's students and graduates will get work experience through the program. Michelle Abarca of the Children's Services Council hopes to take what's learned through FAU's program and scale it in the future. 'Working with FAU is particularly exciting for us because we are a data-driven organization, and with the research that's going to be taking place at FAU, we hope to learn. We hope to be able to replicate some of this at one point,' Abarca said. The program is funded for three years, but Emelianchik-Key and Fields hope to continue it for years to come. 'To be able to do this is a really great honor,' Emelianchik-Key said. This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting

entry.title: Black women on the ballot in the midterms could make history across the country
entry.summary: From the U.S. Senate to the governors mansion, dozens of Black women are on the ballot across the country. Dr. Ndidiamaka Okpareke, a pharmacist and Republican newcomer seeking a New Mexico congressional seat, is one of them. We need adequate representation at the table so that we can pull our communities forward, Okpareke told Scripps News. The daughter of Nigerian immigrants and a mother of three, Okpareke would be the first Black woman to represent New Mexico in Congress if she wins her long-shot bid against a three-term incumbent. The Gen Z Democrat is running in South Carolinas 4th Congressional District in the Upstate, one of the states most conservative districts. She is seeking to become the first Black woman the state has sent to Congress. McClain told Scripps News that many people doubted her candidacy at the start. Now that we are so close to the finish line and with the support that weve been able to get people now realize that we can win this race, McClain said. entry.article_text: Senate to the governor’s mansion, dozens of Black women are on the ballot across the country.Dr. Ndidiamaka Okpareke, a pharmacist and Republican newcomer seeking a New Mexico congressional seat, is one of them.“We need adequate representation at the table so that we can pull our communities forward,” Okpareke told Scripps News.The daughter of Nigerian immigrants and a mother of three, Okpareke would be the first Black woman to represent New Mexico in Congress if she wins her long-shot bid against a three-term incumbent.RELATED STORY | Trump campaigns in Mississippi, highlighting Republicans' challengesSome 1,500 miles away, 25-year-old Courtney McClain is making a similar bid. The Gen Z Democrat is running in South Carolina’s 4th Congressional District in the Upstate, one of the state’s most conservative districts. She is seeking to become the first Black woman the state has sent to Congress.McClain told Scripps News that many people doubted her candidacy at the start.“Now that we are so close to the finish line and with the support that we’ve been able to get people now realize that we can win this race,” McClain said.“STILL CONTINUING TO RUN”Okpareke and McClain are part of a larger group challenging assumptions about Black women’s electability. There are 72 Black women on the midterm ballot, according to data from Rutgers University’s Center for American Women and Politics and Higher Heights. Near majority are Democrats.Four Black women are running for the Senate while 40 Black women nominees are in the running for the lower chamber, two are in the running for governor and 26 are running for other statewide offices.University of Florida professor Sharon Austin told Scripps News these were once officer that women didn't tend to run for, especially women of color.“Now it seems the sky's the limit and more women of color are seeking all offices at all levels,” Austin said.Austin, who has studied Black women in politics, said Black women candidates know the climb to the ballot, let alone victory, is steep.“These are women who know that when they decide to run for office it isn’t going to be easy. They’re going to have to deal with a lot of biases and a lot of bigotry. But many of them are able to overcome it, and they’re still continuing to run,” she said.“There definitely has been progress. There always is going to be bigotry, unfortunately, and there’s always going to be barriers,” Austin added. “But I think there are people in today’s society who are a lot more willing to look beyond race and gender when they cast their votes.”“TAKE YOURSELF OUT OF THE BOX”McClain said she doesn’t want her campaign defined by history-making alone.“Representation isn’t just about what the person looks like, but it’s about what that person can actually bring and do for the community,” McClain added.For Okpareke, a medical professional who says she’s bringing firsthand experience to policy that impacts different communities, representation goes beyond race or gender.“There are boxes that are built for us on both sides of the aisle,” Okpareke said. “We've seen that so often where you align yourself with a certain ideology or a certain way to think and you get boxed in and you can never come out of that.”“So take yourself out of the box, be true to who you are, and stand for the people,” she added.INTERACTIVE | How the midterms could shape the future of Social SecurityKelly Dittmar, director of research at CWAP, told Scripps News the election story this year goes beyond the firsts. Some Black women are leaving Congress, so the overall number may not rise sharply, she said. But the new candidates include younger women and those from different backgrounds who clear new paths and bring complex perspectives to office."We found in our own research that what that means is they're often bringing not only their own voices but also voices from their communities,” Dittmar said. “They’re diversifying the representation among the Black women who are serving.”She said voters are also looking for something new, and women can use the fact that they haven’t been part of the status quo to their advantage.“I think this year we will see a number of cases of success to further prove the case that women can and do win some of the toughest races, that Black women can and do win in majority-white electorates, which has been a bias in a lot of the discussions around when and where Black women should run,” Dittmar said.McClain said that’s the message she is carrying into Election Day.“That excitement. That want for change,” she said. "Not just on being the first Black woman but running on being a candidate that is truly going to represent the Upstate and is truly going to bring change.”“I hope to see a version of America that works for all people, and a version of America that is truly going to be representative of the least of us,” McClain said.Win or lose Tuesday, Okpareke said she hopes to change the conversation about where and when Black women can run for office.“I would just want to inspire anyone from different backgrounds to let them know you can do it,” she said. “You too can stand for and guard and protect and nurture the American dream because it's not going to end with you.”

entry.title: Indian River State College trustees table recommendation to eliminate swimming and diving team
entry.summary: The Indian River State College Board of Trustees has delayed taking action on a recommendation to eliminate the college's swimming and diving team. During a meeting held in Okeechobee, the board voted Tuesday to table the president's recommendation to eliminate the program. WATCH REPORT BELOW: IRSC trustees table recommendation to eliminate swimming, diving team Indian River State College trustees table recommendation to eliminate swimming and diving team Instead, trustees asked the college administration to prepare a comprehensive report on the swimming and diving program. The board requested that the report include input from the community. President Timothy Moore said at Tuesday's meeting that the proposal to cut the programs comes down to money. 'It's a tremendous opportunity to leave this college with that kind of skill, resource and talent here, but it comes at a price,' Moore said. The school president said the program currently costs around $1.4 to $2 million, money that isn't coming in through donations. 'What's required to maintain it as it sits today? We will require $15 to $20 million of an endowment to throw off enough revenue per year to sustain the program as it sits today,' Moore said. There's also a proposal to transition the remaining sports to Division II, resulting in potential savings of around $500,000. But if the swimming and diving program stays, Moore said the school may be forced to cut 50 percent for sports across the board. 'It's elimination of one or impose a penalty across all, and I would imagine that our championships will suffer because of that decision,' Moore said. The administration is expected to present the report at the Board of Trustees Nov. 17 meeting, when recommendations on how to move forward will be considered. This past March, the men's swim and dive team captured its 52nd consecutive national championship title, and the women's team claimed its 48th crown. Former swimmer Ella Smith started a petition last week to save the program, which has more than 12,500 signatures.

entry.title: Martin County approves 1-year pause on new data center development
entry.summary: By a 4-0 vote, commissioners in Martin County on Tuesday unanimously passed a one-year moratorium on data centers as county leaders consider how to handle future development of the facilities. This was the second reading after commissioners moved forward with the moratorium during a meeting held Oct. 13. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Martin County approves 1-year pause on new data center development Tuesday's vote comes after Martin County recently received an application to build its first data center proposed in unincorporated Martin County. That application is for the construction of a hyperscale data center off Kanner Highway west of Interstate 95. However, because the application was submitted before the moratorium, it will not be affected by Tuesday's vote. The proposal comes amid residents' concerns about the future of data center development.

entry.title: Women's hockey growing in South Florida as University of Miami club gains momentum
entry.summary: Women's hockey is growing in South Florida, from the pee-wee level all the way up to the college level, and the University of Miami Women's Hockey Club team is part of that surge. Head coach Justina Holland, a former player, rebooted the women's hockey club program at the University of Miami in 2021. She rebuilt it from the ground up, taking on every task herself as a college student. WATCH BELOW: Women's hockey growing at University of Miami Women's hockey growing at University of Miami 'Yes, all by myself. I did. I had to find some girls that wanted to play. I had to find a league. I did buy jerseys, get ice time, like everything. Every single little thing you can think of, I had to do myself,' Holland said. At first, the team had only six players and no subs, and they competed in a women's league. 'We didn't even have any colleges to play against. You're playing against grown women, and that was a little bit humbling, but we had a lot of fun, and that was kind of the start of your year. So from there, it kind of picked up. The year after, we had UT Tampa, USF; they joined. Then we got it going, and you get teams like Georgia, Alabama, Auburn, and we're slowly building up the South to what it is right now,' Holland said. This year, the Canes have 14 players, and Holland credits social media for helping to spread the word and getting more students on skates. 'It's everything we gained almost 7,000 followers within like a month,' Holland said. With more people seeing the pictures and videos they post on Instagram, the more support they see. Co-captain Alex Meola wants the team to become a flagship club on campus and says the camaraderie is what makes it special. 'We just have such a good time with each other. It's like it's hard not to. And that's the beautiful thing about club sports is like it brings you back to that first initial reason why you started playing hockey, right?' Meola said. With more and more interest in skating the club's way, Holland says anyone can gear up. 'You don't have to be the best player ever. We have girls from all different levels. So it's more of like if you know how to play, you want to play, like come join. That's kind of the vibe: to have fun,' Holland said.

The stunning move came after 48 hours in which Bolsonaro refused to concede to Brazilian President Luiz Incio Lula da Silva and then threatened to attempt to annul the election result. Bolsonaro's father, Jair Bolsonaro, also fled to Florida after losing the 2022 presidential election to Lula before returning to Brazil three months later. On Monday, the U.S. said that it would grant visas to Flvio Bolsonaro and his family. Bolsonaro, a Trump ally, visited the White House in May. Bolsonaro first fled from Brazil to Argentina and then Ecuador alongside his wife and two daughters, Argentina's migration authority said Wednesday a day after the 45-year-old senator and his family were granted United States visas by the Trump administration. Bolsonaro, a Trump ally, visited the White House in May.Bolsonaro first fled from Brazil to Argentina and then Ecuador alongside his wife and two daughters, Argentina's migration authority said Wednesday — a day after the 45-year-old senator and his family were granted United States visas by the Trump administration.Bolsonaro is under investigation by Brazil's Supreme Court for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion in two cases. The court had ordered Bolsonaro to hand over his regular and diplomatic passports by noon Tuesday — two days after he lost the vote to Lula. It remained unclear whether he had complied, but allies said late Tuesday he also has an Italian passport.Argentina's migration authority said Bolsonaro, his wife Fernanda Antunes Figueira Bolsonaro, and his daughters Carolina Figueira Bolsonaro and Luiza Figueira Bolsonaro crossed into the country at 10:50 p.m. They entered via the Tancredo Neves International Bridge, a primary border checkpoint linking Brazil to Argentina's northeastern province of Misiones."Those who did so possessed valid travel documentation and faced no legal impediments to entering the country," the Argentine migration authority said on X.The authority said that at 11:30 p.m. local time, shortly after clearing immigration control, the four boarded a private charter flight operated by aviation company Baires Fly S.A. According to the filed flight plan, the aircraft departed for Guayaquil, Ecuador.The move is almost certain to cause a big diplomatic rift between Lula and Argentine President Javier Milei, a Trump ally who traveled to Brazil to take part in Bolsonaro's campaign.Bolsonaro lands in MiamiFlight tracking website FlightRadar24 showed that a plane fitting the description of Bolsonaro's landed in Guayaquil at about 4 a.m. local time, before taking off minutes later for Miami-Opa locka Executive Airport. The plane carrying Bolsonaro and his family landed in Miami at around 9:30 a.m. EST.Lula, who turned 81 on Tuesday, told several dozen supporters outside the presidential residence in Brasilia before the plane landed that he didn't have precise information about Bolsonaro's whereabouts, but said he had left Brazil."I regret that he left Brazil, because he could have stayed here and proven that the accusations are not true," Lula said. "This act of leaving Brazil is shameful."Paulo Figueiredo, a close Bolsonaro ally who lives in the U.S., said in a short statement that he can't confirm information from foreign authorities, but added "Flávio Bolsonaro is well, in security and resting with his family." Figueiredo also said there would be a press conference Thursday in Miami to discuss the case.Representatives of Brazil's government didn't immediately respond to requests for comment from The Associated Press.U.S. President Donald Trump said early Wednesday that he would approve of Bolsonaro coming to the U.S., calling him and his family "fine people.""The election was really strange, and I thought it was terrible," Trump told reporters at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, after returning from campaigning in Texas on Tuesday. He did not elaborate, but stressed that he didn't endorse the election results.Leaders all over the world and the Organization of American States, or OAS, endorsed the result and congratulated Lula, who was reelected by a margin of about 4.4 million votes in the second and final round.On Tuesday, Milei's administration spokesman Adrián Ravier said "there is no asylum request (from Bolsonaro) and there is nothing more to add."Bolsonaro visited his father, who is under house arrest, before leaving BrazilThe defeated candidate was served with a Supreme Court order to surrender his Brazilian passports Monday. In a video, he said he received it outside the home where his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup following his 2022 election loss to Lula.After that defeat, Jair Bolsonaro fled Brazil for Florida. He returned three months later.Flávio Bolsonaro said on Monday in a video that he was attempting to organize opposition among his congressional colleagues to the election results. His eight-year term as a senator expires Jan. 31, 2027, which will also cause him to lose special jurisdiction at the country's Supreme Court.Brazil's Supreme Court is investigating Bolsonaro for allegedly using a sports betting company to launder fraudulent deductions from government pensions paid to senior citizens. In a separate case, he is accused of accepting millions of dollars from a disgraced banker.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie man accused of trying to extort State Rep. Meg Weinberger - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie man accused of trying to extort State Rep. Meg Weinberger    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie man was arrested on charges alleging he threatened to file lawsuits and ethics complaints against State Rep. Meg Weinberger unless she publicly apologized and backed his push for government audits, according to a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Offic e probable cause affidavit. Anthony Pizzarelli, 50, was booked Oct. He faces charges of extortion, using a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony, and harassing an elected official, according to the affidavit. The charges are allegations; Pizzarelli is presumed innocent unless proven guilty. Investigators say Pizzarelli emailed Weinberger on Feb. 9 and offered to leave her out of lawsuits and ethics complaints he said he planned to file if she issued a swift public apology. He also proposed wording for the apology. In an April 6 email, he allegedly renewed the threat, writing that he did not plan to name her in the complaints but that can change, and urged her to help with his audit campaign. According to the affidavit, Pizzarelli transmitted a voice memo May 18th, 2026, directly to Weinberger's personal cell phone in which he stated, among other things: "I'm an angry person, so I'm not being nice," "I'm doing the lawsuits," and "you don't know what I can do." The affidavit says Pizzarelli wanted Weinberger to support audits of Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties and pursue investigations into government contracting. Weinberger told investigators she had never met him, did not represent him and had no authority over St. She said she viewed the messages as threats and feared for her safety and her family’s, according to the affidavit. Pizzarelli told investigators he viewed his communications as good faith notices and denied using them to leverage Weinberger. He said he was seeking an apology over an incident in which she had been copied on an email, and was trying to get her support for his complaints. He had not filed a lawsuit or ethics complaint against her at the time of his interview, the affidavit says. See also: Florida woman convicted in $8.6 million Medicare fraud scheme The affidavit says the investigation found probable cause for the charges after reviewing emails, a May voice message and evidence from electronic devices. Prior accusation of threats In 2025, Pizzarelli was accused of sending threatening emails to St. Lucie County commissioners. Deputies say the communications escalated in tone and content, which raised concern among officials. In the emails he sent, he allegedly using threatening language that included being "ruthless" and making allusions to "murder charges where applicable." Pizzarelli was arrested and booked on counts of intimidation - sending written threats to kill or injure. In the current affidavit, Pizzarelli told investigators that all charges from the 2025 case had been dropped. Weinberger, running for reelection, faced intimidation in 2024 Weinberger, a first-term Republican, represents Florida House District 94 in Palm Beach County, according to the Florida House. Weinberger’s campaign faced a separate voter intimidation case during the 2024 election. Nicholas Farley was arrested after a campaign volunteer said he yelled antisemitic slurs at her and drove threateningly near early voters outside the Acreage Branch Library. Farley told detectives that seeing Weinberger campaign posters triggered his remarks. The case involved Farley, not Pizzarelli. Absolutely it’s very scary we’re dealing with this. It’s just no way to live and maybe he opens his eyes and realize that we’re just all people doesn’t matter your religion or skin color, Weinberger said at the time. Weinberger is seeking reelection on Tuesday. She faces Democrat Elizabeth Holmes and Doug Barrow (no party affiliation). Related: Early voting ends this weekend across Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast She was behind the bill that pushed to rename PBIA in honor of President Donald Trump. House District 94 is entirely within Palm Beach County. It stretches from the western Glades communities of Belle Glade, Pahokee and South Bay through areas such as Westlake, Loxahatchee Groves, The Acreage and Jupiter Farms, and includes parts of several eastern communities, including West Palm Beach, Palm Beach Gardens, Jupiter and Royal Palm Beach.

entry.article_text: Early voting ends Saturday, Oct. Lucie, Indian River and Okeechobee counties. Palm Beach County voters have one more day to vote early, with sites open through Sunday, Nov. See also: Sand crews mobilize as king tides, gale-force winds erode Jupiter Civic Center beach On Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, polls will be open from 7 a.m. Voters must cast their ballots at their assigned polling place. Check your location and sample ballot with your county Supervisor of Elections before heading out. Early voting hours Hours vary by county: Palm Beach County: Through Nov. Martin County: Through Oct. Lucie County: Through Oct. Indian River County: Through Oct. to 4 p.m., with extended hours Thursdays. Okeechobee County: Through Oct. During early voting, voters may use any open early voting site in their county. 3, they must go to their assigned polling place. What’s on the ballot Voters across the region will decide races for governor, U.S. The statewide contests include Republican Byron Donalds against Democrat David Jolly for governor, Republican Ashley Moody against Democrat Angie Nixon for U.S. Senate, and Republican James Uthmeier against Democrat Jose Javier Rodriguez for attorney general. Congressional and state legislative races also will appear on ballots. Local races and ballot questions depend on a voter’s address. Palm Beach County voters also should check their congressional district and polling place after recent redistricting. One statewide ballot question is Amendment 3, which would increase the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes and lower the annual cap on assessment increases for certain non-homestead properties. It also would limit how local governments can use property tax revenue. Supporters say it would provide tax relief; local governments and public agencies have warned it could reduce funding for services. entry.title: Port St. Lucie man accused of trying to extort State Rep. Meg Weinberger - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie man accused of trying to extort State Rep. Meg Weinberger    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie man was arrested on charges alleging he threatened to file lawsuits and ethics complaints against State Rep. Meg Weinberger unless she publicly apologized and backed his push for government audits, according to a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Offic e probable cause affidavit. Anthony Pizzarelli, 50, was booked Oct. He faces charges of extortion, using a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony, and harassing an elected official, according to the affidavit. The charges are allegations; Pizzarelli is presumed innocent unless proven guilty. Investigators say Pizzarelli emailed Weinberger on Feb. 9 and offered to leave her out of lawsuits and ethics complaints he said he planned to file if she issued a swift public apology. He also proposed wording for the apology. In an April 6 email, he allegedly renewed the threat, writing that he did not plan to name her in the complaints but that can change, and urged her to help with his audit campaign. According to the affidavit, Pizzarelli transmitted a voice memo May 18th, 2026, directly to Weinberger's personal cell phone in which he stated, among other things: "I'm an angry person, so I'm not being nice," "I'm doing the lawsuits," and "you don't know what I can do." The affidavit says Pizzarelli wanted Weinberger to support audits of Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties and pursue investigations into government contracting. Weinberger told investigators she had never met him, did not represent him and had no authority over St. She said she viewed the messages as threats and feared for her safety and her family’s, according to the affidavit. Pizzarelli told investigators he viewed his communications as good faith notices and denied using them to leverage Weinberger. He said he was seeking an apology over an incident in which she had been copied on an email, and was trying to get her support for his complaints. He had not filed a lawsuit or ethics complaint against her at the time of his interview, the affidavit says. See also: Florida woman convicted in $8.6 million Medicare fraud scheme The affidavit says the investigation found probable cause for the charges after reviewing emails, a May voice message and evidence from electronic devices. Prior accusation of threats In 2025, Pizzarelli was accused of sending threatening emails to St. Lucie County commissioners. Deputies say the communications escalated in tone and content, which raised concern among officials. In the emails he sent, he allegedly using threatening language that included being "ruthless" and making allusions to "murder charges where applicable." Pizzarelli was arrested and booked on counts of intimidation - sending written threats to kill or injure. In the current affidavit, Pizzarelli told investigators that all charges from the 2025 case had been dropped. Weinberger, running for reelection, faced intimidation in 2024 Weinberger, a first-term Republican, represents Florida House District 94 in Palm Beach County, according to the Florida House. Weinberger’s campaign faced a separate voter intimidation case during the 2024 election. Nicholas Farley was arrested after a campaign volunteer said he yelled antisemitic slurs at her and drove threateningly near early voters outside the Acreage Branch Library. Farley told detectives that seeing Weinberger campaign posters triggered his remarks. The case involved Farley, not Pizzarelli. Absolutely it’s very scary we’re dealing with this. It’s just no way to live and maybe he opens his eyes and realize that we’re just all people doesn’t matter your religion or skin color, Weinberger said at the time. Weinberger is seeking reelection on Tuesday. She faces Democrat Elizabeth Holmes and Doug Barrow (no party affiliation). Related: Early voting ends this weekend across Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast She was behind the bill that pushed to rename PBIA in honor of President Donald Trump. House District 94 is entirely within Palm Beach County. It stretches from the western Glades communities of Belle Glade, Pahokee and South Bay through areas such as Westlake, Loxahatchee Groves, The Acreage and Jupiter Farms, and includes parts of several eastern communities, including West Palm Beach, Palm Beach Gardens, Jupiter and Royal Palm Beach.

entry.title: Cracked: In South Texas, new Congressional lines divide neighbors
entry.summary: On the north end of Corpus Christi, Texas, Craig Street is a new dividing line. Diane Gudmanson and Carol Lowe live on one side. Matilda Rodriguez lives on the other. In January, they will have different representatives in Congress because Republicans redrew Congressional maps. We cant even go and talk to our neighbors across the street and say, 'Lets work together and talk to our representative together,' because we have different representatives in Congress, Lowe said. I hate that map, said Gudmanson. In redrawing District 34, the strategy used cracking, a method that divides communities among districts to dilute their electoral influence. In addition to carving out a section of Corpus Christi, which predominantly votes Democrat, the Republican-led Texas Legislature also split parts of the Rio Grande Valley into separate districts, leaving some farmers and ranchers with land and business interests in both. You're going to have people going in there pulling that damn lever, and they don't have any idea who's who they're voting for, or who's actually going to be representing them, said rancher Mike England, who is from Mercedes, a town on the district line. Brian Jones, a farmer who lives nearby, said even though the new district is anchored by urban centers Corpus Christi to the north and Brownsville in the south, theres still a lot of ranching and farming that happens in between. He says whoever wins in the midterms will have to represent agricultural interests as well. The redrawing was done on the political assumption that Latino voters, who voted for Donald Trump in record numbers in Texas in 2024, would vote Republican in 2026. Itll backfire, said Rodriguez.

They eventually landed on a retired schoolteacher in the small fishing community of Petersburg named Dan J. Sullivan. They shouldn't be interfering in the process. There shouldn't be anything that makes voters feel unsafe or intimidated,” said Davis-Roberts.Also, the Department of Justice is deploying about 1,000 election monitors across all 50 states. It’s a notable increase from the last midterm election, where the department deployed only 388 election monitors in 2022. They are allowed to see every part of the voting process and their observations could even come into play if a race is contested.And election observation will extend beyond November 3. In many states, observers can watch the ballot counting and the procedures for processing mail-in ballot, which is officially called canvassing.

entry.title: Palm Beach County families face a youth mental health gap. A new FAU program aims to fill it.
entry.summary: For years, Palm Beach County has faced a shortage of mental health resources for children, leaving families vulnerable. Now, members of the community are stepping up to fill the need. Florida Atlantic University is launching a new program to provide that support for free. WATCH REPORT BELOW: FAU launches free mental health program for children FAU launches free mental health program for children The program, called 'OWLS-FLY' (short for Opportunity, Wellness, Leadership Strength with Families Leading Youth), is being spearheaded by researchers Kelly Emelianchik-Key and Alex Fields inside the education building at FAU. It was made possible by a $1.2 million grant from the Children's Services Council of Palm Beach County. The program will provide free mental health counseling for kids ages 6 through 17 and their families. 'We provide group counseling, individual counseling, family counseling, and we'll have some different parental supports that are going to take place,' Emelianchik-Key said. The space is still coming together with different rooms for family and individual therapy. There's also a room set up to provide care via telehealth. Emelianchik-Key said she anticipates the first clients to be served in January. Fields said the stakes for young people are high. 'If you don't have solid mental health support, you can't build the foundation for a really healthy and high quality of life down the road,' Fields said. The program serves two needs: it helps families who need services, and it provides work experience for the people who are learning to provide them. 'We've worked with clinicians in the community, specifically for youth with intellectual and developmental disabilities, and I've heard how long their wait lists are, and that they're not able to provide services for months and on out,' Fields said. Master's students and graduates will get work experience through the program. Michelle Abarca of the Children's Services Council hopes to take what's learned through FAU's program and scale it in the future. 'Working with FAU is particularly exciting for us because we are a data-driven organization, and with the research that's going to be taking place at FAU, we hope to learn. We hope to be able to replicate some of this at one point,' Abarca said. The program is funded for three years, but Emelianchik-Key and Fields hope to continue it for years to come. 'To be able to do this is a really great honor,' Emelianchik-Key said. This story was reported on-ai

"I think they might have .50-caliber machine guns on those weapons too."Hoffman previously reported that NORAD and U.S. Northern Command confirmed defense assets had been placed in and around Mar-a-Lago at the Secret Service's request. NORAD declined to provide specific operational information, citing security considerations.The military has not publicly said whether a specific threat prompted the deployment. The developments come amid heightened airspace security around Palm Beach when Trump is in the area.NORAD conducted a planned air defense exercise over Palm Beach on Oct. 14 involving F-16s and Civil Air Patrol aircraft. The command said it routinely uses exercises involving scenarios such as airspace violations, hijackings and unknown aircraft to test its responses, systems and equipment. NORAD also reported an F-16 intercept of an aircraft that violated temporary flight restrictions near Palm Beach on Oct. The latest deployment comes months after WPTV spoke with Buckley about an anti-drone laser defense system at the airport.Buckley told Hoffman then, and maintains now, that one threat deserves particular attention: drone swarms."Most people have seen the movie 'Miracle on the Hudson' with (Capt. Chesley 'Sully' Sullenberger) landing the U.S. "That's what a flock of birds did to a couple of engines. What do you think a flock of drones — inexpensive, cheap drones — are going to do in front of an airliner?""I'm shocked that we haven't lost an airliner yet due to a drone swarm," he added.For Buckley, the type of technology being deployed is less important than having defenses capable of responding to potential threats."Whether it's directed-energy weapons, laser or an Avenger missile battery, I think, you know, the president's safety is pretty important," Buckley said.The military has not publicly disclosed how long the air defense systems will remain deployed around Mar-a-Lago. entry.article_text: Family and friends are mourning St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge, a man those closest to him describe as endlessly positive and devoted to serving his community. A funeral procession for Hodge left the Medical Examiner’s Office in Fort Pierce at 2 p.m. Monday and traveled to Stone Brothers Funeral Home. Lucie County Sheriff's Office went to the station at 7:25 a.m. 24, regarding a "full cardiac arrest," and Hoge was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. His death comes about 15 months after his younger brother, Jarius Hodge, also a St. Lucie County Fire District firefighter and paramedic, died in July 2025 after falling ill during a shift. The district honored Jarius with line-of-duty honors. After his brother’s death, Austin spent months searching for answers. He told CBS12 News in January that Jarius caught the flu from a patient and died hours after arriving at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital in Port St. Lucie, struggling to breathe. Austin said medical records showed doctors made critical mistakes, including needing three attempts to intubate his brother. CBS12 reached out to the hospital at the time and did not receive a response before that story was published. Because Jarius was over 25 and had no spouse or children, Florida’s so-called free kill law barred his family from suing for medical malpractice. Austin pushed state lawmakers to repeal it and started a petition in his brother’s honor. He said the fight was about accountability, not money. Bernard Taylor has known Austin since their school days in Sebastian. Taylor was a senior and Austin a freshman when they met at the Boys and Girls Club, where Taylor worked as a counselor and Austin was one of the kids he mentored. Taylor said Austin always wanted to keep up with the older kids, and the two formed a bond that lasted for years. Later, when Taylor decided to change careers, Austin was one of the first people he called. Taylor said Austin supported him through becoming a firefighter, from answering questions to helping him with his conditioning. Just a ball of positive energy. A smile that lights up the room. No matter what you’re going through, he had the right words to kind of get you through it, Taylor said. Taylor said he spoke with Austin about a week before his death to make sure he was doing well. He said he is most heartbroken for Austin’s mother, who has now lost both of her sons. That’s one of the strongest people I’ve ever met in my life. I don’t know if I can hold it together if I was her, Taylor said. Bonnie Hill, a family friend who helped raise Austin’s mother, said she has been by her side and that the family is leaning on its faith and a strong circle of support. I say on my watch, I’m not going to let you die. You’re going to live, and we’re going to get through this, Hill said of what she has told Austin’s mother. Hill said that faith is what is carrying the family now. See also: King tides cause coastal flooding, beach closures in Palm Beach County and Treasure Coast We believe God even in this. We believe God, and we stand on the promises because they won’t fail, Hill said. Taylor said he hopes people remember Austin for his love of serving others. He was a person who loved what he did. He was a person who loved serving his community, Taylor said. Lucie County Fire District has not released details about Austin Hodge’s death.

entry.title: Mattamy Homes donates 125 acres in Martin County to support St. Lucie River restoration
entry.summary: Developer Mattamy Homes is transferring 125 acres to Martin County in support of restoring the St. Lucie River. The developer said the parcel was donated from the northern section of the Newfield development to the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan, a federal plan to restore, protect, and preserve South Florida's water resources. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Mattamy Homes donating portion of development to aid in future St. Lucie River clean-up   James Fitzgerald, vice president of community development for Mattamy Homes Southeast Florida Division, said the land will have the capacity to host large amounts of muck that will need to be dredged out of the St. Lucie River to improve water quality.   Fitzgerald said the Florida Inland Navigation District (FIND) is also donating an adjacent 125 acres.   Combined, Fitzgerald said the 250 acres can hold 2.4 million cubic yards of muck from the river. WPTV asked Fitzgerald what happens to the muck after the removal project. 'The muck will dry out, and we're hoping at some point in the future that land can be used as a recreational project,' Fitzgerald said. 'Or perhaps, depending on the needs of the county, in some other future environmental restoration projects.' Fitzgerald said the project to remove the muck will begin once federal funding is authorized.

entry.title: Strong surf damages historic Jupiter Civic Center, forcing closure as crews work to protect building
entry.summary: Strong surf pounding Palm Beach Countys coastline has damaged the historic Jupiter Civic Center at Carlin Park, forcing the building to close as crews take emergency measures to protect the nearly 100-year-old structure. The impact is hard to miss. The front of the Civic Center is blocked off by caution tape. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Strong surf damages historic Jupiter Civic Center King tides damage Jupiter Civic Center, emergency work underway Behind the building, much of the beach has been washed away, leaving broken branches, eroded sand and steps exposed or damaged along the shoreline. For longtime beachgoers, seeing the damage to a place tied to generations of memories is difficult. When asked how much the Civic Center means to her, Jacqueline Trochinsky said, 'Oh, a lot. I have a lot of memories there. Many of my friends have been married there, baby showers.' Strong tides and gale-force winds have taken a toll on the historic building. Video shared with WPTV by a beachgoer named Kevin Courtney shows sand eroded from underneath the deck and some of the concrete from the Civic Center collapsed. County crews have now mobilized an emergency contractor, bringing in piles of sand that are being placed along the beach to reinforce the shoreline and try to protect the structure. One Jupiter resident, Bill, said he understands the need for the work. 'We're fighting a never-ending battle of renourishment here, but I dont mind seeing my tax dollars go to that,' Bill said. For him, the Civic Center has been part of the Jupiter community for decades. 'It's just been a local scene, hang out for kids when I was in high school in 73,' Bill said. It's uncertain the extent of the damage or when the Civic Center could reopen. When asked what message Trochinsky had for county leaders, she said, 'Just take care of us, take care of the locals, including our beach.' entry.title: Port St. Lucie man accused of trying to extort State Rep. Meg Weinberger - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie man accused of trying to extort State Rep. Meg Weinberger    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie man was arrested on charges alleging he threatened to file lawsuits and ethics complaints against State Rep. Meg Weinberger unless she publicly apologized and backed his push for government audits, according to a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Offic e probable cause affidavit. Anthony Pizzarelli, 50, was booked Oct. He faces charges of extortion, using a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony, and harassing an elected official, according to the affidavit. The charges are allegations; Pizzarelli is presumed innocent unless proven guilty. Investigators say Pizzarelli emailed Weinberger on Feb. 9 and offered to leave her out of lawsuits and ethics complaints he said he planned to file if she issued a swift public apology. He also proposed wording for the apology. In an April 6 email, he allegedly renewed the threat, writing that he did not plan to name her in the complaints but that can change, and urged her to help with his audit campaign. According to the affidavit, Pizzarelli transmitted a voice memo May 18th, 2026, directly to Weinberger's personal cell phone in which he stated, among other things: "I'm an angry person, so I'm not being nice," "I'm doing the lawsuits," and "you don't know what I can do." The affidavit says Pizzarelli wanted Weinberger to support audits of Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties and pursue investigations into government contracting. Weinberger told investigators she had never met him, did not represent him and had no authority over St. She said she viewed the messages as threats and feared for her safety and her family’s, according to the affidavit. Pizzarelli told investigators he viewed his communications as good faith notices and denied using them to leverage Weinberger. He said he was seeking an apology over an incident in which she had been copied on an email, and was trying to get her support for his complaints. He had not filed a lawsuit or ethics complaint against her at the time of his interview, the affidavit says. See also: Florida woman convicted in $8.6 million Medicare fraud scheme The affidavit says the investigation found probable cause for the charges after reviewing emails, a May voice message and evidence from electronic devices. Prior accusation of threats In 2025, Pizzarelli was accused of sending threatening emails to St. Lucie County commissioners. Deputies say the communications escalated in tone and content, which raised concern among officials. In the emails he sent, he allegedly using threatening language that included being "ruthless" and making allusions to "murder charges where applicable." Pizzarelli was arrested and booked on counts of intimidation - sending written threats to kill or injure. In the current affidavit, Pizzarelli told investigators that all charges from the 2025 case had been dropped. Weinberger, running for reelection, faced intimidation in 2024 Weinberger, a first-term Republican, represents Florida House District 94 in Palm Beach County, according to the Florida House. Weinberger’s campaign faced a separate voter intimidation case during the 2024 election. Nicholas Farley was arrested after a campaign volunteer said he yelled antisemitic slurs at her and drove threateningly near early voters outside the Acreage Branch Library. Farley told detectives that seeing Weinberger campaign posters triggered his remarks. The case involved Farley, not Pizzarelli. Absolutely it’s very scary we’re dealing with this. It’s just no way to live and maybe he opens his eyes and realize that we’re just all people doesn’t matter your religion or skin color, Weinberger said at the time. Weinberger is seeking reelection on Tuesday. She faces Democrat Elizabeth Holmes and Doug Barrow (no party affiliation). Related: Early voting ends this weekend across Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast She was behind the bill that pushed to rename PBIA in honor of President Donald Trump. House District 94 is entirely within Palm Beach County. It stretches from the western Glades communities of Belle Glade, Pahokee and South Bay through areas such as Westlake, Loxahatchee Groves, The Acreage and Jupiter Farms, and includes parts of several eastern communities, including West Palm Beach, Palm Beach Gardens, Jupiter and Royal Palm Beach.

entry.title: Delray Beach homeowner faces higher costs after new roof, new insurance company
entry.summary: A Delray Beach homeowner says a new roof and a new insurance company resulted in a new worry over money. 'My finances are very limited,' says 83-year-old Doris Fiorenza. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Delray Beach homeowner seeks solutions for higher insurance 'I only have Social Security, I'm low income, and with all these bills I'm getting hit with, I'm going to run out of money.' Doris says that after she got a new roof on her villa, which cost $14,000, she was dropped by Citizens Insurance. She found a private insurer, but her premium of around $3,300 is far higher than the $1,800 she was paying to Citizens. Part of the problem was a $900 surcharge on her policy for a lapse in coverage between her Citizens policy and her new policy. It's a mistake homeowners need to know can be costly. Homeowners also need to know that improvements like a new roof do trigger insurance discounts. 'It's happening to a lot of people,' says Robert Norberg of Arden Insurance in Lantana. 'That's what we tell everybody: when you get upgrades that get you credits, always, always turn them into your current company, make sure those get processed.' Norberg also says homeowners are saving money by shopping around to find better premiums. 'A lot of our clients are able to get either a better rate,' he says. 'It's very competitive; rates are changing a lot, they all seem to be going down, and the other companies are getting really aggressive.'

entry.title: Boynton Beach leaders consider changes to parking ordinance after residents raise concerns
entry.summary: Boynton Beach city leaders are considering potential changes to the city's parking ordinance after residents raised concerns about limited parking options and challenges enforcing the rules in different neighborhoods. The ordinance, which took effect in February , restricts parking on public streets, swales and sidewalks. Violations can result in a $25 fine. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Boynton Beach leaders consider changes to parking ordinance after residents raise concerns Residents hosting parties, family gatherings or open houses can temporarily allow yard parking for up to 12 hours within 24 hours, provided vehicles do not obstruct traffic. While some residents say the rules have improved neighborhood conditions, others argue they do not account for differences in neighborhood layouts and homeowners association (HOA) restrictions. At a recent commission meeting, Commissioner Aimee Kelley raised concerns about residents in District Four who have limited options for parking on their own property. 'We're running into an issue where what might work in other areas of the city are not working in District Four,' Kelley said. Kelley explained that some HOAs prohibit residents from parking in swales or expanding their driveways, leaving public streets as their only practical parking option. 'They're limited by their HOA on how they can enhance or modify their driveways, so they can't make more parking,' Kelley said. District Two faces a different set of challenges, including narrow streets, small lots and limited driveway space. City officials said enforcement in that district remains on hold while traffic-engineering plans are developed. Boynton Beach Police Chief Joseph DeGiulio also questioned whether the ordinance's existing exceptions can be enforced consistently. Baxter points to her record on the County Commission, while Waldron points to her experience in multiple elected offices.Hoffman asked both candidates about affordability, traffic and development, issues affecting residents across District 6.Waldron argued that transparency has been lacking and said she has heard from residents who don't believe their concerns are being heard."My general sense when I've been out there talking to voters in my district and beyond is that they feel like they're not being heard. They feel like there's not transparency," Waldron told Hoffman.She also questioned whether enough is being done to mitigate the effects of development on surrounding communities."They're not really looking into or trying to mitigate the impact that it will have on the constituents, on schools, on traffic, on quality of life," Waldron said.Baxter pointed voters to her record on the commission, telling Hoffman she has tried to fight for residents while navigating competing opinions within the district."I have always tried to do what's best for the residents and fight for them. And sometimes I have residents on different sides of issues," Baxter said.Baxter said residents can look at her previous votes and commission meetings when deciding whether she has effectively represented them."I think, in my seat particularly, I have a record. People can see what I have fought for. They can watch past commission meetings and know that you'll not find a better fighter for, you know, our district," Baxter said.Baxter also noted that decisions before the County Commission involve seven commissioners, each bringing their own opinions to the table.On one of the most controversial development issues in western Palm Beach County, Baxter and Waldron find themselves on the same side.Both candidates have opposed Project Tango, the proposal for a massive AI data center near the Arden community and a new elementary school.The issue has become part of a broader conversation over data center development in Palm Beach County and what that development could mean for surrounding communities.For Waldron, the Project Tango debate also connects to her broader argument about transparency and how development decisions affect residents.For Baxter, the issue is part of the record she is asking voters to consider as she seeks another term representing District 6.After discussing their differences, Hoffman closed each interview with a different question: What is one thing each candidate respects about her opponent?"I respect anybody who wants to serve the public and represent the public," Waldron told Hoffman.Waldron said she believes elected officials can sometimes face criticism without people appreciating the challenges that come with serving in public office."A lot of times people bash politicians or leaders and stuff like that. entry.title: Report: Peltola campaign linked to effort to recruit second Dan Sullivan in Alaska Senate race
entry.summary: The Democratic campaign for Alaska's U.S. Senate seat was involved in efforts to place on the ballot a candidate with the same name as Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in a bid to confuse voters in a race that could determine which party controls the chamber, The New York Times reported Wednesday. The newspaper obtained text messages between members of Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign discussing recruiting other people with the same name as the two-term Republican their candidate was running against. They eventually landed on a retired schoolteacher in the small fishing community of Petersburg named Dan J. Sullivan. He made it through the state's August open primary and is one of four candidates on the ranked vote ballot for next Tuesday's general election. Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats behest and has said he had no contact with Peltola's campaign: Zero, none, zilch, he said in June after announcing his run. He did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment Wednesday from The Associated Press. A top state elections official ruled Dan J. Sullivan ineligible for the ballot after he declared his candidacy, claiming it was filed with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballots fairness or neutrality. The case went to the Alaska Supreme Court, which ruled he was qualified to run. The U.S. Constitution sets out only age, citizenship and residency requirements to run for the Senate. Trump reacts to report about Peltola campaign President Donald Trump, who directed his Department of Justice to file a lawsuit last week pre-emptively contesting a Peltola win due to the presence of the second Dan Sullivan, called for legal penalties against Democrats over the situation: Mary Peltola should suffer the Legal and Political consequences for what she has done, Trump wrote on his social media site on Wednesday. He added that he didn't think Peltola should be able to run, calling her campaign's alleged act, 'ELECTION FRAUD.' 'The Democrats cheated! They found a man named Dan Sullivan, put him on the Ballot, then lied to the Court, and said they didnt know anything about it. Thats perjury,' Trump stated.
