entry.article_text: Three seniors at Alexander W. Dreyfoos School of the Arts have created Prodigy Pro, a free artificial intelligence platform designed to help students turn their ideas into real-world ventures.Co-founders Aiden Azoy and Anthony Tan and Head of Design Mia Rubio developed the platform after attending South Florida business networking events and realizing how few students were in the room.WATCH: Dreyfoos seniors build free AI platform for student entrepreneurs“We attended networking events and we noticed, why are we the youngest people in the room?” Azoy said. “There are so many talented students in our communities where they’re able to pursue their professional careers outside of school.”The students said they wanted to give young people a way to explore their interests, develop practical ideas and participate in West Palm Beach’s growing business community.The founders attend Dreyfoos in downtown West Palm Beach, where new development and the arrival of major companies have fueled the area’s growing reputation as “Wall Street South.”“We go to Dreyfoos, and literally hundreds of feet away are these huge constructions of Related Ross, companies like ServiceNow or even Citadel moving down to South Florida,” Tan said. “We’re right at the forefront of this new business center that is becoming West Palm Beach.”Tan said the students attempted to connect with professionals at local gatherings but struggled to find opportunities intended for people their age.“We tried to go to these meetings, and a lot of the time there wouldn’t be any opportunity for us,” Tan said. “So that’s why we wanted to create our own.”Prodigy Pro was built to help students take the first steps toward developing projects and businesses.“Prodigy Pro is a free AI entrepreneurship platform that helps a student take their idea from an idea to the final product,” Tan said.Azoy said the team created the platform after noticing that many students were not taking their ideas beyond the classroom.“Prodigy Pro is a way for students to build real ventures outside of school and be able to pursue their professional interests,” Azoy said. “We noticed that not enough students are getting out there and really putting their ideas out into the world. We gave them the ability to do that.”Users enter information about an idea and the problem they hope to solve. The platform’s AI then helps organize the concept and identify potential next steps.Rubio designed the user interface and worked to make the process understandable for students who may have little or no previous business experience.“You upload your information and the idea that you really want to pursue,” Rubio said. “And the AI will help you guide and shape and really tell you what your next step is, as well as create roadmaps, reminders and just really help your venture get off the ground.”The platform divides the development process into smaller sections and tasks.“With Prodigy [Pro], we wanted to make the next step super easy and attainable,” Rubio said. “So we grouped things into different sections and made each task super easy for the user to understand, so they know what to do next with their venture.”During a demonstration, the students used concerns about a school bus route to show how a user could enter a problem and explore possible efficiencies. “You input your information, and it really gives you the next steps, what you should do, and you can ask the AI to help develop your venture,” Rubio said.The founders said making Prodigy Pro free was central to their mission. Azoy said students should have access to the same entrepreneurial tools regardless of their school or community’s resources.“It’s completely free for students, and we want to stress that because we want to basically give the message that a student in an underprivileged school or community should have the same exact resources as, you know, a student in a resourced school,” Azoy said.According to the students, Prodigy Pro has grown to more than 15,000 users in 20 countries.The team also competed in the Mott Million Dollar Challenge, a national student entrepreneurship competition.“A few months ago in May, we competed in the Mott Million Dollar Challenge, where we won $7,500 for our venture,” Tan said.Tan said the prize money was reinvested into Prodigy Pro.“A lot of it went into the development of the platform, going through the UI, the back end, also enabling the AI to be free for other students,” he said.The three founders are seniors preparing for life after high school, but they said Prodigy Pro will continue.Asked whether the platform would remain after graduation, Rubio responded, “Yes, of course. It’ll remain to be a free platform for our users.”For Azoy, the larger goal is to show young people that they do not have to wait to begin developing their professional interests.“We really think that it’s important for them to be showing up and, you know, building ventures that really matter because every student has creativity in an underprivileged or privileged school,” Azoy said.The students’ work comes as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into education, business and everyday problem-solving. By making the platform free, the Dreyfoos seniors hope more young people will be able to turn their creativity into action and create opportunities of their own.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Spookyville and Fright Nights return to the South Florida Fairgrounds this October
entry.summary: Whether your idea of Halloween involves collecting candy with the kids or screaming your way through a haunted house, the South Florida Fairgrounds has an event designed for you. This October, the fairgrounds once again become home to two popular seasonal attractions: Spookyville, a family-friendly Halloween celebration at Yesteryear Village, and Fright Nights, a nighttime attraction featuring haunted houses, scare zones, rides, and entertainment. Family-Friendly Fun at Spookyville Spookyville transforms historic Yesteryear Village into a Halloween destination geared toward children and families. Guests can enjoy safe trick-or-treating throughout the village, costume parades, live entertainment, food vendors, and plenty of opportunities for festive family photos. The attraction's historic buildings are decorated with pumpkins, spider webs, fall decorations, and Halloween displays. Visitors can also enjoy rides, a petting zoo, balloon artists, and special performances. Among this year's entertainers is Wizard Aloysius, who brings magic tricks and family-friendly entertainment to the event on select dates. Spookyville runs Oct. 17-18, 23-25 and 30-31. Looking for a Good Scare? When the sun goes down, the atmosphere changes dramatically. Fright Nights returns to the South Florida Fairgrounds with four haunted attractions, roaming scare actors, carnival rides, live entertainment, food vendors, and a midway designed to test visitors' courage. The event has become a Halloween tradition for thrill-seekers across South Florida and offers an alternative to traveling to larger attractions outside the area. During a behind-the-scenes visit, WPTV's T.A. Walker got a firsthand look at what it takes to become one of the monsters responsible for scaring guests. After receiving scare training, costume, and makeup, he attempted life as a Fright Nights scare actor under the pirate persona 'Captain Arby's.' The results were mixed. While a few guests played along, many walked by unfazed, proving that creating a memorable scare is much harder than it looks. Fright Nights runs October 15-17, 22-24, and 29-30. Captain Arbys attempts to scare Fright Nights guestsTwo Experiences, One Destination The South Florida Fairgrounds offers Halloween fans two distinctly different experiences throughout October. Families looking for safe seasonal fun can enjoy Spookyville during the day and evening, while older guests seeking thrills can test their nerves at Fright Nights after dark. Whethe

entry.title: Mattamy Homes donates 125 acres in Martin County to support St. Lucie River restoration - WPTV
entry.summary: Mattamy Homes donates 125 acres in Martin County to support St. Lucie River restoration    WPTV
entry.article_text: Developer Mattamy Homes is transferring 125 acres to Martin County in support of restoring the St. Lucie River.The developer said the parcel was donated from the northern section of the Newfield development to the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan, a federal plan to restore, protect, and preserve South Florida's water resources.WATCH REPORT BELOW: James Fitzgerald, vice president of community development for Mattamy Homes Southeast Florida Division, said the land will have the capacity to host large amounts of muck that will need to be dredged out of the St. Lucie River to improve water quality. Fitzgerald said the Florida Inland Navigation District (FIND) is also donating an adjacent 125 acres. Combined, Fitzgerald said the 250 acres can hold 2.4 million cubic yards of muck from the river.WPTV asked Fitzgerald what happens to the muck after the removal project."The muck will dry out, and we're hoping at some point in the future that land can be used as a recreational project," Fitzgerald said. "Or perhaps, depending on the needs of the county, in some other future environmental restoration projects."Fitzgerald said the project to remove the muck will begin once federal funding is authorized.
